en: The *Brahmasūtra-Śāṅkara-bhāṣya*,
with its commentary *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā* composed by the ascetic Śrī Rāmānanda:
even he who was born as an enemy [to his own brother] attained the great station by seeking refuge in that compassionate one.
I quickly take refuge in that Hari, the supreme one, who has Janaka’s daughter as his lap and whose form is infinite bliss. //1//

I bow to Śiva, the Lord of Kāśī, who—along with the illustrious Gaurī—bestows all goals through his own lotus feet and grants liberation; who destroys the dense forest of obstacles with the sword of his glorious, curved tusk; who is sinless; who, through the humble guise of a leather-clad mendicant, teaches that there is no bliss higher than dispassion; and who is free from inner affliction. 2.
I worship that Goddess Vāṇī, who holds a lute in her hand and whose very body is the Vedas and Shastras; by a mere fragment of whose grace even a mute becomes a scholar.

I have found rest, like a bee, at the lotus feet of the speech of the illustrious Govinda—those words of the venerable Gopāla which reveal the supreme non-duality (paramādvaita), whose face smiles with the light of that revelation, and who attained self-knowledge through Śiva-Rāmārya, the worshipful leader of abundant food who was honored by the gods and nourished by the profuse milk offered by Kāmākṣī. //4//

Having bowed to the illustrious Śaṅkara, the author of the Bhāṣya, and to Vyāsa, who is Hari himself, the author of the Sūtras, I shall speak of the means that cuts the bonds of the web of words for the satisfaction of the Parahaṃsas at the holy site of the Śrībhāṣya. (5)
For one whose mind has become weary from examining extensive texts, this commentary named *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā* has been commenced for that purpose. (6)
"By attaining this glorious commentary on the Śārīraka, may my speech attain purity;
thus, my labor shall be as fruitful as [the sight of] the Gaṅgā, which renders even street-water sacred. (7)
This world is a magical illusion produced by ignorance;
that which is infinite bliss and true knowledge—that I am, the fearless Brahman. //8//
START BsRp_1,1.1.1:
Now, therefore, [arises] the desire to know Brahman (brahmajijñāsā).

Here, indeed, for one who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs according to the injunction for compulsory study—"One's own Vedic portion is to be studied"—[it is said]: "Seek to know that."
The injunction for hearing [the scriptures] is found in such passages as, "He is to be sought, He is to be desired to be known," and "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, is to be heard.
Its meaning is this: one who desires immortality must engage in the inquiry into the non-dual Self by means of the Vedānta texts.

The actual state of affairs is this: by that optional restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), it follows by implication that the activity of self-scriptures is excluded, or else the predominance of the Purāṇas and similar texts among the Vaidikas is set aside.
In this regard, who is the subject of this injunction for hearing [the scripture]—one whose mind has become utterly pure through sacrifices and other rites performed in this life or in another birth?
One inquires: what is the fruit, who is the qualified person, and what is the relationship?

Perceiving him to be desirous of knowledge, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa composed this aphorism— "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman"— in order to determine by means of reasoning the fourfold set of preliminary requirements that motivate the commencement of the scripture consisting of hearing.
But surely, the collection of auxiliary details can be known from the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) situated in proximity to the injunction;

for instance, by the scriptural text—"Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes"—which possesses the logical principle that "whatever is produced is impermanent," and [by the text] "The wise one is neither born nor dies," and "He who indeed... [and so forth].

From such scriptural passages as, "The Infinite (bhūman) is immortal; that which is other than this is afflicted," the discernment is obtained that the Self, as the Infinite, is eternal, whereas that which is other than it is non-eternal and of the nature of ignorance.
The world produced by action—such as agriculture—is the field of enjoyment, meaning it consists of things like grain to be consumed.
Vipaścit is one whose essential nature is eternal knowledge.

"Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, let the Brāhmaṇa attain detachment, for there is nothing uncreated that can be gained by what is created; indeed, everything becomes dear for the sake of the Self"— from such scriptural passages as these, detachment is obtained toward the non-Self alone, that is, toward the entire collection of objects consisting of the body, senses, and so forth,
after having examined them and determined them to be impermanent.
The meaning is that since liberation is not produced by performed action, it does not exist [as a result thereof]; thus one should attain detachment from actions and their fruits.

From the Śruti passage, "Having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, concentrated, and possessing faith, one should see the Self in the very Self," the sixfold group beginning with tranquility (śama) is obtained.
"Having become concentrated" is the reading in the Kāṇva recension.
Cessation (*uparati*) is renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
Through the scriptural statement, "He does not return again," which declares the eternity of liberation—consisting of self-luminous bliss—the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) is obtained.
Thus, it can be understood that the qualified candidate (*adhikārī*) is one who possesses the specific qualifications such as discrimination (*viveka*) and so forth.

Just as in the injunction for the Rātri-sattra sacrifice—"those who perform these nights"—the statement "they attain stability" serves as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for one desiring that stability, so it is here.

Likewise, in the case of "it is to be heard," the primary meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), which is inquiry, is the object of the suffix-meaning, namely the mandate (*niyoga*); and it can be known that the Vedāntas are the object of that inquiry, because after pointing toward the vision of the non-dual Self in the statement "the Self is to be seen," the injunction for inquiry is given in the form "it is to be heard."
For investigation is not the direct cause of perception, because it is not a means of valid cognition; rather, it is such by virtue of being the object of a means of valid cognition.

And the sole authority regarding the non-dual Self is the Vedāntas themselves, according to the Śruti: "That person who is known through the Upaniṣads," and "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of the Vedāntas."
Furthermore, the subject matter of the Vedāntas is the identity of the inner self and Brahman,
according to the scriptural texts: "That thou art" and "I am Brahman."

Thus, the fruit of the method of inquiry is also liberation through the gateway of knowledge, according to such scriptural passages as, "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow," and "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself."

Likewise, the relationship between the qualified seeker and the inquiry consists in the former’s duty to perform it, while the relationship with the result consists in its being attained; thus, as appropriate, this is easily understood.
If it is argued that, for this reason, the aphorism is useless, we say: no.

In the absence of sūtras providing the logical criteria for determining the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of those scriptural passages concerning qualification and so forth, one must investigate: is the qualified person (*adhikārī*) one endowed with the specific attributes such as discrimination (*viveka*) and the rest, or someone else?
Are the Vedāntas already established by the *Pūrvatantra* (Mīmāṃsā), or do they have a subject matter not reached therein?
And is Brahman non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*), or not?

Is liberation another world like heaven and so forth, or is it the very nature of the Self? It is for the removal of such doubt that this Sūtra is necessary, in order to determine— on the basis of scriptural statements— the preliminary qualifications of the seeker and other factors as they appear at first glance.

This has been stated by the venerable Śrīcaraṇas, who are of the nature of Light: "Even though the qualified seeker (adhikārī) and other factors are established through scripture, this aphorism is for the purpose of determining them through reasoning.

For those whose view is that there is no injunction regarding hearing (śravaṇa), it would follow that the aphorism is useless, because in the case of unenjoined hearing, there is no requirement to determine the qualified seeker and so forth. Enough of this digression.

Thus, this Sūtra has a connection with the Śruti because it is raised for the purpose of determining its own meaning through the Śruti passages concerning the qualification (*adhikārin*) and other requirements expected by the injunction to hear [this scripture];

it has a connection with the beginning of the Śāstra because it serves as an introduction (*upoddhāta*) by determining the necessary preliminary conditions (*anubandha*) that cause the commencement of the Śāstra;

and it has a connection with the first chapter (*samanvayādhyāya*) because it explains the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Śruti passages concerning the qualification and other factors with their own respective meanings.

The connection with the chapter (*pāda-saṅgati*) is established by the statement of the concordance (*samanvaya*) of such scriptural passages as "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; thou art That," which contain clear indicators (*liṅga*) of Brahman, such as its being the Self of all.
Similarly, the connection with the scripture (*śruti-saṅgati*) follows because all the sūtras serve to determine the meaning of the scriptures.
Furthermore, the connection within each respective chapter and section should be inferred based on the commonality of the subject matter (*prameya*).

The subject matter (*prameya*) of the entire treatise is Brahman; however, the subjects of the chapters are respectively: the concordance (*samanvaya*), the absence of contradiction (*avirodha*), the means of realization (*sādhana*), and the fruit (*phala*). Among these, the subject matter of the first quarter (*pāda*) is the concordance of those scriptural passages (*śruti*) that contain clear indicatory marks (*liṅga*) of Brahman.
The distinction is that the second and third [sections] concern passages where the indicative marks of Brahman are unclear,
while the fourth quarter concerns the coordination of words alone. Since this section is the first of its kind, no prior connection with a preceding section is required.
Now, the formal inquiry (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced: The subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the treatise on Vedānta-mīmāṃsā, consisting of "listening" as prescribed by the injunction "it is to be heard.
The doubt is whether it should be commenced or not, based on the possibility or impossibility of its subject matter and its purpose.

In that regard, because of the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) which grasps difference—namely, "I am not Brahman"—and with inference (*anumāna*) based on the mark (*liṅga*) of possessing contradictory attributes such as agency and non-agency, the identity of Brahman and the Self, which is the subject matter, is impossible.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the fruit consisting of cessation cannot arise from the knowledge of one who has made a [false] commitment to truth, the inquiry should not be undertaken. In response, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*).
Here, for the sake of making it consistent with the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*), the word "should be performed" (*kartavyā*) must be supplied.
And this supplied word was indeed provided by the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) in the form: "The desire to know Brahman should be performed."

In this context, since the knowledge and the desire denoted by the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) cannot be construed as things to be performed (*kartavya*), the base expresses through non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) the knowledge which is the result;
the suffix expresses through exclusive indication (*jahallakṣaṇā*) the inquiry which is the means to achieve that desire.
Thus, the literal meaning of the Sūtra becomes: "Inquiry must be undertaken for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman."

In this context, since knowledge cannot be its own fruit, its status as a fruit must be explained solely by its function of removing the evil (anartha) consisting of the states of being a knower, an agent, and an enjoyer. Since that evil cannot be removed by mere knowledge if it were real, it must be declared to be superimposed (adhyasta); thus, the superimposition of bondage is indicated by implication. And this [superimposition] is the cause for establishing that the scripture possesses both a subject matter and a purpose.
For thus it is that the treatise ought to be commenced, because it possesses a subject matter and a purpose, like the act of eating and so forth.
The treatise possesses a purpose,
because it is the cause of the knowledge that brings about the cessation of bondage, like the statement "this is a rope" and so forth.
Bondage is removable by knowledge because it is superimposed,
like a snake on a rope;
thus, the purpose [of the inquiry] is established.

Thus, by aphorizing that the fruit [of inquiry] is the cessation of the delusion of misfortune pertaining to the individual soul (*jīva*) through the knowledge of the Brahman as the ultimate reality, it also implicitly indicates the subject matter— the identity of the *jīva* and Brahman—
since the cessation of a delusion in one thing cannot occur through the knowledge of something else.
[Therefore,] the *jīva* is non-different from Brahman.
Because it is the locus of superimposition (adhyāsa) which is to be removed by that knowledge;
for whatever is thus [characterized] is so [established],
just as the "this-portion" (idamaṃśa) is non-different from the mother-of-pearl— thus, superimposition is the cause for the establishment of the object.
Thus, because it possesses both subject matter and purpose, the treatise ought to be commenced.
Herein lies the distinction: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since bondage is real and cannot be ceased by knowledge, liberation must be accomplished through other means;
according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), liberation occurs through knowledge alone.

Having thus kept all this in mind, the venerable author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra), desiring to explain the Brahma-sūtras, first describes—by means of the two introductory commentaries (bhāṣya) concerning the objection to and the resolution of superimposition (adhyāsa)—the fact that the subject matter and the purpose are established by implication, on the grounds that the scriptural meaning in the form of the necessity for inquiry (as stated in the sūtra) would otherwise be untenable; he does so by means of the [sūtra] beginning with: "Of the two spheres of the notions of 'you' and 'I'... (yuṣmadasmatpratyayagocarayoḥ).
By this, the argument that the section on superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is not a commentary (*bhāṣya*) because it does not touch upon the literal meaning of the Sūtra is refuted,
since it does touch upon the implied meaning (*ārthika-artha*).
As for the claim that this commentary (*bhāṣya*) should not be explained because it lacks an invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*), that is not so;

for the purpose of composing the commentary up to the words "the mutual existence [of the two] is even more impossible," there is a recollection of the reality (*tattva*)—which is the meaning of that [invocation]—namely, the inner self (*pratyagartha*) as a mass of consciousness (*vijñānaghana*) free from all afflictions.
Therefore, being faultless, this commentary is indeed to be explained.

In the world, the error "this is silver" regarding a mother-of-pearl shell is observed to be produced by a latent impression (saṃskāra) generated by a prior valid cognition (*pramā*) that apprehended the identity between the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the superimposed particular (*āropya-viśeṣa*), as in the case of real silver where one thinks "this is silver. Therefore, in this instance as well—the superimposition of the non-self ego (*ahaṅkāra*) upon the Self—a prior valid cognition must be posited;
and that [prior cognition] requires a real identity between the Self and the non-self.
For that is not the case;
for instance, the self and the non-self are devoid of identity,
because they are incapable of being identical with one another.

Considering that [the self] is like darkness (tamaḥ) in its lack of luminosity, he establishes—both through reality (*vastutaḥ*), through cognition (*pratītitaḥ*), and through linguistic usage (*vyavahārataḥ*)—the contradiction that serves as the logical reason (*hetu*) with the words "of the objects of the cognitions of *yuṣmad* and *asmat*.

This is because of the rule in the sūtra "pratyayottarapadayośca," which prescribes: "when followed by a suffix (*pratyaya*) or a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*), the substitutes *tvam* and *aham* take the place of the portions ending in *map* of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*."
It should not be argued that [the form] would be *tvanmat-pratyaya-gocayoḥ* (of the objects of your and my cognitions), as in the expressions "your" and "my," or "your son" and "my son";
for this is because of the governing rule "tvamāvekavacane" (the substitutes *tvam* and *aham* occur in the singular).

Furthermore, in this context, since *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not denote a single object, there is a plurality of the referents of *yuṣmad*, and the consciousness that is the referent of *asmad* is also manifold due to its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
If this is so, how is the analysis (*vigraha*) of this commentary to be understood?
It should not be said that the analysis is: "the cognition 'you' is the *yuṣmat*-cognition; the cognition 'we' is the *asmat*-cognition; [the word refers] to the objects of those two."
If it is argued that [the term "you"] is grammatically correct even though its referent is incorrect—
since the non-self, such as the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), cannot be the object of the cognition "you"— we say no; for the word *gocara* (object) here refers to suitability (*yogyatā*).

The conscious self (cidātmā), for its part, is fit to be the object of the notion "I" (asmat-pratyaya), because it is the recipient of the fruit consisting in the cessation of doubt and other such states induced by that notion; thus,
it is not entirely without an object.
And because of the statement in the Bhāṣya: "Because [the Self] is the object of the notion 'I' (asmad-pratyaya).

Although the ego (ahaṅkāra) and so forth are also fit for that [notion], they are nevertheless described as being "fit for the notion 'you' (yuṣmad-pratyaya)" in order to establish their absolute difference from the conscious Self (cid-ātman).
The venerable Āśramaśricaraṇas, however, state in their *Ṭīkāyojanā* as follows: "The conscious being denoted by the word *yuṣmad* is that which is to be addressed;
the conscious being qualified by the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth is denoted by the word *asmad*.

Thus, the rule regarding the substitution of *tvam* and so on applies only when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are used in their primary sense (*svārtha*), and not when they are used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*)."
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the rule: *yuṣmadasmadoḥ ṣaṣṭhīcaturthīdvitīyāsthayorvānāvau* (Pāṇini 7.2.95).

In this context, just as [the substitutes] do not apply to words that indicate [other things], so too they do not apply to pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and pure insentience (*jaḍamātra*) when these are indicated [by the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*], because there is no difference in their being indicators.

If it is intended by this rule that the absence of the *tvam*-substitutes occurs only when those two [words] denote actual linguistic sounds (*śabda*), then in this Bhāṣya, the word *yuṣmat* refers to the objective extrinsic reality (*parāgartha*) which is fit to be the object of a cognition produced by the word *yuṣmad*.
By the word "asmad," the inward self (pratyagātman) is intended, which is capable of being the object of the cognition produced by the word "asmad.
Thus, since the word itself is also understood as the delimitor of the scope of the indicated (lakṣyatāvacchedaka), it does not undergo the substitution of "tvam.
Nor is it the case that only externality (parāktva) and internality (pratyaktva) serve as the delimiters of the scope of the indicated.
It should not be said that [the cognition] does not pertain to the portion consisting of the word's fitness, on the grounds of complexity;
for even the fitness of the words as being contradictory must be stated in order to manifest the contradiction between the external object and the internal cognition.

For this very reason, although one could have said "of these two, which are the objects of the notions of 'this' and 'I'," the word *idam* (this) is used here for the meaning of "I" (*asmadartha*) both in common worldly usage and in the Veda; as in "we are these," or "these are the Videhas."

Thinking that the word *yuṣmad* (you) is not in contradiction with the word *asmat* (we), because one observes its usage in the expression "this is I" (*ayamaham asmi*), it was employed; for when the word *idam* (this) is used, no contradiction is perceived.
By this [argument], since the word *asmat* denotes a conscious being, it ought to have been used first, according to the maxim: "That which is more venerable comes first."
The objection that the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) rule prescribed by the sūtra "tyadādīni sarvair nityam" might apply here is also refuted;

for, as in the sūtra "yuṣmadasmadoḥ," neither the rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) nor *ekaśeṣa* applies here, and furthermore, if *ekaśeṣa* were applied, the intended contradiction would not be manifest.

The elders, however, say: "The mention of *yuṣmad* at the beginning is intended to indicate that, by means of the logic of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropa-apavāda*), one extracts the pure element of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*) from the non-self which constitutes the referent of *yuṣmad*, and then grasps it.
In this context, through the two words *yuṣmad* and *asmat*, the factual opposition between the Self and the non-Self as the "other" (*parāktva*) and the "inner" (*pratyaktva*) is stated;
by the word *pratyaya*, the opposition based on cognition is stated.
That which is cognized is the "cognition" (*pratyaya*), such as the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth; being non-self, it appears as an object of vision.
The Self, however, because it is the very act of cognition, is the "cognizer" (*pratyaya*); it appears through its own self-luminosity.
By the word "object" (*gocara*), a contradiction is stated from the perspective of conventional usage.

The threefold contradiction has been made clear: the referent of "you" (yuṣmad-artha), which is the object of such worldly usage as "I am the agent" by way of obscuring the inner self (pratyag-ātman); and the referent of "we" (asmad-artha), which is the object of such usage as "I am Brahman" by way of the dissolution of the non-self (anātma).

The construction is as follows: "yuṣmad" and "asmat" refer to the words for "you" and "I"; these two are both the cognitions (*pratyaya*) and the objects (*gocara*) of those cognitions, hence they are called "the objects of the cognitions of *yuṣmad* and *asmat*.

Since these two possess threefold contradictory natures, their non-existence as other than each other—that is, their absolute identity (*atyantābheda*) or their being of the same essence (*tādātmya*)—is established once that impossibility has been proven.
To the objection that even if identity (*aikya*) is impossible, why could there not be a relation of identity (*tādātmya*), as in the case of "the white jar," he says: "of the object and the subject.
The sense is that because consciousness (*cit*) and the insentient (*jaḍa*) stand in the relation of subject and object, they cannot have identity, just like a lamp and a jar.
*Yuṣmad* and *asmat* refer to the external (*parāc*) and internal (*pratyak*) realities, respectively.
Alternatively, the analysis [of the compound] is: "they themselves are both the condition (*pratyaya*) and the object (*gocara*).

Here, by means of the two terms *pratyaya* and *gocara*, the fact of being consciousness (*cid-tva*) and non-consciousness (*acid-tva*) is stated as the reason for the inwardness and outwardness (*pratyak-parāgbhāva*) of the Self and the non-Self respectively. Regarding that, he states the reason: "because of the object and the subject" (*viṣaya-viṣayiṇoḥ*).
Because the non-Self is an object of apprehension (*grāhya*), it is non-conscious.
However, because the self is the grasper, its nature as consciousness (citva) must be asserted.

The meaning is that if it were non-conscious (acit), its own apprehension by itself would be impossible due to the contradiction between being both object and agent, which would result in its not being perceived.
Alternatively, the relationship of cause and effect may be stated according to preference.

Now, one might object: "Since the Self (ātman) and the non-Self (anātman) are opposed as being inward and outward, conscious and unconscious, and subject and object—just like darkness and light—their identity or oneness is impossible; and since there is no cognition of such [identity], there can be no superimposition (adhyāsa). Nevertheless, let there be a mutual superimposition of their attributes, such as consciousness and happiness on the one hand, and insentience and suffering on the other. To this, he says: "And of their attributes also... [The full verse: *taddharmāṇāmapi caivaṃ parasparaviparyayaḥ / adhyāso 'nyonyadharmāṇāmiti bhāṣye vyavasthitam //* "And thus, there is a mutual reversal of their attributes; the superimposition of each other's attributes is established in the Bhāṣya. [The commentary: The meaning is that just as there is a superimposition of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) and the object of superimposition (adhyasyamāna), so too there is a superimposition of their respective attributes. For example, the attributes of the Self—such as consciousness, bliss, and purity—are superimposed upon the non-Self, which consists of the body, senses, mind, and intellect; and the attributes of the non-Self—such as insentience, suffering, and impurity—are superimposed upon the Self. This is because they are perceived as being indistinguishable from one another due to the lack of discernment (*aviveka*). Thus, it is established in the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya* that there is a mutual superimposition of the attributes of both. This is the sense. Furthermore, this is not merely a matter of words; rather, it is a fact established by experience, as we observe the usage of terms such as "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am happy," and "I am miserable. This is because the Self and the non-Self are always perceived together, and because the attributes of one are always perceived in association with the other. Therefore, the mutual superimposition of their attributes is proven by the very nature of empirical experience. Thus, it is established in the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya* that there is a mutual superimposition of the attributes of both. This is the sense. Furthermore, this is not merely a matter of words; rather, it is a fact established by experience, as we observe the usage of terms such as "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am happy," and "I am miserable. This is because the Self and the non-Self are always perceived together, and because the attributes of one are always perceived in association with the other. Therefore, the mutual superimposition of their attributes is proven by the very nature of empirical experience. The properties (*dharma*) of those two—the self (*ātman*) and the non-self (*anātman*)—are their "own-properties" (*taddharma*). Regarding these as well, there is the impossibility of their mutual existence.
The meaning is that the existence—that is, the conjunction (*saṃsarga*)—of those various properties in another property-possessor (*dharmī*) is impossible.
For indeed, there can be no exchange of properties without a conjunction of the property-possessors.
In the case of a crystal, there is a connection with the quality of redness due to the proximity of a red object.

Since the Self, whose nature is non-attachment, cannot be connected with anything at all, how could there be a connection with a quality preceded by a connection with its substratum? With this intention, he said: "all the more so" (*sutarām*). Now, one might ask: even if there is no identity between the Self and the non-Self, nor a connection between their respective qualities, why should superimposition (*adhyāsa*) not still occur? To this, he says: "for this reason" (*ityataḥ*).

According to the manner stated above, since there is an absence of identity and so forth, there is an absence of valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding that; therefore, because of the absence of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by such valid cognition—which is the cause of superimposition—it follows that "superimposition ought to be false. In this context, the word *mithyā* signifies both concealment (*apahnava*) and indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*).
And here, the purpose is to negate [superimposition].
Anticipating the objection, "Well then, where and whose superimposition is being negated?", he states—

beginning with the words "the object of the notion of 'I'" (*asmat-pratyaya-gocara*)— that the superimposition of non-self and its attributes upon the Self, and of the Self and its attributes upon the non-self, is being refuted.
Thinking that even the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties possess the fitness for the notion "I am," he distinguishes the Self from them by describing it as "the subject" (*viṣayiṇī*).
This means it is the witness (*sākṣin*) of the intellect and so forth. The reason for its being the witness is stated as "consisting of consciousness" (*cidātmaka*).
The meaning is: "in the aspect of consciousness (cid-aṃśa) which manifests as 'I'";
"of that which is the object of the notion of 'you' (yuṣmat-pratyaya-gocara)" means "that which is fit for the designation 'thou' (tvam-kāra-yogya)."
This means "of this object" (idamartha).

Now, one might ask: how can the intellect and so forth, which appear as "I," have the status of being "this object"? To this he says: "of the object"—meaning, that which is manifested by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin).

The point is that because the intellect (*buddhi*) and other such factors possess the defining characteristic of being manifested by a witness (*sākṣibhāsyatva*), they do not appear as objects of the "this" (*idamartha*), unlike a jar or similar external objects.

Alternatively, [the opponent might argue: the primary nature of the Self—which was described as being the innermost of all (*sarvāntaratva*), as selfhood (*pratyaktva*), as the state of being perceived (*pratītatva*), and as being the object of the empirical usage "I am Brahman" (*brahmāsmi*)—is unestablished, because it is perceived as "I" (*aham*).

Anticipating the objection that [the Self] is like the ego (ahaṅkāra), he says: "the object of the notion of 'I'. This means: it is that which is both the notion (*pratyaya*) of "us" (*asmad*) and the object (*gocara*).
The reason [for its being distinct from the ego] is either its being a manifestation made manifest by the function of the "I" (*ahaṃvṛtti*), or its being the objective field of such manifestation.

The meaning is that in the first example the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*), whereas in the second position that [reason] is unestablished; thus, it is logical that the Self's primary nature consists of subjectivity (*pratyaktva*) and so forth.
Now, one might object: "That which is the object-nature (*viṣayatva*) of the Self is unestablished."
Because it possesses the word "I experience," like the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); to this he says: "as an object" (*viṣayiṇī*).
Whether being denotable (*vācyatva*) or being indicated by secondary implication (*lakṣyatva*) is the reason.
Not the first, because that [reason] is unestablished in the subject (pakṣa);
nor the last, because it is lacking in the corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta)—this is the sense.

One might argue: "Even though in the cognition 'I know the body' there is a relationship of object and subject between the body and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), there could still be an illusory identification (abhedādhyāsa) between the Self and the ego-sense, just as there is an illusory identification of non-difference in the thought 'I am a man'. To this, he says: "Consisting of consciousness" (cidātmaka).

The point is this: although there is superimposition (adhyāsa) because of the similarity between those two [the Self and the ego] due to their respective qualities of being non-material (jaḍa) and limited (alpa), the non-material and limited ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) and so forth are not superimposed upon the undivided conscious Self (cidātman).

Anticipating the objection that—since the ego-sense is manifested as "I" (aham) like the Self, it too possesses subjectivity (pratyaktva) and so on, and therefore the previously mentioned externality (parāktva) and other attributes cannot be established regarding it—the author says: "yuṣmad... (you/that).
The state of being manifested by the activity of the "I" (ahaṃvṛtti) does not exist in the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), because of the contradiction between the status of agent and object;
nor does the state of being manifested by consciousness (cidbhāsyatva) exist in the conscious self (cidātman). Thus, there is a failure of the reason (hetvasiddhi).

Therefore, the point is that although the intellect and so forth possess inwardness (pratyaktva) from the perspective of their appearance, their outwardness (parāktva) and other such qualities are indeed primary.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is "pratyaya" because it is cognized (*prati-yata*) by you; and it is that which is the object of worldly transactions such as agency and so forth.
He states [the following] for the purpose of showing that it is to be abandoned: "of the poison," etc. [The root] *piñ* means "to bind."
The meaning is that it is an "object" (*viṣaya*) because it binds or fetters (*visinoti*).
Let the superimposition of the non-self and its attributes upon the Self be false;
why should the superimposition of the Self and its attributes upon the non-self not also be so?
Anticipating the objection that [the self exists] because of the experience "I am vibrating" or "I am happy," he says: "by its opposite.
Therefore, the opposite of the non-self (anātman) is consciousness (caitanya), which is of a contrary nature.
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of "being in such a state."

It is logical that the superimposition (adhyāsa) of the conscious self, as the subject, and its attributes upon the object— the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) and so forth— is false and non-existent, because the causal conditions for such superimposition are absent. For in this case, there exists neither the latent impression (saṃskāra) deposited by prior valid cognition, nor similarity, nor ignorance (ajñāna).
Because in the self, which is partless, devoid of qualities, and self-luminous, there is no possibility of ignorance, which consists in similarity to qualities or parts.
If it is asked, "But how can the Bhāṣya statement 'of its attributes' be consistent with the self being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa)?", it is replied:
consciousness manifested through a modification of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) is knowledge (jñāna);
that which is manifested as non-different from the object is the flash of awareness (sphuraṇa).

Bliss (*ānanda*) is that which is manifested by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by auspicious karma; thus, due to the distinctions created by the limiting adjuncts of these modifications, knowledge and the other qualities are designated as attributes of the Self.

As it is stated in the *Ṭīkā*: "Bliss, the experience of objects, and eternity—these are attributes which, although not separate [from consciousness], appear as if distinct because of their nature as consciousness.
Therefore, in the view that the Self is the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahma*),...

The purport of the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) commentary is as follows: since the object of the cognition "I am doing" cannot be a superimposition (*adhyāsa*), it must be accepted that this cognition possesses both validity (*prāmāṇya*) and truth (*satyatva*). Furthermore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "I am a man" is merely figurative (*gauṇa*). Consequently, because bondage is real, its cessation—which is the fruit [of the teaching]—cannot occur through knowledge; and because the identity between the bound individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is impossible, there can be no subject matter (*viṣaya*) for the scripture. Therefore, the scripture need not be commenced.
By the inclusion of the word "yukta" (proper), he indicates the weakness of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
To explain: is the non-existence of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) due to its being improper, or because it does not appear, or because of the absence of its cause?
Regarding the first [alternative], he says "even so" (*tathāpi*), meaning that this is accepted.
In accordance with this, the phrase "even though" (*yadyapi*) should be read at the beginning.
The intended meaning is that the impossibility of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the Self, which is non-attached and self-luminous, is actually an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
He states that the second [alternative] is not the case with the words "this" (*ayam*).
The meaning is that the non-appearance of superimposition is unestablished, because of the direct experience of the ignorant person thinking, "I am the agent.
Nor should it be said that this perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) regarding agency and so forth;
for [the Veda], being authorless, is free from defects.

Furthermore, because the sentence "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) has its purport determined by such indicative marks as the introductory context (*upakrama*), it brings about the realization of one's non-agency and identity with Brahman; thus, the erroneous nature of [the prior perception] is ascertained.

Nor should it be argued that the knowledge derived from scripture is sublated simply because it contradicts the more senior means of perception (*pratyakṣa*), for that would lead to the absurd consequence of the doctrine that the body is the self.

The notion "I am a human being" is contradicted by direct perception; furthermore, through such scriptural passages as "Now this [self] is bodiless," it is established that the Self is distinct from the body.

Therefore, it must be accepted that the perception of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—which is tainted by the suspicion of being an error like the cognition "this is silver"—does not possess greater authority than scripture.
Moreover, does "seniority" mean occurring earlier in time, or being the basis upon which the knowledge of scripture depends?
The first [alternative] is not tenable,
because even a senior [cognition], such as the error of silver, is seen to be sublated by a subsequent cognition of mother-of-pearl.

Nor is the second, because when scriptural knowledge arises, it depends on the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] through the linguistic usage of elders, which is rooted in perception and other means of knowledge.

Furthermore, although perception and other means of knowledge depend upon verbal testimony for their empirical validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*), they do not require its ultimate validity (*tāttvika-prāmāṇya*); and since there can be no sublation by scripture regarding that which is not required [by them], [the objection is refuted]. As for the argument that—just as a momentary sacrifice is the cause of a result occurring at a later time by the force of scriptural authority—so too, by the force of the scriptural text "Thus the knower is freed from name and form," it is possible for even the real to cease through knowledge, and therefore the description of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is unnecessary; [this is rejected as follows]: [The response is: No, because the two cases are not analogous. In the case of the sacrifice, the relationship between the action and its fruit is established by scripture, and since that relationship cannot be perceived through other means of knowledge, there is no contradiction. However, in the present case, the cessation of the real is not established by scripture alone, because it is contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge. Moreover, the cessation of the real would imply the non-existence of the Self, which is impossible. Therefore, the description of superimposition is indeed necessary. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the world; rather, what is observed is the cessation of the unreal, such as the cessation of the snake-superimposition upon the rope. Thus, the description of superimposition is appropriate. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not seen even in the case of the body, which is considered real by some; for when the body ceases, it does not become non-existent, but rather becomes unmanifest due to the absence of the conditions for its manifestation. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the pot and other objects, which are considered real by some; for when the pot ceases, it does not become non-existent, but rather becomes unmanifest due to the absence of the conditions for its manifestation. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the Self, which is considered real by all; for if the Self were to cease, it would follow that there is no liberation, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the world, which is considered real by some; for if the world were to cease, it would follow that there is no rebirth, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the Veda, which is considered real by all; for if the Veda were to cease, it would follow that there is no dharma or adharma, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the atoms, which are considered real by some; for if the atoms were to cease, it would follow that there is no creation or dissolution, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the ether, which is considered real by all; for if the ether were to cease, it would follow that there is no space for the movement of things, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the mind, which is considered real by some; for if the mind were to cease, it would follow that there is no experience of pleasure and pain, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is considered real by some; for if the intellect were to cease, it would follow that there is no cognition of objects, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which is considered real by some; for if the ego were to cease, it would follow that there is no sense of "I," and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the senses, which are considered real by some; for if the senses were to cease, it would follow that there is no perception of objects, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which are considered real by some; for if the subtle elements were to cease, it would follow that there is no gross creation, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the mahat-tattva, which is considered real by some; for if the mahat-tattva were to cease, it would follow that there is no evolution of the principles, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), which is considered real by some; for if primordial matter were to cease, it would follow that there is no cycle of birth and death, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the liberated soul (*mukta-ātman*), which is considered real by some; for if the liberated soul were to cease, it would follow that there is no final goal, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the Lord (*īśvara*), which is considered real by some; for if the Lord were to cease, it would follow that there is no dispenser of fruits, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is considered real by some; for if the individual soul were to cease, it would follow that there is no transmigrator, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the world-appearance (*prapañca*), which is considered real by some; for if the world-appearance were to cease, it would follow that there is no ignorance (*avidyā*), and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the truth (*satya*), which is considered real by all; for if the truth were to cease, it would follow that there is no reality, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the Brahman, which is considered real by all; for if the Brahman were to cease, it would follow that there is no ultimate reality, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the absolute (*paramārtha*), which is considered real by some; for if the absolute were to cease, it would follow that there is no liberation, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Furthermore, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the non-dual (*advaita*), which is considered real by some; for if the non-dual were to cease, it would follow that there is no unity, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition is correct. Moreover, the cessation of the real is not observed in the case of the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is considered real by some; for if pure consciousness were to cease, it would follow that there is no witness, and this is unacceptable. Therefore, the cessation of the real is not possible. Consequently, the description of superimposition
As for the claim that [this] is futile, that is not so;
for nowhere is anything seen to be real that can be removed by mere knowledge, and yet the reality of the Self is never seen to cease.
For if there were certainty regarding unfitness [to perform rituals], it would be impossible for the scriptural statement that "the bondage of truth ceases through knowledge" to convey its meaning.
Nor should it be argued that there is no certainty regarding unfitness because we observe the destruction of even true sin upon seeing the Setu (Rāmeśvara),
since that [sin] is destroyed by knowledge only when that knowledge is dependent on faith, ritual observances, and so forth.

Furthermore, since the scripture stating "There is no other path" indicates that bondage ceases through knowledge alone, one must describe its status as a superimposition (adhyasta) in order to justify its being removable by the knowledge derived from scripture. Moreover, what kind of reality can there be for that which is removable by knowledge alone?

First of all, it is not the case that [the world] is not produced from ignorance (ajñāna), because that would contradict the scriptural text, "But Māyā is Prakṛti," since Māyā and avidyā are one and the same.
Nor is it the case that [Brahman] is devoid of its own absence in its own locus, because that would contradict scriptural prohibitions such as, "[Brahman is] neither gross... and so forth.
Nor can it mean "incapability of being sublated by Brahman," because that would contradict scriptural statements regarding the cessation [of ignorance] through knowledge.
If, on the other hand, it means "freedom from sublation at the time of empirical usage," [then...]
In that case, it follows that truth is merely empirical, which amounts to its being superimposed (adhyasta).
And that [superimposition] must indeed be described for the sake of understanding the compatibility with the meaning of the scripture,
just as the sacrificial act has the *apūrva* as its mediating factor.

Nor is there redundancy because that [superimposition] is described in the section on "Difference from That" (*tadanyatva*), since it is merely being recalled at the outset for the purpose of establishing the object and other factors that serve as the basis for activity—the very superimposition already stated therein; such is the direction of the argument.
He shows superimposition (adhyāsa) in two ways with the words "worldly transaction" (lokavyavahāra).

"World" (loka) refers to the object-superimposition (arthādhyāsa), in that one identifies oneself as "I am a man"; the "transaction" (vyavahāra) concerning that [object] is the conceit (abhimāna), which shows the cognition-superimposition (jñānādhyāsa).
He states the definition of the nature of the two-fold superimposition with the words beginning "in each other" and ending with "of the attributes and the substrata.
The substrata of the attributes such as insentience and consciousness are the ego (ahaṅkāra) and the Self (ātman).

Since these two are absolutely distinct, the construction is as follows: through the non-apprehension of their mutual difference, one superimposes upon each other the identity of the other and the attributes of the other in a reversed manner, and thus worldly transaction proceeds.

Therefore, the cognition "this is that" is not a case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), because even though a distinction is conceptually constructed between the objects "that" and "this" due to their difference in time, there is no absolute difference between them; this is why the word "absolute" (*atyanta*) was used.

Nor should it be argued that the phrase "and [their] attributes" (*dharmāṃśca*) is redundant, since the superimposition of attributes is established once the identity of the substrates (*dharmitādātmya*) has been superimposed.

This is for the purpose of making it known that, although the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the substratum (*dharmin*)—such as blindness and other attributes of the sense organs—is not distinct [from them], the superimposition in the form "I am blind" is indeed distinct.
Now, raising the objection that if the Self and the non-Self were mutually superimposed, it would result in the doctrine of Nihilism (*śūnyavāda*), he says: "having coupled the real and the unreal.
The "real" is this consciousness which is not this [body]; its superimposition upon the non-Self consists merely in its association (*saṃsarga*), not in its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

The meaning is that "unreality" has you as its object; because there is superimposition even upon its own nature, the coupling of those two is called superimposition (adhyāsa), and thus it is not a state of emptiness.

Surely, if the words *adhyāsa* (superimposition), *mithunīkaraṇa* (pairing), and *lokavyavahāra* (worldly transaction) have a single meaning, how can there be the use of the suffix *lyap*—which replaces the gerundive suffix *ktvā* to express priority of time—as in "having superimposed" (*adhyasya*) and "having paired" (*mithunīkṛtya*)?
[The answer is: because there is a distinction between individual instances of superimposition.

In that context, the use of *lyap* is intended to indicate that each preceding instance of superimposition serves as the cause for each subsequent instance of superimposition by means of its residual impression (*saṃskāra*), thereby establishing its temporal priority.
He clarifies that very point with the word "natural" (*naisargika*).
The meaning is that the stream of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) within the inner self (*pratyagātman*), by way of the relationship between cause and effect, is beginningless (*anādi*).
[Objection: But since a stream is not a real entity, how can it be beginningless?
If it is asked, "Since individual instances of superimposition (adhyāsa) have a beginning, how can there be beginninglessness?"—

it is replied: Because it is accepted that "beginninglessness of effects" consists in the non-occurrence of the beginningless past time without at least one among the individual instances delimited by the nature of superimposition.
By this, the alternative that [the cognition arises] due to the absence of a cause is refuted,

because the word *naisargika* (inborn) has already stated that the impression (*saṃskāra*) is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*). Nor should it be said that only an impression produced by a previous valid cognition (*pramā*) is the cause.
Because, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a prior experience is the cause [of the subsequent superimposition].
Therefore, it is established that there exists an impression generated by a prior superimposition.
He states the material cause (*upādāna*) of the superimposition: "having false cognition as its cause" (*mithyājñānanimitta*).
It is false and it is ignorance; thus, "mithyājñāna" means false ignorance. That which has that as its cause is "tannimittaḥ.
The meaning is: "having that as its material cause" (tadupādānaka).

Although ignorance is the material cause, because it veils the nature of the Self as it manifests, it is described as a "defect" (doṣa) and as the "limiting adjunct" (upādhi) of the Lord who effects the superimposition of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra-adhyāsa).
The term "cause" (*nimitta*) is used to indicate that [the Self] possesses causality by virtue of being transformed by causes such as mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), time, and karma;
for how could there be an attachment to ignorance (*avidyā*) in the unattached Self, which is self-luminous, given the absence of the causal complex consisting of mental impressions and the like?
The word "false" (*mithyā*) is used for the purpose of dispelling such a doubt.
Just as darkness is established by the experience of owls within the orb of the fierce sun,
so too the ignorance established by the experience "I am ignorant" is impossible to deny.
This is because the imagined [object] does not touch its substrate,
and because knowledge of the eternal nature [of the substrate] is not in contradiction [with it].
Alternatively, the word "mithyā" (false) is used to dispel the doubt that ignorance is merely the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*).
The definition of ignorance (*ajñāna*) stated by the term "false knowledge" (*mithyājñāna*) is: being directly sublatable by knowledge while being false.
This phrase "while being false" is stated in response to one who claims that the prior absence of desire (*icchā-prāgabhāva*) is directly sublatable by knowledge.
The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to bondage (*bandha*), which is sublatable by knowledge through the mediation of the cessation of ignorance.
The definition [of the world] is either falsity while having beginningless material cause (*upādāna*), or else:
"falsity" is for the purpose of excluding Brahman,
and "beginningless" is for the purpose of excluding clay and the like.
The phrase "provided that it is the material cause" is intended to exclude the possibility of a relationship between ignorance (*avidyā*) and the Self (*ātman*).
Now, he seeks to strengthen the doctrine of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), stating: "I am this," and "this is mine.
Among the superimpositions of internal effects, "I am" is the first superimposition.
Nor should it be argued that this is not a false superimposition because the two parts—the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the object of superimposition (*āropya*)—are not perceived;
for, just as in the expression "the iron burns," we perceive both the seer and the seen parts in the expression "I perceive.
By the word *idam*, the aggregate that is the object of experience is denoted.
Here, by the expression "I am this," the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*)—namely, "I am a human"—is shown;
by "this is my body," the superimposition of association (*saṃsargādhyāsa*) is shown.

If it is objected: "But surely the very identity of the body and the self is their relation; so what is the difference between them?"—it is true that identity (*tādātmya*) consists in mutual difference existing while there is oneness of being (*sattaikya*).

In this context, the distinction is that the appearance of the aspect of identity in the form "I am a human being" and the appearance of the aspect of difference in the form of a relation in "this is mine" constitute the difference. Thus, because the causal complex exists and because experience exists, superimposition (adhyāsa) exists; therefore, since there is no contradiction regarding the identity of Brahman and the Self, and since the subject matter and the purpose exist, the scripture should be commenced—such is the purport of the Siddhāntabhāṣya.

And so, having established the subject matter and the purpose which were indicated by implication through the Sūtra, he asks for the definition in order to prove superimposition—which is the cause of those two—by means of its definition, possibility, and proof; thus he says: "He said."

"What is the definition of superimposition (adhyāsa)?"—this is what the proponent of the previous view says. The phrase "he says" (*āha*) is used to indicate that this treatise is a formal debate (*vādakathā*), since its primary purpose is the determination of truth (*tattvanirṇaya*). Thus, the words of another are cited.
The commentary beginning with "He said" and extending up to "How, moreover, in the inner self" is devoted to defining superimposition (*adhyāsa*).
From that point onward, it is devoted to establishing its possibility.
The section beginning with "This very thing called ignorance" and ending with "is evident to all the world" is devoted to providing proof; such is the division.
He states the definition: "It is said—'having the form of memory'.
The word "superimposition" (adhyāsa) is to be supplied [from the previous context].
Here, the definition is simply "the appearance of one thing in another."

The remaining two words are for the purpose of establishing that [meaning]. For instance, "that which is manifested" (*avabhāsa*) refers to an object such as silver; its "unfit locus" (*paratra*) is the meaning of the word *paratra*.
The unfitness of the locus consists either in being the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the superimposed object or in possessing that [absence].

And thus, the meaning is that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) consists in being manifested in that which is conjoined with itself under a single delimitation (*ekāvacchedena*), while simultaneously possessing its own absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
This is a definition common to both beginningless and beginning superimpositions.
The phrase "under a single delimitation" is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Regarding conjunction (*saṃyoga*), although it appears in the tree with which it is conjoined even while its own absolute absence (*svātyantābhāva*) exists there, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the two absolute absences differ—namely, the root and the top [of the tree].

To exclude the over-extension that would apply to a jar (where one might argue that a jar brought later appears on a floor where it was previously absent), the term "conjoined with itself" (*svasaṃsṛjyamāna*) is used;
by this, it is stated that at the time of the absence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), the conjunction of the counter-positive must exist, and thus there is no over-extension.

The phrase "possessing its own absolute non-existence" (*svātyantābhāvavat*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of a smell that is manifested by being delimited by [the locus] *bhūta*.

Since at the time of the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, there exists an absolute non-existence of silver delimited by the property of "this-ness" (*idantva*), there is no lack of extension (*avyāpti*).
Now, it may be argued that this definition is impossible (*asaṃbhava*).
Because of the absence of the causal complex for silver in the mother-of-pearl shell, there is no real relation [between them].

Nor should it be argued that what is called "superimposition" (adhyāsa) is simply the appearance of a remembered real silver elsewhere—in the shell—because that would entail the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*). Therefore, he says: "having the form of memory" (*smṛtirūpa*).
"Smṛti" means that which is remembered, such as real silver and the like; "smṛtirūpa" means having a form like that [remembered object]. The meaning is that it resembles what is being remembered.
By the mention of "resemblance," the superimposed object is distinguished from the object being remembered.
It is stated that there is no "misapprehension of one thing as another" (anyathākhyāti). He establishes this similarity [with the following]: "previously seen," etc.
"Seen" (dṛṣṭa) means the act of seeing (darśana).
Because it appears through the medium of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) as having been seen previously, it is called "the appearance of what was previously seen.

By this, it is stated that the similarity between the object being remembered and the object superimposed consists in their both being objects of a cognition produced by a mental impression; for both memory and superimposition are produced by a mental impression.

Nor should it be argued that because superimposition is produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), it would follow that it is a memory; for we intend to include its production from the contact with a defect (*doṣasaṃprayoga*) as well, and thus it is not produced by latent impressions alone.
Here, the word "contact" (*saṃyoga*) refers to the cognition of the general nature of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Because there is no contact with the sense organs in the superimposition of the ego (ahaṅkāra-adhyāsa), it is thus established—by means of the two terms "of the nature of memory" (*smṛtirūpa*) and "previously seen" (*pūrvadṛṣṭa*)—that silver exists as having arisen in mother-of-pearl and the like through the power of defects (*doṣa*), contact (*saṃprayoga*), and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); therefore, the definition of superimposition as "the appearance of something else" (*paratrāvabhāsya*) is justified.
Others, however, say that by those two terms, the definition of objective superimposition (*kāryādhyāsa-lakṣaṇa*) is stated as being produced by the triad beginning with defects.

Others, however, maintain that "having the form of memory" means being similar to what is being remembered; and this similarity consists in being the object of a cognition not produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because both memory and superimposition are not produced by a *pramāṇa*. [The term "previously seen"] refers to the locus previously perceived or to something belonging to that same class.
Because there is an absence of having been previously seen in the case of a body with newly acquired silver,

they have stated that the definition of empirical superimposition (*prātītikādhyāsa*) consists in being of a nature similar to what was previously seen, while being the object of a cognition not produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
By the two terms "in another" (*paratra*) and "appearance" (*avabhāsa*), the general definition of superimposition has indeed been explained.

In this regard, they say that the two terms beginning with "pramāṇa" (means of valid cognition) are used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the Ganges as it is being remembered and to a brand-new jar.
Therein, regarding the superimposition of an object (*arthādhyāsa*), the construction is: "that which resembles what is being remembered appears elsewhere due to prior perception.
Regarding the superimposition of cognition (*jñānādhyāsa*), however, the sentence should be construed as: "that which resembles memory appears elsewhere due to prior perception. This is the summary.

Now, one might object: "Since there is disagreement among disputants regarding superimposition (adhyāsa), how can the definition stated above be established? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] considers that although there is dispute concerning the nature of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) and the object superimposed (āropya), the definition—"the appearance of one thing in another"—is a universally accepted conclusion (sarvatantra-siddhānta), because it is established through corroborative arguments that a false object appears within a real substrate. Thinking thus, he states the views of those who maintain the theories of *anyathākhyāti* and *ātmakhyāti*: "Some [say] of that... and so forth.

Some proponents of the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) maintain that there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the property of another thing—such as silver located in a different place—onto something else, such as mother-of-pearl, which actually possesses its own constituent properties.

However, the proponents of the theory of self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*) maintain that there is a superimposition of the property of the self, which is of the nature of cognition, onto external objects like mother-of-pearl;
that is to say, they hold that internal silver appears as if it were external. This is the meaning.
He states the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) with the words "some say" (*kecid*).

The meaning is that they assert that when there is a non-apprehension of the difference between two objects— or rather, between an object and its cognition— whose superimposition is established in common worldly experience, an error rooted in that [non-apprehension] arises, resulting in a specific linguistic usage such as "this is silver."

The point is that even by them, a qualified error must be accepted because otherwise qualified conventional usage would be inexplicable; thus, there is agreement regarding the appearance of one thing as another. He states the view of the Śūnyavādins with the words, "But others..."

The meaning is that they describe the "imagination of the contrary nature" (viparītadharmatvakalpanā) of that very substratum, such as mother-of-pearl, as being the imagination of something absolutely non-existent, such as silver—where "contrary" (viparīta) means having a contradictory property (viruddhadharma).
Regarding these views, he states the agreement concerning the definition of "the appearance of one thing as another" (paratra parāvabhāsatva) with the words: "But in every way... (sarvathāpi tu).

The meaning is that even though there is dispute regarding the specific mode—such as whether it is *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension) and so forth—the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) does not abandon its defining characteristic of being "the appearance of one thing in another.

The point is this: since it is impossible for the silver, which is directly perceived, to exist in another place or in the mind, and since it cannot be non-existent because it is directly perceived, and since it cannot truly exist in the mother-of-pearl because its sublation would otherwise be impossible, its nature must necessarily be falsity (*mithyātva*).
He says "And thus" (tathā ca) to show that there is no dependence on reasoning regarding the falsity of what is superimposed, because that is established by experience;
this experience occurs at a time subsequent to the sublation, whereas [the superimposition] occurred prior to it.
Because it is impossible to know [the shell] as "shell-ness," the word "vaccha" expresses the falsity of the silver, which is established by the perception of its sublation (*bādhā*).

Having stated the example for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) upon the attributeless Self, he states the example for the superimposition of the internal difference between Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*), which is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as ignorance (*avidyā*), with the words "one" (*eka*).

The meaning is that, just as with a second moon, a single [object] appears as two when pointed at by a finger. The word "iti" (thus) serves to conclude the section on defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Let it be granted that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) occurs in the case of mother-of-pearl and so forth; [however, the question remains: how can there be superimposition of the Self upon the non-Self? For the Self is not an object of perception, since it is devoid of form and the like. Nor is it an object of inference, because it lacks any inferential mark (*liṅga*). Nor is it an object of verbal testimony (*śabda*), because it is not denoted by any word. Nor is it an object of comparison (*upamāna*), because it has no similarity to anything else. Nor is it an object of presumption (*arthāpatti*), because its existence is established even without it. Nor is it an object of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because it is self-luminous. Therefore, since the Self is not an object of any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it cannot be superimposed upon the non-Self. Furthermore, the non-Self cannot be superimposed upon the Self, because it is an object of perception. Indeed, it is observed that what is perceived is superimposed upon what is remembered, as in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver. But the Self is never perceived, being devoid of form and the like. Thus, since neither the Self nor the non-Self is an object of perception, how can there be superimposition of one upon the other? To this, we reply: it is not the case that only what is perceived can be superimposed upon what is remembered. Rather, it is seen that what is remembered is superimposed upon what is perceived. For example, one who has experienced the taste of a mango may, upon seeing a citron, have the memory of the mango's taste superimposed upon the citron. Similarly, one who has experienced the touch of sandalwood paste may, upon feeling the touch of a stone, have the memory of the sandalwood's touch superimposed upon the stone. Likewise, one who has experienced the smell of a lotus may, upon smelling a blue water lily, have the memory of the lotus's smell superimposed upon the water lily. Therefore, it is established that the superimposition of the non-Self upon the Self is possible. As for the objection that the Self is not an object of perception because it is devoid of form and the like, we reply: the Self is indeed perceived through the internal sense organ (*manas*), which is free from defects such as distance and obstruction, and which possesses the nature of consciousness. Just as the eye perceives color, so too does the internal sense organ perceive the Self, which is of the nature of consciousness. Therefore, the Self is an object of perception. Consequently, the superimposition of the non-Self upon the Self is possible. Furthermore, the superimposition of the Self upon the non-Self is also possible, because the non-Self is perceived. It is observed that what is perceived is superimposed upon what is remembered, as in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver. And the non-Self is perceived. But since [superimposition] is not possible with respect to the Self, he raises an objection with the words, "How then? The pervasion (vyāpti) is observed in cases such as mother-of-pearl: wherever there is the status of being the substratum for immediate superimposition, there is both conjunction with the sense organs and the status of being an object. Intending to show that the status of being the substratum for the Self is impossible because of the absence of those pervading conditions, he says, "With respect to the inner Self" (*pratyagātmani*).
The meaning is: how can there be a superimposition (adhyāsa) upon the inward, full, and sense-ungraspable [Self] of objects such as the ego (ahaṅkāra) and their attributes?
He states the aforementioned pervasion (vyāpti): "For everyone...
Here, "being situated in front" means being in contact with the senses.
One might object: "Let there be objectivity and so forth for the Self as well, in order that it may serve as a substratum. To this he says, "yuṣmad" (you).
Following such scriptural passages as "This inner Self is not grasped by the eye," you declare that the inner Self—which is unworthy of being an object of the notion "this"—is not an object.
The meaning is that if, out of greed for proximity, one were now to admit its objectivity, there would be a subversion of both scripture and established doctrine.
He declares the possibility of superimposition upon the Self with the words, "It is said.
The pervading characteristic of superimposition is merely the appearance of both the substrate and the object of superimposition in a single cognition;
and that consists in being the locus of effects such as the cessation of doubt, which is necessitated by such appearance.
Thinking that objecthood (*viṣayatva*) constituted by a difference from its own manifestation is not pervasive due to its complexity (*gaurava*), he says: "Not, first of all... (*na tāvad iti*).
This self is not, by necessity, an object [of cognition].
He states the reason for this: "our" (asmad).
The meaning is that it appears therein—that is, in the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) denoted by the word "we" (*asmad*), in the form of "I" (*aham*).

The meaning is either this: that in which the conscious self (*cidātmā*), which is our own object, is perceived by way of being reflected—that is the "I-notion" (*ahaṅkāra*) called *asmad-pratyaya*, because it appears therein; or else, [the meaning is] that it is that in which [the self] appears. Nor should it be argued that there is a circularity—namely, that appearance occurs only when superimposition (*adhyāsa*) exists, and superimposition exists only when that [appearance] exists—for [this is not the case] because [the process] is beginningless (*anāditvāt*).
Because that which appears as the self during prior practice can serve as the substratum for subsequent superimposition.
[Objection: How can the Self, which consists of the manifestation (*bhāna*) having the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) as its object—expressed as "I am indeed"—be that which is being manifested?
For without being the object of that [manifestation], it would be impossible for it to partake in its fruit. To this, he says: "And because of its immediacy" (*aparokṣatvācca*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt.
The meaning is "because of its self-luminosity.
He establishes its self-luminosity with the word "pratyak" (the inner self).
The meaning is that the self-luminosity of the Self follows from its well-known status—among everyone from children to scholars—as being free from doubt and other such cognitive states.
Therefore, the sense is that because the Self appears as self-luminous, it is possible for it to be the substrate of superimposition.
Regarding the claim that being the substrate of immediate superimposition is pervaded by being perceptible through sensory contact, he says: "And this [Self] is not...
He states the reason for that: "even though it is not perceptible..."
The meaning is: "even in that which is perceptible by the senses.
The ignorant, who lack discrimination, superimpose upon the sky—which is like a sapphire bowl—such things as being dark or yellow, perceiving it as directly present before them.
Since the quality of being perceptible by the senses does not exist in that case, there is no pervasion (vyāpti) due to this deviation (vyabhicāra).
