By this, the argument that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) cannot occur between the self and the non-self because there is no similarity between them is refuted;
for we observe superimposition even in the absence of such similarity, as in the case of the blue sky.

According to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it should be understood that the sky is cognizable by the Witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) manifested through a visual modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of light.
He concludes the demonstration with the word "evam" (thus).

Now, one might ask: why is superimposition (*adhyāsa*) described here when ignorance (*avidyā*), which was indicated in the aphorism as being destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman, has been set aside? To this he says: "tametam" (this very [superimposition]).

The meaning is that they consider this superimposition—which was introduced, resolved, and characterized by the aforementioned definition—to be ignorance itself, because it is the effect of ignorance.
He states that this [superimposition] is ignorance because it is to be removed by knowledge (*vidyā*), saying "by its discrimination" (*tadvivekena*).
The meaning is: they call that which determines the true nature of the substratum through the negation of the superimposed object "knowledge," for it removes the superimposition.
Nevertheless, setting aside causal ignorance (*kāraṇāvidyā*), why is effect-ignorance (*kāryāvidyā*) described? To this he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).
The meaning is: "when that superimposition (adhyāsa), consisting of ignorance (avidyā), exists according to the logic already stated.

The intention is that since the root ignorance is not seen to cause harm during deep sleep (suṣupti), its description here is for the purpose of making known its harmful nature in its form as an effect. The literal meaning [of the verse] is that the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) is not tainted by the virtues or defects produced by the superimposed object.
Having thus stated the definition and the possibility of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), he states the proof: "Taking this very [superimposition]...

The meaning is that, taking as its cause this aforementioned superimposition—which is established through the direct perception of the witness—threefold worldly activity proceeds: namely, worldly, pertaining to the scriptures of ritual action (*karma-śāstra*), and pertaining to the scriptures of liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*).
Among these, the scriptures of ritual action, such as the *Ṛgveda* and others, are primarily concerned with injunctions and prohibitions.
The distinction is that the Vedānta texts, which are the scriptures of liberation, are devoted to the inner Brahman (pratyag-brahma) which is devoid of injunctions and prohibitions.
Thus, although superimposition (adhyāsa) is established by perception as the cause of worldly transaction, [the author] asks for further proof, saying, "But how?

The analysis of the compound *avidyāvad-viṣayāṇi* is as follows: the self (*ātman*) who possesses superimposition in the form "I am possessed of ignorance" is the knower (*pramātā*); those [scriptures] whose object and locus is such a [knower] are "those whose object is the one possessed of ignorance."

Although it is evident that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have as their object one who possesses ignorance (*avidyāvat*), because the valid cognition—which serves as the cause for the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding various objects of knowledge—resides in a cognizer (*pramātṛ*) whose nature is superimposition (*adhyāsa*);
nevertheless, the construction [of the objection] is: "How then, and by what means of valid cognition, is it established that they have as their object one who possesses ignorance?
Or alternatively: "How can the means of valid cognition have as their object one who is not a knower (*avidvat*)?"
The objection is that [the Veda] would incur invalidity due to defects in its basis (*āśrayadoṣa*).

In response to the inquiry regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein, he states the presumption based on worldly practice (*vyavahārārthāpatti*) and the inference from its mark (*talliṅgānumāna*) with the passage beginning with "It is said" (*ucyate*) and ending with "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The empirical usage (vyavahāra) having Devadatta as its agent is rooted in the superimposition (adhyāsa) of "I" and "mine" upon his body and so forth, because it follows the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of that [superimposition]; whatever is thus is so, just as the usage "the jar is rooted in clay" [is based on the superimposition of clay-ness]. This is the formal argument (prayoga).
In this regard, he demonstrates the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "deha" (body).
It is observed that in the case of Devadatta, during deep sleep, when there is an absence of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), there is an absence of empirical activity (*vyavahāra*);
whereas in the waking and dreaming states, when superimposition exists, there is empirical activity. This positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not explicitly stated because it is obvious.
The meaning is that superimposition (adhyāsa) is established either by this mark (*liṅga*) as its cause, or by the impossibility of the effect in the form of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Now, one might object: "Let worldly transaction be established by the mere conceit of 'I' with respect to the body, which possesses the genus of humanity and so forth; what is the use of the conceit of 'mine' with respect to the senses and other [organs]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For not...
The word "senses" (*indriya*) is also indicative of the marks (*liṅga*) and so forth.
Because of the use of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "perception and so forth" (*pratyakṣādi*), the meaning is as follows:

the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) prompted by perception, inferential marks, and so on—taking the form of "I am the seer," "I am the inferrer," "I am the hearer," and so forth—is not possible without grasping the sense-faculties and other factors as objects of the notion of "mine" (*mamatā*).
Alternatively, the construction is that such conventional usage does not exist when those [faculties] are not appropriated as "mine."
In the former case, since there is a single agent for the actions of non-appropriation and performing, the suffix *ktvā* is grammatically correct.
In the latter case, because non-appropriation and the act of usage have a single identical agent, its correctness [is established]; such is the distinction.

The sense is that if there were no superimposition (adhyāsa) of "mine-ness" upon the senses and so forth, then, like a blind person, there would be no such worldly functioning as being a "seer" and so on.
To the objection that since worldly functioning occurs through the superimposition of the senses alone, the superimposition of the body is redundant, he says: "And not...
The locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the senses is their substratum (*āśraya*).

The meaning is "the body. Now, one might object: "Let the body conjoined with the self be their substratum; what is the use of superimposition (adhyāsa)? To this he replies: "And not by means of that in which the state of being the self has not been superimposed. This means: that in which the state of being the self—that is, identity with the self (ātmatādātmya)—has not been superimposed.

The meaning is that, according to the scriptural text "for [the Self] is unattached," the relationship between the body and the Self is purely superimposed (ādhyāsika), and not one of conjunction (saṃyoga) or the like.
Now, it might be argued: let there be no superimposed relationship of the Self with the body and so forth either.

Because the status of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) is established by its own inherent consciousness, there is no contingency of being a knower during deep sleep (*suṣupti*) due to the cessation of the instruments [of perception]; to this he says: "And not in this... For the state of being a knower consists in being the substratum of valid cognition (*pramā*).
If valid cognition (*pramā*) were merely eternal pure consciousness (*nityacinmātra*), then it would be impossible for it to have a locus, and the sense organs would be rendered useless.
If, on the other hand, it were merely a mental modification (*vṛtti*),
there would follow the consequence of universal blindness.
Because a mental modification (*vṛtti*) is insentient (*jaḍa*), cognition (*bodha*) arising from that modification is the valid knowledge (*pramā*).

The point is this: the state of being the substratum (*āśrayatva*) of that [cognition] for the Self, which is by nature unattached (*asaṅga*), is not possible without the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with the mind that possesses modifications.
The literal meaning is: "when there is no superimposition of the body, nor superimposition of its attributes.
To one who might say, "In that case, let the self not possess the status of a knower," he replies: "And not..."

Therefore, he concludes the result of both inference and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) by stating "therefore" (*tasmāt*), [meaning] that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) must be accepted for the sake of the empirical usage of the self as a knower and so forth;
the meaning is "because of the existence of means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasattvāt*).
Alternatively, having resolved the inquiry regarding the means of valid cognition, he dispels the objection by stating "therefore."
The construction is as follows: since the superimposition of "I" (aham-adhyāsa) is internal to the knower, it is not a defect;
thus, even the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) have as their locus that which possesses ignorance (avidyāvat).
A defect is said to be that which arises subsequently, once the knower already exists.
Just as glass and the like [are external defects],

ignorance (avidyā), however, is not a defect because it is internal to the cognizer; thus, the implication is that there would be no invalidity of perception and the other means of knowledge on that account.

Now, as for the claim that worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is the effect of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that is incorrect because worldly activity is observed even in the case of the learned (*vidvat*), who are devoid of superimposition; therefore, he says: "And with animals, etc. (*paśvādibhiśca*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of dispelling this doubt.

What constitutes "learnedness" (vidvattva): is it the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that "I am Brahman," or is it the conceptual knowledge of the distinction between the Self and the non-Self derived through reasoning?
In the first case, it will be stated in the *Samanvaya-sūtra* that empirical activity continues due to the persistence of sublated superimposition (*bādhitādhyāsānuvṛtti*).
In the second case, because indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) does not remove immediate error (*aparokṣabhramanivartaka*), [empirical activity would persist].

The meaning is that even for those possessing discrimination (vivekin), because they are indistinguishable from animals and the like during the time of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*) due to being equally possessed of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), it is logical that empirical transaction is the effect of superimposition.
Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*): those possessing discrimination are possessed of superimposition, because they possess empirical transaction, just like animals and the like.
Therein, explaining the summary statement, he clarifies the reason through an illustration with the words "just as" (*yathā hi*).
The favorability or unfavorability of consciousness consists in its having as its object that which accomplishes what is desired or undesired;
he illustrates this very point with the word "just as" (*yathā*).
This staff is a means for accomplishing what is undesirable to me,
because it is a staff,
like a staff previously experienced.
The meaning is that they engage in practical activity after inferring: "This grass is a means to achieve what is desired, like the grass previously experienced.
Now, he states the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) with the word "thus" (*evam*).
The logical connection is "even those whose minds are fully developed";
the meaning is "even those who possess discernment.
He states the conclusion: "Therefore," etc.
"By the force of experience" is the meaning.
"Similar" means equal insofar as they are both effects of superimposition.

[Objection: "Surely neither do animals and the like say, 'Our activity proceeds from superimposition,' nor is this perceived by others; therefore, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (sādhyavikala). [Reply: He says "And of animals and the like" to show that this is not so.
They possess only the cognition of the self and the non-self, but not the discrimination between them.

Because there is no such instruction; therefore, the meaning is that their superimposition is established due to the existence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). He concludes with the words "tatsāmānya... (that generality...).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because its similarity to those [animals], such as cattle, consists in being subject to empirical usage (*vyavahāravattva*), it is determined that this empirical usage is common even to those who possess discrimination.
It was stated previously that this commonality of usage is due to its being the effect of superimposition (*adhyāsa*).
In that regard, he recalls the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) mentioned there with the words "tatkā" (arising from that).

The term *tatkāla* means that whose very time is the time of that superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Alternatively, it means that which possesses the stated positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, namely: when there is superimposition, there is worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); and in its absence, as in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is the absence of that [transaction].

Therefore, it is faultless that even for the discerning, there exists the conceit of "I" and "mine" with respect to the body and so forth, due to this empirical mark. Now, one might object: "Even if worldly transactional activity is based on superimposition, ritual activities such as the Jyotiṣṭoma are not produced by superimposition, because they are preceded by the knowledge of a self distinct from the body. Anticipating this objection, he accepts the reason [for their being based on superimposition] by stating: "But in the case of scriptural [activity]... (śāstrīye tu).

Then, raising the objection as to how the fact that Vedic ritual action is produced by superimposition (adhyāsa) can be established, [the author] asks: "Is it merely the cognition of the Self as distinct from the body that is required there, or is it the knowledge of the true nature of the Self?
To the first case, he says, "Even so," meaning that since such a cognition does not sublate superimposition, the establishment of [superimposition] remains intact.

He says that the second [alternative] is not [the case], stating "not by Vedānta. The meaning is that for ritual action, what is required is the knowledge "I am a transmigrating being belonging to a particular caste, afflicted by hunger, thirst, and so forth," and not the knowledge of the true nature of the Self which is the opposite of that, because the latter is useless and would obstruct engagement in action.
He concludes that scriptural action is produced by superimposition with the words "But previously" (*prāk tu*).
He cites scripture as a means of valid cognition regarding superimposition with the words "For just as" (*yathā hi*);
the meaning is that just as perception, inference, and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) are means of valid cognition for superimposition, so too is scripture.

The meaning is as follows: the scripture—such as "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice," "One should not beg after having bathed [for initiation]," "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age," and "One with black hair should establish the sacred fires"—by employing terms such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth, refers to an eligible person who identifies with his caste (varṇa) and other attributes, thereby implying superimposition (adhyāsa). Even though superimposition is thus established by means of proof, since there arises a desire to know "of what is there a superimposition upon what?", he recalls the definition in order to illustrate it, saying: "Superimposition is called... and so on.
He provides an illustration with the words "tadyathā" (for example).
The meaning is that it is illustrated in such a way that its characteristic becomes clear.

One superimposes upon the self as qualified by the body—external objects such as sons and so forth, which are perceived as distinct from one's own body—their attributes, such as totality and the like.
The meaning is that, due to the knowledge of those attributes, one superimposes attributes similar to them upon oneself;

this should be understood because the superimposition of those attributes is impossible when there is direct perception of difference, and because the theory of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension) is not accepted.
He says "likewise" (tathā) to explain that one superimposes the attributes of the body, the senses, and the mind upon the Self characterized by consciousness.

Since the body and so forth, which possess attributes such as thinness, are imagined through identity with the Self, it should be understood that their attributes are directly superimposed upon the Self. He describes the superimposition of the attributes of the mind upon the Witness, whose nature is immediate and unknown, saying: "likewise, the internal organ... (tathāntaḥkaraṇa).
Having explained the superimposition of attributes (*dharmādhyāsa*), he likewise states the superimposition of the substrate (*dharmyadhyāsa*) with the word "thus" (*evam*).
It should be understood that, having superimposed the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) non-differently upon the Witness (*sākṣin*), one then superimposes its attributes, such as desire and the like.
The movements of one's own [mind] are the fluctuations of the mind (*manovṛttayaḥ*).

It is "internal" (*pratyak*) because it moves toward (*añcati*), that is, manifests itself as being of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccitsukhātmaka*), by way of its opposition (*prati-prātilomyena*) to non-existence, insentience, suffering, and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth.

Having thus illustrated the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the non-self and its attributes upon the Self, he now describes the superimposition of the Self upon the non-self as being conjoined with it, saying: "And that... (*tañca*).
In the superimposition of "I," the manifestation of the conscious self (cidātman) must be admitted,
otherwise the world would fall into blindness;
furthermore, there is no manifestation of that which has not been superimposed.
Therefore, just as in the case of silver [superimposed] upon this [shell], the superimposition of association with the Self must be admitted;
and likewise by its reverse.
The "reverse" of that inert object of superimposition is its status as the substrate (adhiṣṭhānatva).
And consciousness exists as that very self; this is the meaning.

In that regard, the distinction is as follows: in ignorance (ajñāna), there is contact with the pure self alone; in the mind (manas), there is contact with the self as conditioned by ignorance; and in the body and so forth, there is contact with the self as conditioned by the mind.

The sense is that, through the superimposition of the intellect and so forth upon the Self, the Self acquires agency and other such qualities; and through the superimposition of the Self upon the intellect and so forth, the intellect and so forth acquire consciousness.
He concludes the described superimposition with the words "Thus, this..."

Because it consists of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of effects is itself beginningless; from superimposition comes the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and from that, further superimposition.
Thus, by way of this continuous flow, its innate nature (*naisargikatva*) is established.
In this manner, both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) have been explained.
Because there is no destruction in the absence of knowledge, it is infinite.
As it is said in the Bhagavad Gītā: "Neither its form is perceived here in such a way, nor its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation.
Having stated the cause, he describes its essential nature with the word "mithyā" (false).

The meaning is as follows: *pratyaya* refers to that which is perceived through false illusion (*mithyāmāyā*), namely the manifold of effects (*kāryaprapañca*) and the cognition thereof; such is its essential nature.
He states its function with the words "agency" (*kartṛtva*), etc. He concludes the proof with the words "all," etc.

Intending that perception alone is the means of knowledge (*māna*) that apprehends the locus of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), while inference and other means serve only for the sake of establishing its possibility, he concludes the section on perception.
Having thus described superimposition, he shows the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) to be accomplished by it, beginning with the words "of this" (*asya*).

Liberation (mokṣa) is the absolute destruction, along with its root, of superimposition (adhyāsa), which is the cause of evils such as agency; by what means is this achieved? To this he says: "By the Self" (ātman). This means:
by the attainment—that is, the unobstructed acquisition through hearing and other means—of the direct realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self.
He states the cause for this knowledge: "All" (sarva).
The meaning is that they are undertaken and studied after being investigated.
It is thus stated that for those who have investigated the Vedāntas, the subject matter is the identity of Brahman and the Self, and liberation is the fruit.
It should be understood that, by implication, those same two (the subject matter and the purpose) belong to the treatise as well, which consists of the investigation of that [Self].

Now, one might object: "Since meditations on the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth appear in the Vedāntas, how can it be said that their sole meaning is the unity of the Self? To this he says: "And just as... (*yathā ca*).
That which pertains to the body (*śarīra*) is the "embodied" (*śārīraka*).
Because it is contemptible, the term refers to the embodied soul (*śārīraka*) dwelling therein; *mīmāṃsā* is the investigation into its being Brahman, and the meaning is "in that [investigation].

Since meditations (*upāsanā*) serve the purpose of attaining knowledge of the oneness of the Self by means of one-pointedness of mind, it will be explained later that the primary purport (*mahātātparya*) of the sentences concerning them also lies in that oneness.

Thus, by means of the statement regarding superimposition (*adhyāsa*), it has been demonstrated that the scripture ought to be commenced, because there is no contradiction in the identity of Brahman and the Self, and because it possesses both a subject matter and a purpose.
Thus ends the first section.

The Vedāntas are the direct subject matter of this inquiry; yet, since there is doubt as to whether they have already been dealt with or not, given that the entire Veda is devoted to injunctions (*vidhi*),
and because injunctions were already investigated by the previous system (*pūrvatantra*) starting from the aphorism "Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) being that the Vedāntas have their objects already understood and thus lack an immediate subject matter, and therefore there is no need for this work, the author says: "The Vedānta...
This means that this is the first aphorism of the collection of sūtras intended to be explained—a treatise consisting of a revered inquiry into the subject matter of the Vedānta.
If the meaning of the Veda were exclusively injunction (*vidhi*), then the omniscient Bādarāyaṇa would not have spoken of the "inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*).
Because there is no means of valid cognition regarding Brahman,

the author of the Sūtras demonstrates by stating that Brahman is the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*) that an investigation into the Vedānta texts— which have Brahman as their subject matter and which are not understood through any other system— is to be commenced.
And the commentator [Śaṅkara] expressed this very point by the phrase "of that which he intends to explain" (*vyācikhyāsitasya*).
Thus ends the second section.

Having thus explained, by means of two sections, the two reasons for the necessity of undertaking the inquiry into the Vedanta—namely, its possession of a subject matter and a purpose, and its not being a repetition of what is already known—the author begins the word-by-word commentary. Furthermore, since there remains doubt regarding the commencement of the treatise due to the presence or absence of a qualified candidate (adhikārin), he establishes the existence of such a candidate by stating that the word *atha* signifies "immediacy" (*ānantarya*). This is expressed in the passage: "Therein, the word *atha*..."

The meaning is "in the sūtra. Since the word *atha* has many meanings— as in the rule "the word *atha* [is used] in the senses of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), immediate succession (*anantara*), commencement (*ārambha*), inquiry (*praśna*), and totality (*kārtsnya*)"— it is in this context of "Now, the instruction on yoga" (*atha yogānuśāsanam*) that...

One might ask: "Why should it not be as in the Sūtras, where the word *atha* signifies 'commencement'—as in 'the Yoga-śāstra is commenced'—so why should it not be so here? To this he says: "It does not have the sense of an introduction (*adhikāra*).
The underlying intention is this: Does the term *jijñāsā* refer primarily to the desire for knowledge (*jñāna-icchā*), or does it indicate the investigation (*vicāra*) itself?

If, in the first case, the word *atha* has the sense of "commencement," the meaning of the Sūtra would be that "the desire for knowledge of Brahman is commenced"; however, this is inconsistent, because such a desire is not something to be commenced.
For a desire is not undertaken in every section; rather, it is through that desire that the inquiry (*vicāra*) is undertaken.

Not the second [alternative], because it is impossible for [the word *atha*] to indicate "investigation" (*vicāra*) without supplying a word expressing an action to be performed (*kartavya*); and if such a word is supplied, the statement of the commencement [of the inquiry] is accomplished by that very word, rendering the word *atha* redundant.

However, since it is more appropriate for the word *atha* to signify immediate succession (*ānantarya*) for the sake of establishing the qualification (*adhikāri*), he now refutes the other possible meaning with the words "of the auspicious rite" (*maṅgalasya*).

The meaning is that the sentence-meaning is the necessity of undertaking the inquiry; for in that context, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the auspicious rite as an agent or in any other such role.
If it is objected: "But surely the author of the Sūtras has already indicated that an auspicious rite must be performed at the beginning of a treatise by using the word *atha*," [the reply is: True.
Its meaning is not auspiciousness; rather, its hearing and recitation perform the function of an auspicious rite.
Its meaning, however, is immediate succession (ānantarya); thus it says, "the meaning is immediate succession. Immediate succession is the absence of any other intervening object.

Through hearing—that is, by the act of listening—the hearing of the syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha* yields the fruit of auspiciousness, just like the hearing of the sounds of conchs, lutes, and other instruments.
As it is said: "In ancient times, these two—the syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—emerged from Brahman after piercing his throat; therefore, both of them are auspicious."
The meaning is that this is because of such a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*).

Now, since the context is that "the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is false," if it is thought that "the phenomenal world is real," then the word *atha* is observed to have the sense of introducing a subsequent matter that is different from the matter previously under discussion.
To the question, "Why should it not be so here? he says: "Because of the preceding" (*pūrva*).

This means "as a result" (*phalataḥ*), i.e., as a result of the inquiry into Brahman. Since there is no specific subject matter (*arthaviśeṣa*) previously introduced prior to the inquiry into Brahman, for which the word *atha* could express a different topic (*arthāntaratva*).
The author of the Sūtras should not state that it is a different subject from anything whatsoever, because there would be no purpose in doing so.

If, however, it is argued that because the previously mentioned subject—which was introduced as the cause for the inquiry into what is to be done (kartavya) denoted by the word *jijñāsā*—is required [as a prerequisite], and that on the strength of this requirement (*apekṣā*), the previously mentioned cause is implied and thus a difference in subject matter is asserted; [then we reply:]

In that case, the status of being a separate meaning (*arthāntaratva*) is included within immediate succession (*ānantarya*), because immediate succession must necessarily be stated for the sake of knowing the relationship between cause and effect.
For when it is said, "This is a separate meaning," the fact that it is a cause is not understood;
however, when it is said, "This is immediately subsequent," the understanding of its causality indeed arises.

Nor should it be argued that there is the consequence of the cognition of "cow" being considered the cause immediately after the cognition of "horse," because such immediate succession is not primary when there is a separation by space or time.
Therefore, immediate succession is primary only between the causal complex and its result.

Because there is no intervention [between the two], once that [meaning] has been stated, it should not be said that it is a different meaning, since it is already knowledge and because it would be redundant—this is the sense.

One should construe the Bhāṣya by supplying the words: "Since the result, namely the inquiry (*vicāra*), necessarily depends on the previously mentioned cause (*hetu*), that which is a different meaning [from the cause] is not a separate meaning of the word *atha*, because it is included within the category of 'immediate sequence' (*ānantarya*)."

Alternatively, the meaning is that the result of that "difference of meaning" (arthāntaratā) which requires a prior subject matter is knowledge; since there is no distinction from immediate succession (ānantarya) by way of that [knowledge], and because that [difference] is not included within the knowledge itself, it is not the meaning of the word *atha*. Now, raising the doubt: even if it has the sense of immediate succession, what is the limit of that succession? He says: "And when...
That which invariably precedes, occurs first, and is the uncommon cause—that is to say, the complete cause.
The meaning is that it must be stated that this very [study] is the limit (avadhi).
Now, one might object: "Just as in the inquiry into Dharma, so too in the inquiry into Brahman, the study of the Veda is a sufficient cause. To this he says: "svādhyāya" (one's own Vedic study).
The meaning is that in the inquiry into Brahman, it is a common cause (sādhāraṇakāraṇa), not a sufficient cause (puṣkalakāraṇa).

[Objection: But surely, according to the principle of "separateness despite conjunction" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), it will be stated in the *Sarvāpekṣā* section that by such scriptural texts as "by sacrifice, by charity," rituals such as sacrifice are enjoined for the sake of knowledge; and thus, the understanding [of ritual] through the *Pūrva-tantra* (the Mīmāṃsā) is a complete cause [for the knowledge of Brahman]. To this, he raises the doubt with "But surely" (*nanu*). Here, in the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), there is a specific [requirement], namely the uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇa-kāraṇa*).

Regarding the Jaimini Sūtra, "But when one [act] serves two purposes, there is a distinctness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvam*), its meaning is as follows: when a single action has two purposes—that is, a connection with multiple results—the "connection" (*saṃyoga*) refers to the sentence that makes known the connection to both; the "distinctness" (*pṛthaktvam*) of that [sentence] is its differentiation, and that is the reason [for the multiplicity of results].

Consequently, here too, although actions such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* have results such as heaven, they also serve the purpose of knowledge because of scriptural statements such as "by sacrifice, by charity," and so forth.
He refutes this with the words "No," and so forth.

The intention is as follows: the thousands of logical arguments found in the previous [Mīmāṃsā] system are not, first of all, a sufficient cause for the knowledge of Brahman or its investigation, because that system has as its sole purpose the determination of Dharma.
Nor is there a determination of karma,
because that serves as the cause for its performance;
for there is no pervasion (vyāpti) between dharma and Brahman, as there is between smoke and fire.
By means of which, through the knowledge of Dharma, the knowledge of Brahman arises;
although ritual actions are causes by way of such means as the discrimination of mother-of-pearl [from silver], nevertheless they do not constitute qualifications for the seeker.
Because even those [karmas] performed in other lifetimes serve as causes for results when they are unknown;
therefore, that which is known as a specific qualification of the agent must be stated as the proximate limit (*ānantarya-avadhi*) for the abundant cause of engagement.
Hence, these are [the] karmas.
Since the comprehension of that [Dharma] or the investigation into its means is not the limit [of the inquiry], the inquiry into Brahman does not follow immediately after the inquiry into Dharma.

Now, one might object: even if there is no relationship of cause and effect between the inquiry into Dharma and the inquiry into Brahman, the word "atha" (then) serves to indicate a sequence by way of expressing immediate succession.

Anticipating the objection that the word "atha" (then) serves to indicate the sequence of sacrificial portions—as in the passage, "He cuts from the heart first, then from the tongue, then from the chest"—the author says: "Just as...

Just as the sequence of sacrificial portions, which is a rule of immediate succession (*ānantarya-niyama*), is the meaning intended by the word "atha," it is not so here that a sequence between the inquiry into Dharma and the inquiry into Brahman is intended;
for since they do not have a single agent, no dependence on sequence exists between them.

Therefore, the meaning is that the word "atha" (then) does not signify sequence. Now, one might ask: why is there no single agent for those two? To this he says: "śeṣa" (subsidiary), referring to those things which are subsidiary to a single primary act.
As in the case of the *avadānas* and the *prayāja* offerings;
and as in the case of the relationship between the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*), such as that between the *prayāja* and the *darśa* sacrifice.
And there is the case of that which possesses the status of being an entitlement for one already entitled (*adhikṛtādhikāratva*),

such as the *godohana* vessel prescribed by the rule "for one desiring cattle, [he should perform the water-carrying] with the *godohana*," which depends upon the water-carrying that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices;

or likewise, the *Soma* sacrifice prescribed for the period subsequent to the *Darśa* by the rule "having sacrificed with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, one should sacrifice with *Soma*," which has the status of being an entitlement for one already entitled to the *Darśa* and so forth— these all share a single agent.

This being the case, since those [elements] grasped by a single injunction of performance can be executed simultaneously, an order is understood through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means when there is a requirement for sequence;
however, there is no such evidence— such as direct statement, indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth— for a relationship of subsidiary and principal between the two desires to know (*jijñāsā*).
But is it not said in the Śruti: "Having completed the life of a student, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller, and then renounce"?
And: "Having studied the Vedas according to rule, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma, and having offered sacrifices to the best of one's ability, one should fix the mind on liberation."

It is not so, because the Smṛti text "one should renounce even from the stage of studentship" (*brahmacaryādeva pravrajet*) and "the pure-souled one attains liberation indeed in the first stage of life" (*āsādayati śuddhātmā mokṣaṃ vai prathamāśrame*) indicate that the qualification for [renunciation] is established by the Smṛti itself.
Thus, from the two scriptural and traditional texts cited by you, it is understood that those two scriptural and traditional passages have as their subject matter those whose minds are impure.
This is what is meant: if the mind has been purified by actions performed in previous births, then one should renounce even while still a student (*brahmacārin*) and desire to know Brahman;
but when it is known through passion that the mind is not yet pure, then one should become a householder.

Even there, if it remains impure, one should become a forest-dweller; even there, if it remains impure, one should likewise await the [proper] time, for one should renounce when purity is attained in the forest.
And thus says the Śruti: "On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce."
Therefore, the point is that there is no evidence whatsoever for these two [Mīmāṃsās] having the relationship of a primary subject and its subordinate topic (*adhikṛtādhikāratva*).
Now, one might object: "Let it be that the two Mīmāṃsās lack the relationship of subordinate and principal (*śeṣaśeṣitva*) or the relationship of primary subject and its subordinate topic;
nevertheless, since they both have the single fruit of liberation (*mokṣa*), they must certainly have a single agent."

For those who advocate for the combination [of means] say: "Liberation results from both knowledge and action. And because there is a single authorship, since the object to be investigated is one—the meaning of the Veda—this is so even as in the case of the six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya, which have a single result, namely heaven.

Anticipating the objection that "since the twelve chapters have a single object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*), a sequence is intended between them, and therefore the word *atha* signifies sequence," he says "phalety" (due to the difference in results).
The ellipsis is: "sequence is not intended because of the difference in results and the difference in the objects of inquiry.

This is just as, for example, there is no sequence intended among the *saurya*, *āryamaṇa*, and *prājāpatya* oblations due to the difference in their results—namely, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), heaven (*svarga*), and long life (*āyus*).

The sense is that, just as there is no requirement for a sequential order between the systems of medicine and erotics because their objects of inquiry differ, likewise there is no requirement for a sequential order between the two Mīmāṃsās.
In this regard, he explains the difference in their results with the words "abhyudaya" (prosperity) and so forth.

That which arises by being directed toward sense objects is "abhyudaya"—namely, pleasure dependent on sense objects such as heaven; and the meaning is that this is the result of the [Pūrva] Mīmāṃsā, which has the knowledge of Dharma as its purpose.
He states "And that" to show that there is not only a difference in the nature of the result, but also in its cause;
he says "niḥśreyasa" to indicate that the fruit of the inquiry (mīmāṃsā), which is the cause for the knowledge of Brahman, is indeed opposed to that [other inquiry].
The meaning is that "niḥśreyasa"—the eternal, independent good—is liberation (mokṣa), and that is its fruit.
And he says "nor" (na ca) to show that the knowledge of Brahman does not require any performance other than its own arising;
the sense is that there is no combination [of the two paths] because of the difference in their nature, cause, and result.
He explains the difference in the objects of inquiry with the words "and that which is to be brought into being" (bhavyaśca).
"One who comes into being" is *bhavya*;
the meaning is "that which is to be accomplished. He states the reason for its being something to be accomplished with the word "no."
If that is so, then [the cognition] would be insubstantial;
he says "no"—"puruṣa... etc. The meaning is: because its basis, that is, its cause, is the activity of the person, namely effort (prayatna).

The meaning is that because it is to be accomplished through human effort (*kṛti-sādhyatvāt*), the property (*dharma*) does not exist at the time of the knowledge that generates that effort; this is not due to its being non-existent in an absolute sense (*tucchatvāt*).
He states the distinction of Brahman from dharma with the words "But here" (*iha tu*);
the meaning is "in the Uttara-mīmāṃsā."
That which has come into being is incurable.
The reason for this is "because it is eternal," meaning because it exists at all times.

Having stated the difference in essential nature between *dharma* and *brahman* by way of their being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*), he states it also by way of their cause with the word "not" (*na*).
The meaning is that [Brahman] is not dependent on human action (*kṛti*), unlike *dharma*.
He also states the difference by way of their means of knowledge (*māna*) with the word "injunction" (*codanā*).
In this context, *codanā* is a statement that makes known what was previously unknown.

Its "activity" (*pravṛtti*) consists in its capacity to produce cognition; and because of its distinction from that [other means of knowledge], there is a difference in the object of inquiry—this is the meaning.
He explains the summary statement with the words: "For that which... (*yā hi*).

The definition of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: a sentence such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" informs a person by indeed impelling them toward its own object—namely, *dharma* consisting of an efficient force (*bhāvanā*) wherein sacrifice and the like are the instruments and heaven and the like are the results, or toward the injunction (*niyoga*) concerning the sacrifice and so forth which are the causes of the result, or toward the sacrifice and so forth which are the means to one's welfare.

However, a statement such as "This Self is Brahman" merely informs the referent of "thou" (*tvaṃ-padārtha*), which is Brahman alone, free from phenomenal expansion (*aprapañca*); it does not impel [the person], because there is no [prescriptive] object [to be acted upon]. This is the meaning.
[Objection: "But surely the object [of the Veda] is indeed comprehension. To this he replies: "Not the person.
He states the reason why the person does not engage in comprehension through the injunction regarding Brahman by means of the preceding sentence: "Of comprehension...
He provides an illustration for the point that a thing itself, as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is not an instigator toward the knowledge produced by itself: "Just as..."

Since understanding arises from the mere act of hearing [the words], and since an injunction is inapplicable once [understanding] has arisen, there is no human activity directed toward the cognition of the sentence-meaning.

And thus, since there is a difference between the objects of inquiry— dharma being the object of a cognition that impels one to action, and Brahman being the object of a neutral cognition— [the two inquiries are distinct].
The sense is that the word *atha* does not serve the purpose of indicating a sequence between those two [inquiry and knowledge].

Thus, since no other meaning for the word *atha* is possible, and given that it expresses immediate succession (*ānantarya*), one must state the sufficient cause (*puṣkalakāraṇa*) as its point of reference; therefore he says, "Therefore," and so forth.
It is taught.
The word "sūtrakṛtā" (by the author of the Sūtras) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the agent]. To the question "What is that?", he says: "It is said.
That the validity of discernment (*viveka*) and the others is established by scripture has already been stated previously.

*Śama* is the cessation of the mind from worldly activities; *dama* is the cessation of the external organs; *uparati* is the renunciation of obligatory and other prescribed rites for the sake of knowledge;
and *titikṣā* is the endurance of the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat.
The stabilization of the mind through the abandonment of sleep, laziness, and negligence is *samādhi*.
Faith is the state of being convinced of everything.
The attainment of these six qualities constitutes the perfection of tranquility (*śama*) and the other virtues.
In this context, it should be understood that discrimination (*viveka*) and the other qualities serve as qualifications for the seeker (*adhikārin*) by virtue of being successive causes.

He states that these are the causes for the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the words "among them" (*teṣu*). Even for one who engages in the inquiry into Brahman out of mere curiosity, the knowledge of it does not arise until the attainment of the fruit; thus, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established.
He concludes the explanation of the word *atha* with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Now, one might object that the aforementioned discrimination (*viveka*) and so forth are not possible,

because the fruit of action is eternal according to such scriptural passages as, "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed imperishable," and thus detachment (*vairāgya*) cannot be established from it.

The liberation of the individual soul (jīva) as having the nature of Brahman is untenable, because of their difference and because, like a clod of earth or similar objects, such a state would not constitute the goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha). Consequently, the desire for liberation (mumukṣā) would be impossible. To resolve this objection, the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is used; he explains that word as follows: "the word 'ataḥ'."

The word *atha* (then), signifying immediate succession, implies by its very nature that the fourfold [means] beginning with discrimination (*viveka*) constitute the causes for the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*). The word *ataḥ* (therefore) is a restatement intended to refute any objection regarding this implied causality;
such is the meaning. He explains what was stated with the words "because" (*yasmāt*).
The word "therefore" (tasmāt) is connected with what follows.

The scriptural passage beginning with "Just as here... (*tadyatheha*), which possesses the logic that "whatever is small is mortal" and "whatever is created is impermanent," sublates the scriptural statement regarding the inexhaustibility of the fruits of ritual action (*karmaphala*).

Therefore, the sense is that the attainment of dispassion (*vairāgya*) results from the discernment (*viveka*) of the impermanence of everything other than the Self, according to the scripture: "Other than this, everything is afflicted" (*ato 'nyadārtam*).
He fosters the desire for liberation with the word "tathā" (so).

The meaning is that just as the Veda demonstrates the impermanence of the fruits of ritual action, so too does it demonstrate that through the knowledge of Brahman one attains the shoreless, self-luminous bliss in which the wind of sorrow has been stilled.
The sense is that by the mention of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon [the self] as being a living being and so forth, the possibility of its being Brahman has already been stated.

Thus, having established through the words *atha* and *ataḥ* that there exists an eligible candidate (*adhikārī*) possessing the complete causes [for inquiry], he says "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) to indicate that the scripture should be commenced.

For the purpose of completing the sentence of the aphorism and for the purpose of connecting it with the supplied word "should be done" (*kartavya*), he shows the meaning of the individual components by stating his preferred compound, in order to indicate that the term *brahmajijñāsā* points to "inquiry" (*vicāra*) through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*). [He begins: "Of Brahman... (*brahmaṇaḥ*)...
Thus [it is said].

Now, one might ask: why could there not be a dative compound (caturthī-samāsa) such as *brahmaṇe jijñāsā* ("the desire for Brahman"), just as in the case of *dharmāya jijñāsā* ("the desire for dharma")?
It is replied: for the primary meaning of the word *jijñāsā* is "desire" (*icchā*).

For that [action], the object (karman) as its primary factor is required first, and the result (phala) afterwards; therefore, at the outset, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is appropriate for the sake of understanding the object. Once the object has been stated, the result is understood by implication.
This is because the fruit belongs to the object of desire itself;
just as when one says "the desire for heaven," heaven acquires the status of being the fruit, so it is here.
For this very reason, in the expression "inquiry into Dharma" (*dharmajijñāsā*), a genitive compound is shown by taking the word "desire" (*icchā*)—as in the phrase "for that is his desire to know."

However, since investigation (*vicāra*) consists of mental effort and is thus of the nature of a *kleśa*, one first desires its fruit; therefore, the fourth compound (*caturthī-samāsa*) was stated as "the desire to know for the sake of Dharma" (*dharmāya jijñāsā*).
Likewise, if the Commentator (*Vṛttikāra*) had said "the desire to know Brahman" (*brahmaṇe jijñāsā*), that would have been acceptable because Brahman, being knowledge itself, is the fruit.
Now, he states the meaning of the word "Brahman": "And Brahman... (*brahma ca*).

One might object: "In the Vedas and in common usage, the word *brahman* is employed to denote the caste of Brāhmaṇas (*brāhmaṇatva-jāti*), the individual soul (*jīva*), the Veda, and the lotus-seated god (Brahmā), as seen in such scriptural passages as: 'This [world] is Brahman, the Kṣatriya is Brahman; Brahman comes forth; Brahman is the Self-existent (*svayambhū*); Brahman is Prajāpati. To address this doubt, he says: "For this very reason. This means:
precisely because [otherwise] there would arise the consequence of inconsistency with the sūtras that establish the definition of being the cause of the universe.
He refutes the statement made in another commentary—that the sixth case ending is used in the sense of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*)—by saying "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇa iti*).
The "remainder" refers to a general relation (*sambandha-sāmānyam*).
In the word *jijñāsā*, knowledge is the object of the desire expressed by the suffix *san*.
The object (*karman*) of that knowledge is Brahman;

for in that case, since an action involving an object cannot be known without knowledge of the object, and since desire is produced by knowledge of its object, the object itself—which is required first—is what must be expressed by the genitive case, not the residual relation (*śeṣa*). This is the meaning.

[Objection: "But surely the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and so forth are something else entirely; let them be the object of action (karman), while Brahman is connected as the principal beneficiary (śeṣin). To this, he replies with the words "jijñāsyāntare" (by another object of inquiry).

The sense is that by abandoning the action (karman) explicitly stated in the scripture and imagining something else not stated, one follows the maxim: "Casting away the lump of food, he licks his hand.
With a hidden intention, the objection is raised: "But surely... [and so on].

The meaning is that, because of the rule "the sixth case [is used] in the sense of the remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*), although a mere relationship is understood by the genitive, it culminates in the status of being an object (*karmatva*) when there is a requirement for a specific relation due to the proximity of a transitive action.
As if not understanding this intention, he states the reply: "Even so... (*evam api*).

The meaning is that even though the status of being an object (*karman*) is directly evident through the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti," which prescribes such a status when there is a connection with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix— since the word *jijñāsā* ends in the suffix *ākāra* (i.e., *-ana*)— the proponent of the "remainder" (*śeṣavādī*) abandons this required and primary objecthood and instead postulates an indirect, non-verbal [objecthood].
The proponent of the "remainder" reveals his own intention by saying, "It is not useless."
By means of the genitive of residue (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) related to Brahman is proposed.

In that context, the investigation of those things which depend upon Brahman—namely, its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), reasoning (*yukti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), means of attainment (*sādhana*), and fruit (*phala*)—is also proposed;
for even that desire to know is related to Brahman, since it has the purpose of attaining knowledge of Brahman.

However, with the intention that if the genitive were taken in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), the inquiry would be proposed as having Brahman alone as its object, it is stated that the genitive is used in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Therefore, my effort is not in vain;
the meaning is that it has as its purpose and fruit the proposal of an inquiry into all things related to Brahman, including Brahman itself.
The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) states that this fruit of your effort is not appropriate,

because when the investigation of Brahman— the primary subject— is formally proposed by the Sūtra, the investigation of its auxiliary elements is already implied by that proposal; he then explains the summarized meaning of "not the primary [subject]" (*na pradhāna*) with an illustration, beginning with the words "Brahman indeed," and so forth.

And because it follows the fundamental scripture (mūla-śruti), "Desire to know that" (*tadvijijñāsasva*), he states [the genitive case] is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*) with the words, "and because of conformity with scripture" (*śrutyanugamācca*).
This means that one attains the fact that the scripture and the sūtra have a single identical meaning.
He explains the etymological meaning of the word *jijñāsā* as "to know" (*jñātum*).
Now, since desire is not observed toward an object that has not been cognized, it must be said that the knowledge of the object is the root of that desire.
But since the knowledge of Brahman is itself the fruit of the desire to know (jijñāsā), how can it be its root? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because [it is] cognition... and so forth.

The object of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is that very knowledge consisting of an undivided direct realization (*akhaṇḍa-sākṣātkāra-vṛtti-jñāna*), which has as its limit or culmination consciousness manifested in the form of the cessation of obstructions;
that alone is the fruit.

However, it will be explained below that the "root" is the initial, superficial knowledge (*āpātajñāna*); thus, because there is a distinction between the knowledge that is the fruit and the knowledge that is the root, there is no logical inconsistency in the desire to know. This is the meaning.

[Objection: But surely the village is the object (*karman*) of the act of going, and its attainment is the fruit (*phala*); thus, because of this distinction, it was stated that "the fruit is indeed the object. To this, he replies with the word "fruit" (*phala*).
The meaning is that although there is a distinction between those two in relation to another action, since desire has the fruit as its object, the fruit itself is the object.
Now, one might object that since knowledge (*jñāna*) and realization (*avagati*) are identical, the statement regarding their distinction is improper; to this he says: "by knowledge" (*jñānena*).
The meaning is that there is a distinction in that *jñāna* is the mental modification (*vṛtti*), while *avagati* is its fruit. [The word] "to realize" (*avagantum*) means to manifest.
He clarifies that realization is the fruit [of knowledge] with the word "Brahman.
He states the reason expressed by the particle "hi" (for) with the words "niḥśeṣa... (without remainder).
The meaning is: because it destroys that misfortune which has ignorance as its seed and its beginning.
Having explained the meaning of the individual parts, he states the meaning of the sentence of the Sūtra with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).
Here, he indicates by means of the suffix *tavya* that the suffix *san* signifies "investigation" (*vicāra*).

Since the qualification of the seeker has been established by the two words "Now" (*atha*) and "Therefore" (*ataḥ*), the meaning is that an investigation must be undertaken for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman.
Thus ends the third section.

In the first exposition (*varṇaka*), by stating that bondage is superimposed (*adhyasta*), it was shown that even if the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and other requirements are well-known, there remains a doubt regarding the commencement of the scripture based on whether Brahman is known or unknown—which determines whether the subject matter and other requirements are possible or impossible. To state the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says: "But that [Brahman]...
The word "but" (*punaḥ*) serves to indicate a different exposition.
If the knowledge of Brahman already existed prior to the inquiry into the Vedānta, then it would lack the status of being a subject matter (*viṣayatva*), defined as being previously unknown.
One should not consider that, due to the absence of ignorance, there is also no fruit consisting of its cessation;
for if it were unknown to anyone at all, then inquiry could not be undertaken with that as its objective, since it is impossible to aim for what is unknown.

And likewise, since it is impossible to propound [the truth] through a treatise consisting of inquiry or through the Vedāntas for one who has not ascended to the knowledge of Brahman, there is no relationship in the form of being the subject matter of that [treatise]; consequently, because knowledge does not arise, the fruit also does not exist, and thus the treatise is not to be commenced—this is the meaning.

He establishes the conclusion that [the inquiry] ought to be undertaken because the object and other factors are attained through common consensus (*āpātaprasiddhi*), beginning with the words "It is said" (*ucyate*).
The meaning is: "First of all, it is well-known.
This is because existence (*astitva*) is not the subject under discussion, and thus the word "exists" (*asti*) is intended to signify what is commonly established.
Now, by what means of knowledge is Brahman established?

Nor can it be said that this is established by the scriptural text, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," because the word *brahman* lacks a grasped conventional relation (*saṃgati*) in the world, and thus a sentence composed of it would be non-cognitive. Anticipating this objection, he states that through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *brahman*, there is first the establishment of both the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) and the attributed (*saguṇa*) Brahman. [He says: "Of the word *brahman*..."
The word "hi" has this meaning: it is known that there must be some referent [for the term *brahman*], because its usage in the Śruti and the Sūtra would otherwise be inexplicable;
for one never observes the use of meaningless words in authoritative statements (*pramāṇavākya*).
And that object is determined by its etymology to be of the nature of greatness, because of the traditional rule (smaraṇa) that "the root bṛh means to grow.
And that growth is unlimited greatness, since there is no factor to restrict it.
Furthermore, it is understood from its usage together with the term "infinite" (*ananta*) in the scriptures that [the greatness] is unlimited;
for such boundless greatness is impossible if one possesses defects such as finitude or is devoid of qualities such as omniscience,
since in the world it is well known that those who lack qualities and possess defects are considered small.

Therefore, from the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "that which expands" (*bṛṃhaṇāt*), eternity (*nityatva*)—characterized by the absence of limitation in terms of space, time, and substance—is understood.
Purity (*śuddhatva*) is the state of being devoid of defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*).
Enlightenment (*buddhatva*) is the absence of insentience (*jāḍya*).
Even at the time of bondage, its state of being bound by itself and its state of liberation are perceived;
thus, it is well known to be devoid of all defects and free from qualities (*nirguṇa*).
Likewise, that which is denoted by the word "That" (*tatpada*) is well known to possess qualities such as omniscience.

Because if there were a remainder of either the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) or the task to be accomplished (*kārya*), it would follow that they are few, and thereby one would obtain only partial omniscience and the capacity for only partial action.

Having thus stated that the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) is justified because the word "That" (*tat-pada*) is not established as authoritative—being merely superficial and failing to remove ignorance—he further states that it is justified by the Brahmin’s well-known identity with the meaning of the word "Thou" (*tvaṃ-padārtha*): "Of all," meaning that Brahman is well-known through its non-difference from this Self (*ātman*) which belongs to every person in the world.
Now, as to the question "What is the well-known nature of the Self?", he says: "For everyone...
It is not that one does not perceive "I am," but rather that one certainly does perceive it;
this very perception is the well-known nature of the Self as Being-Consciousness (saccidātman). This is the meaning.
Anticipating the objection that the self cannot exist because it is empty, he says, "If indeed...
The meaning is this: if the self were empty and yet perceived, the world would know "I do not exist";
however, the world knows "I am," therefore the existence of the self is established.
He states what follows for Brahman even if the Self is well-known: "And the Self," etc.
The intention is that this is based on such scriptural texts as "This Self is Brahman.
He recalls the defect stated regarding the position that [Brahman] is well-known by means of the prima facie argument: "If," etc.
The meaning is that, due to the absence of non-cognition (*ajñātatva*), there is an absence of objects and so forth, which results in the conclusion that [the Self] is not an object of inquiry.

Just as "this is silver" is, in reality, the well-known cognition of mother-of-pearl, so too "I am" is, in reality, the well-known cognition of Brahman by virtue of the commonality of its nature as existence and consciousness;

however, this [cognition] does not have as its object the specific quality of being the Brahman of perfect bliss, because otherwise it would follow that there could be no dispute among proponents [regarding this].
For when the specific nature of the mother-of-pearl is perceived, there is no conflicting doubt as to whether it is silver, vermilion, or something else.

Therefore, because such a conflict would otherwise be inexplicable, and because the particularity remains unknown despite the general object being established, he establishes the proof of the object and so forth with the words beginning "No" (na).

It should be understood that the relationship between the universal and the particular is imagined based on the distinctions denoted by terms such as "Being" (sat), "Consciousness" (cit), and "Fullness" (pūrṇa) within the Self itself.
In this regard, he presents various misconceptions through the sequence of coarse and subtle [views], beginning with "the body alone" and so forth.
"Ordinary people" refers to those devoid of knowledge of the scriptures.
Having stated the views outside the Vedas, he states the view of the logicians and others: "it exists," and so on.
He states the Sāṃkhya view with the words "the enjoyer" (*bhoktā*).

Regarding the point of contention as to whether the self (*ātman*) is of the nature of the body and so forth, or distinct from it—having set forth the positions of the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the void;

and regarding the further point of contention as to whether that which is distinct [from them] possesses agency and so forth, or not—having presented the positions of the Logicians (*tārkika*) and the Sāṃkhyas, [he concludes that the self] is indeed non-agent, yet distinct from God (*īśvara*).
Regarding the point of contention as to whether [He exists] or not, he states the view of the Yogins: "There exists a Lord distinct from that [world].
Taking up His state of being unsurpassed, the Yogins declare that the Lord is endowed with omniscience and other such qualities.
Having stated the position of difference, he states the position of the established tenet (siddhānta): "That is the Self of the enjoyer."

The meaning is that the Vedāntins declare that the Lord is the Self, the very nature of the experiencing individual soul (*jīva*), who is a non-agent and a witness. He concludes the conflicting views with the words, "Thus, many...

The detailed exposition and refutation of these conflicting views have been shown through the presentation of the *Vivaraṇa* for the sake of easy understanding; therefore, [the discussion] is concluded here.

In this regard, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) relies on both reasoning and scripture: [the reasoning] such as "The individual soul (jīva) is indeed Brahman, because it possesses selfhood (ātmatva), just like Brahman," and [the scripture] such as "That thou art" (tattvam asi), which exists as an uncontradicted authority.

Others, however, [assert] through fallacious reasoning such as: "The body and so forth are the self, because they are the object of the notion of 'I', whereas that which is different from them— such as a jar— is not," and so on.
"This very person consists of food" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1); in the "Dialogue of the Senses," "the eye and the others said to speech," and "the mind said";
"this which consists of consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5);
"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1).
The distinction is that they have relied upon fallacious statements such as "the agent, the cognizer, the non-eater, the other" and "He who controls [it] from within.
The body and so forth are the non-Self (anātman).

By means of such logical arguments as "because it is composed of material elements" and "because it is an object of perception," [it is established that] "the one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of the repetition [of that term]."
The fallacious nature [of these views] will be explained by such sūtras as these.

Now, one might object: "Let there be these conflicting opinions; nevertheless, whatever view a person has faith in, his own goal will be accomplished by resorting to that. What is the need for undertaking an inquiry into Brahman? To this, he says: "In that regard, without having investigated...
The actual state of things is that liberation occurs only through the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self.
If one resorts to other doctrines, liberation cannot be achieved because of the absence of that [true knowledge].

Furthermore, by knowing the Self otherwise, one falls into the dark well of saṃsāra through that sin, according to the Śruti: "Into blind darkness they enter, those people who are slayers of the Self."
"What sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self— he who represents himself as one thing when he is actually another?"
The meaning is that this is because of such scriptural statements.

Therefore, he concludes the meaning of the sūtra—namely, that "therefore, for the sake of the fruit of supreme beatitude (niḥśreyasa), inquiry into the Vedānta must be undertaken by all those desiring liberation"—with the words "tasmāt" (therefore).
This is because, since bondage is superimposed, there exists a subject matter and so forth, and thus [the inquiry] is not redundant.

The meaning is that this inquiry—Mīmāṃsā, which is the revered investigation whose subject matter is the Vedānta—is commenced for the sake of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa), because its qualified seeker has been found, its subject matter and so forth are established from beginning to end, and its instruments are those logical arguments (tarka) residing in other systems that do not contradict the Vedānta.
Now, one might object: since there is no word denoting "inquiry" in the Sūtra itself, how can its commencement be the meaning of the Sūtra? To this, he says: "Brahman... [and so on].
The intention is that, by means of the statement regarding the desire for knowledge of Brahman, [the Sūtra] indicates inquiry and declares its necessity.
Thus, the four meanings of the first Sūtra have been shown through the fourfold exposition.
And it is an ornament for a Sūtra to possess multiple meanings.
Now, does this Sūtra initiate the treatise while standing outside it, or by being included within it?
In the first case, it would be something to be rejected,
because of its lack of connection with the treatise.
In the second case, its producer must be stated;
yet it cannot be its own producer, because a thing cannot arise from itself, which would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
"And we do not perceive any other commencement [of the treatise].

It is said in reply: This treatise, having been commenced according to the rule of hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*), establishes the very commencement of the treatise as being internal to the treatise itself.
Just as the rule of study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), though internal to the Veda, impels one toward the study of the entire Veda, so it is here; thus, there is no fault. //1//
[The Brahman is that] from which there is the origin and so forth of this [world]. (BS 1.1.2)

Having established the commencement of the treatise by means of the first sūtra and being about to begin the treatise itself, the author recounts what has preceded in order to state the connection between the preceding and succeeding sections, beginning with the word "Brahman.
It was stated that one desiring liberation must undertake an inquiry into the Vedānta for the sake of knowing Brahman.

Although, by stating that Brahman is the object of inquiry, the inquiries into the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth are implicitly promised, [the author proceeds] because such inquiry cannot be carried out without first establishing the means of knowledge regarding Brahman.

In order to know its true nature, a definition must first be stated; however, [the author] first raises an objection that such a definition is impossible, and while honoring the author of the Sūtras, he determines the very Sūtra concerning the definition by asking: "What is its defining characteristic?
The word "kim" (what) is used here in the sense of an objection.
The meaning is that there is no characteristic at all.
Because this [objection] arises by way of an objection (*ākṣepa*), there is a connection by way of objection.

Since the Vedānta texts—which illuminate the characteristics and contain clear marks of Brahman—are stated to be in harmony (*samanvaya*) with respect to Brahman, the object characterized, there is a connection with the Śruti, the Śāstra, the Book (*adhyāya*), and the Section (*pāda*).
For instance, the scriptural passage beginning with "That from which indeed these beings are born" is the subject matter.
The doubt is whether this constitutes a definition of Brahman or not.

In this regard, the distinction is that according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), liberation is not established because the true nature of Brahman is not established, whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is so established.

Although, in the case of an objection (*ākṣepa*) or a connection (*saṃgati*), it need not be stated separately because its result is simply the result of the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), as it has been said: "In the case of an objection, a refutation (*apavāda*), a preliminary topic (*prāsaṅga*), a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), or an action (*karma*), the purpose (*prayojana*) need not be stated; nor [need it be stated] for that which proceeds by way of 'having done' (*kṛtvā*)."
Nevertheless, it should be understood that this has been stated for the sake of clarity.

Where the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by means of a conclusion from a previous section (*adhikaraṇa-siddhānta*), there the connection is one of exception (*apavādika*). The "attainment" (*prāpti*) is the deliberation for the purpose of that [exception]. In that case, the prima facie position reached is "no."
Because origination and so forth, being attributes of the world, cannot serve as the definition of Brahman;

nor should it be said that the definition is "being the agent while being the material cause of the world," for since there is no example of an agent who is also the material cause, inference cannot proceed.
Nor should it be argued that since the definition of the Brahman taught in the Śruti is established by the Śruti itself, what is the use of inference;
for inference serves as a support for the Śruti, and in its absence or in case of conflict with it, the meaning of the Śruti would not be established.
Nor should it be argued that either being the agent of the world or being the material cause should serve as the definition individually.

Since it is impossible for that which is distinct from the mere agent to be Brahman due to its factual limitation, this being the position reached, [we reply]: because inference— which is merely a human construction— is unstable and lacks independence regarding supersensuous objects,
the dual causality declared by the faultless Śruti as being non-human in origin is established through the analogy of pleasure and so forth.
Because it is possible to conceive [of it], he establishes that very definition with the words: "From which the origin and so forth of this [proceed]" (*janmādy asya yataḥ*).

Although here the definition is presented as the causality of the world's origin, maintenance, and dissolution, nevertheless, later on, in the section beginning with "And the material cause" (*prakṛtiś ca*), [it will be further clarified].

Its being the cause does not consist merely in agency, but rather in having the dual nature of both agency and material causality (*upādānatva*). Taking this—which will be explained later—as established, it is stated that the definition consists in being the cause of both; thus, there is no tautology. Now, one might ask: how can the causality of the qualityless Brahman, which is the object of inquiry, serve as its definition? It is said: just as silver [is defined by its appearance].
Just as the definition of mother-of-pearl is "that which is silver is mother-of-pearl," so too, Brahman is defined as "that which is the cause of the world.
Thus, the causality attributed to it is merely adventitious (taṭastha), and this constitutes the flawless definition of Brahman.
He explains the Sūtra with the words beginning "birth" (janma), etc.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, all the word-meanings (*padārtha*) serve as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), which is the meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*).

Just as in the case of Devadatta’s "variegated cows," where the variegated cows are the qualifier, so too here, "birth" is the qualifier for the aggregate (*samāhāra*) indicated by the neuter singular [ending]—namely, the aggregate of birth, subsistence, and dissolution.

And thus, the meaning is that a *bahuvrīhi* compound in which the subordinate part of the summarized meaning (*samāsārthaikadeśa*)—in this case, "birth"—is understood as a qualifying attribute (*tadguṇa*) is called a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*.

In that context, it is improper to prescribe Brahman-hood for that which is the cause of birth; for when something is known to be distinct from the causes of maintenance and dissolution, it is impossible to know it as Brahman.

Therefore, it should be understood that the sūtra indicates a collective compound (samāhāra) because it considers the three causalities—defined by birth, subsistence, and dissolution—together as the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
Now, one might ask: how is the "beginning-ness" (āditva) of birth to be known, given that saṃsāra is beginningless? To this, he says: "And of birth... (janmanaśca).

The meaning is that, having understood the primacy [of Brahman] both from the root scripture (*mūlaśruti*) and from the nature of reality (*vastugati*), the author of the Sūtras spoke of the "origin and so forth" (*janmādi*) of the sun with reference to that [primacy].
Anticipating the objection that the word *idam* (this) denotes only perceptible objects, he states "of this" (*asya*) to indicate that it denotes all effects that are present.
He says "the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) because the world, beginning with ether (*viyat*), is eternal and thus lacks a connection to birth and so forth.

The intention is that the connection of the great elements (mahābhūtas) with their objects and so forth, including their birth and other states, will be explained. Now, one might object: "Since the world's birth and other states lack a connection to Brahman, they cannot serve as its definition. Anticipating this doubt, he states the meaning of the ablative case—*yataḥ*—"in order to show that being the cause of that [world] is the defining characteristic.

By the word *yat*, the Reality which is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite, and of the nature of Bliss is expressed, because this has been determined by the scriptural passage, 'Verily, from Bliss [alone...]'."
