And thus, it should be understood that the definition by intrinsic nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) is established.

Having stated the meaning of the term (*padārtha*), he explains the meaning of the sentence of the Sūtra—by supplying the word "that" (*tat*) and by connecting it with the word "Brahman" from the preceding Sūtra—starting with the words "of this" (*asya*), etc.
The specific attributes of the world serve to establish the possibility of the Cause possessing omniscience and other such qualities.

Just as a potter, having first conceived in his mind the form of a pot—characterized by a broad base and a rounded belly—as something undifferentiated from the mere word "pot," then manifests that pot externally by defining it through its own nature, so too is it inferred that the Supreme Cause likewise manifests itself through the nature of name and form; thinking thus, he says, "by name and form.
Here, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of "being in such a state" (*itthaṃbhāve*).
The first effect is produced by a conscious agent, because it is an effect, like a pot; thus, the [theories of] Pradhāna and Śūnya are refuted.
He refutes the notion that [the world] is produced by individual souls (jīvas) such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others with the word "aneka" (many).
In rites such as the Śrāddha and the Vaiśvānareṣṭi, there is a separate mention because of the distinction between the agent and the enjoyer in the case of the father and the son.

According to the scriptural texts, "He who creates Brahmā in the beginning" and "All these emerge from the Self," individual souls—by way of the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of the gross and subtle bodies—are effects; therefore, since they fall within the world itself, [they cannot be its cause].

He establishes the omniscience of the cause with the words "pratiniyata" and so forth. The meaning is: that which is the basis for those actions and their fruits whose locations, times, and causes are fixed and determined.
For instance, the summit of Mount Meru is the location for the fruit of action that is heaven.
After the fall of the body, the time [of death] and the causes such as dying during the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) have been determined accordingly.
In this way, the distribution of regions and so forth regarding villages and other rewards for royal service is to be understood.
And just as the fruit of service is given by one who knows the regions and so forth, so too is the fruit of karma.
The sense is that omniscience is established because [the Lord] is the fruit [of such knowledge]. He establishes His omnipotence with the words "even by the mind.

Now, one might object: since there are other modifications of being (bhāvavikāra), such as growth and transformation, why are they not included under the phrase "birth and so forth"? To this he replies: "Of the others..."
The meaning is that growth and transformation are included within birth, while decay is included within destruction.
Now, it may be argued that the body is born, exists, [grows, transforms, decays, and perishes].
It increases, it transforms, and it diminishes.
One might ask: "Could this statement of the sage Yāska, 'it perishes,' not be the source of this Sūtra? To this he says:

"Yāska... It is said that the sage Yāska, having perceived the sixfold marks such as birth and so forth through direct observation in material objects during the period of stability of the great elements already produced, composed the statement in the *Nirukta*. If one were to take that as the basis and hold that the meaning of the Sūtra is the definition of Brahman as the cause of the sixfold marks such as birth, then the author of the Sūtra [would have failed to provide] the definition of Brahman.

The meaning is this: lest there arise the suspicion that [the six states] are not included [in the Sūtra] but rather that the characteristics of the great elements (mahābhūtas) are being stated, it is intended that only those states such as birth (janman) and so forth which are mentioned in the Śruti are taken here.

If even the etymological explanation (nirukta) has the Śruti as its source, and if the meaning is that the "birth and so forth" of the great elements constitutes the "birth and so forth" [of Brahman], then let that very Śruti be the source for the Sūtra.
The sense is: "What is the use of this useless excrescence (antargaḍu) that is the Nirukta?
If there were a cause of the world other than Brahman, then the definition of Brahman would suffer from defects such as over-extension (ativyāpti) and so forth;
therefore, in order to exclude that possibility, the Sūtra on the definition [of Brahman] establishes that the birth and so forth of the world are not possible without Brahman.
The reasoning that "because other causes are impossible" has been stated in brief;
it will be explained in detail in the Tarkapāda. Now, he demonstrates it concisely with the words beginning "not as stated," and so forth.

In the course of explaining the four qualifiers of the world—beginning with "distinguished by name-and-form" (*nāmarūpābhyāṃ vyākṛta*)—the refutation of Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), the Void (*śūnya*), and the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*) was demonstrated.

This is because it is impossible for insentient atoms to act spontaneously; because, since it is established by inference that anything other than the individual soul is necessarily devoid of knowledge, an omniscient Lord is not proven to exist, and thus there would be no creator for them.
The sense is that it is impossible for [Prakṛti] to be the originator of the world.
Regarding the Lokāyata who claims that the diverse world arises from its own inherent nature (svabhāva) alone, he says "na ca" (and not).
The syntactical connection is that it is impossible to conceive of the origination and so forth of the world [from such a cause].
Does "self" mean that it is its own cause by its very nature (*svabhāva*), or does it mean independence from causes?
Not the first, because it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). It is not the second either; thus he says: "qualified," etc.

The meaning is that specific, non-common factors—namely place, time, and causal conditions—are appropriated by those seeking an effect; therefore, it is not logical for an effect to be independent of its causes.

The implication is that if there were no dependence [on these], people seeking grain would not engage in activity directed toward specific plots of land, at times such as the rainy season, or with causal conditions such as seeds.

The commentary states that the origin and so forth of the world are not possible except through an Īśvara characterized by the previously mentioned attributes such as omniscience; thus, it expresses the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that "there is no effect without a creator. By this, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is known: "whatever is an effect has a creator. The author presents the delusion of the logicians (*tārkika*), who think: "This very knowledge of pervasion, while establishing a creator in the subject (*pakṣa*) of the world, establishes an omniscient Īśvara—what need is there for scripture? He introduces this with the words "etadeva" (this very [knowledge]).
The construction of the sentence is as follows: they consider that this very inference alone is the means of proof (*sādhana*), and not scripture (*śruti*).

Alternatively, the meaning is: they consider that this very knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti-jñāna*), being accepted by us merely as a reasoning that supports scripture, is an independent inference (*anumāna*).
The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) and so forth.
Alternatively, the meaning is that they consider this very definition, when conjoined with the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*), to be inference as an independent means of knowledge.
In that regard, the distinction is as follows: from the cognition of pervasion, the existence of a creator of the world is established;
subsequently, that creator—
He is omniscient because he is the cause of the world;
by contrast, [it is not so] in the case of a potter and the like. Thus, the establishment of his omniscience is derived from this defining characteristic.
In this context, by the phrase "they think," the fallacious nature of the inference is indicated.

For instance, first of all, a living being (*jīva*) cannot be the agent of a sprout and so forth, because there is a necessary rule that what is distinct from a living being must be insentient, like a jar; and since there is no other agent at all, as determined by negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the knowledge of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, "whatever is an effect has an agent"—is unestablished.

However, in the case of inference based on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) or marks (*liṅga*), there is a sublation (*bādha*); for it is impossible for one who is bodiless to possess knowledge of birth, and because the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is knowledge is produced by the mind" contradicts this, eternal knowledge cannot be established, resulting in the certainty of the absence of such knowledge.
Therefore, regarding supersensuous objects, scripture alone is the refuge.
The sense is that inference is merely a supporting argument (*yukti*) for the purpose of establishing the possibility of the meaning of the scripture; it is not independent.

An objector from the Vaiśeṣika school raises an objection with the word "nanu": "But is this not improper? For, intending to include inference within the scope of scripture, your own author of the Sūtras would have presented only inference.
Thus, the sense is that the statement regarding the fallacy of inference—namely, "therefore they think"—is improper.

If the Śrutis did not possess independent authority, then the author of the Sūtras would not have investigated their purport by means of the aphorism "But that [Brahman], because of the harmony [of the texts]" (samanvayāt) and so forth;

therefore, since the subsequent sūtras are for the purpose of investigating the Śrutis, it is established even in the sūtra concerning "origination and so forth" (janmādi) that it is the Śruti alone that is independently investigated, and not inference—thus he refutes [the objection] with "No. Furthermore, the comprehension of Brahman is desired by the seeker of liberation, for the sake of which this treatise is commenced.
And that [knowledge] does not arise from inference,
because of the scriptural text, "But him, who is known through the Upaniṣads.
Therefore, he says "the meaning of the sentence" (vākyārtha), indicating that inference is not to be investigated.

The meaning is that the comprehension of Brahman, which arises through the ascertainment [of truth] resulting from the investigation of the sentence and its meaning—namely, the determination of the intended purport (*tātparya*) and the ascertainment of the possibility of the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—leads to liberation. "Possibility" (*saṃbhava*) here means the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*). Now, one might ask: is inference entirely disregarded? To this he replies: "But when [the means of knowledge] exist... and so forth.

The subject under dispute has non-different material and instrumental causes, because it is an effect, like the threads produced from a spider; the subject under dispute has a conscious nature as its material cause.
The meaning is that the inference— "because it is an effect, like pleasure and so forth"— is required for the firm establishment of the meaning of the scripture.
Firmness (dārḍhya) means the cessation of doubt and error.
The meaning of the scriptural statement "it is to be reflected upon" (mantavyaḥ) is that the meaning heard [from scripture] is to be rendered probable through reasoning (tarka).

For example, suppose a certain man from the Gandhāra country were abandoned by thieves in another forest with his eyes bound; once released from those bonds, a wise and intelligent man, capable of following the path described [to him] and himself skilled in reasoning, would reach his own country. In exactly the same way, here in this forest, one's true nature has been led away from the bliss of its own essence by ignorance, desire, and so forth.

"Though cast into saṃsāra by some teacher overcome with compassion, you are not a transmigrating being; rather, having been taught your true nature through the instruction 'That thou art,' if you yourself are skilled in reasoning, you would know your own nature, and not otherwise.
Thus, the Śruti shows its dependence on reasoning that conforms to the human intellect, saying "the wise man."
The meaning is: "from the scripture concerning the Self.
Now, an objection is raised: it is not proper for Brahman to require reflection (*manana*) and so forth, because it is the subject matter of the Veda, just like *dharma*.
But since it is the *śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, and so forth that are required, he says "no.
It should be explained as follows: just as with respect to *dharma* which is to be investigated, so too with respect to *brahman* which is to be investigated.
"Experience" (*anubhava*) refers to the experience of the wise, known as the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of *brahman*.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadāt*), reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are included.
He states the reason for this with the words "anubhava" (experience):

because for the sake of liberation, verbal knowledge of Brahman must culminate in direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*); and since [Brahman] is the already-established reality that is one's own inner self (*pratyagbhūta-siddha-brahma*), it is possible for such knowledge to have direct realization as its fruit.
Therefore, the requirement for reflection (*manana*) and so forth is logical in that case.

However, regarding *dharma*, which is by nature eternally beyond the senses and is yet to be established, direct perception is neither required nor possible; thus, for the sake of performance, only the determination [of its nature] through scripture (*śruti*) is required.

The meaning is this: while indicators (*liṅga*) and the rest—being included within scripture itself—are required as means for determination by way of being subordinate to scripture, reflection and the rest are not required, because they are of no use.
Direct assertion (*śruti*) is a word that is independent [of other words].
Indicative power (*liṅga*) is the capacity of a word to manifest its meaning.
A sentence (*vākya*) is a word that requires another word capable [of syntactic connection].
*Prakaraṇa* (context) is the principal sentence that depends upon subsidiary sentences.
*Sthāna* (position) is the connection, in due order, of items listed in a specific sequence with other items listed in that same sequence;

for example, ten sacrifices such as the *Aindrāgna* are listed in sequence, and ten mantras beginning with "Indrāgnī rocanā divi" are likewise listed; therein, the first mantra is applied to the first sacrifice.
Thus, the rest should be inferred.
"Commonality of name" (*samākhyā*) refers to identity of designation; for example, the application of mantras designated as *ādhvaryava* to a rite designated as *ādhvaryava*. This is the distinction.
Thus, first of all, in the inference that "Brahman requires reflection and so forth,
because it is the subject matter of the Veda, like Dharma," the property of Dharma is taken as the probandum (sādhya), and its unfitness for direct experience [is established].

It has been stated that "not requiring experience" (*anapekṣitānubhavatva*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Furthermore, it has been stated that due to the absence of this adjunct, Brahman does not require reflection (*manana*) and so forth.

In that case, if you were to assert that Brahman is identical to Dharma merely by virtue of being the subject matter of the Veda, then—just as with Dharma—the qualities of being achievable through human effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), as well as injunctions (*vidhi*), prohibitions (*niṣedha*), alternatives (*vikalpa*), general rules (*utsarga*), and exceptions (*apavāda*), would likewise apply to Brahman.
[The author] states the refutation of the opposing view with the words beginning "puruṣa... and so forth.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: because the acquisition of its own nature—that is, its production—depends upon human activity, the authority of the Vedas (*śruti*) and other sources resides solely in the Dharma [itself].
He clarifies that *dharma* is something to be accomplished by means of the example of worldly action with the words "to do" (*kartum*).
The meaning is "just as in the world.
He clarifies the example with the word "as" (*yathā*).
He states the illustrative example with the word "tathā" (so).
Having stated that it is possible for *dharma* to be performed or not performed, he states that it is possible for it to be performed otherwise with the word "udita" (arisen).
Having established that *dharma* is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), he states its fitness for injunctions and so forth with the word "vidhi" (injunction).

The meaning is that those injunctions and prohibitions, as well as options and the like, which are purposeful and find scope when *dharma* is the object to be established, would likewise apply to *brahman*.
Examples of such injunctions and prohibitions include "one should sacrifice" and "one should not drink liquor.
An example of a possible option is "one should sacrifice with rice or with barley," while the choice between taking up or not taking up [the ritual vessels] is a matter of personal preference.
Regarding the two options of offering after sunrise or before sunrise, there is a settled alternative.
The general rule is "one shall not kill," while the exception is "one should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma."
Likewise, the distinction is that "he offers in the Āhavanīya fire" is a general rule (utsarga), while "he offers at every step of the horse" is an exception (apavāda).
He rules out the objection that these [rules] might apply to Brahman by saying "no," and so forth.
Because its object is an existing reality;
up to this point, [it has been shown that] this reality is thus.
"It is not so":
this is a conceptualization regarding the mode [of being], such as "a jar" or "a cloth.
"It exists" or "it does not exist": this is a conceptualization regarding the essential nature of existence.

[Objection: But surely, even regarding real entities such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "it exists" or "it does not exist" are observed among disputants. To this, he says: "But the conceptualizations... The literal meaning is as follows: the recollection of alternatives such as existence and non-existence is a human intellect; rooted in that, the conceptualizations of doubt and error are mere fluctuations of the mind and do not possess the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*). The underlying intention (*bhāva*) is this: since a thing (*dharma*) can be acted upon exactly as it is known, all conceptualizations based on human intellect in accordance with the scriptures are indeed of the nature of valid cognition.
"By parity with that [case], all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding Brahman would also be [considered] true.
To one who says "it is so even there," he replies: "No.

If the knowledge of an established entity (*siddhavastu*) were to arise in dependence upon human intellect, just like the knowledge of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then conceptual constructions regarding the established would indeed be true.
The cognition of an established object is not produced by a person; rather, it is born from the object as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And since the object has a single nature, only one cognition is valid;
the meaning is that other conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are simply non-correspondent with reality (*ayathārtha*).
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "For it is not [the case] with respect to a post," and so forth.
The meaning is that once the restriction "it is indeed a post" is established, all conceptual constructions (vikalpas) are not in accordance with reality (yathārtha).
In that context, knowledge which is dependent upon the actual object is what is in accordance with reality.
He analyzes what is dependent on a person as being false with the word "therein" (tatra).
This means "in the case of a post. He extends the principle stated regarding the post to jars and other objects with the word "thus" (evam).
He states the subject at hand: "In that case, being so.

This means that since the validity of knowledge regarding an established object depends upon the thing itself, the knowledge of Brahman is likewise produced by the thing itself and is true; it is not dependent on the person, because its object is an existing reality, just like the knowledge of a post.

Therefore, the meaning is that all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are dependent upon the means of proof (*sādhya*) regarding an object to be established, but not regarding an already established object; thus, because of this distinction, there is no similarity of properties (*dharma-sāmya*), and it follows that the realization [of Brahman] does not depend on reflection (*manana*) and so forth, as in the case of the statement "He is a Brāhmaṇa.
Now, one might object: "In that case, Brahman must be within the scope of perception and other such means of knowledge, since it is distinct from *dharma*."
Like a jar and so forth;
and thus, in the *Janmādi-sūtra*, the inference regarding the cause of the world is to be investigated,
because it possesses validity with respect to an already established fact (*siddhārtha*).
He raises an objection: "Not [Scripture]," because Scripture lacks authority regarding established facts (*siddhārtha*), and thus an inquiry into it would be fruitless.

The sense is: "Since it has been established that [the subject] is the object of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), the inquiry should apply to those other means of knowledge alone"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) should be asked:
does the inference that "whatever is an effect is born from Brahman" establish Brahman, or is it that "whatever is an effect has a cause"?
It is not the first, because the universal concomitance (vyāpti) is unestablished; thus he says, "No."

The meaning is that because Brahman cannot be grasped by the senses, it is impossible to apprehend its pervasion (*vyāpti*) through perception; therefore, it does not fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
To the question "Why is it ungraspable by the senses?", he says: "By its very nature," based on the Vedic scripture: "The Self-existent pierced the openings [of the senses] outward."
The meaning is that this is because Brahman is devoid of form and other such qualities.

To the question, "Even if it is not perceptible by the senses, why could the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) not occur?", he says: "For when..."—the remainder of the sentence being "that [perception] does not exist."
The meaning is that a perceptual observation of the pervasion—that "this effect is born from Brahman"—is not possible because Brahman is beyond the senses.
Regarding the second [alternative], even if the cause is established, its being Brahman cannot be known without scripture; thus he says: "merely the effect.

Since a connection has been made such that, without scripture, there is no attainment of the certainty that "Brahman is the cause of the world," therefore, for the sake of attaining that certainty, scripture alone must be primarily investigated.

He concludes that inference, by means of generalities such as being the material cause (*upādānatva*)—just as in the case of clay and so forth—is to be considered as a subordinate factor for the purpose of establishing the possibility of the scriptural meaning, namely that Brahman consists of its own effects; thus he says, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

He asks what the subject passage (*viṣayavākya*) for this sūtra is: "But what [is it]? (*kiṃ punar iti*). The meaning is: what is the passage intended to be examined here regarding Brahman for the purpose of defining its characteristics?
For here, having first declared in the first aphorism that the inquiry into Brahman is for a qualified seeker, the definition of one who desires to know Brahman is stated in the second aphorism.

Likewise, in the Śruti as well, Brahman is made known to the seeker of liberation who desires to know Brahman by restating the defining characteristic of being the cause of the universe; thus, in order to demonstrate that the aphorism follows the sequence of the scriptural meaning, he recites the passage beginning with "Bhṛgu" along with its introduction.
"Teach me"—that is, remind me; the meaning is "instruct me.
Here, the singular number in the word "yena" (by which) is intended, because if there were plurality, it would be impossible to enjoin [the realization of] Brahman-hood.
The intermediate sentence is: "That which is the cause of the world is one.
The distinction between the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) is either: "That which is the one cause is Brahman," or "That which is the cause is the one Brahman.

Anticipating the question, "What then is the definition of its essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*)?", he states—beginning with the words "And of that"—the meaning of the word *yataḥ* as determined from the remainder of the passage: "Being, Consciousness, Bliss" (*satya-jñāna-ānanda*).

He states that sentences from other Vedic branches (śākhā) such as "He who is omniscient," "From Him this Brahman, name, form, and food are born," and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" are also the subject matter [of the inquiry], by saying "others as well.
He explains that they are of this very same nature by the words "eternal," etc.
Thus, in all the branches, the statements defining the two characteristics are in harmony with Brahman, which is the object of the desire to know.
Thus, it is established that liberation results from that knowledge. //2//
Because [Brahman] has the sacred teaching as its source. (Sūtra 1.1.3)
I worship Śrī Rāma, the knower of all, who is to be known through the Vedas, whose very breath is the Vedas—the powers of knowledge regarding all things. //1//
Introducing the subsequent sutra while stating its connection by way of restating the preceding topic, [the commentator] says: "The world...

By the statement that the conscious Brahman is the cause of the world, the author of the sutras has effectively asserted its omniscience, because a creation by a conscious being must be preceded by knowledge.
And thus, Brahman is omniscient because it is the cause of all; for whoever is the maker of something is the knower of that thing.
As it has been established that [the world] is like a potter,

the meaning is that he speaks in order to strengthen that very same omniscience through the reason of being the author of the Veda, thereby refuting [theories such as] Primordial Matter (pradhāna) and so forth;
for these two reasons establish the same single object.
The intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṃgati*) consists in having the same subject matter.

Alternatively, the status of the Veda as the cause [of the world] is stated by way of an objection (*ākṣepa-saṃgati*): since the Veda is eternal, Brahman cannot be the cause of everything; [to this it is replied: "The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvāṅgirasa are the breath of this Great Being."
Thus, the subject matter is this statement; the doubt is whether it establishes the omniscience of Brahman by virtue of being the cause of the Veda, or whether it does not establish it.

In that regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it does not establish it, because if the Veda were of human origin—like grammar and other sciences—it would lack authority due to its dependence on a foundational source of knowledge. In this view, the result is the failure to establish the sentience of the cause of the world.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), that [omniscience] is established.

Since this Vedāntic statement, which possesses clear marks of Brahman, is shown to be in harmony with the author of the Veda, there is a connection with the Śruti, the Śāstra, the Book (Adhyāya), and the Section (Pāda).
In this manner, the connections with Śruti and so forth are to be inferred up to the end of the Pāda.
For indeed, the capacity to illuminate all objects is perceived in the Veda.
That [power of manifestation] is preceded by a power residing in the Brahman which is its material cause, or it resides in that [Brahman] itself;
for it is a power of manifestation,
or because it is a power residing in an effect.

Just as in the case of the power of a lamp, by virtue of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the Veda, Brahman’s status as the witness of all (*sarvasākṣitva*)— in the form of the capacity to illuminate all objects connected to itself— is established. Alternatively, just as students compose the Veda after knowing its prior sequence, so too the Supreme Lord— who possesses the aid of *māyā* with its diverse qualities and consists solely of unobscured, infinite, self-luminous consciousness— [produces the Veda] possessing a sequence similar to the sequence of the previous kalpa created by Himself.
Since he creates the mass of the Vedas and their meanings while knowing them simultaneously, the Veda is not of human origin.
For where the knowledge of a sentence is preceded by the knowledge of its meaning and serves as the cause for the creation of that sentence, there it is of human origin;
but here, because of simultaneity, such [human authorship] does not exist.

Therefore, he establishes the conclusion that the author of the Veda, like the Veda itself, must necessarily know its meaning as being connected to himself; thus, he is "omniscient. He explains the words of the Sūtra—"The Teacher"—with the intention of applying the aphorism according to two types of logical connection (*saṃgati*): namely, that Brahman is omniscient because it is the cause of the scripture, and that it is the cause of all things. He comments on the phrase "of the great" (*mahataḥ*) as follows: [He explains: "Of the great... [and so forth].
The qualifications of the Veda are for the sake of establishing its omniscience:
therein lies its greatness in terms of both its textual extent and its meaning;
and it possesses the status of a *śāstra* because it teaches what is beneficial.
Considering that the word "śāstra" (treatise) is intended to indicate sound in general, he says: "aneka... (many).

The ten fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*)—namely, the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*) consisting of Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Chandas, and Jyotiṣa—are the means for knowing the meaning of the Vedas.
The meaning is: "of one who is assisted by these."
By this, the authority of the Veda is indicated through its being accepted by Manu and others.
He states that its authority also follows from its lack of non-comprehensiveness—saying "like a lamp.
Although it possesses the power to illuminate all objects, because it is insentient, it is like an omniscient being; its "source" (yoni) is both the material cause (upādāna) and the agent (kartṛ).
Now, one might object: "Even if the Veda possesses that quality of an omniscient being—which is the capacity to know all objects—how can its source be omniscient? To this, he says: "For not...
Since that capacity cannot exist in the effect without its presence in the material cause, the source of the Veda must be omniscient;
as for the inference, it has already been shown previously.
Nor does it follow that [the Veda] is produced by ignorance;
the point is that even though it possesses power, it is insentient.
The Veda is produced by one who possesses knowledge of an object greater than its own subject matter, because it is a statement of valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
There is another inference: "like grammar, the Rāmāyaṇa, and so forth.
Regarding that, he states the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "whatever...
*Vistara* means an abundance of words.
By stating that [the author] is small in scope in terms of meaning (*arthataḥ*), he indicates that the knowledge of the author regarding the subject matter (*artha*) is superior;
moreover, an abundance of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is observed in the Veda.
Here is the construction: whatever scripture arises from whichever authoritative person (*āpta*), that person possesses knowledge of a subject matter greater than that scripture.

Thus it is well known that even grammatical treatises such as those of Pāṇini, whose subject matter consists of only a portion of what is to be known—such as the correctness of words—arise from one who knows more than that.

If even a treatise with limited scope can arise from one who knows more, then, according to the scriptural passage beginning "From Him, the Great," since the Veda—characterized by its many branches and so forth—arose effortlessly, like a person's exhalation, from the Great, the unlimited, the Real Source of all beings; [how much more so could this Upanishad arise from Him].
Since his very existence implies both omniscience and omnipotence, what more need be said?
In that regard, in order to dispel the suspicion that the Veda is of human origin, he states the meaning of the term "breathing forth" (*niḥśvasita*) found in the Śruti: "without effort.
This means without the exertion involved in cognizing an object through other means of knowledge, according to the analogy of the blinking of an eye.

Here, by means of inference, for the sake of strengthening the omniscience declared in the scripture "He who is all-knowing," we establish merely the existence of knowledge of the primary meaning in the author of the Veda— just as in the case of Pāṇini and others— but not that such knowledge of the meaning is the cause of the Veda; for that would contradict the *niḥśvasita* (breath) scripture,
and because the status of being the author of the Veda is possible through mere knowledge of the Veda, just as in the case of a student.

This is the distinction: the student is dependent on others, whereas the Lord, by his own memory, manifests at the beginning of the aeon the very sequence of the Vedas he himself created to Brahmā and others; because his knowledge is unobstructed, he knows their meaning as something that cannot be avoided, and thus he is "all-knowing"—this is beyond reproach.
Now, following the definition of Brahman, since there is a desire to know its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he states another exposition with the words "ata eva" (for this very reason).
Since both the definition and the means of valid cognition have the determination of Brahman as their purpose, they share a single result; this constitutes their logical connection (*saṅgati*).
Regarding the doubt as to whether or not the scriptural text, "But that person who is known through the Upaniṣads," declares that Brahman is to be known solely through the Vedas:

Since, by means of the effect as a logical mark (*kāryaliṅga*) alone, parsimony (*lāghava*) establishes a single, omniscient creator who is Brahman, [the opponent] concludes that [Brahman] is not [known through scripture]. To this, the author of the Siddhānta replies with the aphorism "Because [Brahman] has scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*).
He explains this [saying], "As it has been stated."

In every case, one should understand that the pair of arguments for the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) constitutes the seed of doubt. Here, the distinction is that the result of the prima facie view is the establishment of the necessity of investigating inference alone, whereas the result of the final conclusion is the [establishment of the necessity of investigating] the Vedāntas.
The attainment of Brahman through inference and other means was incidentally refuted in the preceding Sūtra.

Furthermore, because the multiplicity of the world's manifold diversity contradicts its having a single creator—just as a palace and the like do—the principle of parsimony (lāghava) does not apply here.

Nor is it possible for a single creator to exist simply by virtue of being omniscient; for if one were to claim that the knowledge of omniscience arises from the knowledge of unity, and conversely that the knowledge of unity arises from that [omniscience], this would result in a circular argument (anyonyāśraya). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Precisely from the scripture" (śāstrādeva).
"What is that treatise?"—to this he says: "The treatise.
He raises an objection regarding its separate composition: "For what purpose?"—the meaning is:
"What is the purpose for which it was shown by that reason?"
He states "It is said" (ucyate) to show that this separate sūtra is intended to dispel the doubt that the inference characterized by birth and so forth might be presented independently. //3//
But that [Brahman is the cause] because of the harmony [of all scriptural texts]. (BS 1.1.4)

There arises a doubt as to whether the Vedāntas have as their primary purport the established Brahman (*siddhabrahma*) or the task to be accomplished (*kārya*), based on the presence or absence of the consequences of fruitlessness (*niṣphalatva*) and dependence (*sāpekṣatva*). In response to this, following the connection by way of an objection (*ākṣepasaṃgati*) through the second interpretation (*varṇaka*) of the previous sūtra, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "But how [is it]... and so forth.

This is because the concordance (*samanvaya*) of passages such as "Being alone, my dear," which possess clear marks of Brahman such as being the Self of all, has already been stated to refer to Brahman.
The connections with the Śruti and other sources are as follows:

the distinction is that, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the engagement of those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) in the Vedāntas is not established, whereas according to the final conclusion (siddhānta), it is established.
The reason for the objection "How so? is given by the phrase "yāvatā" (since).

Since the Jaimini-sūtra has demonstrated that the scripture—the Veda—is intent upon action (*kriyā*), it follows that because the Vedāntas do not have action as their purpose, they would result in meaninglessness, which is to say, a lack of any fruitful purpose; this is the connection of the sūtra's meaning.

In the first sūtra, it was stated that the Veda—which is the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) by the injunction of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) having study as its instrument—has as its purpose a fruitful meaning.

In the second sūtra, "Dharma is a matter characterized by injunction (*codanālakṣaṇo'rtho dharmaḥ*)," it is established that since dharma is something to be accomplished (*kārya*), injunction is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, the status of the Veda as a source of valid knowledge is pervaded by its being directed toward action (*kāryaparatva*). In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether or not there is validity regarding dharma in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest," because the authority of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is pervaded by its having action as its purpose, and because dharma is not perceived in these explanatory passages which do not concern action.
Their "uselessness" means that their purpose is fruitless.
And it is not logical for those [texts] included within the injunction to study to possess authority regarding a proven matter that is fruitless;
therefore, it is said that their authority is non-eternal.
The meaning is that because of the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), the pervaded (*vyāpya*) validity (*prāmāṇya*) simply does not exist.

Thus, even regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the sūtra: "But because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, they [the mantras] should serve the purpose of praising the injunctions"—namely, that they have action (*kriyā*) as their ultimate goal.
The sense is that this was demonstrated when it was argued that [mantric validity] is non-eternal (*anitya*).
Vāyu is indeed the deity that moves most swiftly; therefore, a ritual action dedicated to that deity will yield its fruit very quickly.

Thus, by way of praising the objects to be performed, the explanatory passages (arthavādas)—such as "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu"—form a single syntactical unit with the injunctive sentences. Consequently, the arthavādas become purposeful.
In short, because they aim toward fruitful action through the indication of praise, the arthavādas are authoritative means of knowledge.
Is it not the case that it is improper for the Vedāntas, which are grasped by the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), to be purposeless? To this, he says: "The agent," etc.

We do not establish the purposelessness of the Vedāntas; rather, since what is already established in the world is known through other means of knowledge (*māna*), lacks fruitfulness, and because if they were directed toward an already established Brahman, there would follow the contingencies of dependence on other means of knowledge and lack of fruitfulness—resulting in the loss of their authority—we [hold otherwise].

We maintain that it must be stated that [the Upanishads] have the ritual action as their ultimate purpose by way of illuminating the agent, the deity, and the fruit of the remaining parts of the ritual.
In this regard, however, sentences concerning the meaning of the word *tat* (That) serve to praise the agent and the deity,
while sentences such as those concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) serve to praise the fruit.

Now, one might object: since the Vedāntas are studied in a separate context (*prakaraṇāntara*) without reference to any specific ritual action (*karmaviśeṣa*), how can they be subordinate to that [action], given the lack of evidence?
Anticipating this dissatisfaction, he states another position: "meditation" (*upāsanā*).
The injunction for meditation is: "One who desires liberation, having superimposed the non-difference of the unreal [self] and Brahman, should meditate [with the thought], 'I am Brahman'."

The word "etcetera" (ādi) refers to hearing [the Veda] and so forth. The meaning is that one must state its being intent upon an effect (kāryaparatva). Now, one might ask: "Why should one state that it is intent upon an effect—which has not been heard—while setting aside the Brahman which has been heard? To this he says: "For not... (na hi).
"Pariṣṭhita" means situated firmly on all sides and in every respect, established, and independent of any further action;
that is to say, it is "accomplished. Its "pratipādana" is the making known by means of the Veda that which was previously unknown.
That is not possible;
for when a sentence accords with a matter that is capable of being known through other means of knowledge, it is merely reiterative (anuvādaka),
like the sentence, "Fire is the remedy for cold."
But in the case of contradiction, because it would fail to convey [the truth],
the meaning is that it would be like the sentence "The sacrificial post is the sun"; thus,
it is established that such a thing is not the meaning of the Veda.

Having stated that [the object] is like a jar because it is capable of being known through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), he says "likewise" (*tathā*) because [such a statement] would be fruitless.
The meaning is that this is not possible because there is no result in making known what is already established, and because it does not concern what is to be avoided or sought after;
for the result [of knowledge] consists indeed in the attainment of happiness and the removal of suffering.

And that [attainment] is to be accomplished through engagement and desisting; these two arise from the cognitions of what is to be adopted—which is the effect of the effort of engagement—and what is to be rejected—which is the effect of the effort of desisting—not from the cognition of what is already established. This is the intended meaning.

Then, raising the objection as to how the Vedic declarations concerning established facts (siddhabodhivedavādānām) can have any fruitfulness, he explains the summary statement beginning with "of the tradition" (āmnāyasya) with the words "for this very reason" (ata eva).
The meaning is: precisely because there is no fruit from the knowledge of an already established entity.

Just as the sentence "That Agni, obstructed by the gods, wept,"—by way of censuring silver as being born of tears—serves as a supplement to the prohibition of giving [silver] on the sacrificial grass (barhis), so too do the Vedāntas serve as supplements to injunctions and the like.
The meaning is that [the mantra] must be expressed.

Now, one might object: "Let it be granted that these [mantras] possess independence like other mantras, rather than forming a single syntactical unit with an injunction (vidhi) like an explanatory passage (arthavāda). Anticipating this doubt, he states the failure of the example with the words "And of the mantras... In the first chapter, under the section defining the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), after the discussion of arthavādas, the discussion of mantras was undertaken: because in the mantra "For the sake of food, thee" (*iṣe tvā*), the act of cutting the branch is understood through the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "I cut" (*chinadmi*).

In passages such as "Agni is the head," since there is a cognition of the action, its means, and the deity, the mantras are enjoined for use in the sacrifice by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and other means.

Regarding the doubt as to whether they assist in the sacrifice by producing an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) through mere recitation, or rather by the seen means of reminding one of the meaning—[the prima facie view is:
the mantras have an unseen purpose, because the meaning of the mantra, which was understood at the time of study, can be remembered even through reflection (*cintā*) and so forth.

This being the prima facie view, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: "But the meaning of the sentence is not different"—because there is no difference in the meaning of sentences between worldly usage and the Veda, and because it is possible for mantra-sentences to assist the sacrifice through their visible function of manifesting their own meaning;
for when a visible purpose is possible, the postulation of an invisible one (*adṛṣṭa*) is untenable.

The status of mantras as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) of ritual action is established through the medium of the recollection of the action and its means, which is required for the performance that yields the fruit.
The restrictive rule (*niyama*) that "the object must be remembered by means of mantras alone," however, serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Likewise, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) form syntactic units with injunctions (*vidhi*) through the mediation of the meaning of the words of praise.
However, the distinction is that mantras possess syntactic unity with those [injunctions] by means of the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence.
Now, one might object: "Let it be that sentences situated within the context of ritual action (karma-prakaraṇa) have syntactic unity with injunctions;
but why should the Vedāntas not have validity regarding established entities (siddha)? To this, he says: "Nowhere... [na kvacid iti].
The meaning is that the Vedāntas possess purpose solely by being syntactically unified with injunctions, because they do not make known an already established fact, just like mantras and arthavādas.
To the objection that it might be postulated even though it is not seen elsewhere, he replies: "Or [it is] appropriate. The word "not" is to be supplied from the previous context.
The meaning is that [this is not so], because it has already been stated that there is no purpose for [such a postulation] once [the goal] is established.

"In that case, let an injunction be postulated for Brahman itself as its own object; what is the use of [regarding] the Vedāntas as supplementary to an injunction? To this he says: "And not... Now, an objection is raised: "In the case of 'He offers with curd,' an injunction is seen regarding the already established curd"; to this he replies: "Action...
Because curd, as a means of action, is something to be accomplished by virtue of being employed, it is the object of the injunction.
The meaning is that because actionless Brahman cannot be accomplished by any means whatsoever, it cannot be an object of injunction. He concludes the Bhaṭṭa view with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).
Then, expressing his own lack of conviction, he states another position with the word "Now" (atha).
He explains the sūtra of the established conclusion with the words "the word 'but' (tu).
He asks for the reason regarding the proposition that "that Brahman has the Vedānta as its means of valid cognition" by asking "how?
He states the reason with the word "because" (sam).
Therefore, the reason is simply "being the object of the purport of the positive concomitance" (*anvayatātparyaviṣayatvam*).
The prefix *sam-* is included within the proposition itself to indicate that the correctness of the purport consists in its having an indivisible entity (*akhaṇḍārtha*) as its object.
Thus, Brahman as an indivisible whole is the object of the valid knowledge produced by the Vedāntas.

Because it is the intended object (*tātparyaviṣaya*) of the Vedānta; for whatever is the intended object of a particular statement is the object of knowledge (*prameya*) of that statement, just as *dharma* is the object of knowledge of the ritual (*karman*) statements— such is the formal argument (*prayoga*).
The indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of the sentence-meaning consists in its being non-composite (*asaṃsṛṣṭatva*).

And the property of a sentence having an indivisible meaning consists in its generating a valid cognition whose object is the relation of those word-meanings which are presented by the words themselves.
Nor is this [definition] unestablished.

In common worldly usage, definitional statements such as "the moon is that which possesses preeminent light" serve as the cause for the valid cognition of the mere individual entity, the moon, through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Furthermore, the secondary indication of all words is not contradictory, because it is accepted that a single eulogy is the object indicated by all the words of an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
Likewise, since Brahman appears as an undivided whole through words such as "Truth" and "Knowledge," there is no failure of the thesis (pakṣāsiddhi).

Nor is there a lack of proof for the reason, because the purport of the Vedānta texts regarding the non-dual, indivisible Brahman is determined by such indicative marks as the opening statements (*upakrama*) and so forth.
He shows the opening statement in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Being alone, my dear... (*sadeva somyedam*).
Uddālaka said to his son: "O gentle one, O handsome one,
this entire world,
prior to its origin, was in the beginning only Brahman, which is Being and is indestructible."
By the word "eva" (only/alone), the separate existence of the world is negated.
The three words "one only, without a second" are intended to exclude internal differences as well as differences from those of the same or different classes.
Having thus introduced Brahman as being without a second, the text concludes by stating, "All this has that as its self."
This uniformity between the introduction and the conclusion is an indicator of the intended meaning (tātparya-liṅga),
just as there is a ninefold repetition of "That thou art" (tattvam asi).

The fact that Brahman—which is devoid of form and the like and is without a second—is "unprecedented" (apūrva) because it cannot be known through other means of knowledge, has been stated [by the scripture]: "In this very place, my dear, you do not perceive That which truly exists.
The meaning is that you do not know the innermost Brahman residing within the aggregate [of the body].
Furthermore, the fruit for the knower resulting from the knowledge of Brahman has been stated: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in the Absolute]."
For as long as his body is not liberated, there is only a delay until the fall of that body;
then, immediately after the fall of the body, the knower shall attain Brahman—
the meaning is that he experiences the liberation of the bodiless state (videhakaivalya).
The passage beginning with "having entered by means of this living self" (*anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya*) is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of knowing the non-dual [Self].
Through analogies such as clay and so forth, the logical argument has been stated that there is no modification apart from the material cause (*prakṛti*).

Thus, these six kinds of indicators of the purport (*tātparya-liṅga*), whether individually or collectively, are seen in every Vedānta text; therefore, he recites the opening sentence of the Aitareya Upaniṣad: "The Self, verily... (*ātmā vā iti*).
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the concluding statement of the Madhu-kāṇḍa says "That is this" (tadetad) for the purpose of showing that the True Self is devoid of distinctions:
"That Brahman, which through its powers of illusion (māyā) has many forms,
is this [which is] immediate."
"Apūrva" means devoid of a cause. "Anapara" means devoid of an effect.
"Anantara" means that there is no other distinct category of existence intervening between this [state].
The meaning is "of a single flavor.
It is "without exterior" and "non-dual.
He establishes its immediacy by saying "this."
"Experiencing everything" means *sarvānubhūḥ*;
the sense is that it is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
Having spoken the statements of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas, he states the statement of the *Atharva* Veda: "This is indeed Brahman."
The meaning is that this collection of objects in the eastern direction, which previously appeared as if it were non-Brahman to the learned, is in reality the immortal Brahman alone.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), statements such as "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) and so forth are included.
Now, let it be granted that Brahman is the intended object of the [scriptural] purport; however—

To the objection that the meaning of the Vedāntas might indeed be something to be accomplished (kārya), he says: "And not [so]. The meaning is that when the purport (tātparya) of the Vedāntas is determined to be Brahman, it is not logical for them to have an injunction as their meaning, according to the maxim: "That which a word aims at is its meaning. Regarding the claim that, by the logic of the arthavāda, the Vedāntas serve to praise the agent and so forth, he says: "And not of those... [the Vedāntas].
For them, the state of being a praiser of action does not shine forth; rather, through knowledge, action—which is its means—is destroyed.
The meaning is that this is according to the Śruti: "In that state of knowledge, who is the agent, by what instrument, and upon what object could one look?
The point is that since explanatory passages (arthavādas) lack a fruit in their own literal sense, they possess the character of praise.

Regarding the claim that Brahman, being an established entity, is cognizable through other means of knowledge and is therefore not the subject matter of the Veda, he says: "And not by [other means]," etc.
The connection is: "without the scripture [saying] 'That thou art'.
Dharma is not the subject matter of the Veda.
Because it is an object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), like cooking, it is cognizable through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*).
If it is argued that because *dharma* cannot be determined without the Veda, it is not cognizable by other means of knowledge, then the same applies to Brahman as well.
Having restated the objection that Brahman is not the subject matter of the Veda because it is fruitless (*niṣphala*), he refutes it with the words "As for what was said," and so forth.
Because of being devoid [of attributes] and because of being distinct— this refers to Brahman, as is understood from the context.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated— that "the Vedāntas have meditation (upāsanā) as their primary purport"— is this true only of passages concerning the vital breath (prāṇa), the five fires (pañcāgni), and so forth, or of all [Vedāntic texts]?
Therein, he marks the first [alternative] with the words "the deity and so forth.
The meaning of the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to qualities such as being the eldest (jyeṣṭhatva) and the result.
It is not the second [alternative].

Because it is impossible to assume that passages such as "Truth, Knowledge," which are devoid of injunctions and are fruitful in their own literal sense, have meditation (upāsanā) as their intended purpose;
furthermore, regarding the Brahman that is their referent, its status as a subordinate element (śeṣatva) must occur either prior to or subsequent to knowledge.
As for the first case, even if that [Brahman]—possessing superimposed qualities—is subordinate to it, the second case is not so; thus he says: "But not so."
The meaning is that [the self] is like the deities such as Prāṇa.
When the identity expressed in "I am Brahman" is realized, there is an absence of any fruit for the Brahman-Self because it is devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted.

And because the cause—the knowledge of the duality between the object of worship and the worshipper—is destroyed, there is no remainder of the practice of worship; thus he says, "In [the state of] oneness.

He says "no" to the idea that there is an injunction for the re-emergence of dualistic knowledge through the force of its residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), adding "for not," with the word "of the firm" being understood as the ellipsis.
Certainty regarding its being an error constitutes firmness;
however, that which arises from mental conditioning (saṃskāra) is not a cause for a [positive] injunction once it has been ascertained as an error.
"By which" refers to this.
The meaning is: "by virtue of the existence of the cause in the act of meditation.
He restates that being for the purpose of action (*kriyārthakatva*) pervades the authority of the Veda—introducing this with "Even though" (*yadyapi*).
This refers to the fact that [the Veda] consists of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), including explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and so forth.
And thus, the sense is that because of the absence of the pervader (vyāpaka), there is an inference of the absence of the pervaded (vyāpya) within the Vedāntas.

In the inference— "The Vedāntas are not authoritative with respect to their own meaning, because they do not have action as their purpose, like the passage 'He wept' (so 'rodīt)'— he states that "being fruitless in purpose" is a limiting condition (upādhi), saying "nevertheless" (tathāpi).
The meaning is: even though explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) lack authoritative status with respect to their own literal meaning;
[this refers to] that which has them as its object, namely the instrument for that [knowledge].
The phrase "with respect to its own meaning" implies "in the case of Brahman as the Self."

The point is this: since the Vedāntas are established as authoritative with respect to their own subject matter by virtue of being the means for producing knowledge that bears fruit, "having action as its purpose" cannot be their pervader (*vyāpaka*).
[Objection: Granted, let it be that "having action as its purpose" is not the pervader of Vedic authority;
however, it may still be its pervaded (*vyāpya*).
Because that [logical mark] is absent, it is difficult to know the validity of the Vedāntas through inference;
to this he says, "Not so" (*na ca*).
The meaning is: there is no such thing as the validity of the Veda being observed anywhere else as something accessible to inference, which would require a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).

The meaning is as follows: because the Veda possesses self-evident validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) like the sense of sight and other faculties, it does not depend upon the observation of pervasion (*vyāpti*), logical marks (*liṅga*), and so forth.

However, when there is doubt regarding its validity, certainty of validity arises from the fact that its purport consists of an uncontradicted object that is conducive to a result (*phalavat*), and not merely from its having action as its subject matter;
for there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a sentence such as "He might fall into a well."
He concludes for the sake of the [specific] color [of the argument]: "Therefore" (tasmāt).
This means "because of the concordance" (samanvayāt).
It is established that the authority of injunctive statements (*vidhi-vākya*)—on the grounds that their meaning is unknown and they possess a fruit—is equally applicable to the Vedāntas as well.

Thus, the view of those atheists (brahmanāstika) who seek the derivation of word-meanings from established usage has been refuted by the statement that Brahman, because it is not amenable to other means of knowledge and because [the inquiry into it] is fruitful, is knowable solely through the Vedāntas.

Now, another exposition of the Sūtra is commenced in order to refute the view of the Vṛttikāras—who, while asserting that all words possess a power (*śakti*) directed toward an object associated with an action, maintain that Brahman is taught by the Vedāntas as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to an injunction (*vidhi*), and not independently.

In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether the Vedāntas teach Brahman as a subordinate element to an injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*) or independently, based on the presence or absence of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) regarding an already established entity. Regarding this, he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*): "In this matter, others... [and so forth].
Thus,
the meaning is that the Vṛttikāras raise a prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the statement that Brahman is to be known through the Vedāntas;
in this prima facie view, liberation results from meditative worship (*upāsanā*).
In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the result [of knowledge] arises solely from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
An injunction (*vidhi*) is a mandate (*niyoga*); its object (*viṣaya*) is comprehension (*pratipatti*), which is worship (*upāsanā*).

To the inquiry "What is the object of this [comprehension]?", he says "comprehension" (*pratipatti*), meaning that Brahman is presented by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) precisely for the purpose of an injunction.
The meaning is: "by being the object of an injunction and the object of comprehension.
He provides an example regarding the attainment of that which is subordinate to a sentence whose primary purport is an injunction—namely, "just as" [in the case of]:

"He binds the animal to the sacrificial post (yūpa)," "He offers the oblation in the Āhavanīya fire," and "One should sacrifice to Indra. When there arises the expectancy regarding these injunctions, "What are the sacrificial posts and so forth?", [the answer is given by the texts] "He fashions the sacrificial post," and so on.

The meaning is that Brahman is presented in the same way as other things are presented by sentences intended solely for injunctions—just as wood that has been refined by processing such as planing into eight facets is called a *yūpa* (sacrificial post); just as fire refined by the rite of *ādhāna* (consecration) is called the *āhavanīya*; and just as [the deity] with the thunderbolt in hand who shatters forts is [presented].

The word "api" (also) is used to dispel the doubt that even in the case of a sentence subordinate to an injunction (*vidhiparavākya*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if it were to convey another meaning. The sense is that although other things not known from other means of knowledge are mentioned as being subsidiary (*śeṣatvena*), they are not mentioned as being primary (*pradhānatvena*); thus, there is no syntactical split, because only a difference in the primary object constitutes a syntactical split.

One might object: "How can Brahman, which is the subject matter of the intended meaning as determined by the sixfold marks [of textual interpretation], be subordinate to an injunction? Thus he raises the doubt with the word "kutaḥ" (whence?).
For the determination of the intention of a scripture occurs through the usage of elders.
And in the usage of elders, a novel employment of words is observed as being directed toward the activity or cessation of activity of the listener.
Therefore, those two alone are the purposes of the scripture as well;
and since those two are produced by the knowledge of what is to be done (*kārya*), the scripture has as its primary object that which is to be done.
Consequently, he states that Brahman is subordinate to what is to be done, beginning with the words "engagement" (*pravṛtti*).
He states the consensus of the elders regarding the fact that the treatise is centered on *niyoga* (an injunction), beginning with the words "For it is not thus," and so forth.
[The terms] *kriyā*, *kārya*, and *niyoga*— [...are synonymous.]
*Vidhi*, *dharma*, and *apūrva* are synonymous.
When there is the inquiry as to what the meaning of the Veda is, the author of the Śābara-bhāṣya stated: "For [it] is seen," etc., referring to that Veda.
Regarding the point that "the object [of the Veda] is its meaning," he cites the commentary from the *Codanā-sūtra*: "Codanā.
The meaning is that a sentence which impels one toward action—namely, toward a ritual injunction (*niyoga*)—by means of knowledge, is called *codanā*.
Having stated the consensus of Śabarasvāmin, he states the consensus of Jaimini: "The knowledge of that."
The indicator of that Dharma is the instruction consisting of non-human prescriptive sentences;
the meaning is that it is not distinct from Dharma.
He cites the sūtra—"tadbhūtānām" (of those [words] which have come into being)—regarding the point that words possess their power (*śakti*) with respect to meanings connected to an action (*kārya*).

The meaning is that in that Veda, there must be a collective recitation—that is, a simultaneous utterance—of words whose established meanings refer to existing things (*bhūtārtha*), together with a word expressing an action (*kriyārtha*), such as an optative suffix (*liṅ*) which denotes what is to be done (*kārya*).
This is because the knowledge of the meaning of individual words is the cause for the cognition of the effect that constitutes the sentence-meaning.

The underlying idea is that words, which possess the capacity to denote meanings connected to what is to be done, bring about the sentence-meaning—which is precisely the "to-be-done" (*kārya*)—by means of the recollection of the word-meanings, in conjunction with a word denoting an action.
He states the conclusion: "Therefore.
Since the elders have spoken thus, therefore the scripture consists solely of sentences enjoining and prohibiting.
However, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like are exhausted by being subordinate to that [injunction].
Therefore, there is a commonality of "scriptural character" (*śāstratva*) with that [body of] ritual injunctions (*karmaśāstra*).
Consequently, the meaning is that the Upaniṣads (*vedānta*) must possess purposefulness precisely by having an injunction as their primary purport.
[Objection: But surely, since neither a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) nor an injunction (*vidheya*) is observed in the Vedāntas, how can there be a cognition of something to be done (*kārya*)?
To this, he says: "And when [it exists]," etc. [Objection:
But surely, a difference in subject matter (*arthabheda*) has been stated here between these two sections by the authors of the *Jijñāsā-sūtras* for Dharma and Brahman.
Because if they had a single purpose, the division of the treatise would be untenable.
In that case, since there is a difference in the objects of inquiry (*jijñāsya*) between the two sections, a difference in their results must be stated.
And thus, knowledge cannot be something to be enjoined for the sake of the fruit of liberation.

If liberation were produced by an action that must be performed (*vidheyakriyājanyatva*), it would follow that it is no different from the fruit of ritual action (*karmaphala*); and if there is no difference, the distinction between what is to be known through inquiry (*jijñāsya*) would not be established.

Therefore, one might object: "Since liberation is eternally established and distinct from the fruits of ritual action, an injunction for the knowledge that manifests it is improper"—this is the doubt expressed by the words "nanviheti.
To this, [the author replies]: the distinction of liberation from the fruit of ritual action is unestablished; therefore, knowledge must be enjoined for that purpose.

Nor should it be argued that, since even among those [Vedic texts] not taught by the Vedas there is something to be investigated that possesses a fruitful result, the distinction [between the Vedas and other texts] is unestablished; for this is indeed accepted.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the aphorism regarding Brahman as the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*), because the author of the Sūtras presents Brahman as subordinate to the injunction to know (*jñāna-vidhi*). Thus he refutes [the objection] with the word "no" (*na*).

He clarifies that Brahman is enjoined by an injunction with the words "The Self, verily... It should be understood that in the statement "One who knows Brahman," the injunction is transformed to mean: "One who desires the state of Brahman should perform the knowledge of Brahman. "Loka" means the nature of knowledge.
He shows the very meaning of the Vedāntas by the word "eternal" (nitya).
Now, one might ask: what is the fruit of the injunction? To that he says: "from the meditation upon that.

The meaning is that liberation, as declared in the scripture—"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"—is the result, which, unlike heaven, is not well-known in the world; it is attained through the meditation on the inner Self as Brahman.

He states the objection [to the view] that Brahman is not accepted as being supplementary to an injunction regarding the meditation (*upāsanā*) that is to be performed: "If it were not to be performed," and so forth. The meaning is that if there were a cognition of an already established entity unconnected to an injunction, there would be no result such as engagement in action, and thus the Vedāntas would be rendered futile.
The doubt introduced by "nanu" has a clear meaning.
He refutes [the objection] by means of a disparity in the example, saying "it might be" (syāt).
The meaning is: "if it were thus, then this [word] would indeed possess a meaning. He states the meaning of the word "thus" (evam) with "that which" (yat).

Furthermore, if liberation were to arise from knowledge alone, then there would be no injunction for reflection (*manana*) and so forth subsequent to the knowledge produced by hearing (*śravaṇa*); moreover, because of that injunction, liberation would be something to be accomplished through action. To this he says: "It is to be heard" (*śrotavya*).
This is because words possess the power to denote only that which is connected to an action (*kāryānvita-śakti*).
Since scripture consists precisely of that which has activity and so forth as its fruit,

and since there is an absence of fruit in the case of an already established entity, and because the injunctions for reflection and so on are directed toward what is to be accomplished, he concludes the prima facie view with the words "Therefore."
The Vedāntas are not intent upon injunctions, because, while possessing their own fruit, they lack a person to be enjoined (niyojya),

like the sentence "This is not a snake. He establishes the final position— introducing it with "here"— by providing two qualifications in the reason to exclude the sentences "He wept" and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice."
Regarding the claim that knowledge must be enjoined for one who desires liberation and is thus the person to be directed (*niyojya*), he says "no"—
liberation is not produced by an injunction.
The meaning is that [the Self] is distinct from the fruit of action, just like the Self [itself].
To explain the aforementioned reason, he elaborates upon action and its fruit with the words beginning "the bodily" and ending with "he reiterates the described cycle of transmigration."
Now— after the study of the Veda;

"therefore"— because the Veda is intent upon fruitful meaning— the meaning of the aphorism is that an inquiry into the sentences concerning ritual action must be undertaken for the sake of determining Dharma.
He says "even unrighteousness" (adharmo 'pi) to show that it is not only the action called dharma, but unrighteousness as well;
the meaning is "by means of the authority of prohibitive statements.
Having spoken of action, he speaks of its fruit: "of those two" (tayoḥ).

Liberation (mokṣa), however, is beyond the senses, free from sorrow, not an object of enjoyment for the body and so forth, not produced by sense-objects and the like, and is not well-known to those who do not know the Self; thus, the qualifiers such as "perception" and so on are employed to demonstrate its distinctness.

Having stated the fruit of action in general, he elaborates separately upon the fruit of dharma—beginning with "humanity" and so forth. The meaning of the word "anu" (following) is that [the fruits] accord with experience, according to the Śruti: "That is one human bliss; a hundredfold greater than that is the bliss of the Gandharvas and so forth."
And therefore, the meaning is: "because of the gradations of pleasure";
however, liberation is unsurpassed.
Furthermore, there is a distinction in that the means for achieving that [liberation], which is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), is of a single form; moreover,

he states the distinction that while only one who is endowed with the fourfold means is eligible for liberation through knowledge, eligibility for ritual action (*karman*) is of various kinds— beginning with the word "dharma."
The meaning is that it is not only understood, but is also well-known.
"Desire" (arthitva) is the longing for a result;
"capacity" (sāmarthya) is worldly [resources] such as sons and so forth.
From the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the qualities of] being learned and not being censured by the scriptures are understood.
Furthermore, he states the distinction that while the fruit of action is to be attained through the path, liberation is eternally attained— thus saying "likewise" (*tathā*).

The meaning is that, through the excellence of mental steadiness attained in worship (*upāsanā*), one's departure for the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) by way of the path beginning with light (*arciḥ*) is heard in the scripture in the passage starting with "They [go] to the light" (*te 'rciṣam*). Furthermore:
"The Agnihotra sacrifice, austerity, truthfulness, the preservation of the Vedas, hospitality, and the Vaiśvadeva offering—this is designated as *iṣṭa* (sacrificial rites)."
The construction of ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as temples for the deities,
the gift of food, and the establishment of groves— this is designated as *pūrta*.
Protecting those who have come for refuge, non-violence toward living beings,
and whatever gift is given outside the sacrificial altar— this is designated as "given" (datta).
"In that case as well" means "even in the world of the moon. *Saṃpāta* refers to action (*karman*), because by means of it one "falls together"— that is, goes— from this world to that world.
The meaning is that they remain for as long as the karma to be experienced lasts, and then return again.
Having described the gradations of happiness among those who have gone upwards from the human state, he now speaks of those who have gone downwards—beginning with "In the same way.
Now, describing the gradations of suffering, its causes, and those who practice them, he elaborates upon the fruit of unrighteousness (adharma)—beginning with "In the same way upwards."
He concludes the detailed exposition of the two kinds of karmic fruits for the sake of knowing their distinct characteristics from liberation with the word "thus" (*evam*).
The meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes egoism (*asmitā*), desire (*kāma*), anger (*krodha*), and fear (*bhaya*).
The relevant *smṛti* passage is: "Having abandoned him, they [go] to the vast world of heaven," and so forth.
Since an increase in flame is observed to follow from an increase in fuel-wood, it is logical to infer a gradation in the means (sādhana) based on the gradation in the result.
He cites the Śruti to this effect with the words "And thus... (tathā ca).

Liberation is not the fruit of action, because it possesses attributes such as being contrary to the fruits of action, being beyond the senses, being free from sorrow, and being incapable of being experienced by the body and so forth; this is established by inference through the method of difference (*vyatireka*), like heaven and other such rewards. He cites the scriptural passage supported by this reasoning: "The bodiless," etc.
The word *vāva* is used for emphasis.
The meaning is that the Self, being in reality bodiless (*videha*), is not touched at all by worldly pleasure and pain.
If liberation were the fruit of dharma in the form of meditation (*upāsanā*), [then it would be subject to decay].
He states that "dharmakāryatve hi" [in the case of being an effect of dharma] because it would be improper to negate that very thing which exists as the beloved (*priya*).
Now, one might object: what is called the "beloved" is merely sensual pleasure (*vaiṣayika-sukha*), and it is that which is negated; however, liberation (*mokṣa*) is indeed the fruit of dharma.
He raises the objection that this is due to the power of karma to produce diverse results—namely, "the state of being bodiless" (*aśarīratvam*).
He explains that "bodilessness" means the self's lack of attachment to a body;
since this is beginningless, it cannot be produced by karma, and thus he says: "No."
It is bodiless, devoid of a gross body;
it is the one eternal reality abiding within many impermanent bodies;
it is the great, all-pervading.
He excludes [the notion of] relative magnitude by using the word "all-pervading" (vibhu).

The meaning is that having known that Self, the wise man does not experience transmigratory existence, which is characterized by sorrow. He cites scripture regarding the absence of the subtle body with the words "without breath" (aprāṇa).
Because the powers of action and knowledge belonging to the vital breath (prāṇa) and the mind (manas) are negated,
and since the organs of action and knowledge are dependent upon them, they too are negated;
