It was stated previously that there is no disparity [between the two cases], because even when the action of karma is not intended to be expressed, just as the sun— which is of the nature of light— is metaphorically designated as the "agent" (kartṛ) by virtue of being, in some sense, the locus of the activity of shining, so too the conscious self (cidātman) is metaphorically designated as the agent of the act of seeing, which is its own conscious nature. Now, however, just as for a potter the act of seeing consists of a modification (vṛtti) of his own limiting adjunct, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), so too for the Lord (Īśvara), it consists of a modification of his own limiting adjunct, ignorance (avidyā).

At the conclusion of the dissolution, when the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the various creations have been awakened, a certain transformation (*pariṇāma*) directed toward creation occurs; therefore, it indicates that within her, there exists a vision (*īkṣaṇa*) regarding all effects that lie dormant in subtle form,
and because that [vision] is an effect and because action (*karman*) exists therein, her agency is primary— this is emphasized by the word "sutarām" (all the more).

Now, one might object: "How can the Lord—who is pure consciousness as the prototype (bimba) conditioned by Māyā—be the primary agent with respect to seeing, given the absence of any volitional action?
We say no; for agency belongs only to one who possesses knowledge conducive to the effect, and since the Lord also possesses eternal knowledge conducive to seeing.
Nor should it be argued that since agency is established by eternal knowledge alone, what is the use of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa);
for such an argument would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), whereby one might as well ask what is the use of space (ākāśa) when sound could arise from air and so forth alone.

Therefore, since it is heard in scripture that [Brahman] "saw" just as space is the cause of air and the rest, this "seeing"—which is heard to be adventitious—must be accepted as the cause of space and the other elements. This suffices.

The meaning is that when the unmanifest (avyākṛta) exists in a subtle state, it is desired to be manifested—that is, to be made gross. Having raised the objection that while the act of seeing whose nature is consciousness colored by the effects of the unmanifest does not depend on an instrument, one must still specify an instrument for the seeing that takes the form of a mental modification (vṛtti), he says: "Moreover, [it belongs] to one possessed of ignorance and so forth.
The sense is that, since there is no rule that what is known by one must be known by another, even the Māyin (the Lord), though bodiless, can be the instrumental agent of produced seeing.

Raising the objection that there is indeed a pervasion (vyāpti) such that whatever knowledge is produced must be accomplished by means of a body, he states "And the two mantras" to refute it through scripture.
"Effect" refers to the body;
"cause" refers to the sense organs.
The power (*śakti*) of this Lord is *māyā*; it is "supreme" (*parā*) in relation to its own effects, and it is twofold because it produces diverse effects.
However, one might object that it is established merely by tradition (*aitihya*) and not by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); to this he says: "It is heard."

The creative activity that occurs by means of the power of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) is "natural" (*svābhāvikī*); the meaning is that it arises because [Brahman] consists of beginningless *māyā*.

Furthermore, the "power of knowledge"—that is, of consciousness—is its clarity through being reflected in the modifications of *māyā*; the "activity" of that [clarity] is the productivity and subjectivity of Brahman as the original image (*bimba*), which is also natural. This is another interpretation.
Though handless, he is a grasper;
though footless, he is swift.
The meaning is that the Lord has no dependence on worldly causes for his own activity.
The meaning is: the foremost, without beginning, the Person, infinite, great, and all-pervading.
He raises the objection of a departure from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*) with the words "But surely" (*nanu*).

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: since ignorance, attachment, and so forth—which are the obstructive causes regarding knowledge—do not exist apart from the Lord (*īśvara*), there is no one other than the Lord.

He replies to this, stating that there is no departure from established tenets, because he has already stated that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Thus he says: "To this, it is replied."
The conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) consisting of words and the cognitions produced by them is brought about by that [superimposition], that is, by the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
The word "unconfused" (*asaṃkīrṇa*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
To the question, "How can there be non-confusion if there is no distinction [between the Self and the adjuncts]? he replies: "And brought about by that... and so forth.
The meaning is that [the distinction] is produced by the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Regarding the word "thus" (*tathā*):
the cause of the connection with the body and so forth is non-discrimination (*aviveka*), which is beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*); the meaning is that it is produced by that [ignorance].

For the distinction— that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the reflection in ignorance (*avidyā*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is the original image-consciousness (*bimba-caitanya*)— has its existence dependent upon ignorance;
this is because an eternal distinction cannot be an effect.
The distinction between the knower and so forth, produced by the intellect and its functions, is itself an effect; this is the discernment.
Now, one might ask: how can there be non-discernment regarding the Self, which is partless and self-luminous?
To this, he says: "And it is seen."
In reality, the notion "I am a man" is an irrefutable error, since it is observed with respect to the Self—which is distinct from the body and so forth and is self-luminous.
And the meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that this [notion] is imagined through mere false cognition—that is, through ignorance established by delusion, which is measured by false cognition.
Alternatively, he states the common worldly experience regarding the aforementioned false cognition: "And it is seen," etc.

The third case ending is used here in the sense of "in this manner. The meaning is that it is perceived by way of its nature as an error; or alternatively, the meaning is that it is perceived solely through a succession of prior errors, and not as an object of valid cognition (*prameya*).
He states that even for the immutable (kūṭastha), a causal status based on māyā is logical, with the words "But as... (yathā tu).
As for the objection that it is impossible to grasp the power of words regarding that which is not an object of knowledge (avedya), that is not so;

for words such as "Being" (sat) and others, whose powers are understood in common worldly usage in the sense of "unsublated" and so forth, function as indicators (lakṣaka) of the undivided Brahman by virtue of being a portion of their own primary denotable meaning (vācya). Thus it is established. //5//
If it is argued that [the term "Self"] is used in a secondary sense, we say no, because of the word "Self."
He states the doubt to be refuted by the subsequent sūtra with the words "here he says.

[The phrase] "even otherwise" means even in the case of insentience (*acetanatva*). Now, one might ask: what similarity does the *pradhāna* have with a sentient being (*cetana*) such that its "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) could be considered figurative? To this, he replies with the words "just as... (*yathā*).
The meaning is that "similarity" refers to the performance of functions according to a fixed sequence.
Regarding the phrase "because of the statement being mostly figurative," the meaning is because it is recited in a context abounding in secondary (gauṇa) meanings.
If it is argued that the term "seeing" (īkṣati) is used in a figurative sense because [the subject] is insentient—just as it is for water and fire—the answer is no.
He states the meaning of the Sūtra—"from the word *ātman* and from the certainty of [the Self's] being sentient"—with the words "As has been said," and so forth.

That aforementioned entity denoted by the word *sat*, this very deity who is the seer, though previously beyond perception (*parokṣā*), says: "Come now (*hanta*); immediately after the creation of the elements, these three created things—namely fire, water, and food—are here.
Because they are beyond perception, the word *devatāḥ* (deities) is used in the accusative plural.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Having entered into those [elements] by means of this living self (*jīva*), which is my own essential nature (*svarūpa*) experienced in previous kalpas, I shall make their names and forms gross for the sake of being objects of enjoyment.

This is because it is well-known in common usage, and because of the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) from the verbal root *jīv* (in the sense of "to sustain life"), namely that one "lives" (*jīvati*) because one sustains the vital breaths (*prāṇān dhārayati*).
"But this [is not so]" means:

however, in our own position, since it is observed in the world that the difference between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) is merely conceptualized, it is logical that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the Self of Being (*sat*).

Having stated that the *pradhāna* is not the referent of the word "Being" because of the term "Self" (*ātman*) applied to the individual soul, he explains the reason in another way—that the *pradhāna* is not [the referent] because of the term "Self" applied to the individual soul within Being—saying "likewise."
That which is called "Being" (sat), this subtle essence within the minute, this entire world has that as its self;
that Being alone is the truth.
Because modification is unreal,
that existent entity is the Self of all. O Śvetaketu!
And you are not a transmigrating being;
rather, the meaning of the Śruti is that you are that very Brahman, which is real, uncontradicted, and the Self of all—
thus it teaches here.
Therefore, because it is conscious by nature and exists, the completion of the sentence is that it is indeed conscious.
Regarding the claim that the "seeing" of the existent [Being] is figurative, as in the case of water and fire, he says: "But in the case of water and fire..."
The differentiation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is creation;
the restriction [of elements] starting from the "seizing of the foot" (*ājipada*) is governance.

Since water and fire are objects of sight and are both created and governed, they lack consciousness. Because there is an obstacle to the primary sense of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) [being applied to them] and no proof for it, it is logical that this "seeing" is secondary (*gauṇa*).

The interpretation is as follows: the quality is the performance of an action like that of a conscious being; the meaning of "Fire thought" (*teja aikṣata*) is the performance of an action like that of a conscious being.
Alternatively, by the word "fire," its substrate, Being (*sat*), is indicated.
And so, he states that the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) belongs primarily to [the Existent] with the words "Of those two" (*tayoḥ*).
This might be so if the seeing of the Existent were primary; but why is that? To this he replies: "But of the Existent" (*satastu*).

Since there can be no doubt between the primary and the secondary when they are not equal, and because of the word "Self" (*ātman*), the meaning is that the seeing of the Existent is primary, as the context of the secondary would otherwise be determinative. //6//
Because liberation is taught for one who is devoted to that [Brahman]. (BS 1.1.7)

He raises the objection that the word *ātman* is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) for the *pradhāna* because it possesses the quality of acting for its own benefit—this is done with the words beginning "Now" (*atha*).
He replies that the word *ātman* is primary (*mukhya*) even when applied to the *pradhāna*, because words have multiple meanings—this he states with "Or rather" (*athavā*).
As an illustration of this multiplicity of meaning, he provides the example: "Just as... (*yathā*).

The meaning is that, just as the word "light" (*jyotis*) is used in its primary sense in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice—which involves a thousand sacrificial fees—due to its application in common worldly usage and in reference to fire, so it is here.

He states the meaning of the Sūtra with the words beginning with "no," etc., on the grounds that liberation is heard to be attained by one who is "established in Being" (*sanniṣṭha*), that is, one whose realization of non-difference is fixed upon that reality which is Being.
The Śruti has already been explained under the Sūtra on "Harmonization" (*Samanvaya*).
Having stated "for the sake of harm," he elaborates with the words "if [it were] for one who is ignorant.

It is said that a certain wicked person spoke to a blind man who had fallen onto the path through a great forest and was desiring to go to his own kinsmen's city, saying: "Why do you remain here, long-lived one, in such suffering?"
And that blind man, having heard those pleasant words and considering him a trusted friend,
said: "Oh, what good fortune for me, that you speak thus to me, a wretch incapable of reaching my desired city!"
Desiring to deceive him, he brought a young rogue bull and had the blind man seize its tail;
he then instructed the blind man,
"This young bull will lead you to the city."
"Do not abandon your tail.
And that blind man, out of excessive faith, did not abandon it; failing to attain his desired object, he instead encountered a succession of calamities.
The meaning is: "by that same principle."

"Such being the case" means that in the absence of knowledge of the Self, one would be frustrated—that is, one would not attain liberation, but on the contrary, would encounter misfortune and transmigrate.
[Objection: But let this statement be for the purpose of meditating on the identification of the individual soul (jīva) with Pradhāna.
Regarding this, he says: "And this being so.
This means: when one's own cognition is uncontradicted.
It is observed that someone who has been falsely accused of theft is released when he grasps a heated axe with truthfulness.

By means of that illustration, liberation is taught for one who possesses the conviction "I am" regarding the true Brahman, just as the Śruti teaches: "He who has a false conviction grasps a heated axe; he is not burned, and then he is released.
That teaching is not tenable on the view of identification (saṃpat), as the author says with the words "otherwise" (anyathā). Uktha is the vital breath (prāṇa), because it raises up the body.

Therefore, because the instruction regarding liberation is given, and because it is improper to resort to a secondary sense when the primary sense is possible, he says "api ca" (furthermore) to show that the word *ātman* is used in its primary sense where it exists.

The meaning is that even in common expressions such as "I am the self" (*aham ātmā*)—which might sometimes refer to a servant or the like—the word *ātman* would not be used in a secondary sense; rather, it must be understood in its primary sense everywhere.

The metaphorical designation of "sentience" (cetanatva) is applied to the primary elements and so forth because sentience is their very identity in all cases; this is the meaning. It has been stated that the word "self" (ātman) is unique to the sentient being alone.

Granted that [the word ‘ātman’] may be common to all pervasive entities, nevertheless, since there is no decisive evidence here in this Śruti passage—even though it might refer to the Pradhāna—it does not function as denoting the Pradhāna; thus he says: "Even though it is common.
But in the case of its denoting a conscious being, the context and the word ‘Śvetaketu’ serve as decisive evidence; thus he says: "But the subject under discussion...
He clarifies the decisiveness of the accompanying word (upapada) with: "For not..."
What follows from that? To this he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He refutes the example given—that the word *ātman* has multiple meanings like the word *jyotis*—by stating: "The light" (*jyotiḥ*). [An objection is raised:
"In that case, how is there the usage of the word in the phrase 'one should sacrifice with light' (*jyotiṣā yajeta*) regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice?"
Regarding this, he says: "By way of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
In the explanatory passage, "These indeed are those lights which are its *stomas*," a similarity with fire is imagined.

The *stomas*—namely, the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, *trivṛt-saptadaśa*, and *trivṛt-ekaviṃśa*—are groups of verses denoted by the word "lights" through the quality of illuminating their respective objects.

And likewise, in the case of the term *jyotiṣṭoma*—meaning "that which has the *jyotis* chants as its *stomas*"—the word *jyotis* is used in a secondary (figurative) sense; this is the meaning [of the present sūtra].

Now, one might object: it would have been more appropriate to dispel the doubt regarding the word *ātman* being used in a secondary sense with respect to the *pradhāna* in the preceding sūtra itself (*ātma-śabdāt*).

For when the primary meaning can be stated with brevity, there is no need for the effort of a separate sūtra to dispel a doubt about figurative usage or polysemy, since such a doubt is inherently weak.
And thus, explaining the sūtra as a response to an objection (*śaṅkottara*) does not appear very elegant; therefore, out of dissatisfaction, he says "or else" (*athavā*).

The meaning is: that word "Self" (*ātman*) from which all doubts regarding its being figurative or having multiple meanings have been dispelled—of that [word], the state of being so is "that-ness" (*tattā*); by means of that.
From that [it follows].

The meaning is that, in view of the reason "because [the Self] is non-different from the individual soul (jīva)" when the word "Self" is used for the Existent (sat), the teaching of liberation is itself an independent reason for refuting the Pradhāna as the cause. //7//
And because there is no statement regarding [the self] as something to be abandoned. (BS 1.1.8)

One might object: "Is it not the case that, just as someone wishing to point out the star Arundhatī points to a nearby, large star and instructs it to be Arundhatī, so too is there an instruction that the Pradhāna itself—the entity denoted by the word 'Sat'—is the Self? This is the meaning of the question, "Why [not]? (kutaśca): why is it that the Pradhāna is not the referent of the word 'Sat'?
He states that the "ca" (and) in the Sūtra is for the purpose of collecting what has not been explicitly mentioned, saying "the word 'ca'.
He explains this with the words "even though," where the word "api" (even/also) indicates that [the object] does not exist at all.

When his son had returned after studying the Vedas, being conceited, the father said to him: "O son, have you also asked about that Ātman which is indicated—that is, obtainable solely through instruction—in the presence of the Guru;
by the hearing, reflection, and realization of which there arises [the capacity for] the hearing and so forth of another? This is the grammatical connection.
The son raises an objection, wondering how one thing could be known when another remains unknown: "How? (katham).
The meaning is: "O Venerable One, how indeed could that be so?"
He states that there is no difference between the effect and its cause with the words "just as" (*yathā*).
"By the mass" (*piṇḍena*) means by its own form (*svarūpeṇa*);
the word "by [it] being known" (*vijñātena*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Regarding this, he states the reasoning: "by speech" (*vācā*). That which is commenced by speech—that is, by the organ of speech—is a modification, and thus it is called "a product of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*).
Now, one might object: is it not the case that only the name (*nāman*) is commenced by speech?
Anticipating the objection that [the effect] is not [merely] a pot or the like, he states that modification is merely a name:
"This modification is a mere name; it is spoken of by speech alone.
In reality, it does not exist as distinct from the cause; therefore, it is indeed false."
This is the intended meaning:
[one might argue that] if the modification (*vikāra*) is false, then its cause, which is non-different from it, must also be false; to this he says "clay" (*mṛttikā*).
The cause possesses an existence distinct from the effect, yet the effect is not distinct from the cause;

therefore, since there is no nature of the effect apart from the cause, the knowledge of that [cause] arises through the knowledge of the cause. This being established, he states the application to the case at hand with the word "evam" (thus):

just as clay is real, so too Brahman alone is real, while transformations such as ether and the rest are false; thus, when the knowledge of Brahman occurs, nothing remains to be known. This is the meaning.

Although knowledge of the modifications arises from knowing the primary cause (pradhāna) due to their identity with it, such is not the case for the Puruṣas, because they are not modifications of the pradhāna; thus he says "and not" (na ca).
The sense is that since we, the individual souls (jīvas), have the nature of Being (sadrūpa), there is knowledge [of ourselves] when that [Being] is known. //8//
Because of its merging [into Brahman] during deep sleep.
"From what [reason]? means for what further reason.

The construction of the Sūtra is as follows: because of the scriptural teaching that in deep sleep the individual soul (jīva) merges even into its own Self, which is Being, it is indeed Being and Consciousness.
Just as this state of sleeping occurs, so too in deep sleep (suṣupti), when the name "he sleeps" (svapiti) applies, the person (puruṣa) becomes united with Being (sat) and attains oneness.
Even though there is oneness with Being, how is the application of the name [“sleeping”] possible?
To that, he says: “his own” (svam).
In this regard, he states what is well-known in the world: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
The meaning is: because one has gone into (*apīta*) one's own true self (*svam sadātmānam*), therefore [it is so].
He explains the purport of the scripture with the words beginning with "This" (*eṣa*).

How is the refutation of the Pradhāna established by this much? To this he says: "by its own word. Although the root *i*, which generally means "to go," can also mean "to dissolve" when preceded by a prefix, one might wonder how there can be a dissolution of the eternal individual soul (*jīva*). Anticipating this objection, he states that it occurs through the dissolution of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); thus, he mentions the adjuncts of the waking and dreaming states with the word "mind" (*manas*).
The functions of the senses and the mind are limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Through them, because of the connection between the Self and specific gross objects such as jars and the like, the Self perceives those sensory objects; having fallen into the delusion of identity with the body as a gross particularity, it wakes up under the designation of "the Universal" (*viśva*).

Being characterized by the mind which is the substratum for the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the waking state, it is designated as "the Radiant" (*taijasa*); while dreaming, perceiving the transformations of *māyā* aided by diverse impressions, it is that which is denoted by the word "mind" in the scriptural passage, "O dear one, that is the mind."
It comes to pass.

The meaning is that when both the gross and subtle adjuncts (upādhi) have ceased, because the specific conceits such as "I am a man" or "I am an agent" no longer exist, that Self is metaphorically designated as "dissolved.

Now, one might object that since the etymological explanation of the term "he sleeps" (svapiti) is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda), it is not necessarily literal; to this he replies with the word "yathā" (as).
This is the etymological derivation of the word *hṛdaya*:
because they lead (*nayanti*) the food that has been eaten after it has been liquefied and digest it (*jarayanti*), the waters themselves are the referent of the term *aśanāyā*.
Because it leads (*nayate*) the water that has been drunk and dries it up (*śoṣayati*), fire itself is *udanya*.
Here, the lengthening [of the vowel] is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
He says "thus" (*evam*) to indicate that this etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is likewise consistent with the facts.
And he says "not" (*na ca*) to show that this [derivation] is not tenable under the theory of *pradhāna* (primordial matter).
Anticipating the objection that the word *sva* (own) possesses the power to denote not only the self (*ātman*) but also what belongs to the self (*ātmiya*), he says: "If...
The meaning is that "embracing" (*saṃpariṣvaṅga*) by the conscious one—the Lord who is the reflected consciousness—refers to non-difference through the absence of the delusion of difference. //9//
Because of the commonality of destination. (BS 1.1.10)

Since the cognitions produced by the various Vedānta texts are generally concerned with a conscious cause, the meaning of the Sūtra—that the non-conscious cannot be the cause of the world—is stated by way of negative inference (vyatireka) in the passage beginning with "yadi tārkika... and ending with "na tv etat," where "anything else" refers to atoms and so forth.
"But not this" [refers to the conscious Brahman].
The meaning is that there would be a discrepancy in their respective cognitions. "Moving apart" (vipratiṣṭheran) means they would go forth in various directions, toward different quarters.
The vital breaths, such as sight and the rest, manifest according to their respective physical seats (golaka).

Immediately after the vital breaths (prāṇas) are the deities, such as the Sun and others, who are their sustainers; immediately after those are the "worlds" (lokas), which means the sense-objects, so called because they are perceived (lokyante).

Now, since the Vedāntas possess intrinsic authority (svataḥ-prāmāṇya) and thus each can independently determine its own meaning, what is the purpose of establishing a commonality of purport (gati-sāmānya)? To this he replies: "And great... (mahacca).

Regarding the fact that the Vedāntas’ status as a means of valid knowledge consists in their being the cause for the comprehension of a single [non-dual] reality— which serves to remove doubt— he provides an illustration with the words "the eye" (*cakṣuriti*).
Just as all eyes are the cause for the comprehension of a single form, and just as the ears are the cause for the comprehension of sound, and the nose and other senses are so for smell and the rest;
Thus, the meaning is that the uniformity of the purport of the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman is the cause for the firmness of their authority. //10//
And because it is so stated in scripture. (BS 1.1.11)

Having thus refuted the concordance of the Vedāntas with the non-conscious by means of such indicative marks as "seeing" (īkṣati), he now refutes it by means of words denoting a conscious being as well—namely, the Sūtra: "And because [it] is heard [to be so].
He explains the Sūtra with the words: "By its own word.
The word "all-knowing" (sarvavit) is the designator of that which is conscious (svasya cetanasya).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: since the Supreme Lord is omniscient—as established by the scriptural passage, "He who knows all, the knower of time, the controller of time, the possessor of qualities, the knower of all sciences," and "He is the omniscient cause"—the cause cannot be insentient.
He is the lord of the individual souls (jīvas), who are themselves the lords of their instruments.
He concludes the meaning of the section with the words, "Therefore... (tasmāt).
Considering that [qualities] such as vision, the self, and sound are likewise inappropriate for atoms and so forth, he says: "Or else, something else. (11)
The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of the repetition. (BS 1.1.12)
By restating what has preceded, he introduces the composition of the subsequent sūtras with the words "beginning with birth" (*janmādi*).
Since the first sūtra serves as the introduction to the entire treatise, it is said that [the discussion] begins from the sūtra concerning birth and so forth.

By refuting the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all Vedāntas with the effect (the world) or with non-sentient principles such as *pradhāna*, it has been explained that they have Brahman as their sole purport.

Therefore, since the subject matter of the first chapter has been completed, the question is: what is the reason for beginning the subsequent text? He says—*ucyate* (it is said)—that the reason is precisely the inquiry arising from the fact that in the Vedāntas, sentences concerning Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa*) and Brahman without attributes (*nirguṇa*) are found in abundance; therein, one must determine which sentence achieves its harmony (*samanvaya*) in the attributeless Brahman through the injunction for meditation on the qualified Brahman, and which achieves harmony directly in Brahman itself without any intention to convey attributes. Thus he says: *ucyate*.
Thus, summarizing the meaning of the statements regarding that which possesses qualities and that which is devoid of qualities, he says: "For it is of two forms.
The entire world is a modification consisting of name and form.
The meaning of the sentence is that its distinction consists in specific qualities such as having golden hair and beard.
He cites the passage beginning with "For where... and so forth:
in that state of ignorance, indeed, when duality is imagined as it were, then one, being this [self], sees another; thus the object appears as something characterized by the adjunct of the visible.

At that time when, for the wise one, the entire world has become nothing but the Self (*ātman*) at the moment of realization, then—by virtue of the rhetorical challenge "who would see whom by what?"—the reality free of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika-tattva*) shines forth.
When the wise one is certain of the *bhūman* (the Infinite), he perceives no second thing whatsoever; that non-dual *bhūman* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*).
Now, immediately after the description of the attributeless, the one with attributes (*saguṇa*) is described.
Where one abides in that which possesses qualities, there one perceives a second; that is limited and finite.
But that which is the Plenum (bhūman) is immortal and eternal.
Now, [the word] "atha" [is used].
This is to be explained as before.

The Wise One is the Supreme Self alone; having fashioned all forms and created names, He enters into the intellect and other faculties, abiding there under the designation of the individual soul (jīva) and engaging in worldly activity. Though one knows Him who possesses qualities (saguṇa) as being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), one becomes immortal.
That from which parts (kalā) or portions have departed is "partless" (niṣkala).
Therefore, due to being partless, it is "actionless" (niṣkriya);
consequently, it is "quiescent" (śānta) and immutable.

"Niravadya" means free from faults such as passion (*rāga*) and the like. "Nirañjana" means free from "añjana"—that is, free from the connection with fundamental darkness (*mūlatamas*) or [the cycle of] *dharma* and so forth.

Furthermore, it is the supreme (*parama*), most excellent (*utkṛṣṭa*) bridge (*setu*) to immortality (*amṛta*), that is, to liberation (*mokṣa*), because it abides in the state of mental modification (*vṛtti*) arising from its own words, and thus, like a worldly bridge, it is the means of attainment.

Just as a fire is extinguished when its fuel is burnt, so too, having burnt away ignorance and that which is born of it, one should know the Self to be tranquil and devoid of qualities; this is the meaning.
"Not this, not this" has already been explained.
It is devoid of duality such as the gross and so forth.
Regarding the two forms, he cites scripture: "deficient," etc.
That which is the locus of duality—the deficient, limited, qualified form—is other than the unqualified [Brahman].

Thus, it is complete, devoid of attributes (nirguṇa), and distinct from that which possesses attributes (saguṇa); this is the meaning. To the objection that it is contradictory for a single entity to have two forms, he says: "by means of knowledge" (vidyā). That which is the object of knowledge is the knowable, whose attributelessness is real; that which is the object of ignorance is the object of meditation, whose possession of attributes is imagined. Thus, there is no contradiction.
Therein, he explains the scope of ignorance with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

For the sake of knowledge devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa-jñāna*), meditations (*upāsanā*) directed toward various specific fruits are enjoined by relying on the superimposed phenomenal world (*āropita-prapañca*) prior to its sublation (*bādha*), according to the maxim of the "sugarcane on the tongue.

Since their primary fruit is knowledge through the medium of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*), it should be understood that even the great purport (*mahātātparya*) of those scriptural passages lies in Brahman.
For meditations such as "Brahman is name," the fruit is prosperity consisting of acting according to one's desires and so forth;

for meditations such as the "small [ether]," the fruit is prosperity consisting of acting according to one's desires and so forth; and for meditations such as the "small [ether]," the fruit is gradual liberation.
The distinction is that the fruit of meditations such as the Udgītha is the successful accomplishment of ritual action;
this is because these meditations are purely mental and are internal auxiliaries to knowledge.
The sense is that this is the injunction regarding the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa).
Now, an objection is raised: "Since the Brahman to be meditated upon is one, how can there be a distinction among the meditations?
To this, he says: "Of these... (teṣām iti).
The specific qualities are those such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth;
the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are the heart and so forth.
Here, [the author] himself raises an objection and then resolves it with the word "one" (*eka*).

The sense is this: although there is no difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because there is a distinction between the forms of the objects of meditation as conditioned by their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is a difference among the meditations, and consequently, a difference in their fruits.
Whatever qualities people meditate upon that Supreme Self with—as they would a king—He possesses those very qualities for them; that is their fruit.
*Kratu* means resolve, intention, or meditation.
In this world, whatever kind of meditation one possesses, upon death one becomes of such a form as that which was meditated upon.

Regarding this very point, the Lord’s own statement is cited: "And from memory" (smṛteśca). Now, an objection is raised: since the Self is non-differentiated and without degrees among all beings, how can there be scriptural declarations concerning the relative gradation between the object of worship and the worshiper? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution: "Even though it is one," and so forth.

Due to the gradations of purity among the aforementioned limiting adjuncts (upādhis), there arise specific distinctions consisting of gradations in the powers (śaktis) whose nature is sovereignty, knowledge, and bliss.
Through these, it is heard in scripture that there is a gradation of manifestation for the Self—which is uniform in nature—progressively from humans up to Hiraṇyagarbha.

The meaning is that he who knows and worships the Self as its own true nature more fully—that is, more manifestly (āvistarām)—"attains that," as indicated by the suffix -tara (in the word *āvistarām*).

Thus, the meaning is that the self with a low-grade limiting adjunct (upādhi) is the worshipper, while the Lord with a high-grade limiting adjunct is the object of worship; therefore, this gradation based on limiting adjuncts is not contradictory.
Regarding this point, he cites the Bhagavadgītā as scriptural authority (smṛti).
In this context, it is stated that even the sun and other such entities are not to be meditated upon as the individual soul (*jīva*), but rather as the Lord (*īśvara*).
Regarding this, he cites the agreement of the author of the Sūtras with the words "evam" (thus). Here, "udaya" means non-connection.

Having stated that the composition of the subsequent sūtras begins in order to declare that a sentence in which a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is intended to be expressed is devoted to meditation (*upāsana*), he says "In this way,
immediately," etc., to establish the conclusion that a sentence in which [an adjunct] is not intended is devoted to the Brahman as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).
The sheaths beginning with the one made of food (*annamaya*) are specific limiting adjuncts.
The "course of the statement" (vākyagati) is its intended meaning (*tātparya*).
He concludes the justification for the undertaking [of the discussion] with the words, "Thus, even though it is one...
He states, "And that which... in order to establish the general principle of the course already stated as if it were an established fact (*siddhavat*).
Food is well known;
the vital breath, mind, and intellect take the form of Hiraṇyagarbha; and the reflection-consciousness is Īśvara, who is Bliss.

According to the Śruti, the ultimate truth is that the modifications of these five are the internal ones—the five sheaths (kośas) consisting of food and so forth, namely the body, vital breath, mind, intellect, and the individual soul (jīva).

In the preceding section, it was stated that because the figurative and primary senses of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) are not equal, there is no doubt [regarding which sense applies], and thus the occurrence of a figurative term in the context (*prāyapāṭha*) is not determinative. Now, since the suffix *mayaṭ* has both primary senses—denoting a modification (*vikāra*) and abundance (*prācurya*)—there arises a doubt. In this case of doubt, because the occurrence of the word in the context of modification is more frequent, one might conclude that the subject of the section on bliss (*ānandādhikāra*), the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), is the individual soul (*jīva*). To address this counter-example, the proponent states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) preceded by the inquiry: "What, then, [is the conclusion]? (beginning with *kim iti*).
He asks for the reason for taking the term *ānandamaya* in its non-primary sense with the words "Why?
He states the reason based on its inclusion in a series primarily consisting of modifications with the words "beginning with *annamaya*.
The connections with the Śruti and other authorities are indeed clear.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), according to the opinion of the Vṛttikāra, the fruit is the attainment of "the pleasant" and so forth through the meditation on the individual soul (*jīva*);
however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is the meditation on Brahman—this is the distinction. He raises an objection with the words: "But even so... (*athāpi*).
He refutes [the objection] with the words "it would not be so. He explains what was summarized with the word "primary";
the meaning is "the Supreme Self" (paramātman).

To the objection, "Even if it possesses a body, why could it not be the Lord (Īśvara)? he says, "And not... The meaning is that its status as a living soul (jīvatva) would be unavoidable. Now, having raised the doubt—"Even with the repetition of the word 'bliss' (ānanda), how can the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) be Brahman?"—in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma [he replies]:

Just as the term *jyotiṣpada* refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, so too the term *ānandamaya* occurring in the context of the *ānandamaya* section refers to the *ānandamaya* itself; intending that its repetition serves as the proof for its being Brahman, he says:
"having introduced the *ānandamaya*."
*Rasa* means essence;
that is to say, bliss.
This is the world.
Even though this space is full of bliss, if it were not the impeller of the witness, then who else could move,
or who could distinguish, breathe, or live? Therefore, it is this very [space] that causes bliss.
The meaning is "he causes to rejoice.

This is the present investigation into the gradations of bliss, beginning with the bliss of human youths—as will be described in the passage starting with "He should be young, a youth who is virtuous," and ending with the bliss of Brahman.
According to the view of certain partial authorities (ekadeśins), the meaning of the verb *upasaṃkrāmati* is that the knower "attains" [the bliss].

In the primary doctrine, however, it should be understood that the "transference" of the wise consists in the dissolution of the sheaths (kośas) into their state as being merely the Self (pratyag-mātratva).
The remainder has already been explained.
He says, "And in another scriptural passage," for the purpose of establishing the uniformity of the path—that the comprehension of Brahman through the word "bliss" (ānanda) is the same everywhere.
Thinking that there is a sublation [of the Self] due to the proximity of the non-primary [Self] indicated by the gender, he says: "Not that one.

Anticipating the objection that being the innermost of all is not heard in scripture, he explains that because nothing else is mentioned beyond it, it is the innermost of all: "The primary," and so on. "The worldly understanding," etc.
The meaning is that it follows its coarse apprehension.
Just as copper takes the form of a crucible, the vital breath (prāṇa) takes the form of the body; this is its similarity with the body.
Likewise, the mind takes the form of the vital breath and is equal to it; thus he says "by the former."
The previous limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), which was the sheath of consciousness (*vijñānakośa*), produced the conceptualization of having parts;
thus, the two marks—namely, "being embodied" because it is known by the body—are weak.

Therefore, the sense is that due to the absence of such auxiliary factors, the proximity of the modification (*vikāra*) is set aside by the two qualities of repetition (*abhyāsa*) and being the innermost of all (*sarvāntaratva*). //12//
If it be argued that [the Self] is not [denoted by the word "Brahman"] because of words denoting modification, we say no, because of abundance. (BS 1.1.13)

Anticipating the objection that the suffix *mayaṭ* heard here must signify a modification (*vikāra*), he states "In the case of modification," etc., to show that this is not so, because *mayaṭ* is also prescribed in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*).

The meaning of the rule is: "The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs after a word standing in the nominative case (*tat-prathamā-samarthāt*) when there is to be an expression (*vacane*) of something currently under discussion (*prakṛta*) as characterized by abundance. Thus, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied when abundance is implied.

In this context, by the inclusion of the word "vacana" (statement), the predominance and distinction of the subject under discussion are established, because such a usage of the suffix *mayaṭ* is attested in the world,
as in the expression "the sacrifice consists primarily of food" (*annamayo yajñaḥ*).

For here, the word *anna* (food) signifies abundance, as it is used in the sense "there is plenty of food in this," being capable of the nominative case; therefore, the suffix *mayaṭ* is seen to denote the abundance of the food which is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) of the sacrifice, and not merely the base itself—this is how it should be understood. //13//
And because there is a designation of that [Brahman] as the cause. (BS 1.1.14)
Considering that the word "ca" (and) in the Sūtra has the sense of including what has not been mentioned, he explains it with the words "itaśca" (for this reason also).
And that which was not mentioned—the ascertainment of the unsurpassable nature of the bliss of Brahman—was stated previously. //14//
And it is proclaimed as being based precisely on the wording of the mantras. (BS 1.1.15)
Having stated the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is Brahman, he states the context (*prakaraṇa*):
"Because it is thus the subject under discussion, therefore that very Brahman mentioned in the mantra-text (*māntravarṇika*) is celebrated in the sentence 'consisting of bliss' (*ānandamaya*).
[Objection: But what is the insistence that only that which is stated in the mantra should be accepted here?
Regarding this, he says:
"The mantra is the means because it consists of the explanation of the mantra for the sake of the Brahmin; the mantra, however, is the goal."
This has been stated as "because there is no contradiction";
the meaning is that these two stand in the relationship of means and end.
To the objection that, in that case, even the [selfs] consisting of food and so forth would possess the nature of Brahman based on the description in the mantras, he says: "And not..."
Furthermore, the Bhṛgu-vallī, which was proclaimed to Bhṛgu and taught by Varuṇa, culminates in bliss (ānanda) at the fifth stage.
By the principle of location, he states that the Brahma-vallī, which has the same subject matter, culminates in the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), saying: "It culminates in this alone. (15)
Not the other, because it is not possible.
That Lord performed austerity, which means he engaged in contemplation regarding creation;
"abhidhyāna" means desire. "May I become many"—this is the non-differentiation [of the Self from the world]. //16//
And because there is a designation of difference. (BS 1.1.17)
In the context of the section [on the Self], that essence consists of bliss.

Now, one might ask: "Even in the absence of the distinction between the attainer and the object to be attained, why should there not be non-difference? To this he says: "For it is not merely the attained [object]."

One might raise the objection: "If there must necessarily be a distinction between the non-attainer and the one to be attained, then there would be a contradiction with the Śruti and Smṛti. This is the sense of the question, "How [could that be]?
The connection is as follows: since it has been stated by you, "Because of this," how then could there be no contradiction with the Śruti and Smṛti?
He accepts the raised objection, saying, "Certainly."

One might object that, since there is no difference [between the self and the knower], the statement that the Self is attained by the Self through itself is contradicted; anticipating this, he says "even so" (*tathāpi*) to show that there is no contradiction because the difference is merely imagined.
The meaning is "even though there is non-difference";
it refers to a worldly delusion.

The meaning is that, due to the delusion born of one's own ignorance regarding the Self—which is non-different from the body and so forth—the statement that the Supreme Self is an object of knowledge arises from the error of perceiving duality.

It is "to be sought" (anveṣṭavya) in the sense of being known as distinct from the body and other such things; it is "to be attained" through the knowledge of discrimination, meaning it is to be directly realized.
For that purpose, it is to be heard;
and since "knowing" (vijñāna) refers to profound reflection (nididhyāsana) or direct realization (sākṣātkāra), there is no tautology because this restates the meaning of another Vedic text.
[Objection: But let it be that difference is indeed real.
Regarding this, he says: "It is denied.

If it is argued that there is no individual soul (*jīva*) as a seer distinct from this Lord (*īśvara*), then because of the difference [between them], even the Lord would be false; therefore, he says: "The Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*).
Since the Lord is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and exists separately from the individual soul—which is a conceptual construct as a reflection of ignorance (*avidyā*)—He is not false.

Regarding the point that although the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is non-different from the imagined (*kalpita*), the substrate is nevertheless different from it, he states an illustrative example with the word "just as" (*yathā*).

[The author] says "or just as" (*yathā vā*) to provide another example for the falsity of mere non-difference, out of dissatisfaction with the view that the thread mounted on the rope is false even in itself, whereas the individual soul (*jīva*) is not.
[Objection: But surely, on the strength of the Sūtra, difference is real; to this he says: "And such [as this]"—the meaning is that it is merely imagined.
This is because there is no word in the Sūtra stating that "difference is real."
The intention is that this is also because the sūtras beginning with "tadananyatvam" (the non-difference from that) follow the Śruti. //17//
And because it is based on desire, there is no dependence upon inference. (BBs 1.1.18)

"Surely, let the *pradhāna*, which consists predominantly of *sattva* whose nature is bliss, be that which is 'consisting of bliss' (*ānandamaya*"); to this he replies: "And because of desire" (*kāmācca*).
That which is to be understood through inference is the "inferential" (*ānumānika*).
Anticipating the objection of tautology, he says: "Because of seeing" (īkṣateḥ) //18//
And in this [context], he teaches its application to this [state]. (BBs 1.19)

The construction is as follows: since it teaches the union of the individual soul (jīva)—who possesses the awakening whose object is that which consists of bliss (ānandamaya)—with that [bliss] by means of the locative case "in this" (*asmin*), which denotes the object, it cannot be the Pradhāna.
To the objection that the individual soul also has a connection with the Pradhāna, he says: "as its self" (*tadātmanā*).
To the objection that the individual soul has identity with the individual soul, he says: "liberation" (*muktiḥ*).
In that which is invisible, devoid of the gross phenomenal world,

free from the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra)— which is the self's own nature consisting of mere connection to the self— and distinct from that which can be designated by words; in that which is other than such [objects].

The meaning is as follows: *nilayana* is that place of total dissolution, which is *māyā*; when this wise one attains a firm, excellent state of the mind within the Brahman that is void of that [māyā], such that there is fearlessness (*abhaya*), then at that very moment he attains the fearless Brahman.
Furthermore, the construction is: "As soon as this person perceives even the slightest (*aram*) interval (*antara*)—that is, even a minute difference—then at that moment he has fear."

He refutes the opinion of the author of the *Vṛtti* with the words "But this... (*idaṃ tu*). The syntactical connection is as follows: since the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*) is present here in the opponent's interpretation, it must be explained how—without any cause and quite arbitrarily—the same *mayaṭ* occurring within a single context can be taken to mean "modification" at the beginning and "abundance" (*prācurya*) at the end; for by what analogy could such a "half-old-woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) approach be resorted to? This is what must be stated.
Having considered the question, it is suspected that "māntra" [is the answer]. The response is clear:
it is not heard [in the text] as "kimāntara" (what is internal).
Alternatively, having raised the doubt as to whether Brahman is not heard of even as something internal in reality, he accepts the first alternative, saying: "To this it is replied: although...

He states "nevertheless" because of the scriptural mention of the suffix *-maya* supported by its occurrence in a context primarily dealing with modifications (*vikāra*), and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of having parts.
That which arises from the sight of a desired object is "pleasure" (*priya*).
Joy arises from mindfulness;
that joy, when intensified through the absence of fear, is supreme delight (pramoda);
bliss (ānanda), however, is the cause.
The meaning of the Śruti is that the Self is the consciousness within the image (bimba-caitanya), which is the pure Brahman situated between the head and the tail;
he states the second [point] with the words "therein, that which... (tatra yad iti).
That Brahman which is the subject under discussion in the mantra— as being hidden in the cave and situated within all—

is recognized here in the statement concerning the "tail" by virtue of the word "Brahman. It is precisely for the purpose of making that very Brahman known that the cave, in the form of the five sheaths, has been elaborated upon.
It was stated that they are postulated [as supports] because there is no intended meaning (tātparya) in them regarding that [support].

Thus, the meaning is that when the sentence concerning the tail is devoted to Brahman—which is the subject under discussion and the primary topic—there is no fault such as the abandonment of the subject matter (prakṛtahāni).
One raises an objection, saying "But surely," [arguing] that Brahman’s status as the primary topic is contradicted by the scriptural mention of a "tail."
In this context, since the word "Brahman" (brahman) brings about the recognition of the Brahman under discussion as the primary subject, a conflict arises with the word "tail" (puccha).

Considering that within a single sentence, between two words heard at the beginning and at the end, the first—which has not yet encountered any contradiction—is stronger, and thus the status of being a subordinate quality (guṇatva) implied by the word "tail" must be set aside, he says: "Because it is the subject under discussion" (prakṛtatvāt).

He states the alternative possibility for this [interpretation] with the words "Now, an objection... (*nanu*). He says, "To this it is replied" (*atrocyate*), because the status of being both a member (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) is contradictory for one and the same thing.

In that regard, in order to remove the contradiction, he says, "By one or the other," meaning that if Brahman is accepted in either one of the two sentences, then Brahman must be accepted in the sentence concerning the tail (*puccha*).

And he says "also" (api ca) because it is so from the remainder of the sentence; the meaning is that there is also a verse regarding that Brahman. He asks for the interpretation of the word "tail" (puccha): "But how [is this]? (kathaṃ punar iti).
Even for you, the primary meaning of the word "tail" (puccha) cannot be asserted,
because Brahman lacks the nature of being a tail consisting of bliss (ānandamaya). Furthermore, when the term "tail" is used figuratively, it is more appropriate that it signifies its locus (ādhāra).
This is because [the term] attains its etymological basis through the application of the word *pratiṣṭhā*, and because the word *brahman* thereby acquires its primary meaning;
furthermore, in your own position, the word *brahman* would also have to indicate a mere part [of the whole]. To this he replies: "This is not a fault."
By the word "puccha" (tail), mere substratum-ness is expressed. "Pratiṣṭhā" (foundation) means having a single nest;
that is to say, there is one primary nest or locus for the world together with its material cause.
Now, one might object: "The commentators themselves accept that the Taittirīya passage is connected with Brahman;
so why do you cite it here as being non-different [from Brahman]? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "Moreover" (*apica*).

Since there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that wherever there is possession of attributes (*saviśeṣatva*), there is the state of being within the range of speech and mind, he says, "non-different" (*nirviśeṣam*), meaning that by stating the absence of the pervader (*vyāpakābhāva*) here, the attributeless nature is expressed.
The meaning is that they turn back because they are incapable.
Since that which possesses distinctions is false, the state of fearlessness is also untenable.
Therefore, the intention is that the sentence concerning the tail alone is the illustrative example for the sake of attaining non-distinctive knowledge.

By the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*), it was stated that there is a sublation of the scriptural texts concerning the featureless (*nirviśeṣa*) when there is a qualified statement (*saviśeṣokti*).
He states another defect with the words "Furthermore" (*api ca*).
Since abundance is the primary meaning of the suffix, the meaning of the stem (*prakṛtyartha*) is its qualifier.

That which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of a distinction—that is, its opposite—requires a smallness [of that correlate]; for example, in the expression "a village consisting mostly of Brahmins," there is a smallness of Śūdras.
Let it be so; what is the fault?
To this he replies: "And thus...
This fault does not arise when the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is predominant; for in the expression "the sun is abundant light," even a slight darkness is not perceived.
However, one should consider that there would be the defect of [the term] *ānandamaya* having the characteristic of "abundant bliss" (*pracurānanda*).
Furthermore, because it is distinct [from Brahman], it cannot be Brahman, just like a pot; thus he says: "in every body.
Now, if it is argued that the word *ānanda*, being repeated, indicates the *ānandamaya* by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and thus the repetition is established, he says: "And if..."

The sense is this: if it were already determined that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is Brahman, then the repetition would be established by knowing that the word "bliss" refers to that [Brahman]; and once that [repetition] is established, its determination [as Brahman] would follow—thus there would be a circular argument (*parasparāśraya*).
He states that this repetition refers to the Brahman that is the tail: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).
"Approaching" (*upasaṃkramaṇa*) means "attaining.

One might object: "But surely, by beginning with the knower of Brahman in the words 'He who knows thus' and then indicating the fruit through the statement regarding approaching, that [fruit] would not be established if he were not Brahman?"—this is the doubt expressed by the word "nanu.

Accepting that "approaching" means "attainment," [the author] replies "This is not so," stating that by the mention of the attainment of the qualified [Brahman], the fruit of attaining the qualifier is also stated.

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it is stated that through knowledge there is the sublation (*bādha*) of the sheaths; thus, the attainment of the innermost bliss (*pratyagānanda*), which is the limit of that sublation, is implied. This is made explicit by the following verse, as the author says:
"That too... [and] "...because of its dependence on that.
The meaning is: because its object is the Brahman that is the tail of the desirer.
Regarding what was stated—that the Brahmavallī is completed at the fifth station because it is in the Ānandamaya, as in the case of the Bhṛguvallī—he says: "As for that which... [yattv iti].
The meaning is "but that which...
The intention is that the [notion of] location is sublated by the direct mention of the suffix *mayaṭ* and by such indicative marks as having parts (*sāvayavatva*).
"Transcending the range" (*gocarātikrama*) means the absence of being an object of perception (*gocaratvābhāva*).

He says "the Sūtras" [in the phrase] "sūtrāṇi," meaning that when there is a conflict between the Veda and the Sūtras, one must interpret the Sūtras otherwise according to the principle "but where there is no subordinate quality, an improper assumption [is not to be made].
Previously, it was stated by the reasoning that "because of the prior mention of seeing, there is no doubt" that the context of the majority of readings (*prāyapāṭha*) is not determinative.

Now, however, since the word "tail" (*puccha*) can equally denote either a support or a limb through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is a doubt; therefore, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—lacking the reasoning for the conclusion of the previous section—that the context of the majority of readings determines [the meaning], based on the word "tail."
And thus, there is a connection by way of a counter-example:
in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the fruit is meditation on the qualified [Brahman], whereas in the final conclusion (siddhānta), the fruit is the realization of the unqualified [Brahman].
The connections with the Śruti and other sources are indeed clear from the statement regarding the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts.
By the term *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) in the Sūtra, the word *brahman* found in that passage is indicated.
That by which something is modified is a "modification" (*vikāra*), namely, a limb or part.
"Prāyāpatti" means the attainment of the sequence of parts in the intellect; for here,
the sheaths (kośas) are conceived as the limbs of a bird for the purpose of knowing the Brahman under discussion.
There is no intention [to convey] this here.

In that context, after the other limbs of the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) have been mentioned, when something must be stated as its "tail" (puccha), it is Brahman, which is the subject under discussion, that is denoted by the word "tail.
The meaning is that it must necessarily be stated as the substratum of the one consisting of bliss.
And because there is a designation of its cause. //14//
This is because that Brahman is designated as the cause of all effects.

Since the individual soul (jīva), consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), is an effect characterized by distinctions such as "dear" and so forth, it is not logical for Brahman to be subordinate to it; this is the meaning.
And it is precisely that which is described in the words of the mantra [that is celebrated here]. //15//

That Brahman, whose knowledge is said to lead to liberation in the passage "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and which is described in the mantra as "Truth, Knowledge," is celebrated right here in this sentence concerning the tail, because of its connection with the word "Brahman."
The meaning is that [the Self] consists of infinite bliss;
it cannot be either of the other two, because they are untenable. //16//
The other [interpretation], that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) here is the individual soul (*jīva*), is not to be accepted;
the meaning is that [in that case] the status of being the creator of all and so forth would be untenable.
And because there is a designation of difference. (Sūtra 1.1.17)

The meaning is that because of the statement of difference—namely, "this one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), having obtained the essence of Brahman (brahmarasa), becomes blissful"—it [the ānandamaya] is not what is being propounded [as Brahman].

Having raised the objection that the ānandamaya is Brahman because it is situated in the fifth place in the Taittirīyaka, just like the "bliss" (ānanda) situated in the Bhṛguvallī, he says: "And because of desire, there is no dependence on inference" (1.1.18).

The bliss of desire (*kāmānanda*) is so called because it is desired; since the fifth [sheath] in the *Bhṛguvallī* is seen as Brahman, there is no need for an inference that the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is also Brahman, because that would contradict the suffix *mayaṭ*, which signifies a modification (*vikāra*).

Having raised the objection that, due to the mention of difference, the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahman*) must be what is to be known here, he says: "And [the scripture] teaches its union with this [self] in this [state]. (Sūtra 1.1.19)

Since the one described as "that one" (sa ekaḥ) is concluded as being within the inner self (pratīci) by virtue of being hidden in the cave, and since the scripture beginning with "for when" (yadā hi) teaches the attainment of the state of Brahman for the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya)—who possesses the realization "I alone am the supreme Brahman" regarding the Brahman declared in the "tail" passage—it follows that the mention of the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) is for the purpose of knowing the identity with the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇabrahma). With this intention, he says: "The others also... (1.1.19).
[The Self] is within [the body], because there is instruction regarding its attributes [there]. (BS 1.1.20)
"Because of the teaching of His attributes within [the heart].
He cites the passage from the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "Now, he who...
Here, the word "now" (*atha*) signifies the commencement of the meditation (*upāsti*).
The golden one is a transformation of light;
though the Puruṣa is all-pervading, he is seen by the practitioners as possessing a form.
He describes that form: "golden," and so forth.
"Pranakhah" means the tip of the nail; the prefix "ā" in "ā-pranakhāt" is used in the sense of inclusion (abhividhi). He specifies a particular quality of his eyes with the word "tasya":

the "āsah" (tail-end) of a monkey (kapih/markaṭasya) is exceedingly radiant, and his two eyes are like that lotus (puṇḍarīkam)—meaning they are as luminous as a lotus that has just blossomed and is red. This is the meaning.
Having stated the solar orb as the locus for the purpose of worship and having described its form, he provides its name: "Its [name] is 'ud'. He then etymologically explains that name: "He (sa)."
"Udita" means risen;
the meaning is that he is untouched by all evil.
He states the result of ignorance regarding his name: "He rises and sets."

Immediately after stating that the meditation concerns Āditya as the abode of the deity, he says "Now" (atha) to indicate that the same meditation is also stated with reference to the self, namely the body. Just as in the previous case, where the determination of the Nirguṇa was reached by virtue of many authorities—such as the word *brahman*, the word *ānandamaya*, and the repetition of the word *ānanda*—here, by virtue of many authorities such as its having form (*rūpavattva*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is set forth to provide an exception (*apavāda*) to the previously established general rule of the Nirguṇa concordance, following the analogy of the previous example: "The golden one is the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus he says: "The transmigrating soul... (*saṃsārī*).
In this context, the fruit of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final (uttarapakṣa) positions is the meditation on the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman respectively.
Furthermore, because of the mention of the eyes as the locus (*akṣiṇī*), the connection is that [the object of meditation] is the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*).
He cites the scripture: "This very one... (*sa eṣa*).
The Person abiding in the sun is the lord of whatever worlds there are above that sun, as well as of the enjoyments of the gods;
this same Person abiding in the eye is the lord of those worlds which are below this eye.
Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that he is the lord of those enjoyments which are human desires;
therefore, from this scriptural statement, the sense is that [the Self] is subject to transmigratory existence.
The connection is: "from the scriptural statement without qualification, 'He is the Lord of all.'"
Yama, the lord of beings, and Indra and the others who are the guardians of beings, are indeed this very one. Furthermore,

just as a dam is that which holds back waters so that they do not intermingle in the world, so too is he alone the "dam" (setu) because he is the cause of the boundaries for these worlds, such as the castes and stages of life.
Therefore, the meaning is that he is the Lord of all.
He explains the Sūtra with the words "He who is this...
Although, within a single sentence, the latter part should be interpreted in accordance with what was heard first, [the following applies].
Nevertheless, in this context, the quality of possessing form mentioned first is fruitless and could be attributed to Īśvara for the sake of meditation; however,
freedom from all evil and attachment, as well as oneness with the Self of all, are fruitful.
And it is powerful because the individual soul (jīva) cannot be led [to the world of Brahman].
Nor should it be argued that, based on the Śruti statement, "Indeed, evil does not reach the gods," the solar jīva is likewise untouched by evil;

for the purport of that Śruti passage concerns the fact that the gods—who are currently ineligible for ritual action—have no connection with the evil being performed [at that time], or rather, that they do not experience its fruit.

Intending to show that it is impossible [for them] as long as their accumulated sins have not ceased and their merit is not exhausted—expressed in the words, "they enter the world of mortals"—he says: "And the departure from all evil belongs to the Supreme Self alone.
He states the state of universal identity with the word "likewise" (tathā).
Here, by the pronouns "that" (tat), the Person seen in the eye is referred to.
The change in gender is in relation to the *ṛc* and other [Vedic meters].
An *uktha* is a specific type of recitation (*śastra*);
by association with that, the *sāman* is a hymn of praise (*stotra*).
A *śastra* other than the *uktha* is called *ṛc*;
the *yajurveda* is *yajuḥ*;
"Brahman" means the three Vedas—this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "consisting of earth, fire, and so forth":

the Ṛg-veda, from the perspective of the deities (*ādhidaivata*), is said by the Śruti to be fivefold, consisting of the white forms located in the earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the stars, and the sun;
and the Sāman is likewise said to be fivefold, consisting of the extremely black forms located in fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the sun.

Internally, however, the *Ṛg* is fourfold, consisting of speech, sight, hearing, and the white light-form situated in the eye; and the *Sāman* is also said to be fourfold, consisting of breath, shadow, the self (ātman), and the mind, which is the extremely dark blue form situated in the eye.
Having thus sequentially enumerated the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*, the Śruti says "of that" (*tasya*).

The meaning is that those two joints which are the *geṣṇas* (limbs) consisting of the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* belonging to that [Self] residing in the sun, are themselves the two joints (*parvaṇī*) of the one residing in the eye.
"And that" means the state of having the *Ṛk*, *Sāman*, and *Geya* as its essence.
He states another indicative mark for its being sung by all singers: "Now, those... etc.
In that regard, "in the world," those who possess the acquisition of wealth are "dhanasanayaḥ"; the meaning is that they are possessed of prosperity.
[Objection: But in the world, kings are praised, not the Lord; therefore, he says "whatever...":
"whatever" refers to prosperity such as cattle and wealth, and "glory" (śrī) refers to splendor.

Vigor (*ūrjitatva*) is strength; the meaning is that the *sattva*, *rajas*, and so forth endowed with that [vigor] are merely portions of me, and therefore their manifestation belongs to the Lord alone.
"Unrestrained" (*niraṅkuśam*) means not dependent on anything else.
The meaning is that this form of manifold appearance is "māyā" because it is a transformation of māyā, and has been created by me.
This is stated [in the scripture] with the passage beginning "without sound," etc.; and he says "moreover" (api ca) to show that this statement refers to that which is to be known (the Brahman).
If so, from where does the form arise?
Regarding this, he says "all" (*sarva*).

Having supplied the word "where" (*yatra*) [from the previous context], the construction is as follows: where [the Lord] is spoken of as the object of meditation, there His possession of form is established on account of His being the cause of all, and is indicated by such scriptural passages as "possessing all actions" (*sarvakarmā*).
He refutes the claim that the Lord's sovereignty is limited by saying "sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*).

The meaning is that the distinction between meditation on the internal self (*adhyātma*) and meditation on the divine (*adhidaivata*), as well as their separate practice, is intended solely for that purpose [of mastery], and not for the sake of delimiting sovereignty. //20//
And [the Self] is distinct [from the individual soul] because of the designation of difference. (BS 1.1.21)

An objection is raised: "Since the injunction for meditation is made with reference to the object of meditation, it must be stated that the agent of the enjoined action and the object [of that action] are established from another source, just as in the case of rice and other grains. Anticipating this, he says "bhedā" (due to difference). He states the meaning of the Sūtra—"asti" (He exists)—to show that because the difference between Āditya, the individual soul (jīva), and the Lord is mentioned in another Śruti, the Lord is established as distinct from the individual soul. To exclude the rays residing in Āditya, he says "ādityād antaraḥ" (within Āditya); and to exclude the individual soul, he says "yam" (whom).
"How can there be the status of a controller for one who is bodiless?
To this he says: "Of whom...
He states the meaning of the term *antaryāmin* (inner ruler): "He who..."
To refute the notion that it is not the Self, he says: "This is your [Self]" (eṣa ta ātmā). The meaning is: "This is your own essential nature.
The sense is that this is because the scriptural teaching regarding its being within the sun is the same for both.
Therefore, it is established that the Supreme alone is to be meditated upon in the Udgītha, which has the sun and other such things as its locus. //21//
It is space, because of its characteristic mark. (BS 1.1.22)

Let it be that weak indicative marks (liṅga) such as "possessing form" are set aside by the non-deviating brahman-indicative marks such as "untouched by evil. However, in this case, the scriptural mention (śruti) of the word "ether" (ākāśa) is stronger than the indicative mark; thus, having reached the prima facie view through this counter-example, he replies: "The ether [is Brahman], because of its indicative marks.
He cites the Chāndogya passage: "This... and so forth.
The Brahmin Śālāvatya asks King Jaivali,
"What is the support of this world of earth and of all other things?
The king replies, "It is space (ākāśa)."
The distinction is as follows: in the passage "That which is this space," it is determined that space is Brahman because of the hearing of bliss, which is its unique attribute;
whereas in the passage "Space, indeed, by name," it is so determined because of the supplementary statement "that is Brahman. Thus has it been established.
Name-and-form are the cause of arising and persistence; they are that which,
when divided, exists within.
Alternatively, the meaning is that they exist in the middle because they are conceptualized as such.
Regarding the *akṣa* [the syllable "a"]: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is meditation on the *udgītha* as the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*);
in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is as Brahman; this is the result.

Since the reconciliation (*samanvaya*) of passages containing clear marks of Brahman (*spaṣṭabrahmaliṅga*) has been stated regarding the object of worship (*upāsya*), the connections with scripture and so forth (*śrutyādisaṃgati*) apply up to this point.
Here, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is clear:
because air (*vāyu*) and the rest are also causes of fire (*tejas*) and the other elements, there is a sublation of the scriptural mention of the word "only" (*evakāra*).
He says, "It is true that it has been shown," because otherwise there would be a restriction of all scriptural testimony (*śruti*) to objects other than space (*ākāśa*).
The intention is that since Brahman is the self of all, the scriptural statement, "From that alone everything [arises]," is logical.
Likewise, [Brahman's] being the substratum of the dissolution of all things [is established].
He states that "supreme greatness" and "being the ultimate support even during its persistence" are clear marks (liṅga) of Brahman by the passage beginning with "likewise, space," etc.;
[the term] "rāti" refers to the giver of wealth.
In the reading "rātriḥ," the meaning is "friend.
He states another indicative mark with the words "api ca" (and also).
Three individuals—the two Brahmins Dālbhya and Śālāvatya and the King—being experts in the Udgītha-vidyā, deliberated together.

"What is the ultimate resort of the *udgītha*? In this regard, Śālāvatya, having criticized the position of Dālbhya— that heaven itself is the ultimate resort of the *udgītha* performed by means of life-force (*prāṇa*) and the waters that have come from heaven— on the grounds of its lack of a firm foundation, [states that] even for heaven, this [earth] is the cause by way of ritual action (*karman*).
"The world is its foundation," he said.
Having criticized that position of Śālāvatya with the words, "Indeed, your Sāman, O Śālāvatya, is finite," the King speaks of the infinite space (ākāśa) alone;
the meaning is that if the elemental space (bhūtākāśa) were intended, the defect of finitude would remain as it was.
Anticipating the objection that "surely it has not been heard that space is infinite," he says: "And that.

The point is that because the *udgītha* is identified with space (*ākāśa*) through the process of meditative superimposition (*saṃpādana*), its infinity and other qualities do not belong to it inherently;
rather, they belong to that syllable *oṃ*, which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*.
This [Self] consists of space,
is supreme, and is superior to other imperishables (akṣara) because it is preeminent through qualities such as being the most excellent essence (rasatama).
The meaning is "the best. Alternatively, *paraḥ* is an indeclinable ending in *s*, as seen in the usage *paraḥ kṛtsnam*.
And this is "parovarīyān," meaning it is more excellent than the most excellent; that is,
it is superior because of its preeminence.
He recalls what was stated—that the word "ether" (ākāśa) is stronger because of its being directly heard—by saying "yat punar" ("as for that which...").

He states, "To this we reply," indicating that it is proper to set aside a single scriptural statement according to the maxim "one may sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family," in order to favor the many indicative marks such as infinity and so forth, which are supported by the words "only" (eva) and "all" (sarva).
