Furthermore, the particle "api" (also/even) indicates that there is no fixed rule that the element [ether] must be understood first from the word "ākāśa."
Regarding this, he states the reasoning: "And it has been shown.
The sense is that even Brahman, as a secondary (gauṇa) meaning of the word "ākāśa," is first apprehended, because of the frequent usage of that word and its synonyms for Brahman.
In the imperishable, immutable, and ethereal space, the Ṛg-verses and the Vedas exist;
the meaning is that in this imperishable, all the gods are established as the source of authority.
One should meditate upon the syllable Om as bliss (kaṃ), Brahman, and the pervasive ether (khaṃ).
He cites another scriptural usage: "The ancient ether" (*khaṃ purāṇam*). The meaning is that Brahman is all-pervading and beginningless.
This is from the *Chāndogya*: "Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman."
The distinction is that [the passage] "Oṃ, Khaṃ is Brahman, Khaṃ is ancient" belongs to the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Furthermore, in that very same context, the subsequent [passage] should be interpreted in accordance with the preceding one,
provided it is possible to do so.
Where it is impossible [to determine the meaning], there the first [passage] should be interpreted according to the subsequent one; thus he says: "vākya... (in the verse).
Therefore, he concludes that the sentence is consistent with Brahman as the object of meditation: "tasmāt" (therefore). //22//
For this very reason, he is Prāṇa. (BsRp_1,1.9.23)
He extends the logic stated in the passage concerning space to the subsequent passage: "For this very reason, [the word] *prāṇa* [is used].
The word "Udgītha" in the commentary is for the purpose of indicating that this belongs to the section on the Udgītha.
The syntactical connection is: "It is heard in the section on the Udgītha."
A certain seer, Cākrāyaṇa, said to the Prastotṛ priest: "O Prastotṛ,
which deity is to be meditated upon as accompanying the Prastāva section of the Sāman?"
"If you recite that before me, who am learned, without knowing it, your head shall fall off.
Then, being afraid, he asked: "Which deity is that?"
The answer is: "In breath.
This means that they enter into and dissolve completely with reference to the breath; they emerge and arise with reference to it.
He explains what was stated—that because this is an extended application (*atideśa*), the doubt and so forth are to be understood as being the same as before—by saying "prāṇa" and so on.
The individual soul (*jīva*), which has the mind as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), is bound by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is Brahman; during deep sleep, it becomes one with it.
The meaning is that those who know the Self—which impels the vital breath (the wind) and bestows existence and manifestation upon it—are the knowers of Brahman.
He raises the objection that, since the meaning has already been established by the preceding [sūtra], this separate sūtra is redundant: "But [it is] as before.
Considering that this sūtra of extended application (atideśa-sūtra) is intended to dispel a further doubt, he states the objection: "No;
even in the primary [case]."
In that case, the connection is to be understood everywhere in this manner: "the eye also goes there," and so forth.

Now, one might ask: since here the dissolution and emergence of the sense organs into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) are heard of, how is the consistency with the remainder of the passage—which teaches the dissolution into the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so on—established? To this, he says: "because [the senses] have the vital breath as their essence."
For there is the scriptural text: "This is indeed its essence.

The sense organs, which consist of the subtle body (liṅga-ātman), are the essences of the unevolved elements (apañcīkṛta-bhūtas); since it is established that the elements also dissolve into the vital breath (prāṇa) by virtue of the stated dissolution of those [organs], the consistency of the remainder of the passage is maintained—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, he states "Moreover" (api ca) to show that the vital breath is not Brahman because it is mentioned alongside non-Brahman entities.
When asked by the Udgātṛ and Pratihartṛ priests, "What is the deity in the Udgītha and the Pratihāra?", Cākrāyaṇa pointed out the sun and food, as the Śruti states:
"He said, 'The sun,'" and "He said, 'Food. This refers to their proximity as common factors.

The result of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, since the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is determined by the force of the first-occurring word "breath" (*prāṇa*) supported by its proximity (*saṃnidhi*), the meditation on the *prastāva* is performed through the perspective of that [primary breath]. In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the meditation consists of viewing it as Brahman.
The distinction is that this section is an extension (*atideśa*) of the previous one, and thus its connection with the preceding is precisely that of an extended application.

Having stated that, according to the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "they become" (*bhavanti*) as "beings" (*bhūtāni*), the dissolution and emergence of whatever possesses the nature of becoming—namely, the entire range of effects—is not tenable in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is a modification of air; he then says "even when" (*yadāpi*) to show that even if one accepts the conventional meaning (*rūḍhārtha*) of the word *bhūta*, it still serves to determine Brahman as the cause, because the elemental vital breath cannot be the source of origin (*bhūtayoni*) for the elements. This is the meaning.
The text raises a doubt regarding its being the source [of speech] by means of a scriptural passage, beginning with "Now, however" (*nanu*).

The meaning is that when the individual soul (*jīva*) is in deep sleep and becomes one with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is Brahman, then speech and the other senses, along with their objects, merge into this *prāṇa*.

To this, he replies: "Even there," stating that because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being the substratum for the dissolution of all things—which is not distinct from the individual soul—the *prāṇa* here is not the primary vital breath.
He says, "That is incorrect," because an indicative mark (*liṅga*) contained within its own sentence is stronger than the proximity of another sentence.
The meaning is: "vākyaśeṣa" refers to being part of a single syntactical unit; its "strength" is the indicative mark contained therein, and [the author speaks] by means of that.

By the restrictive particle "eva" (only) in the phrase "prāṇam eva," and by the indicative mark of being the source of all beings, he states that the word "prāṇa" indicates (*lakṣya*) Brahman as its cause, just as in the case of the word "ākāśa."
He states that the examples provided by the authors of the commentaries (*vṛttikṛt*) are untenable due to the absence of doubt, beginning with the words "In this case" (*atra*).
Having stated the difference between the words, he elaborates on the context with the words "And for whom" (*yasya ca*). //23//
[The word "light" refers to Brahman] because it denotes that which possesses feet. (BS 1.1.24)
"Because of the mention of the feet as light.
He cites the Chāndogya Upaniṣad itself with the words "this.
The word "atha" (now) is for the purpose of indicating the sequence following the meditation on Brahman through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Gāyatrī.
Therefore, that light which shines beyond the sky—that is, beyond the heavenly world—is superposed upon this very light, namely the digestive fire within the body.
Where does it shine? To this he says: "on all sides" (*viśvataḥ*).

"Above all classes of living beings" means above everything from the world of Bhūr onwards; "in those highest worlds" refers to those beyond which no higher exist (*anuttama*). The meaning is that [the Self] is the supreme reality situated within the body, transcending the entire sphere of saṃsāra.
Stating that this does not have the same meaning as the preceding verse, he provides a counter-example: "In another sense... (*arthāntareti*).

In this context, although there is no explicit mark (*liṅga*) of Brahman within its own sentence, there is the mark of being "a foot of him" in the preceding sentence; thus, there is a connection with the [previous] section (*pāda*).
The distinction between the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions lies in the fact that the fruit is the meditation upon either the insentient light or Brahman.
Now, one might object: since it is opposed to the darkness of ignorance, Brahman is also well-known as a denotation of the word "light" (*jyotis*).
"No," he says, "it is the eye.
That which exists in the night (*śarvarī*) is *śārvaram*;
that is to say, blue.
By this, it is stated by implication that darkness is a positive entity (bhāvarūpa), because it possesses the quality of obscuring and because it possesses form, like a wall.
He states the supporting indicative marks (liṅga) for the scriptural mention of light with the words "tathā" and so forth.
He says "na hi" [it is not so], meaning that radiance, which consists of luminous form, is indeed the indicative mark of fire alone.
Fearing that there might be no boundary [to the world], he says, "Beyond the sky," to show that such is not the case because it is so stated in the scripture;
the words "declare the boundary" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Someone objects that the Brāhmaṇa passage is useless, on the grounds that like Brahman, the effect (the world) also possesses a boundary—this objection is introduced with "But surely... (nanu).
The proponent of the partial view (ekadeśin) says: "Let it be so.
The meaning is that there exists some supersensible light produced in heaven and other realms beyond the sky, on the authority of the sacred scriptures (śruti).
Having raised the objection that, according to the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*), that which is a fruitless matter cannot be the subject matter (*artha*) of scripture, he says "No.
Anticipating the doubt that meditation (*dhyāna*) might be the fruit, he states "This very [thing]" and so forth, asserting that there is no meditation whatsoever for that which is fruitless.
Any other purpose refers to such things as the destruction of darkness (*tamonāśa*).

Having accepted that light (*tejas*) is not made tripartite (*atrivṛtkṛta*) and thus stated its lack of fruitfulness, he says "of those" (*tāsām*) to show that such [non-tripartite] light does not exist at all.

The meaning is: since it was stated without qualification—"having divided each one of these deities, namely light, water, and food, into two parts, and having again divided each of those portions into two, and having cast [each part] from its own portion into the other two portions, let me make them tripartite like a three-stranded rope"—there is nothing whatsoever that remains untripartitely composed.

Furthermore, in this context, by the word "yat" (that) in the phrase "yadataḥ paraḥ," the state of having heaven as its boundary—which is well-known from another source—is restated for the purpose of meditation.
He says "na ca" (and not), meaning that such a state of the non-tripartite [ether] is not well-known anywhere else.
Once the partial view has been refuted, the proponent of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣin) states directly: "Let it be then..."
The construction is as follows: a specific region, shining intensely beyond the sky, is a particular portion of the splendor of the sun and the Ādityas;
its "appropriation" for the purpose of meditation is not contradictory. That very [splendor] is meditated upon within the light of the belly.
The sense is that this is because it too possesses the nature of light (*tejas*).
One might suggest that even for Brahman, its location in a specific place should be postulated for the purpose of meditation;
to this he says, "But not... (*na tv iti*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: even though there is a distinction, it is not logical to postulate that a portion of Brahman is shining intensely beyond the sky, for that which is without spatial extension (*niṣpradeśa*) and without parts (*niravayava*).
The sense is that this would result in an unwarranted complexity (*apramāṇika-gaurava*).
To the question "What follows from that?", he replies with the words "sārūpya" (similarity).

Just as the perception of Prajāpati’s head is heard in the case of the *vyāhṛti* "Bhūḥ" due to the similarity of oneness, so too, since non-Brahman-hood is well-known in the case of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) through the scriptural mention of sound and so forth, the similarity of being an insentient light must be stated; this is the meaning.
That which is well known as the cognition of heat through the touch of the body—that is the perception of that digestive fire.
The meaning is that the hearing of sound by means of covering the ears is itself its [the ear's] faculty of hearing.
He states another indicative mark for the insentience of light with the words "This very... (tadetad).
The meaning is "light.
He is *cakṣuṣya*, beneficial to the eyes and handsome; he is *śruta*, renowned.
"And there is nothing else either": the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that there is no other characteristic of Brahman (*brahmaliṅga*) whatsoever.

Having raised the objection—"Surely the Brahman mentioned in the preceding sentence, 'Three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven,' should be understood here by the word 'light' (*jyotis*)"—he says: "And there is not."

Now, it might be argued that Brahman has been described by means of its being the self of all and its immortality; to this he says: "Even so" (athāpi). The meaning is: "in some way through the medium of the Vedic hymns. The point is that because of the difference in case endings—such as *divi* and *dive*—there is no recognition [of the same word].
"Prākṛta" means born of *prakṛti*, that is to say, an effect.
He rejects [the idea of] conduct with the word "pāda."
"Indeed, this entire world is the Gāyatrī"; "Speech is the Gāyatrī"; "This earth is [the Gāyatrī]"; "This body is [the Gāyatrī]";

"That which is the heart in this person is [the Gāyatrī]"; and "These vital breaths are [the Gāyatrī]"—thus, the Gāyatrī consists of sixfold aspects composed of the elements, speech, earth, body, heart, and vital breaths;
it has four feet by means of its six syllables.

As for what was said: "All that expansion (*prapañca*) is of such a measure— that is, it is the majesty (*mahiman*), the manifestation (*vibhūti*), of this Brahman who conforms to the *gāyatrī*— but the Person (*puruṣa*), being the form of the complete Brahman, is therefore greater than, that is, superior to, the expansion."
He speaks of the very preeminence [of the Lord] in the word "foot":
the entire world is one foot, or part, as the Smṛti says: "Pervading this whole world, I remain with but a single part."
Of this Puruṣa, there exists an immortal form consisting of three quarters in the heaven that is his own self-luminous nature;
or, for the purpose of meditation, it is said to be in the heaven of the solar orb;
the meaning is that there exists an infinite Brahman-nature beyond the imagined world.

Just as in common parlance one says "three-quarters" to indicate that it is more than three-fourths, so too it is said to be "immortal by three-quarters" (tripāda-amṛta) for the purpose of making known that it is superior;
it should be understood that the state of having exactly three quarters is not intended.

Regarding the phrase "that which is beyond this," since the word *yat* denotes a well-known entity, he states "therein" (*tatra*) to show that the Brahman established in the preceding passage is what must be understood.

Now, one might object: "In the case of the passage 'That which belongs to Agni is the eight-potherd [cake],' it is observed that the word *yat* has a meaning not previously mentioned in the context. To this he replies: "having abandoned that [objection]. In that case, because there was no other means of establishing the sacrifice (*yāga*), and since it was something new (*apūrva*), one had no choice but to resort to the fact that *yat* has an unestablished meaning. Here, however, since Brahman—already established by the preceding statement—is recognized through its connection with heaven, it is certain that *yat* refers to that very same entity; therefore, the word *jyotis*, which shares the same referent as *yat*, must have that same meaning as well. This is the sense.
He says "not only" (na kevalam) because it is so even by the logic of the tongs (saṃdaṃśanyāya).
The meaning is that since the term "Brahman" recurs later in the passage "All this, indeed, is Brahman," the intervening statement concerning light must refer to Brahman.
This is established by the context (prakaraṇāt).

The meaning is: [this is established] by the direct statement (*śruti*) of the word "foot" in relation to the subject under discussion, and by the indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as its connection with heaven and its being a foot of the earth.
Therefore, it is refuted that the contradiction of the word "light" (*jyotis*) by the context (*prakaraṇa*) is not tenable; for [the word "light"] is not a non-distinguishing factor.
The meaning is that [the word "light"] lacks the capacity to exclude Brahman.
The sense is that one who has not studied the Vedas does not know that Great One—the consciousness by which the sun is kindled and illumined, and which causes the sun to shine and manifest.

Having accepted that the word "light" (jyotis) has its primary denotative power (śakti) only in the effect-light and thus stated that it indicates the causal Brahman, [the author] asserts that it also possesses denotative power in Brahman itself, saying "or else" (yadvā).
The meaning is that even in dense darkness, people carry out activities such as sitting and so forth by means of the light of speech alone.

"May the clarified butter (ājya) enjoy [it] and drink [it]"—this is a praise of the clarified butter, implying that the mind becomes the illuminating light. Just as one who follows another walking also possesses movement, so too might everything have its own inherent manifestation; therefore, he says: "By his light."
The meaning is that the gods worship Brahman—which is not limited by time—as the witness of the lights such as the sun, and as life and immortality.

He states with the words "To this it is replied," and so forth, that it is appropriate to attribute to Brahman qualities such as having heaven as its boundary for the purpose of meditation, just as the quality of being fire is attributed to women.
The grammatical connection is: "even beyond heaven."
He states that there is no rule of similarity between the superimposed object, the object of meditation, and the objective support by saying "even for another.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it will become the light of Brahman.
He says "it is not deficient" because of the Vedic scripture: "In whatever manner one meditates upon it, such indeed becomes the fruit."

One might ask: why should the fruit of meditation not be of a single uniform nature, just like the fruit of knowledge? To this he says: "For where... (yatra hi). The meaning is: because the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is one. But he says that the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) is manifold: "But where... (yatra tu).

The Lord eats food in the form of the individual soul (jīva), thus he is "the eater of food" (annāda); or, he is the giver of food on all sides. Or, because he gives wealth (vasu) and gold, he is "the giver of wealth" (vasudāna). He who knows this connection with these specific qualities finds wealth and possesses a radiant digestive fire. Of names, speech is the highest.
The first phrase, "the mind indeed is greater than speech" or "a specific form [of speech] is greater," is intended to include the scriptural injunctions regarding meditation on specific forms.
He raises an objection based on proximity, thinking that direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is stronger: "But how then?
Then he says, "This is not so," meaning that the later scriptural statement is governed by the earlier scriptural statement.

The construction is as follows: "when [the object] is referred to by the power of the pronoun itself"—that is, by the capacity of the pronoun, which consists in its denoting what is proximate (saṃnihitavācitva), and by the force of that [capacity].
The meaning is: "by virtue of the coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word *yat* [which stands for the object], etc. //24//

If it be argued that [the passage] does not refer to Brahman because it mentions a meter, we say no; for there is an injunction to fix the mind [on Brahman] in that way, and such is seen [in other texts]. (BBs 1.1.25)
The partisan (ekadeśin) refutes the doubt that "Brahman is not the subject under discussion because of the mention of *chandas* (metre)" with the word "How so?
He establishes that doubt with the words beginning "Not this," and so forth.
The fact that [Brahman] has four feet and so on has already been explained previously.
The meaning is that whoever knows this Madhu-vidyā— which constitutes the secret essence of the Vedas— in the manner described, attains Brahman, which is devoid of rising and setting.
Thus, the intention is that the word "Brahman" is appropriately applied to the Gāyatrī because it is a Veda.

Regarding the use of the word *gāyatrī* to indicate Brahman through the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its being the material cause, he states the reason for this by saying "for not in the syllables," pointing out the lack of logical inconsistency as the seed [of the definition].
As to how even Brahman can possess the nature of being the self of all, he says there: "and the effect."

Nor should it be said that the attribution of being the self of all is for the purpose of meditation on the Gāyatrī; the sense is that since meditation on that which is inherently the self of all is possible, the attribution of something unreal (asad) is inappropriate.
He explains the remainder of the sūtra, "For thus is the vision," with the words: "so elsewhere."
That which is seen is "darśana"; it means that which has been perceived.
The followers of the Ṛgveda, the Bahvṛcas, meditate upon this Supreme Self as connected with the Great Hymn (mahad-uktha) in the ritual recitation.

The meaning is that this very [Brahman] is what those belonging to the Yajurveda worship in the fire, based on the Śruti text in the *Agnirahasya*: "This very one, as Fire, the Adhvaryus worship"; and this very one is what the Chanters, the Sāmavedins, worship in the Mahāvrata sacrifice, as seen in the *Aitareyaka*.
Having explained that the word *gāyatrī* is indicative of Brahman, he says "another [view]" to indicate that it is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*).
"Directly" means,
that is to say, without even grasping the literal meaning [of the word *gāyatrī*].
Previously, however, both Gāyatrī and Brahman were indicated by the word *gāyatrī* through non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) because [Gāyatrī] was to be meditated upon.
Nor is there an impossibility of the grammatical connection (anvaya) "the Gāyatrī is everything," because—
just as in the case of "the pot has color" where color connects with the individual (vyakti), which is one part of the referent of the word "pot"— here too,

the connection of being the self of all can occur with Brahman, the primary entity, who is inherent in the Gāyatrī and constitutes one part of the referent of the word "Gāyatrī. This is the intended meaning.

And thus, the meaning of this portion of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the Sūtra is as follows: "In that way"—that is, because of the commonality of the quality of having four quarters (*catuṣpāttva*) like the *Gāyatrī*—the word *Gāyatrī*, which is a "bestowal of the mind" (*cetorpaṇa*) since by it the mind is bestowed upon Brahman, denotes Brahman alone; therefore, because of its direct declaration (*nigada*), the claim that it denotes a meter (*chandas*) is unestablished. Now, he explains the remainder of the Sūtra, "For there is a scriptural vision to that effect" (*tathā hi darśanam*), with the word "in that way" (*tathā*).

In the Saṃvarga-vidyā, it is stated that with respect to the divine (ādhidaiva), fire, sun, moon, and water dissolve into air; and with respect to the self (adhyātma), speech, sight, hearing, mind, and breath merge into the vital breath (prāṇa).
These, indeed, are the five others belonging to the divine realm.
The other five internal [factors], when combined, constitute the number ten and are thus called "Kṛta.
Indeed, there are four throws known as Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali, which respectively consist of four, three, two, and one [pips].
Among these, the Kṛta throw consists of ten.
Because three are included within four, two within three, and one within two;
and thus, by way of the quality of being tenfold, wind and the others are expressed by the word "the made" (*kṛta*).
Having thus introduced the state of being "made" for wind and the others, he says: "This very... (*saiṣā*).
The feminine gender is used in reference to that which is to be enjoined.
The term *virāṭ* denotes a meter, according to the Vedic revelation: "The *virāṭ* consists of ten syllables."
By virtue of their commonality in being tenfold, the wind and the other elements are called *virāj*.
Thus, through the medium of this tenfold nature, the state of being the *kṛta* [world] and the state of being *virāj* are to be meditated upon within the wind and the others.
Among these, from the meditation on the state of being *virāj*, everything becomes his food.
According to the Vedic scripture, "Food is Virāj," one becomes an eater of food by meditating on it as such, because one who has performed that meditation becomes an eater of food.
For it appears as if one eats food that has already been prepared, which includes within itself the three throws (*tryaṅka*) and so forth;

therefore, victory in other forms of gambling is said in the Śruti to result from victory at *kṛta*: "When the *kṛtāya* has been won, the lower throws gather unto it. *Ayaḥ* means gambling; *kṛtāyaḥ* is the gambling known as *kṛta*; to him by whom that has been won—
The lower ones, such as the three-syllabled [virāj] and so forth, join together—that is, they submit;
the meaning is that they become conquered by it.
And thus, this Virāj, consisting of the tenfold nature beginning with Vāyu and designated by the word "Kṛta," is food.

The meaning is "because it has been performed," such as eating food and so forth. "In every way" means even if the word *gāyatrī* functions as an indicator (*lakṣaka*) or is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*).
By the phrase "here another says," the author indicates through the word "another" that his own view does not accept the figurative interpretation (*gauṇatva*).

For in the view of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication), the identity of Gāyatrī with speech—as in "Speech indeed is Gāyatrī"—and her etymological name derived from "she sings (*gāyati*) and she protects (*trāyate*"), are both more appropriately established as attributes for meditation;
whereas in the figurative view, since the term "Gāyatrī" is abandoned, both of these [identity and etymology] would have to be justified merely by her being the self of all.

Therefore, the mark of the individual soul (jīva) is stronger; thus, he presents the prima facie view by way of a counter-example, beginning with "the embodied one" (śārīra).
Anticipating this objection, he refutes it by stating, "This is not a fault," on the grounds that [the passage] would otherwise be established as having a different purpose.

He states the reason for its being devoted to the injunction of tranquility (*śama*) with the words, "for which reason" (*yatkāraṇam*). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: because it speaks thus, therefore it is devoted to the injunction of tranquility.
[In this context, the word "here" (atra) is intended to refer back to the Brahman under discussion, and not to refer back to the world,
because there is no purpose in qualifying the world here.
Even though there is no purpose here, wherever there is a purpose, the qualification of the world certainly occurs.]
Just as in the statement "All this is indeed the Self," a qualification is necessary for the sake of strengthening the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) regarding sublation,
because that sentence has as its object Brahman as the Knowable (jñeya).

But here, in the case of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), there is no necessity for such sublation; since Brahman is the object of worship, it remains the same across all subjects. [The phrase] "and not 'śama'" means that if both tranquility (*śama*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) were enjoined, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
He states that even for the individual soul (*jīva*), the possibility of possessing all actions and so forth exists through the succession of births, in the verse beginning with "sarvakarma":
"one whose [actions] are all actions," and "one whose objects of enjoyment are all desires."
The meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "possessing all fragrances, possessing all tastes," and so forth,
is as follows: "the size of the tip of a goad" (*ārāgramātra*) means having the dimension of the tip of an iron rod pierced through by a goad.

He states the meaning of the Sūtra—"In all cases" (*sarvatra*)—to show that because it is taught here that Brahman, who is established everywhere, is the object of meditation, the individual soul (*jīva*) is not the object of meditation.
Where no specific fruit is mentioned, it should be understood that the establishment of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is the fruit.
Although Brahman is thus free from all desire (*nirākāṅkṣa*), its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consists predominantly of the mind (*manaḥ*).
Because the pronoun within the compound "prāṇaḥ śarīram asya" (of whom the vital breath is the body) requires a proximate substantive to be supplied, it is connected with Brahman.

He says this because we observe that even though the phrase "I make a pleasant seat for thee" (syonaṃ te sadanaṃ karomi)—which serves the purpose of consecration—is itself complete in its requirements, it is nevertheless referred to by the word "in that" (tasmin), which does require a complement, as in "sit upon it" (tasmin sīda).
To this it is replied: "A pleasant vessel for thee, [intended] for the sacrificial cake" (puroḍāśasya); such is the meaning of the Vedic text.
Since the individual soul (jīva) might also be understood as being proximate due to these indicative marks, he says: "But the soul...

For these two indicative marks, though well-known in the world, do not bring the soul into proximity, because one who is suffering is unfit for meditation and because there would be no fruit [of such meditation].

Therefore, according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice, the meaning is that Brahman itself—whose nature is bliss and which is desired by all—is the objective correlate (*anubandhi*) of the act of meditation.
Furthermore, he states "not so" (*na ca*) because the direct statement (*śruti*) of the word "Brahman" sets aside the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The collective sense is that a context (*prakaraṇa*) possessing a fruit, when supported by the expectancy of one of its parts, is stronger than a fruitless indicative mark. //1//
And because the qualities intended [to be expressed] are applicable [to Him]. (1.2.2)

The result of the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) regarding an object is its "appropriation" (*upādāna*), that is, its acceptance; and since this exists in the case of the qualities under discussion, he says "nevertheless, by means of appropriation" to indicate the figurative application (*upacāra*) of the intention to speak. Now, one might ask: how could there be such a cognition as "this is to be grasped" and "this is to be abandoned" in the Veda, given the absence of intention to speak and the like? To this, he replies: "But as for appropriation and non-appropriation..."

Tātparya (purport) is a property of the word consisting in its conduciveness to the comprehension of a meaning that possesses a result; the meaning is that the understanding of those two [the purport and the meaning] occurs through the knowledge of that [purport] by means of the introductory statements and so forth.
"In that case" (tadiha) [means as follows].
Therefore, for that reason;
the meaning is "because it possesses [that] intended purport. He states the proof for its being the self of all with the words "and likewise" (tathā ca).
He who is worn out and aged, who leans on a staff and moves about—that too is you alone.
He who is born as a child—that too is you alone. "Possessing ears everywhere" means one whose auditory organs (śrotra) reach in all directions, toward all quarters.
The statement that he is the self of all is made because hands and other limbs are present in all living beings. //2//
But because of the impossibility [of such qualities], it is not the embodied soul.
[Objection: If the attributes of the individual soul (jīva) are indeed applied to Brahman, then why are the attributes of Brahman not likewise applied to the individual soul?
To this, he says: "Because of impossibility" (*anupapatteḥ*).
He explains the Sūtra [by referring] to what precedes it.
The logic previously stated regarding [the Self] being the essence of all and so forth applies here:
the properties of the imagined are connected to the substratum, but the properties of the substratum are not imagined; this is the intended meaning.
At the time of the knowledge of the foundation of the lake (hradhiṣṭhāna-jñāna), because of the absence of imagined phenomena (kalpita-dharma), he is "speechless" (avākī);
that which is speech itself is "speech" (vāk), and one who possesses that [speech] is "possessing-speech" (vākī); one who does not possess it is "speechless" (avākī).
The meaning is "without sense-faculties. He has no regard or desire for anything whatsoever; thus he is "disregarding," which means he is eternally satisfied.
Since the impossibility of [the soul] being superior and so forth is established, the "embodied one" (śārīra) mentioned in the Sūtra is the reason for that limitation.
However, he states with the words "It is true," etc., that this [limitation] applies only to the individual soul (jīva) and not to the Lord (īśvara). //3//
And because of the designation of [the Self] as both the object and the agent of action. (BS 1.2.4)
The connection [of the sentence] is: "he designates by way of being the attainer.
He states another meaning for the phrase "designation as object and agent" with the words: "likewise, as the object of meditation" (tathopāsya). //4//
Because there is a distinction in sound. (BBs 1.2.5)

The unity of meaning (*ekārthatva*) refers to the identity of the context (*prakaraṇa*). In the word *antarātman*, the elision of the case-ending is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). The distinction between the two words consists in the difference of their case-endings.
Therefore, there is a difference between their respective objects; such is the meaning of the sūtra. //5//
And because of tradition (smṛti). BBs_1,2.6.

Because the Smṛti speaks of the distinction between the one dwelling in the heart and the individual soul (jīva), he states here as well that the one dwelling in the heart is the Lord consisting of mind (manomaya)—this is expressed by the words "and because of the Smṛti.
"Beings" refers to the individual souls;
"machine" refers to the body.

Here, in order to dispel the misconception that the author of the Sūtras has stated a distinction between the truths (satya-bheda), he raises and refutes an objection—though one already refuted in the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*—with the words "Here [the opponent] says," and so forth. He states, "True," meaning: according to the method you have described, there is indeed only oneness in reality; however, the distinction is merely imagined and is merely restated in the Sūtras. //6//
If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the cause] because of its smallness and because of the designation of that [smallness], we say no; for it is to be perceived as such, and it is like space.
"Arbhakauka" means that whose abode (*oka*) is small; the state of being such is "arbhakatva," from which follows its smallness (*alpatva*).
He says "by its own word" (*svaśabdena*) to show that even by a word expressing smallness, such as "smaller" (*aṇīyān*), this is heard in scripture.
He explains that this is not a fault with the words "not, first of all" (*na tāvat*).
"In any way" means even with respect to the state of Brahman.

The sense is that since the nature of Brahman is impossible without the abandonment of limitations, and since upon such abandonment Brahman itself becomes the object of worship, this is the intended meaning.
He provides an illustration for the statement regarding the limitation of the All-pervasive Lord: "as in the case of the Equal One.
The meaning is that, just as there is a statement of limitation with respect to the Lord of All residing in Ayodhyā, so too is He described in that way as being meditated upon within the small heart.
Now, why is it generally said to be in the heart alone?
Regarding this, he says: "Therein.
In the heart, the modification of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) becomes the grasper of the Supreme Self;
therefore, the meaning is that it is so called because it is the locus for the manifestation of the Lord (īśvara).
He states that even some creeper of doubt has been severed by the sword of the analogy of space, with the words beginning "In that regard, when it is suspected...
The underlying sense is that although space occupies different locations, there is no real division or the like [in its nature]. //7//
If it is argued that there is the attainment of enjoyment [of the fruits of karma], we say no, because of the difference in nature.

He explains the doubt— that because of the consequence of experiencing undesirable things, the individual soul (jīva) alone must be the one meditated upon as being within the heart— by stating "like space" (vyomavat):
Brahman would be an experiencer, because it is sentient while residing within the heart.

And [the author] refutes the statement "because it is non-different from the individual soul (jīva), it is like the individual soul" with the words: "No, because of the difference in nature" (*vaiśeṣyāt*).
The meaning is that the possession of merit and demerit (*dharmādharmavattva*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
This very thing is *vaiśeṣyam* (distinction);
the suffix *-ṣyañ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*),
or it has the meaning of "excess" (*atiśaya*) of distinction (*viśeṣa*).

The meaning of the sūtra is that the excellence (*atiśaya*) consists in the fact that dharma and so forth serve as the cause of their own results within their own substratum; therefore [the self is one].
Furthermore, for those who argue that there are many liberated selves (*vibhava*), it would follow that all selves would be experiencers within a single body.
He says "sarvagata" (all-pervading) to show that we are not to be questioned, as the rebuttal—that enjoyment occurs only in a body earned by one's own karma—is the same [for both sides].
However, in reality, it will be explained later that for them alone there is a confusion of enjoyments.

Having determined through scripture that Brahman is non-different from the individual soul (jīva), he states "yathāśāstram" (according to scripture) to show that the inference of its being an enjoyer is sublated by the very scripture upon which it depends.
To desire only the face of an aged woman while not desiring her limbs is the "half-old-woman" maxim (*ardhajaratīyanyāya*).
And that is not appropriate here;
for it is not reasonable to accept non-difference [of the self from the body] and yet abandon its being a non-enjoyer (*abhoktṛtva*).
He says, "And the scripture," because it precludes the state of being an enjoyer for the very purpose of establishing non-difference through scripture itself.
[The opponent objects: "But I have not grasped oneness through scripture, such that there would be a sublation of the basis upon which [the argument] depends."

However, fearing that [the soul] might be apprehended as such according to your statement, he says "But if it were not apprehended" (*athāgṛhītam*) and so forth, [arguing] that because the distinction between being an enjoyer and a non-enjoyer is established through the imagined difference between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).
He also applies the Sūtra to this point—that the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) possesses the specific quality of being untouched by imagined [attributes]—by saying "That [Sūtra] says" (*tadāha*).
Since there is no sublation regarding Brahman being the one within the heart (*hārda*), it is established that the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā passage is connected with Brahman as the object of meditation. //8//
The Self [is the object of the word "I"], because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving. 1.2.9.
And from the context;
because of the mention of "self" and "the moving and the unmoving":
"He for whom the world, beginning with the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, is the food."
Even death, which is the slayer of all living beings, serves as a mere seasoning for its rice-like meal, like clarified butter used to flavor food;
that eater—in whom one abides through the conceptualization of non-difference within pure consciousness alone—is the Pure Brahman. Who knows it "thus" (itthā), meaning in this way?
It means that no one knows it without the means of mental purification and the like, even though it is the very substratum of the Lord.
He states the seed of doubt with the words "viśeṣa" (particularity): [the question] "Tell me about Agni" refers to Agni,
while "This doubt which arises when one has died" refers to the individual soul (jīva).

The meaning is that the question regarding Brahman is found in the words "other than dharma," the question regarding Agni is in the words "he spoke of that Agni, the source of the worlds," and the answer for the other two [questions] is found in the words "Come, I shall declare this to you."

It was stated previously that Brahman does not possess the status of an enjoyer; taking that as a premise, the opponent sets forth the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "What, then, [is it]?
Out of dissatisfaction with the idea that the preceding section concerned Agni, he says "or the individual soul (jīva)."

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is meditation on the individual soul (*jīva*); in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman—thus there is a difference in the result.
In the prima facie view, the word "odana" (rice) denotes that which is to be enjoyed.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the word "rice" (*odana*) is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) for whatever effect is presented by the words "Brahmin" and "Kṣatriya.

And here, the quality (*guṇa*) is understood to be the perishability inherent in ordinary rice, which is brought to mind by the term "sprinkling with death," because a figurative word grasps a quality that is proximate to it.

And thus, because everything appears as something subject to destruction, it is by this inferential mark (*liṅga*) that he says "the Lord eats"; [the author] states "this is not a fault" because of its proximity.
The meaning is that enjoyment has been mentioned previously in the phrase "he eats the sweet pippala fruit. // 9 // // 10 //
"The two selves have entered the cave, for that is seen [in scripture]. (BS 1.2.11)
He states that the sentence immediately following the one by Aṭṭra also possesses coherence (*samanvaya*) with respect to the Knowable Self, beginning with the words "guhām" (the cave).

"Drinking" (*pibantau*) means experiencing the "Ṛta"—that is, the inevitable fruit of action—in the world, which is the body produced by well-performed deeds (*sukṛta*). It is called "parārdha" because it is a place worthy of being the half of the Supreme Brahman.

The heart is the supreme, most excellent [abode]; within it is a cave, which is either of the nature of space or of the nature of consciousness. Having entered that [cave], those two—those who know Brahman and those who perform ritual acts—reside there as mutual opposites, like shade and sunlight.
"Those who have piled the fire thrice" (triṇāciketa) means those by whom the Nāciketa fire has been established three times; they too speak thus—this is the meaning.
It should be understood that there is a triad consisting of the study of the Nāciketa passages, the knowledge of their meaning, and the performance of them.

Since both the individual soul (jīva) as delimited by the intellect (buddhi) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) have been introduced as the subject matter, he states the doubt with the word "therein" (tatra).
He himself states the result of the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions with the words beginning "if," etc.;
the meaning is that even that [result] pertains to the distinction of the individual soul from the intellect.
When a human being has died and passed away, there arises this doubt and uncertainty: some say that there is an enjoyer in the next world, while others say there is not.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Instructed by you, may I come to know this reality of the Self."
The meaning is that even that [the Self within the eye] is the nature of the Supreme Self.
He raises a doubt by pointing out the impossibility of both being enjoyers, saying "here he says.

He explains that just as the word "umbrella-bearer" refers to those who are traveling, so too the word "drinker" refers to the two who have entered [the body] through *ajahallakṣaṇā* (indication without abandoning the primary meaning), saying "here it is replied."
He states "or else" (yadvā) to show that the two [factors] conducive to drinking are indicated by the word denoting the agent of drinking.
The nature of being conducive, consisting in possessing an action that invariably precedes [the result], is common to both the agent and the instigator, according to the maxim:
"he who causes another to act necessarily acts himself. This is the intended meaning.
In this case, the base (*prakṛti*) has its primary meaning, while there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*);
however, the action (*kṛti*) is mixed,
as the meaning of the suffix is primary.
However, they say that by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*), through non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), "causing to drink" (*pāyana*) is what is indicated.

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says "buddhi" [etc. to show that by the agent-denoting suffix *śatṛ* in the word "apibantau," the state of being a factor of action (*kārakatva*) common to both the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*) is what is indicated;
for in the expression "the fuel logs cook" (*edhāṃsi pacanti*), the state of being a factor of action is indicated by the verb.

The sense is that *prakṛti* alone is the primary [meaning]. To the objection that the two "drinkers" (*pātārau*) should be understood as the well-known birds, he says "And not... He raises the prima facie view by means of an analogy: just as the word *brahmakṣatra* refers to impermanent things because of its proximity to the word *mṛtyu*, so too here the word *pibantau* refers to the two living beings (the individual soul and the intellect) because of its proximity to the word *guhā*. What...?
The word "tāvat" means "the object," which is the result.
When one member possessing a genus is established, the second [member] to be apprehended must necessarily be of the same genus.
Because it is simpler to grasp the individual alone;
it is not a different class,
due to the conceptual complexity of postulating both the universal and the individual.

Nor should it be argued that the intellect itself, as an agent, may be the "second" to the living being (jīva) because it belongs to the same class; for consciousness, which is the very nature of the jīva, is more intimate than agency. Thus, since in common experience a second entity is observed to possess an intimate genus, the second to the jīva must indeed be a conscious being. He states the meaning of the Sūtra: "And upon hearing the number... etc.

Having known the Ancient One, the beginningless Person, who dwells in the cave of the intellect, situated in the body— a deep abyss crowded with manifold misfortunes— one abandons both joy and sorrow.
He is supreme and most excellent.

The construction is as follows: "He who knows the Brahman deposited in that cave—the intellect (buddhi)—which is the sky (vyoman) within the space of the heart (hārdākāśa), enjoys all desires. "Seek" means "investigate. //11//
And because of the qualification. (BBs 1.2.12)
He states the indicative mark consisting of the qualifiers such as "the goer" and "that which is to be gone to" with the words, "And because of the qualifier.
That living being [reaches] the supreme further shore of the path—that is, the way of saṃsāra.
What is that?
The meaning is that one attains the *pada*, the essential nature, of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self whose nature is all-pervasive (*vyāpanaśīla*).
It is difficult to see (*durdarśa*) and difficult to know (*durjñāna*);

the reason for this is that it is hidden (*gūḍha*), veiled by *māyā*, entered into by *māyā*, and subsequently placed within the cave (*guhāhita*), situated in the depths through the door of the cave.

Thus, having brought the self that had gone outward back within, through the process of dissolving the gross, subtle, and causal bodies by means of internal yoga (adhyātmayoga)—which is the concentration of the mind upon the innermost self (pratyagātman)—one attains realization; the meaning is that one knows [Brahman] through the mental modification (vṛtti) born of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya).

He concludes that in this context of "drinking the Truth" (ṛtapāna), the referent of the term "That" (tatpadārtha), namely Brahman, is taught as the meaning of the sentence by way of restating the individual soul (jīva): "Therefore, here... (tasmād iha).
He extends the aforementioned principle [to other cases] with the word "eṣa" (this).
"Dvā dvā" (two by two);
the form "ākāra" is used for the dual number according to Vedic usage.
They are "joined" (sayujau) because they are joined together like two birds, existing in the relationship of the controlled and the controller.

They are "friends" (sakhāyau), meaning they possess a common nature by virtue of being conscious. The meaning is that they both abide by resorting to the same tree—the body, which is subject to destruction.
"Having entered the cave" means up to this point;
these two are the two selves, because of the observation of their respective characteristics, as he says: "Of the two, one..."
And he says "and because of the qualification" [in the verse], namely "and in the next [verse]":
the individual soul (jīva), being immersed in the body due to its lack of sovereignty—that is, the non-perception of its own lordship—grieves.
He explains the meaning of the word "immersed" as "being deluded."

The meaning is that he is deluded, thinking "I am a man. When, through the practice of meditation and so forth, he perceives at the stage of the maturation of meditation the Lord— who is distinct from the qualified form (viśeṣarūpa) as pure, purified consciousness— as his own inner self (pratyaktvena), then he attains, as it were, His majesty, which is His true nature (svarūpa).
The meaning is that one then becomes free from sorrow.

Having reflected upon the statement "Two birds... by taking it as referring to the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), he now sets aside that reflection and reveals another interpretation: "the other," etc.
Otherwise, the meaning is that there would be a difference in nature from the intellect (*buddhi*) by virtue of being intended as the primary referent of the word.
He raises the objection that the word "sattva" refers to the intellect—namely, that "sattva" means the intellect—with the words "the word *sattva*.
He then says "nor even," [meaning] that if the subject matter of the prima facie view were both the intellect and the individual soul (*jīva*), that would not be the case.
The position of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) would hold true only if a transmigrating being distinct from the intellect were understood here;
however, it is not a transmigrating being that is intended here, but rather the meaning of "Thou" (tvam-artha) purified [of adjuncts], which is Brahman. This is the sense.
And the meaning is that this is consistent with the Śruti and Smṛti; "iti" is the ellipsis.
"By that much" means by the mere explanation of the mantra.
"In this very way" means precisely when the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman is stated.

For it is not proper to conclude merely on the basis of the discrimination that "the living self (jīva) is distinct from the intellect," because such knowledge of difference is erroneous and fruitless; this is the sense.
Ignorance (avidyā) does not destroy nor produce any of its own effects within one who possesses true knowledge.
The meaning is that [ignorance] does not come because it has been burnt by the fire of knowledge belonging to oneself;
or alternatively, the meaning is that ignorance does not approach.
Regarding the position that this statement refers to the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman, he raises an objection: "How?"
He says, "It is said," to show that one need not distress the mind by pondering over the logic here, since the statement that the Buddha is an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) is not intended as a literal truth.
The meaning is that, for the sake of realizing his nature as Brahman, he casts the attribute of being an enjoyer upon the head of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
To the question, "If the individual soul (*jīva*) is in reality not an enjoyer, how can there be the notion of being an enjoyer? he replies, "For this... [is so].
The intellect (*buddhi*), imagined as non-different from the mind (*citta*), undergoes transformation into the form of pleasure and so forth.

The meaning is that the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) appears for the conscious self (*cidātman*) due to its non-discrimination from the intellect; that is, it possesses consciousness manifested through the modifications (*vṛtti*) of the intellect in the form of pleasure and so forth.
This state of being an enjoyer is rooted in ignorance (*avidyaka*).
Regarding the phrase "not in reality," he states the proof with the words "and thus" (*tathā ca*).
The meaning is that when, during the state of ignorance (*avidyā*), consciousness appears as if divided,
then [attributes such as] being the seer and so forth do not exist in the reality that has been known.
Therefore, it is established that the sentence "drinking the ṛta" itself is the subject matter of the section concerning the cave (guhādhikaraṇa). //12//
[The intermediate state exists] because of its arising within [the womb]. (BBs 1.2.13)
[The phrase] "before rebirth" [is explained].
He cites the passage concerning the Upakośala-vidyā, beginning with "He who...
That location in the eye is suitable for Brahman because of its non-attachment; the meaning is that whatever is cast into it goes only between the two paths, namely, the eyelashes.
He states a doubt regarding the vision (darśana) based on its being either worldly or scriptural, using the word "tatra" [therein].
Just as previously, following the sentience mentioned first in the phrase "the two drinking," the later-mentioned entry into the cave and so forth were interpreted accordingly;

likewise here too, following the fact that it is "seen"—that is, its visibility—the immortality and other qualities should be interpreted as being imagined for the purpose of meditation. Thus he presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of the example: "the shadow-self."
The fruit [of this discussion] is that in the prima facie view there is meditation on the reflection, whereas in the final conclusion there is meditation on Brahman;
thus it is said, "as if well-known."
The meaning is "by way of being visible.
He states another alternative merely as a possibility with the words beginning "of the conscious self" (*vijñānātmanaḥ*),
just as in the case of [the statement] "the mind is Brahman" (*mano brahma*).

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the sentence "This is Brahman" (*etad brahma iti*) is headed by the word *iti*, it does not have its own literal meaning as its primary purport.

The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, maintains that it refers to the Supreme Lord alone; for while in the passage "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" (*mano brahmety upāsīta*) the word *iti* refers to the mental cognition (*pratyaya*), here—in the construction "He said, 'Brahman'" (*brahmety uvāca*)—the word *iti* relates to the speech itself and thus has its own literal meaning as its purport, making the two cases dissimilar.

According to the principle that "corroboration by many authorities supports the intended meaning," the visible mark [of the eye] is sublated by the two scriptural passages concerning the Self and Brahman, which are supported by this reasoning; thus he says, "The center of blessings" (*saṃyadvāma*).
"Blessings" (*vāmāni*) refers to the fruits of actions; they "converge toward" (*saṃyanti*), meaning they arise, with reference to this Person in the eye.
The meaning is that He is the cause for the arising of all fruits.
He says that this very one is also the bestower of fruits upon the worlds—namely, "Vāmanī.
The meaning is that he leads the fruits, that is, he causes them to reach the worlds. He says "Bhāmanī" because he leads the lights (bhāmāni), that is, the rays of light.
The meaning is that it illuminates all objects. //13//
And because of the designation of place and so forth. (1.2.14)

The construction of the sūtra is as follows: because the location, name, and form are taught in another Vedic text (Śrutyantara) for the purpose of meditation, there is no fault in the statement here that [the Self] resides in the eye.
"Impossibility" (anavakḷpti) means the assumption of what is not established; the syntactical connection is that this would be the case only if it were specified in this very context.
Anticipating the objection that stating such a multitude of inappropriate qualities would constitute a lack of resolution, he states the reasoning: "Even though it is devoid of qualities," etc. (14).
And precisely because of the designation of [the self] as distinguished by pleasure. (BBs 1.2.15)
He states that Brahman must also be understood from the context by saying, "qualified by bliss.

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: because the previously mentioned Brahman—qualified by the attribute of bliss through a conceptual differentiation for the purpose of meditation—is denoted by the pronoun "this" (*ya eṣa*), the Inner One must be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Now, one might object that the reflected self (*chāyātman*), brought forward by the mark of being visible (*dṛśyatva*), which is more powerful than the context, is the referent of the pronoun; to this, he says, "But the Teacher [says]... (*ācāryastu*).
A certain religious student named Upakośala attended upon his teacher Jābāla as a servant of the sacred fires for twelve years.

When Jābāla had departed for another country without having instructed him, [Upakośala’s father] out of compassion taught him the knowledge of the Self through the words "Breath is Brahman," using the household fire (gārhapatya) and the other fires as symbols, and then said: "But the teacher...
The meaning is that he [the father] spoke thus because the teacher would tell him the path beginning with light (arcis) for the attainment of the fruit of the knowledge of the Self.
Subsequently, the Teacher, having arrived, said, "This which is in the eye," and thus described the path beginning with light (*arcis*).
In this way, the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of the passage concerning the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) spoken by the fires must be asserted with the passage concerning the path;

and that unity is established when the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) refers back to the Self under discussion. Therefore, the sense is that the context (*prakaraṇa*), which effects such syntactic unity, is more powerful than the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that would otherwise divide the sentence.
The scripture explains this: "It is said.

The meaning is: I know that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the *sūtrātman*, is Brahman because of its vastness (*bṛhat*); however, I am unable to know the pleasure of the sense objects (*ka*) and the elemental ether (*kha*) as Brahman.
Of what nature is space (*kha*)?
That which is bliss (*kaṃ*) is itself space; thus, by qualifying space with bliss, its status as a mere physical element is excluded. Likewise, of what nature is bliss (*kaṃ*)?

"That which is space (kha) is indeed bliss (kam)"—by thus qualifying [bliss] with "pervasion" (vibhutva), he excludes its being a product by means of a negative formulation (vyatireka), stating "therein, space," and so forth.
The sense is that meditation on a mere symbol (pratīkadhyāna) is not intended here, because it would contradict the Śruti statement "the knowledge of the Self" (ātmavidyā).
[The term] "sāmaya" [is used].
"Disease" (āmaya) refers to defects such as dependence on external means for accomplishment, impermanence, and so forth; the meaning is "accompanied by those.
Having stated the fault in grasping [the two] individually, he states the result of grasping them as a pair: "mutually," etc.
The meaning is that [the two words] have distinct referents.
Now, one might ask: if Brahman alone is the object of meditation here, what is the purpose of the other word "Brahman"? To this he says: "Therein" (*tatra*).
This means that by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatvena*), it serves to exclude [the possibility of] the ether being an elemental substance (*bhūtatva*).
The analysis of the compound is: "that whose head is the word *brahman* is the *tattva*.
[The opponent asks: "What fault is there in its being an object of study?
To this, he replies: "For it is desired," and so forth.
The intention is that by the mention of the path (*mārga*), it is understood that this is the knowledge of the supreme qualities (*suguṇavidyā*).
Furthermore, he states that the subject under discussion is Brahman because of the concluding summary using the term "knowledge of the Self" (*ātmavidyā*): "And each [one]...
Gārhapatya taught: "Earth, fire, food, and the sun—these are my four bodies, my manifestation."
"The waters, the quarters, the stars, and the moon"—thus spoke the Anvāhāryapacana fire.
"The vital breath, space, the sky, and lightning"—thus the Āhavanīya fire proclaimed its own greatness; such is the division. This knowledge of our fires has been stated individually for each.
The meaning is that we previously met and declared "the life-breath is Brahman" with respect to the knowledge of the Self (ātmavidyā).
To the objection that Brahman might be spoken of by the fires [of the body] and the shadow-self by the teacher—due to the difference in speakers—the author says: "But the teacher... [etc.].
The meaning is that because there is certainty regarding the unity of the sentence, there is no difference in meaning even when there is a difference among the speakers. //15//
And because the scripture describes the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads. (BS 1.2.16)

The meaning of the Sūtra is stated as follows: "Because of the indicative mark (liṅga) consisting in the fact that the destination well-known from Śruti and Smṛti for one by whom the Upaniṣad—the secret doctrine of the meditation on the qualified Brahman—is heard and practiced, is mentioned here. He explains this with the words "And for this reason" (itaśca);
the syntactical connection is: "because it is seen [in scripture], therefore it is so here. He cites the Śruti with the words "Now" (atha).
The meaning is "immediately after the fall of the body.

One's own duty (*svadharma*) is austerity (*tapas*). Having meditated upon the Self through austerity, celibacy, faith, and knowledge, one attains by means of that knowledge of meditation the higher path, the path of the gods (*devayāna*), and not the northern path. Through the door of the sun, they go to the abode of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahma*).
This indeed is Brahman—the subtle body (*liṅga-ātman*) in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, which is the abode of the individual and collective forms of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
In reality, however, this is of the nature of the immortal and so forth, devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), and the substratum of all.
Therefore, the meaning is that having attained the effected Brahman (*kārya-brahma*) and known its true nature as attributeless, they are liberated.
Fire alone is the deity of light; in this same way, the deities of day and so forth have been declared in the Smṛti.

When this worshipper has died, whether his sons and others perform the funeral rites and other honors for the corpse or do not perform them, in either case, by the power of their meditation, they proceed in succession to the deities beginning with Light (arcis).
From the Ārcis fire, one goes to the day;
from the day, to the bright fortnight.
There [he goes] to the northern course, from there to the year, and from there to the world of the gods.
From there [he goes] to Vāyu,
from Vāyu to Āditya, and from there to Candra.

Having gone from the moon to lightning, a non-human person (*amānava*) comes from the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) and leads the worshippers situated there in the world of lightning to the effected world of Brahmā (*kārya-brahmaloka*).

This is the "Path of the Gods" (*devapatha*), distinguished by the deities beginning with Light (*arcis*), and it is also called the "Path of Brahmā" (*brahmapatha*) because of its connection with the Brahmā who is to be reached.

These worshippers, attaining this effected Brahmā, do not return to this creation of Manu (*mānava-sarga*), which is subject to the cycle of birth and death; the meaning is that they do not come back. //16//
It is not the other [the individual soul], because of its lack of stability and because of impossibility. (BS 1.2.17)
"The eye has arrived" means "it approaches.
The sense is that the status of being an object of meditation cannot always be established for that which is unstable.
Furthermore, because it is not separated [from oneself], that which resides in one's own eye is the object of worship;
yet, seeing it with one's own eyes is not possible, and so he says: "This which...
Well then, let there be worship of that which is seen by another; to this he says: "Nor..."
The meaning is "due to the excessive complexity of the conceptual construction" (kalpanāgaurava).
Regarding the fact that [the reflection] is established by reasoning as being non-abiding, he cites scripture: "of this" (asya).
The meaning is that following the destruction—that is, the non-perception—of the object which produces the shadow, this shadow-self perishes.
He rejects [the opponent's view] with "so be it" (*tatheti*).
The meaning is that since the manifestation of the *jīva* occurs as "I" even for one blind from birth without distinction, it is incorrect to say that the eye alone is its locus.
As for the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*): [it refers to the fact that the *jīva* is perceived through other means].
The word "in the Śruti" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Now, one might object that the statement "From the eye the sun was born" and "The sun sets" is contradicted by the common notion that the gods are immortal; anticipating this doubt, he says: "Immortality also...
From fear—out of dread—of this Lord, the wind blows.
Agni and Indra each perform their respective functions.
In view of what has been stated, death is the fifth; the meaning is that it runs near those whose lifespan has reached its end.
Regarding the perspective of the Lord (Īśvara), it is said that he is "seen."
Regarding this, he says: "In this [case].
"Seeing" (darśana) means direct experience.
For that [seeing] which has been heard in the scripture, the scripture itself must be postulated as the instrument (karaṇa).
Because of proximity.
Thus, the meaning is that the experience of the learned, which is produced by the sacred teaching (śāstra), is stated for the purpose of praising meditation (upāsanā).
Therefore, it is established that the passage concerning the Upakośala-vidyā is consistently interpreted as referring to Brahman, the object of meditation. //17//
The Antaryāmin (the Inner Ruler) is [Brahman], because its attributes are designated in relation to the divine realm, the worlds, and so forth. (BS 1.2.18)
"The Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) [is Brahman] because of the designation of its attributes in relation to the divine and other spheres.
He cites the passage from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad with the words "He who... He states the meaning as it appears regarding the Inner Controller-Brahman with the word "here."
By the passage beginning with "He who on earth," the Controller is heard in reference to the deities such as Earth;
likewise, by "He who in all worlds" in reference to the worlds (adhiloka),
and by "He who in all Vedas" in reference to the Vedas (adhiveda).
The division is as follows: "He who [dwells] in all sacrifices" refers to the sacrificial (adhiyajña);
"He who [dwells] in all beings" refers to the elemental (adhibhūta);
and from "He who dwells in the vital breath" up to "He who [dwells] in the self" refers to the spiritual (adhyātma).
A doubt arises from the possibility or impossibility of a bodiless being exercising control.

In the preceding section, the mention of abodes such as the earth was stated as an illustration to establish that the Lord has His station in the eye; here, the objection is raised that this illustrative statement refers to the Lord, and this objection is subsequently resolved—thus constitutes the connection by way of an objection (*ākṣepasaṃgati*).
Therefore, its status as a "sprout" is due to its prior fruit;

however, it should be understood that the intermediate fruit is the meditation on a non-supreme deity according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), whereas in the final conclusion (siddhānta) it is the knowledge of Brahman as the inner self (pratyagbrahma).
Expressing his own lack of approval, he states an alternative view with the words "or else" (athavā).
The underlying sense is that since there is an absence of fruit when the meaning is uncertain, that which lacks a fruit cannot be the purpose of the Veda.
And so it is heard in the Veda:
The earth is the abode and the body of that deity;
"world" (loka) means the eye— so called because one perceives by means of it—
and "light" (jyotis) means the mind, which illuminates all objects.

Because the determination of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) as one through the application of scriptural methods and so forth renders the position of multiple deities untenable, the author—expressing dissatisfaction with that view—states, "or the yogin.

Since it would involve the fault of postulating an unestablished means (*aprasiddhasādhanakalpanā-gaurava*) to assume that an adventitiously perfected being is the inner controller, he establishes his own conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the inner controller is indeed eternally perfected, stating, "this being the case" (*evaṃ prāpte*).
He provides another reason for rejecting the deities, stating, "whom the earth [does not know]."
He refutes the argument that "the Lord is not a controller because he is bodiless,
like a jar," by stating: "This is not a fault."
Alternatively, the reason (hetu) may be either "the state of being devoid of a body other than that which one governs" or "the state of not being connected with a body.
In the first case, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the individual soul (jīva), who governs its own body.
But the second [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), because God possesses all things acquired through His own ignorance; thus he says: "those whom He controls.
This was stated in accordance with worldly perception, namely that the controller is one who possesses a body.
In reality, however, the activity of the insentient due to the proximity of the sentient is its being governed; this state of being governed constitutes its status as a "controller.

And this is possible for the conscious self (cidātman) through its inconceivable power of māyā even without a body. [Objection: If there is a controller for the individual soul (jīva), who controls the body, then there must be another controller for that one as well, leading to an infinite regress. To this, he says: "And of that too... [referring to the verse].

The meaning is that the sovereignty of the Lord as the controller of all is heard in scripture to be unrestrained; therefore, there is no infinite regress, because the assumption of another controller for Him would contradict scripture.

Alternatively, since the statement that the individual soul (jīva) is a controller is made by conceiving of a distinction from the Lord, there is no infinite regress due to the absence of any real distinction [between them]. //18//
And it is not based on the Smṛti, because there is no mention of qualities not belonging to that [Smṛti]. (BBs 1.2.19)
He states that "it is beyond reasoning" (*apratarkya*) because it is not an object of logical inquiry as to how the *pradhāna* proceeds through the sequence beginning with the *mahat*.
Since it is devoid of form and other qualities, it is unknowable;
the meaning is that, due to its insentience (*jaḍatva*), it remains as if dormant in all directions.
That which is non-primary is insentient;
the meaning of the reason is that it is because [the scripture] designates its properties (dharmas). //19//
For both [schools] also study this [self] as distinct from the body.
He states the doubt to be refuted by the *Attara-sūtra* with the words "If [it were] the Pradhāna," and so forth.
And the phrase "and being immortal" means that for one who is subject to destruction, the experience of another body would be impossible.

Just as in the action of going whose agent is Devadatta, the village is the object and not Devadatta, so too in the actions of seeing and so forth whose agent is the self, the non-self is the object and not the self, because it is impossible for an action to have its own agent as its object; thus he says: "In the agent... (kartari).
In an action, the agent is subordinate and the object is primary;
since it is contradictory for one and the same entity to possess both subordination and primacy within a single action, the meaning is that the agent cannot simultaneously be the object.

"One should not make the Self, the seer of seeing, an object of that very seeing which is itself seen," according to such scriptural passages; therefore, he says "no" to the claim that qualities such as being unseen belong to the embodied soul.
Having stated the reason implied by the word "also" (api), he states the reason explicitly expressed in the words "moreover, both.
To dispel the delusion of real difference arising from the Sūtra's mention of "by way of distinction" (bhedena), he raises an objection: "How so? (katham).

Now, one might raise the objection that there is no contradiction here because the individual soul (*jīva*) is the enjoyer, whereas the Lord (*īśvara*) is not the enjoyer; this is expressed by the phrase "What then?
The proponent of the previous view replies, "Not another," asserting that the distinction between these two is contradicted by scripture.
He states the meaning of the scripture itself with the words "herein.
Anticipating another possible interpretation of the scripture, he refutes it with the words beginning "by another controller," and so forth.
It is not merely a case of prohibiting what was never even suggested.

However, he states "aviśeṣa" (without distinction) because, if the scriptural statement denying other seers were taken as a denial of an inner controller within [the Self], there would be a contradiction with the general [scriptural] teaching.
Therefore, the mention of a difference between seers in the Sūtra and in the Śruti passage, "He who dwells in the Self," is untenable.

When it is argued that difference is refuted by the supplementary statement "not another" (*nānyaḥ*), [the author] provides the resolution: "To this it is replied," meaning that difference is merely imagined through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and is restated [by scripture] in both the Śruti and the Sūtra. To the question, "Why might difference not be real? he says: "For [Brahman] is one."
The meaning is as follows: because it is impossible for both [the self and the pot] to be objects of the cognition "I" out of respect [for the authority of scripture], only one can be that object.
Since that which is its object—like a pot—is not the self, a real plurality of selves does not exist.
"And therefore... [refers to this].
The meaning is that because the acceptance of imagined difference (kalpitabheda) is admitted, everything that depends on difference is logically consistent.
Therefore, it is established that the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa is harmonized with Brahman, which is the object of knowledge. //20//
That which possesses qualities such as invisibility [is Brahman], because its attributes are declared [in scripture]. (BS 1.2.21)
"Because of the mention of attributes such as invisibility [it refers to Brahman]. He cites the passage from the *Muṇḍaka Upani�sapad*: "Now," etc.
After the description of action and the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) consisting of ritual, that by which the attributeless [Brahman] is known is called the higher knowledge (*parā vidyā*).
He points that very [Brahman] out by means of a description of its characteristics with the words "that which" (yattat).
It is "unseeable" (adreśyam), meaning invisible by the organs of knowledge; it is "ungraspable" (agrāhyam), meaning ungraspable by the organs of action.
Lineage (*gotra*) refers to family descent;
caste (*varṇa*) refers to birth as a Brahmin and so forth; "empty of eye and ear" means being without eye or ear.
"Devoid of hands and feet" means lacking the organs of knowledge and action; "all-pervading" means sovereign.
It is "subtle" because it is difficult to know.
By the two terms "eternal" (nitya) and "indestructible" (avyaya), the destruction and decay [of the soul] are excluded.

The grammatical connection is as follows: that which the wise—the learned—behold as the source (yoni) and the primordial nature (prakṛti) of all beings, that is the Imperishable (akṣara); one should know that as the Supreme (para).
Since qualities such as "being invisible" (adreśyatva) are common to both Brahman and the Pradhāna, a doubt arises.
