By way of a counter-example—since qualities belonging to a conscious being, such as "being a seer" (draṣṭṛtva), are not heard of here as in the previous case—the opponent sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it must be the Pradhāna.
In this prima facie view, there would be meditation upon the Pradhāna and so forth.
In the final conclusion, the realization of the attributeless [Brahman] is the fruit.
The meaning is that the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*), which is the silkworm, emits threads from its own body and withdraws them again.
"For one who lives mindfully.
[Objection: But was not the Pradhāna already refuted previously? How is it being raised again? To this, he says: "Moreover" (api ca).

Here, one raises an objection, saying "But [the word] 'yaḥ'," on the grounds that a supplementary portion of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) contradicting the primary subject is heard and thus impossible. In response, he says "To this it is replied," explaining that because the element *akṣara* is heard in the ablative case, there is a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the primordial material cause (*bhūtaprakṛti*), whereas the omniscience and other attributes belong to the Lord (*īśvara*), the efficient cause of the world, who is denoted by the nominative form of the word *para*.

He establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) according to the maxim "But when there is doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the supplementary portion of the sentence" (*saṃdigdhe tu vākyaśeṣāt*), saying "Thus, such being the case."

One might object: "It is incorrect to determine that the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) is the Lord (*īśvara*) on the basis of the supplementary statement 'He who is omniscient,' since there is no means of recognition for the source of beings in that supplementary statement. [The author replies:

"From the syllable (*akṣara*) it arises," because the fifth case ending is prescribed by the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.30), which assigns the technical designation of *apādāna* (ablative) to the material cause (*prakṛti*).

He provides the resolution, stating "To this it is replied," that there is recognition of the Imperishable (akṣara) mentioned as the material cause by the indicative mark of being the material cause in the concluding phrase "from that" (tasmāt), which is the source of beings (bhūtayoni).
This effect is Brahman, whose nature is subtle, namely name and form.

The gross [form] is food, meaning rice and so forth. Regarding the argument that the source of beings (bhūtayoni) is non-conscious because of the recognition [of it] through the scriptural mention of the "syllable" (akṣara) in the fifth case-ending, he says: "beyond the syllable."

He says that this word "akṣara" does not refer to the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), because the source of beings—which was previously described as being attainable through higher knowledge (*paravidyā*)—has already been identified as Brahman by the scriptural mention of "akṣara" in the passage "One knows the akṣara, the Puruṣa," which possesses the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being an object of knowledge. He explains this with the words "by which":
by means of which knowledge one knows the all-knowing Puruṣa, the akṣara who is the source of beings—that is, that Brahma-knowledge—to a worthy disciple.

The meaning is that, beginning with the words "One should declare," and stating "Indeed, he is without breath, without mind, pure" and "Higher than the high Imperishable," it is understood that the Supreme Source of beings (bhūtayoni) is the one being described.
Then, raising the doubt as to what the referent of the word "Imperishable" (akṣara) in the ablative case is, he says "How so? in order to state that it will be explained as ignorance (ajñāna).
He states that even by the designation "higher knowledge" (paravidyā), its object is Brahman, saying "Moreover" (apica).
Now, one might object: "But the knowledge of the Pradhāna is also 'higher' because it has the Cause as its object"; to this he says: "The distinction between higher and lower.

The meaning is that, having censured the lower knowledge on account of its impermanent fruit, the text concludes by declaring the knowledge of Brahman for the sake of one seeking liberation. Thus is the sense of the remainder of the passage.
To the objection that even the knowledge of Pradhāna might be considered "higher" because its fruit is liberation, he says: "And not...

Now, one might argue that in the subsequent passage, "He who is all-knowing," the subject of higher knowledge is stated, whereas by the statement regarding the "unseen," the knowledge of Pradhāna is being described; to this he replies: "And three..."
For this reason as well, he states that the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) is Brahman, beginning with the words "In what" (*kasmin*).
If the single abode and material cause were merely insentient, then even if that [cause] were known, there would be no knowledge of the selves (*ātman*), which are not its effects.
Similarly, if the individual soul (*jīva*) were known, there would be no knowledge of the objects of experience (*bhogya*), which are not its effects. This is the meaning.
And by the term "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā), he states that the source of beings is Brahman, saying: "Moreover" (apica).
He [the sage] spoke of the knowledge of Brahman—the foundation and the culminating ground of all sciences—as the knowledge of Brahman.
Because all sciences and the fruits of those sciences are included within Brahman, the knowledge of Brahman is the foundation of all sciences.
Now, one might ask: for what purpose is the lower knowledge (apara-vidyā) mentioned in the context of the higher [knowledge]? To this he says:
"The lower... The term *plavāḥ* means those which float or move; they are perishable, being incapable of producing results that are firm and eternal.
There are sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), together with the wife and the sacrificer, making eighteen;
they are designated as "forms of sacrifice" (*yajñarūpa*) because they are defined by the name "sacrifice.
For instance, they are called *ṛtvij* because they solicit during the ritual seasons (*ṛtu*) and cause the sacrifice to be performed.

One who sacrifices is a *yajamāna*; according to the rule "the word *pati* takes the substitution of *na* when connected with sacrifice" (*apatyurno yajñasaṃyoge*), the word *pati* undergoes the substitution of *na* in connection with sacrifice, thus forming *patnī*.
In this way, since the basis for the application of names such as *ṛtvij* and others is the sacrifice, they are of the nature of sacrifice.

The meaning is that those fools who are satisfied with the thought, "This very ritual action— which yields inferior and impermanent results as taught in the Vedas— is the highest good, and nothing else such as the knowledge of the Self," undergo birth and death again and again.
Therefore, there is the rule that one must approach a teacher for the sake of knowing that, namely, for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman.
He [the author] precludes the status of a teacher for one who, though devoted to Brahman, has not studied the Vedas by using the term "learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*).
The phrase "the effect is non-different from its material cause" serves as an illustration regarding this point.
He says, "Moreover, they are gross," because even if there were complete identity, an undesirable consequence would follow. //21//
And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, it is neither of the other two. (BS 1.2.22)

He explains the two reasons—“because of the qualification” and “because of the statement of difference”—by analyzing them as follows, beginning with the words "For [the text] qualifies [it]" and so on:
"Divine" means consisting of light, self-luminous;
"formless" means full.
The Person (puruṣa) is the inner self (pratyagātman) dwelling within the city (puriśaya).
He is "with the external and internal" because he abides as the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) together with both the external—the gross—and the internal—the subtle causal body;
for it is thus well-known in the Śrutis. This is the meaning.
The body, consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*); limitation (*pariccheda*) is its smallness due to that [body].
The meaning is that the properties of that body, such as insentience and materiality, belong to it.
[Objection: But if the word "imperishable" (*akṣara*) refers to *pradhāna*, would not the thesis that *pradhāna* is "without sound" (*aśabdatva*) be contradicted?

Regarding this, he says: "The syllable (akṣara) is the unmanifest (avyākṛta). It is called the syllable because it pervades—that is, it extends through—the entire collection of its own transformations; it is unmanifest because it is not clearly differentiated.
"Beginningless" means as follows:
God is the seed of name-and-form; His nature is that of power (*śakti*). Because it is dependent upon another, even the material cause (*upādāna*) is called "power."

"Bhūtasūkṣma" refers to that wherein the subtle impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the elements reside; it is "that which has the Lord as its substratum," meaning the Lord who is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is its support.
It is this very pure consciousness that serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord.

As for the interpretation of those who maintain the doctrine of manifold souls—that it means "that which has the Lord as its substratum and object"—that falls outside the scope of the commentary (*bhāṣya*).

For, in the passage, "In this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof," the Śruti declares that the unmanifest (avyākṛta) has consciousness as its substratum through the relationship of being woven; thus, there is no basis for the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of the word "substratum" [as referring to Māyā].
Furthermore, there is no evidence whatsoever for a difference between the Root-Nature (mūlaprakṛti) [and Brahman].
Nor is the Śruti text, "Indra by means of his magical powers (māyābhiḥ)," a proof [for such a difference].

By the force of numerous Śrutis such as "the one unborn" (*ajāmekām*), aided by the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghava-tarka*), that Śruti merely restates the distinctions of Māyā according to the differences in the cognitions [of individual souls].
As it was said by Sureśvarācārya: "In reality, however, not even the slightest distinction of ignorance (*avidyā*) exists here.
The teachers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, as well as the authors of the Purāṇas and Itihāsas, declare the oneness of the root-primal nature (*mūla-prakṛti*).
If it is objected: "But if ignorance is one and the same, how can there be the distinction between bondage and liberation?
Nor should it be said that no such distinction exists, for that would result in the subversion of engagement in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth."
It is said: For even those who maintain that ignorance (*avidyā*) is manifold must admit that it possesses parts (*sāṃśatva*) by virtue of its being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*).

Thus, the systematic distinction between individual souls (*jīva*)—who are conditioned by specific parts of ignorance transformed into the form of their own respective inauspicious aggregates—is established.
Liberation occurs for that person in whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) knowledge arises, through the destruction of the part of ignorance that undergoes transformation within that internal organ.
And thus, there is the attainment of the bliss of one's own true nature by the listener,
the engagement in hearing and so forth, and the experience of the realized ones.
Thus, the entire treatise on liberation while living (*jīvanmukti-śāstra*) remains uncontradicted.
Nor does this result in no distinction from the position of multiple souls (*nānājīva-pakṣa*), because there is no plurality of the root-primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*); so, enough of this.
The reason for its being "other" is stated as "unchanging.

Now, one might object: since the author of the Sūtras has declared in the Śruti that there is a designation of difference from Pradhāna, how can it be explained here by a statement of difference from ignorance (ajñāna)?
To this, he says: "Not here."

The meaning is that *pradhāna* is simply ignorance (*ajñāna*), because it is designated as such by virtue of its being the effect; for anything other than that [ignorance] lacks any basis in valid cognition (*apramāṇika*).
Therefore, having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that here ignorance alone is the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), it is subsequently refuted.
It should be understood that by the refutation of that [soul], the Pradhāna postulated by the Sāṃkhyas is effectively refuted as well. //22//
And because of the presentation of form. (BBs 1.2.23)
First, according to the opinion of the author of the *Vṛtti*, he explains the Sūtra with the words "Moreover" (*apica*) and so forth.
The Śruti states: "Prāṇa, mind, all the senses, space, wind, light, water, and earth.
Here, "fire" (*agni*) refers to the heavenly world (*dyuloka*).
According to the Vedic scripture, "That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire";
the connection is that the Vedas are speech;
and by the words "from the feet," the meaning is "the two feet."
The meaning is that he who possesses this form is the inner self (antarātman) of all living beings. "Of limited majesty" means of small power.

Just as someone who knows Brahman sings the Sāman chant "I am food" for the purpose of manifesting his own nature as the Self of all, but does not intend to assert that he is actually food—since that would yield no fruit—so it is here as well; thus he says: "I am food."
He refutes the commentary of the author of the *Vṛtti* with the words "others, however" (*anye punar*).

The meaning is that, according to the connection with the scriptural passage, "This Inner Self of all beings, the Sūtrātman, is born from this source of beings," Hiraṇyagarbha is presented here as being born.
The word "niradikṣat" means "he spoke."

The meaning is that Agni is the heavenly world (dyuloka) of which [the universe] consists, and since the sun is the form of its fuel (samid), it is from that Agni of the heavenly world that [Agni] was born; for another Vedic text states: "Therefore, the sun itself is the fuel."
Therefore, the intended meaning is that even in the intermediate passage, only the act of creation is to be described, not the form [of the source].

Regarding what was stated—that in the verse "Agni is the head," the intention is to express that the source of beings (bhūtayoni) is the Self of all—he says in response: "Even its being the Self of all..."
Now, one might object: "Since the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha has not been mentioned elsewhere, how can it be stated here?

To this he says: "By the Śruti... [The verse continues: "In the beginning he came into being; having been born, he alone became the lord and master of the multitude of beings through the grace of the Lord."
That Sūtrātman supported this heaven and this earth, as well as everything gross.

Since the word *ka* is a name for Prajāpati, it lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and thus the form *smā* would be inappropriate; therefore, it should be explained by dropping the vowel *e* [from *eka*] as *ekasmai*, meaning "to the one God, the Self of Prāṇa, let us worship with oblation, let us serve Him.
This is because of the Vedic scripture: "Which one is the single God? Prāṇa."
Alternatively, the meaning is "to that one God from whom this [universe] has arisen," because another Vedic scripture states, "The one God is hidden in all beings.
Now, one might ask: how can He be the self of other beings?
Regarding this, he says: "Modification.

Due to the performance of the accumulation of excellent worship and ritual action (*karma*) in a previous kalpa, in this kalpa there arises a collective subtle body (*samaṣṭi-liṅga-śarīra*), which consists of the organs of knowledge and action, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the self; it is pervasive throughout all individual subtle bodies (*vyaṣṭi-liṅga*) of all living beings and is contained within all living beings.
The meaning is that it is logical for that which has such a nature—the thread-self (sūtrātman)—to be the inner self of all beings.
Regarding his own position, he states the meaning of the Sūtra: "In this view," etc.

The meaning is that since all action—whether Vedic or Smārta—and austerity, along with their fruits, reside in the Person alone, and because of the presentation of the form of being the inner self of all, the scriptural statement is consistently applicable to the Source of Beings as the object of knowledge. //23//
Vaiśvānara [is the Self], because of the specific nature of the common term. (BS 1.2.24)
Regarding Vaiśvānara, the Chāndogya Upaniṣad provides an illustration: "Who is our self?
Prācīnaśāla, Satyayajña, Indradyumna, Jana, and Buḍila, having come together, conducted an inquiry, asking: "Who is our self? What is Brahman?"

The two words [of the text] are for the purpose of making known that the Self alone is Brahman. Those five also went to Uddālaka for the sake of certainty; he too did not know it correctly. Therefore, all six, together with Uddālaka, approached King Aśvapati Kaikeya and said: "The Self..."
"You have requested it; remember that very [teaching], so speak to us.
But the king, in order to dispel their delusion, questioned each of them individually: "Whom do you worship as the Self?
And Prācīnaśāla and the others replied to him one by one in turn: "I know heaven alone as Vaiśvānara."
"I know only Āditya; I know only Vāyu; I know only Ākāśa."
"Only water," [he said].
"I know the earth alone.

Then the king, having assigned to the six—beginning with the sky and the sun—their respective qualities of intense brilliance, multiformity, the nature of diverse paths, abundance, speed, and being the foundation;

"O sirs, if you were to hold the view that each individual limb of the Lord Vaiśvānara— such as the sky, the sun, and so forth— is Vaiśvānara itself without first asking me, then you would suffer, respectively, the falling off of your head, blindness, being measured out [and cast away], the dissolution of your body, the bursting of your bladder,
and the withering of your feet. Thus he spoke, censuring the worship of each part individually.
The heavenly world, characterized by the quality of great splendor (*sutejas*), is the head of this Vaiśvānara Self;

the sun, characterized by the quality of universal form (*viśvarūpa*), is his eye. Having thus taught that the heavenly world, the sun, and so forth constitute the head and other parts [of the body], the scripture prescribes the meditation on the complete Vaiśvānara with the words, "But he who... (*yastvetam*).
He is called *abhivimāna* because he measures—that is, knows—the universe directly and through immediate perception (*aparokṣatayā*).
The meaning is that that disciple of his enjoys enjoyment everywhere from that Omniscient One.
"Worlds" refers to the realms such as Bhūr and so forth; "beings" refers to bodies.
The distinction is that "ātman" refers to the self and "jīva" to the living being.
He whose splendor and radiance are excellent—that heavenly world—is "Sutejas.
All forms belong to this Sun.

According to the Vedic scripture, "This is white, this is blue," that wind whose path—meaning its course—is separate and of various kinds possesses the quality of having manifold courses; its vital breath (prāṇa) is characterized by this.
Its abundance is its pervasiveness, and space (ākāśa), which has that as its quality, is its "intermediate space" (saṃdeha), meaning the middle of the body.
The waters possess the quality of being *rayi* (wealth) and *dhana* (property), and his bladder is their locus;
the earth possesses the quality of being the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), and his feet are that [foundation].
He establishes his status as the substratum for the oblation with the words beginning "the chest indeed," and so forth.

Previously, it was stated that a common attribute such as "invisibility" found in the opening of a passage is established as residing in Brahman by means of an indicative mark (liṅga) such as "omniscience" found in the remainder of the passage;

likewise, here too, the opponent raises a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) by means of an analogy—that the common term "Vaiśvānara" found in the opening is established as residing in the digestive fire (jāṭhara) by means of the indicative mark of being the "locus of the oblation" found in the remainder of the passage—beginning with the words "But what [is it]? and so forth.
The fruit of the prima facie and final conclusions (siddhānta) regarding the digestive fire and Brahman, respectively, is meditation (dhyāna).
That which is eaten is food;
the meaning is that that by which it is digested exists within this human body.
He states another alternative: "or merely fire."
The gods made Vaiśvānara Agni—the banner and sign of the days, namely the Sun—for the sake of the entire world;
for by the rising of the sun, the activities of the day proceed—this is the meaning. The word "Vaiśvānara" is to be supplied [from the previous verse].
For indeed, because he is the bestower of happiness (*kaṃ*) upon the worlds, the King Vaiśvānara is the Lord (*īśvara*) whose glory (*śrī*) is directed toward him;
therefore, "may we abide in the good thought (*sumati*) of that Vaiśvānara," meaning: "may his auspicious intention be directed toward us.
Expressing dissatisfaction with all three positions, he states another alternative beginning with "atha" and so forth.
The meaning is: "because of the scriptural text, 'The Self is indeed Vaiśvānara.
"Kevalatva" (the state of being alone) means the absence of the word "Vaiśvānara.
In this context, the primary prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) is Vaiśvānara.

Because it possesses the characteristic mark of being the substratum for the oblation of the Prāṇāgnihotra, and because it pervades the body, its nature as the Self (ātman) is established; furthermore, through the scriptural imagination of having heaven as its head and so forth, its vastness establishes its nature as Brahman—this is what should be meditated upon.
He states the final conclusion: "Therefore, this [is so]."

The meaning is that, because there is a distinction between the two common scriptural passages situated at the beginning, it is appropriate that they refer to the Lord who is the Self of all—on account of the mark (*liṅga*) of the "body of the three worlds" which is heard first and is primary—rather than referring to the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) on account of the mark of being the locus of the oblation, which is heard later and is merely imagined.
[Objection: But how can there be any distinction for that which is devoid of attributes? To this, he says: "For here... (*atra hi*).
The meaning is that, having entered into another state, he exists as the self of the three worlds.
If it is argued that a specific conceptualization is made even for the digestive fire (jāṭhara) for the sake of meditation, we say no,
because that would result in the fallacy of conceiving what is unreal.
However, because the Lord is the material cause (*upādāna*), He is already existent; let Him be spoken of for the sake of meditation. To this he says: "Because He is the cause" (*kāraṇatvāt*).
He states other indicative marks with the words beginning "He in all... and so forth.
The meaning is that, just as a reed or cotton thrown into fire is consumed, even so is [the sin] of this wise man. //24//
"That which is being remembered would be inference" (BBs 1.2.25).

Anticipating the objection that praise is possible even through the imposition of what is unreal, and thus there would be no need for the foundational scripture (*mūla-śruti*), he says: "Even though it is praise.
He reads the word *tathāpi* (even so) according to its meaning as *stutitvam api* (even the state of being praise).
The meaning is that praise in the form of having heaven as one's head and so forth cannot be performed by a mere human being without [the authority of] scripture.
The meaning is that since praise arises from an existing form, there is no superimposition of what is non-existent. //25//

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of the meditation on the small ether] because of its being mentioned among sound and so forth, and because of its abiding within, we say no; for there is instruction regarding such a vision, because [those qualities] are impossible [in the individual soul], and they also study this as the Puruṣa. (BS 1.2.26)
In order to state the movement of sound and the other [objects], he raises an objection to the stated conclusion and provides a resolution with the words "From sound and the rest" (*śabdādibhyaḥ*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: the word "fire" (*agni*) heard in the *Agnirahasya* within the Vaiśvānara-vidyā—namely, "This very one is the fire Vaiśvānara"—is not possible [to apply] to the Lord (*īśvara*).
He states the meaning of the word "and the rest" (*ādi*) contained in the Sūtra with the words "from the word 'and the rest'" (*ādiśabdāt*).
"Bhaktam" means food; "homīyam" means the material for the oblation;
the meaning is that the Prāṇāgnihotra is to be performed with that.

In the *Agnirahasya* of the Vājasaneyins, after teaching the Vaiśvānara-vidyā in detail, it is stated: "He who knows this Agni Vaiśvānara as being of the form of man, established within man—he eats food everywhere. [The author] says "so" (*tathā*) because this state of being situated within the body is possible in the case of the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), owing to its well-known status.

In this Sūtra, although the inclusion of "internal abiding" (*antaḥpratiṣṭhāna*) is possible through the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) alone, its separate mention is intended to indicate that it is a common characteristic (*sādhāraṇaliṅga*).

Furthermore, the argument based on the power of sound (*śabda*) and so forth serves as a supplementary reason (*abhyuccaya*) leading to the conclusion that this [being] is the gastric fire (*jāṭhara*).

Even though it may appear that characteristics such as having heaven as the head (*dyumūrdhatva*) favor the Lord (*īśvara*), while being the substratum of oblations (*homādhāratva*) and so forth favor the gastric fire, nevertheless, the supreme divine characteristic cannot possibly belong to the gastric fire.
To explain why he is "powerful," he says "or else" (*athavā*).
The meaning is that this is the instruction regarding his being the "heavenly-headed one" (*dyumūrdhan*) and so forth.

The meaning is that one should meditate upon him who, as the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*), has pervaded and extended across this earth and even the sky—those two, heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), known as *rodasī*—as well as the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) between them, in the form of light (*bhānu*).
Since that which is merely insentient cannot be an object of meditation, he says "Or rather" (*athavā*).
He establishes his own position with the words "Not so, because of the instruction regarding the vision [of the Lord]" (*na tathādṛṣṭyupadeśāt*).

Having stated that the Supreme Lord—who possesses the head of heaven and other attributes—is indicated by the two words *agni* and *vaiśvānara*, which denote the gastric fire as a symbol to be meditated upon through the vision of the Supreme Lord, he states another alternative: "Or rather, [the term] 'gastric' (*jāṭhara*)."
In this view, the distinction is that the Lord is the primary object of worship here, whereas in the previous case He was subordinate.
By the two words expressing the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the meaning is that He is indicated (*lakṣya*) as being conditioned by them.
He explains the impossibility—which is the seed of the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—with the words "If, however... (*yadi ca*).

He explains the remainder of the sūtra beginning with "puruṣam api" as follows: "yadi ca kevalaḥ. The intended meaning is that [the person] is devoid of being a symbol or an adjunct of Īśvara; the word "tadā" (then) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Yat" means "yaḥ," which is the person (puruṣaḥ).
The meaning of the Śruti is that this very Agni has the gastric fire (jāṭhara) designated by the term Vaiśvānara as its limiting adjunct (upādhi).
The meaning is that he who knows this eats everywhere.

Having stated that "personhood" (puruṣatva)—that is, fullness—is not present in the insentient gastric fire, [the text] says in an alternative reading—"But those who..."—to declare that "person-shaped-ness" (puruṣavidhatva), i.e., having the form of a body, does not belong to it.

[Objection: But surely, since the gastric fire also pervades the body, it too would possess the form of man (puruṣavidhatva). To this he says: "And the state of being man-like [is established] from the context.
Being man-like does not mean merely pervading the body; rather, it means having the shape of the Virāj-body.

The meaning is that the Lord's state of being man-like consists in His having the form of the cosmic person (adhidaiva) and, with respect to the self (adhyātma), in His perfection within the limbs of the worshipper, from the head down to the chin. //26//
For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor a living being. (BBs 1.2.27)
The perfection [of all qualities] in the limbs of the Lord will be stated later.
Having thus refuted the gastric fire (jāṭhara), he refutes the two alternative positions with the words "for this very reason" (ata eva).
He explains the Sūtra with the passage beginning "yat punar... and so forth.
The state of having heaven as its head and so forth,
the sharing in the fruits of all worlds,
and the complete burning away of all evils.
The reasons stated at the beginning regarding the words *ātman* and *brahman* are recalled by the passage beginning with "for [the greatness] of the elemental fire" (*na hi bhūtāgneḥ*).
The intention is that the majesty was described through the vision of the Lord (Īśvara) by means of the mantra "He who [shines] with light" (*yo bhānunā*). //27//
Jaimini maintains that there is no contradiction even with direct perception. (BS 1.2.28)

It was previously stated that the words *agni* and *vaiśvānara* are indicative (*lakṣaka*) of the Lord (*īśvara*). Now, even if it is accepted that the Blessed One Vaiśvānara— in the form of the Virāj-puruṣa— is to be meditated upon within the self (*adhyātma*) by superimposing [his parts] from the head down to the chin after discarding the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the symbols (*pratīka*), there is no contradiction regarding the two words in their application to the Lord.
Because it is primary by way of its yogic application (*yogavṛtti*), and because qualities such as "abiding within" (*antaḥsthatva*) are possible therein, he says: "even directly" (*sākṣād api*).
He explains the meaning of the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) by saying: "without even" (*vinā eva*).

The meaning is that Jaimini considers there to be no contradiction with sound and other [sensory objects], even though the Lord is the object of meditation, provided there is a connection with the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*).

This "abiding within" (*antasthatva*) is not said to mean residing in the stomach; rather, in the body of a person—which consists of a collection of parts from the nails to the hair—limbs from the head down to the chin are established like branches on a tree, and Vaiśvānara, being fully present in those, is said to be "established within the person."

Therefore, just as a bird on a branch is situated within the tree, so too is Vaiśvānara situated within the person; this is stated by the passage beginning with "for here [he is] not of the form of a person.

Since words such as "fire" (agni) denote the Lord (Īśvara), the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) is not what is being referred to. Here, because the Lord is superimposed upon the limbs of the person, the meaning is that He possesses the form of a person and is situated within it.
He states another alternative with the words "or else" (athavā).
"The state of being man-like" (puruṣavidhatva) is as explained previously.
"Being situated within" (antaḥsthatva) means being intermediate, that is, being a witness (sākṣitva).
Having thus explained the state of abiding within in the Lord, he explains the terms "sound" and so forth: "And when it is determined...
This person (*nara*) is the individual soul (*jīva*), because he is the self of all;
or, he is the agent (*nara*) who creates all modifications (*vikāra*).

*Viśvānara* means "one to whom all (*viśve*) men (*narāḥ*), that is, all living beings, belong" either by way of being his self or by way of being subject to his control. The secondary suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*) is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), as in the case of *rakṣa* becoming *rākṣasa*.
The lengthening of the first member of the compound is according to the rule "in *nara*, when a name [is formed]."
The word *agni* is a form derived from the root *ag*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *nip*.
It is called *agni* because it leads (*aṅgayati*) or causes [the agent] to reach the goal; that is, it brings about the fruit of action, and thus it is said to be a leader (*agraṇī*).
Alternatively, it is *agni* because it has gone (*aga*) everywhere (*abhitaḥ*).
For one who worships Vaiśvānara, the Prāṇāgnihotra is prescribed as an ancillary part of that knowledge to be performed before feeding the guest;

for that purpose, the conceptualization of the three sacrificial fires and so forth must be interpreted in a way that does not contradict the primary subject. Thus he says: "The Gārhapatya... (Sūtra 28).
"It is because of manifestation," says Āśmarathya. (BsRp_1,2.7.29)

"Exceeding measure" (*atimātra*) means having transcended all dimensions; the meaning is "of that All-pervading One" (*vibhoḥ*). For the sake of favoring the lay devotees (*upāsaka*), He manifests as being "measured by a span" (*prādeśamātra*);
or, He is measured—that is, manifested—within specific locations (*pradeśeṣu*), hence He is called "measured by a span. //29//
Bādari [maintains that the fruit arises] from recollection. (BBs 1.2.30)
He states another opinion with the words "anusmṛteḥ" (from remembrance).
"Measured by a span" means measured by a mind [the size of] a span; that is the meaning.
"In some way or other" means—
The meaning is that the state of being the size of a span (prādeśamātratva), which resides in the mind and is imagined within the object of remembrance by means of memory, is the basis for the Śruti.
He states another meaning of the Sūtra: "prādeśa... [Sūtra 1.3.24].
"It is because of the attainment [of Brahman], so Jaimini says; for scripture shows it thus. (BS 1.2.31)
Now, he states the interpretation of the scriptural passage concerning the "span-long" (prādeśamātra) measurement: "On account of attaining" (saṃpatteḥ).
He cites the Brāhmaṇa text: "As if span-long.

Although the Lord is unlimited, the gods, having correctly understood Him as conceived through the metaphorical attribution of being span-long, attained Him—the very Lord—by attaining Him as their own inner Self (pratyak).
Indeed, in former times,
I shall then declare to you those parts beginning with heaven, in such a way that they do not exceed the measure of a span (*prādeśa*).

Having made a promise to Prācīnaśāla and others, saying, "I shall identify Vaiśvānara with the internal limbs beginning with the head," the King, pointing to his own head and showing it with his hand, said: "This indeed is my head; that which stands above, transcending the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, is the heavenly world (dyuloka), which is Vaiśvānara."
"His head" means up to that point;
the meaning is that by identifying the internal head with the divine head, it should be meditated upon.
In this same manner, one should apply this reasoning to the eyes and the other [senses].

Showing his own eyes, he said, "This indeed is the one of good luster; the sun is the eye of Vaiśvānara. By the word "nose," that which resides in it—namely, the vital breath (prāṇa)—is indicated. Regarding that internal vital breath, he prescribes the visualization of the cosmic vital breath, Vāyu, saying "the nose. In all these instances, the word *vaiśvānara* refers to the limbs [of the body].

The mouth is the primary [part]; in that [mouth], one should perceive the vast sky as the presiding deity (adhidaiva). In the saliva located in the mouth, one should perceive the water; and in the water contained in the bladder, denoted by the word "ra" (wealth), one should perceive the water. At the chin, the earth, which is the support, should be perceived in the form of the feet. Now, one might object: since there is a difference between the two meditations due to a disparity in their qualities, how can the mention of the "span-long" [person] found in the Chāndogya be explained in accordance with the Śruti of the Agnirahasya? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even though," and so forth.
The identity of the knowledge, established by a greater degree of recognition despite this slight discrepancy, is not lost;

for it will be stated later that the principle holds that even when there is a difference of recensional branches (*śākhā*), the meditation on Vaiśvānara and others perceived in all branches is one and the same.
Furthermore, the quality of "standing upon" (*atiṣṭhātva*) should be combined from the Chāndogya.
And the quality of having a universal form (viśvarūpatva) is to be accepted by the followers of the Vājasaneyi school.
Thus, while the possession of great splendor is common to both the heaven and the sun, there is a distribution of the qualities of being the support and having a universal form [to each].

Vijñāna is profound contemplation (*nididhyāsana*).

From the first word [of the compound], reflection (*manana*), faith (*śraddhā*), hearing (*śravaṇa*), purity of mind (*manaḥ-śuddhi*), steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*), and the actions that cause it are included.
These, beginning with hearing and so forth, are the marks (*liṅga*) of the knowable reality, Brahman.

Thus, having set aside the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of direct scriptural statements (*śruti*) and indicative marks (*liṅga*), he says "In that [context], that which... to show that the Satya Brahman under discussion is the possessor of the attribute of "muchness" (*bhūmatva*) denoted by the word *bhūman*.

Furthermore, according to the maxim "that which is remote is stronger than even that which is proximate if it possesses expectancy," he says "And thus... to show that, having seen the proximate and self-sufficient vital breath, the Self situated at the beginning of the passage—which requires the *bhūman* passage for its own exposition—must be understood here as the *bhūman*.

Furthermore, since the passage begins with "the further shore of sorrow" (*śokasya pāram*) and concludes with "the further shore of darkness" (*tamasaḥ pāram*), and because it is impossible to cross over sorrow without uprooting its very source,
the term "sorrow" (*śoka*) here refers to the fundamental darkness (*mūlatamas*).
He states that the Self is Brahman on the basis of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of being cognizable through the knowledge that removes [ignorance], saying "and not elsewhere.
The connection is that the Brāhmaṇa declares the dependence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon the Self. Now, one might object: let this final Brāhmaṇa be intended as referring to Brahman.
Then, one might suspect that the previously mentioned "plurality" (bhūman) is actually the vital breath (prāṇa); [the author] raises this doubt with the words "at the end of the section.
He refutes it, saying "No," because the word "that" (tat) refers back to the plurality (bhūman). //8//
And because of the attainment of dharma.
Regarding the state of the Infinite (bhūman) being Brahman, the author states another indicative mark: "Dharma...
This is the Sūtra.

Having restated what was said—that the characteristics of the Infinite, namely bliss and immortality, are to be applied to the vital breaths (prāṇas)—he refutes that by beginning with the words "yo 'pyasau" (And as for that...).
When adjuncts such as the intellect (buddhi) are present, the Self possesses the status of a seer and so forth;

in their absence, as in deep sleep, that [status] is absent. To convey this state of non-attachment, the Praśnopaniṣad, referring to the Supreme Self, states: "He does not hear, he does not see. Likewise, in that very same text, the nature of the Self is declared to be bliss, not that of the vital breath (prāṇa).

The meaning is: because another Vedic scripture declares that bliss belongs to the Self alone; therefore [the Self is not happiness]. "Sāmayam" means accompanied by *āmaya*, which refers to defects such as destruction and the like. "Ārtam" means perishable.
"That alone is below, that is above" declares its omnipresence;
"That alone is all this" declares its being the Self of all.
Therefore, it is established that the section concerning the Infinite (Bhūma) is in harmony with the attributeless Brahman. //9//
The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports everything up to the ether. (BS 1.3.10)
"Because it supports that which extends to the ends of space.
The *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* recites: "In what, then?

When Gārgī asked Yājñavalkya, the sage, "Upon what is all that which has been, that which is, and that which will be woven," he replied that the unevolved space (*avyākṛtākāśa*) is the support for everything that is merely an effect.
Regarding the second question, "In what is space woven? that sage replied:
"That is the substrate of the undifferentiated (avyākṛta); it is this Imperishable (akṣara) whose nature is not gross and so forth. A doubt arises because the word "akṣara" is used in both instances.

Just as the word *satya* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of Brahman, and thus it is said that "Brahman is the ground" (*brahma bhūma*), so too the word *akṣara* is conventionally established in the sense of a phoneme (*varṇa*); this constitutes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by way of analogy.

In this regard, the distinction is that the fruit in the prima facie view is the meditation (*upāsti*) on the syllable *oṃ*, whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahmadhī*).

[Objection: But surely the word *akṣara* is primary even with respect to Brahman, because it does not perish (*na kṣarati*) due to its immobility and indestructibility; to this he replies: "because of the transgression of established usage. The meaning is that according to the maxim, "conventional meaning sets aside etymological derivation," [the word cannot apply to Brahman]. Having raised the doubt as to how the syllable *oṃ* can be the substratum of all, he says "the syllable *oṃ*" to show that this is for the purpose of meditation, just as its being the self of all is stated in another Vedic text.
Because the intent [of the text] is determined to be that the world, up to the ether, rests upon Him through the question and answer, it does not serve the purpose of meditation;

therefore, by the force of those indicative marks (liṅga), one should accept the etymological sense (yogavṛtti) while setting aside the conventional sense (rūḍhi). He establishes this conclusion with the words beginning "Thus" (evam) and so forth. //10//
And she [is the cause] because of her command. (BS 1.3.11)

Having treated space as an element, he raises a doubt with the words "this might be the case. He says "and that" (sā ca) to show that it is not so, because the scripture here teaches that [the creation] has an intelligent agent as its creator.
He explains the Sūtra with the words "and that" (sā ca).
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of excluding the [elemental] ether from being the [referent].

Since the elemental ether, being included among the effects, cannot logically be the substratum of all effects mentioned in scripture, it follows that the "ether" is actually unmanifest ignorance (*avyākṛtājñāna*), which is designated by the term "Pradhāna. Therefore, because the Imperishable (*akṣara*) is its substratum, the Imperishable is not the Pradhāna; this is the meaning.
[The phrase] "in the support" (*vidhṛtau*) means in the state of being held as an object. //11//
And because of the exclusion of other states. (BBs 1.3.12)
He explains the Sūtra by means of a question: "What is this?
He dispels the misconception that it is a mere exclusion from the nature of a jar by saying: "This.
The meaning is that the Śruti excludes the Imperishable (akṣara) as the support of everything up to the end of space on the grounds of its being insentient.
He also applies the Sūtra with the intent of refuting the [existence of] the individual soul (jīva), using the word "tathā" (so).
The meaning of the Sūtra is that "anyabhāvaḥ" means difference, and [the soul is not the Imperishable] because that difference is negated.
If it is then argued that the purified individual soul itself is the Imperishable and not the Supreme [Self], he says: "no" (na hi).
The meaning is that once [the body] is purified, there is no state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*).
Therefore, it is established that the *Gārgī-brāhmaṇa* is consistent with the attributeless Imperishable (*akṣara*). //12//
He [is the Self], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing. (BS 1.3.13)
"He is [the one] because of the designation of him as the object of the act of seeing.
He cites the *Praśna Upaniṣad*: "This...
The teacher Pippalāda, being questioned by Satyakāma, says:
O Satyakāma,
this very syllable *oṃ* is that Brahman which is both the supreme, attributeless (*nirguṇa*) and the non-supreme, qualified (*saguṇa*).
For it is its symbol (*pratīka*), just as an image is of Viṣṇu.

Therefore, having introduced the subject that "the knower who knows the Praṇava as Brahman-Ātman, by this very meditation on the syllable Oṃ—which is the abode and the means of attainment—attains, according to his meditation, either the higher or the lower [Brahman]," the text speaks [later] after describing the meditation on the one-measure and two-measure Oṃs: "But he who... (yaḥ punar iti).
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of "being such" (*itthaṃbhāve*), because the non-difference between Brahman and the *oṃkāra* is established from the outset.

For that *oṃkāra* which has one measure (*ekamātraḥ*) is that whose single measure— the letter *a*, the first among the three measures beginning with *a*— is correctly known by one who knows its seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, as well as its manifestation (*vibhūti*) as the waking state and the rest.

Thus, when there is a correct knowledge of the manifestation (*vibhūti*) of the two measures (*mātrā*), one who meditates upon the *oṃ* syllable as the Puruṣa—consisting of two measures and likewise three measures—goes to the world of Brahman through the door of the sun by means of the Sāman chants meditated upon as the manifestations of the *oṃ* syllable, and beholds the Supreme Self, the Puruṣa; such is the meaning.
He states the doubt and its seed with the words beginning "What... and so forth.
The meaning is: "in this sentence consisting of three morae.

The topical connection (*prasaṅga-saṃgati*) is that, since the syllable *oṃ* was mentioned previously as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is now determined that what is to be meditated upon is present in the mind.

Alternatively, whereas previously it was stated that the word *akṣara*, which is conventionally established in the sense of a "phoneme" (*varṇa*), applies to Brahman on the basis of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Similarly here as well, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of an analogy—that the word "Supreme" (*para*) refers to Hiraṇyagarbha because it serves as an indicator for the attainment of the world of Brahmā—by stating, "In that case, the other [is meant].
The fruit in both cases is the meditation upon the two forms of the Supreme Brahman, the effected (*kārya*) and the supreme (*para*); "he" refers to the meditator.

One might object: "Is it not heard in scripture that even for one who meditates on Brahman, there is at least some small fruit—namely, that 'the Lord, the giver of wealth, has entered into the sun' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1), and thus he obtains wealth"? To this, the author says: "No. Even though it may be so in other cases, here it is not appropriate for one who knows the Supreme (paravida) to attain the non-supreme (apara), because the opening statement of the passage—"He who knows the Supreme follows after the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1)—is contradicted by such an interpretation. Therefore, the attainment of the non-supreme by one who knows the Supreme is illogical due to the contradiction with the introductory context.

Nor should it be said that only the attainment of the "other" (the Supreme) is mentioned here; for since the "other" is all-pervading, its attainment would be possible right here, rendering the journey by way of the sun purposeless.

Therefore, the meaning is that the scriptural term "the other Person" (*paraṃ puruṣam*) must be set aside by the inferential mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the attainment of the "not-other," which is supported by the opening statement (*upakrama*).
He asks about the scope of what is heard from another [scripture] with the words "nanu" (but surely).
The meaning of the resolution is that the *piṇḍa* is the gross Virāṭ, and in relation to that, the *sūtra* possesses the quality of being "higher" (*para*).
Since it has been asserted that the word "parameṣṭhin" in the *sūtra* refers to the Lord (*īśvara*), he explains it as "the Supreme One alone" (*parameva*).
The meaning is that this lay follower perceives that Supreme Person beyond this Hiranyagarbha as "I am Brahman.
[Objection: But let there be another [object] even for the scope of such perception;
to this, he says: "In that case, because of the verb *abhidhyai* (to meditate upon)."
[Objection: Since perception requires the reality of its object because it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), let the Supreme (*para*) be the object of perception as something real;
but why could the other [the lower], which is to be meditated upon (*dhyātavya*), not be unreal? To this, he says: "That very one" (*sa eva*).

Because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) from the two scriptural passages, the word *sa* (that) in the Sūtra is explained as "this very same one. Here, the construction of the Sūtra is as follows: that which is to be meditated upon in the syllable *Oṃ* is indeed the Supreme Self (*para evātmā*).
Because the quality of being "worthy of seeing" (īkṣaṇīyatva) is mentioned in the supplementary portion [of the passage],
and because there is recognition of the same scripture here— [realizing] "this is that very same one"—
one might object: "But surely, due to the difference in words, there is no recognition," and thus he raises the doubt with the word "nanu."

Having accepted the distinction between the terms "the higher than the high" (*parātpara*) and "the highest" (*para*), he states that there is no contradiction with the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) expressed by the two scriptural passages in the words "herein.

Now, one might object: since the phrase "from this, the highest, which consists of the mass of living beings" (*etasmājjīvaghanātparāt*) refers back to the object of meditation introduced at the beginning, the Self to be seen must be different from the object of meditation; therefore, he says: "And not so herein."
Because meditation (*dhyāna*) and the vision of its fruit have the same object in this world, that which is to be meditated upon is precisely that which is to be seen.
Thus, the intention is that there is a unity of statement between the opening and the conclusion.

Regarding the phrase "He is led up to the world of Brahman by the Sāmans" and "From this mass of living beings," the Lord of the world of Brahman—who is most proximate—is referred to; he explains this by means of a question, beginning with "Who then... and so forth.
The sense is that this follows from the sūtra "In a concrete form, [the suffix] ghan.
A *saindhavakhilya* is a lump of salt.
That which has a limited state (*khilyabhāva*)—that is, a state of being small like a fragment—is called a *khilyabhāva*.

He states that by this term "the world of Brahman" (brahmaloka) is referred to, saying "the other. He demonstrates the indication (lakṣaṇā) of the word *jīvaghana* as referring to the world of Brahman, saying "for of the individual souls," etc. The meaning is: the "mass" (*ghana*) or aggregate of individual souls (*jīva*) who identify with the individual instruments (*vyaṣṭi-karaṇa*), [is found] in that which identifies with all instruments; thus it is the "mass of individual souls" (*jīvaghana*). Because it belongs to that [world of Brahman], the world is indicated through a successive connection (*paraṃparā-sambandha*).

Therefore, "higher" means pure, transcending all worlds. Furthermore, because the word *parapuruṣa* (the Supreme Person) has its primary application (*mukhyatva*) in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), He alone is the object of meditation; thus he says, "the higher.
Since there is nothing else whatsoever higher than Him, He alone is the primary "higher," and not the *sūtrātman* who is higher than the individual body (*piṇḍa*). This is the meaning.

Furthermore, since "the Supreme" (para) was established at the beginning of the passage, he states that it is indeed the Supreme Brahman alone that is to be meditated upon here in the remainder of the sentence, by saying: "both the higher and the lower.
And he says "just as" because there is an indicative mark (liṅga) of the cessation of evil;
"pādodara" means a serpent.

"Regarding this, it is said: By means of the meditation on the Supreme Brahman within the syllable *oṃ*, one goes to the world of Brahman through the door of the sun; having beheld the Supreme Brahman, one attains that very same state which is peaceful, fearless, and supreme—thus he states there is no contradiction.

In this way, by means of the two scriptural passages concerning the "Supreme Person," which are supported by the context establishing syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*), the recognition of the Supreme Brahman sets aside the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of reaching the world of Brahman;
thus it is established that the sentence is consistent with Brahman as the object of meditation on the *praṇava*. //13//
The small [ether] [is Brahman],
because of the subsequent [scriptural passages]. (BS 1.3.14)
The small [self] is [the Brahman] because of subsequent [scriptural] passages.
He cites the Chandogya: "Now" (atha).
The word "now" indicates the commencement of the Dahara-vidyā immediately after the Bhūma-vidyā.
The body is called the "city of Brahman" because it is the locus for the manifestation of Brahman.

Within this city, that which is well-known as the small (*dahara*) lotus of the heart—in that heart, that which is designated by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), namely Brahman—is what must be sought; the meaning is that it is to be investigated and known.
Here, the ether is the object of inquiry.
First, the doubt must be formulated as to whether [the city] is that which stands within it.
In that regard, if it were the ether (ākāśa), then there would be two doubts.
Having stated one doubt arising from the word "ether," he states another doubt arising from the word "city of Brahman" (brahmapura) with the words: "Likewise, regarding 'the city of Brahman'..."
Regarding this word "city," there is a doubt as to whether it is the city of the individual soul (jīva) or of Brahman;
the construction is that [the discussion proceeds] while that doubt exists.
Because the word *parapuruṣa* (the Supreme Person) has its primary meaning in Brahman, it was stated that Brahman is the object of meditation.

Similarly, here too, since the word *ākāśa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), the opponent establishes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of an analogy—that the elemental ether is the object of meditation—beginning with the words "In that [context], the ether...

The connections with the scriptures (*śruti*) and so forth are established because the subsequent Prajāpati section and the present Dahara section are shown to be in harmony (*samanvaya*) with both the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*) Brahman.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is meditation on the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) and so forth; in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), through meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahma*), there arises the cognition of the unqualified (*nirguṇa*). Thus, there is a difference in the result.
Furthermore, one should not suspect that this [present discussion] is a mere repetition of the sūtra "The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks" (*ākāśas talliṅgāt*).

In this context, because there is an absence of clear indicative marks for the small ether (*daharākāśa*) being Brahman— despite the connection with indicative marks such as its being "that which is within" (to be sought after) and its being situated within the ether—
it may be asked: how can the elemental ether possess smallness,
and how can one and the same thing be both the object of comparison and the subject of comparison?

Having raised the doubt, "How is it that He is heard of in scripture as the substratum of all— as in the passage beginning, 'Both heaven and earth are contained within Him, as well as both fire and wind'?"— the author refutes it step by step with the words beginning "Of Him" (tasya).
[The smallness] is relative to the heart.
The meaning is that there is similarity due to the imagined distinctions for the sake of meditation, while there is the state of being the support of all because of its own inherent oneness.

Now, one might object that the word "self" (*ātman*) in the phrase "this is the self" is not appropriate when applied to the [gross] element; anticipating this lack of conviction, he says, "Or rather."
"By devotion" means by way of association with the quality of consciousness (caitanya).
To the objection that the primary Brahman should be understood [here], he says: "For not..."
Let it be that the lord of the city is the individual soul (jīva), but as for the ether residing within the heart, it is Brahman; to this he says: "Therein.
The meaning is that since the lord of the city himself can possibly reside within that [ether], there is no need for anything else.
To the question, "How can that which is all-pervading be situated within? he says: "The mind" (*manaḥ*).

He says: "The ether" (*ākāśa*), meaning that by the word "ether," the small space (*dahara*) is drawn back [as the subject], and the aforementioned similes and so forth will apply with the intention of expressing its non-difference from Brahman.

Now, raising the objection that it is improper for the individual soul (*jīva*) to be the referent of the word "ether," he states an alternative position—that the elemental ether itself might be the small space, and something situated within it should be meditated upon—by saying: "Nor here" (*na cātra*).

The meaning is that the thing which is the ultimate limit is [the referent], because the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is mentioned by that word as its qualifier and as its locus. Alternatively, the doubt that this [sūtra] has already been covered by the rule "The ether [is Brahman], on account of its characteristic marks" (*ākāśastalliṅgāt*)— since the small ether is determined to be Brahman by such marks as being "to be sought after"— must be dispelled here.
The meaning is that because qualities such as being "to be sought after" are apprehended as attributes of another [entity], there is no indicative mark (liṅga) for the secret [Brahman] being Brahman.

He establishes the final conclusion—that the scriptural mention of mere space is sublated by the scriptural passage concerning the Self endowed with indicative marks such as being "free from sin"—with the words beginning "the Supreme Lord," etc.
The connection is that this occurs "after first raising an objection regarding space."
If they should say to that teacher,
"The heart itself is small, and the space within it is even smaller; what is there in this small space that can be investigated and known?",
then that teacher should speak for the purpose of removing the notion of the smallness of the space.
He states the purport of the sentence with the word "therein" (tatra).
The phrase "he causes [the student] to turn away" implies that it is the Teacher who does so.

An objection is raised: "But since the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) is understood through the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word *ākāśa*, how can it be excluded? Anticipating this, he says: "Even though... [and so on].
If it is argued that a simile is observed even when there is non-difference—as in the expression, "The battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa was like that between Rāma and Rāvaṇa"—we say no.

Scholars of poetry maintain that this is the figure of speech called *ananvaya* (non-comparison), because when there is non-difference, similarity cannot be logically connected; thus, the intent is to show that the battle is beyond comparison.
Having restated what was previously mentioned, he refutes it with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely).

In passages such as "He appears as if embraced by Sītā, endowed with the luster of his bow," the recourse to a distinction based on difference—due to the distinct qualifiers consisting of the union with luster and the embrace of Sītā—is made out of necessity to establish the relationship of subject and object of comparison for the one and the same Śrī Rāma; thus, it should be regarded as not being a valid example [of the figure in question].
In this case, such a reliance [on the literal sense] is not appropriate,
because there is a consistent interpretation (gati) based on the sūtra's intent being the negation of smallness.

Furthermore, he says "Moreover" (apica), because as long as the inner nature of the space within the heart is not relinquished, it is illogical for it to be similar to the all-pervading external space due to its smallness.

The point is that if "interiority" were abandoned, there would be no similarity because of absolute non-difference. Now, one might ask: why could the intention not be the removal of the smallness of the space within the heart (hārdākāśa) and its being [merely] of such a size? To this he says: "both.
Therefore, the point is that the intention lies precisely in the removal of smallness.
Thus, it has been stated that the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is not the elemental ether because it is compared to space;
and for the same reason—based on such indicative marks as being the support of all—it is said [to be non-elemental] with the words beginning "nor... (*na ca*).
One who is free from hunger—that is, free from the desire to eat—is "one devoid of hunger" (*vijighatsa*).
The meaning is that [the city] is devoid of hunger.

One should understand the relationship expressed by the genitive case heard last—which is dependent on the word "Brahman" heard first—as a mere connection, and not as the relationship of owner and owned (svasvāmibhāva) implied by the genitive in the phrase "the city of Brahman. This is because of the maxim: "That which is dependent is sublated by that which is independent. Thus he says: "To this we reply."
He states the proof for the relationship of the body with Brahman, which consists in its being the locus of that [Brahman’s] perception, with the word "sa" (He).
The grammatical connection is: "He is the Puruṣa because He lies (śaya) within the cities (puri), that is, within the bodies (pūrṣu)."

Now, one might object that since the word *brahman* is used in its primary sense for the individual soul (*jīva*)—which, through food and so forth, is the cause of the body's growth—the meaning of the genitive case cannot be interpreted in any other way; to this, he says: "Or else.

The individual soul is *brahman* because it causes the body to grow (*bṛṃhayati*); let the heart be the "abode of Brahman" (*brahmaveśma*) in the city belonging to that [soul], just as there is the presence of Maitra in the king's city. This is the meaning.
He states that the one within the small space (dahara) is the Supreme Self (paramātman) also because of the mark of infinite fruit, beginning with the words "tadyathā" (just as). Now,

immediately after the dispassion toward the fruits of action, those who— having understood through the instruction of a teacher the Self as the small one in this state of life, and having experienced by means of meditation the qualities such as "true desires" (satyakāma) and so forth residing therein— depart for the next world, for them there is infinite sovereignty in all worlds.
The meaning is that movement and so forth occur by its own will.

Having recalled the argument—that the characteristics mentioned regarding the "small" (dahara) are established otherwise because they are qualities of that which resides within it—he refutes them with the words "As for what was said... and so on.

Regarding the claim that the small one must first be sought after because the subsequent description of the nature of space would otherwise be inexplicable, he raises an objection to this alternative explanation with the word "But surely... (nanu).
This is the true nature of space.

Having dispelled the seed of the misconception that space is limited by means of a simile, he states that because of the mention of things situated within it, the object of meditation is precisely what is situated therein; this is the meaning.
To the objection that, in that case, the entire world would be the object of meditation, he says: "It is not so."
"Let it be so; what is the fault?
To this he replies with the word "tatra" (in that case).

The meaning is: having drawn in the small ether (*daharākāśa*) by means of the two pronouns and having stated its qualities such as being the Self, the remainder of the passage declares that it is precisely that [ether] which is to be meditated upon along with those qualities; thus, there is a contradiction.
He states "therefore" (tasmāt) to show that, by virtue of its fitness, the heart is to be understood even though it is separated from it by the word "that" (tat) in the phrase "what is within that.
Alternatively, he indicates the construction: "both that [ether] and what is within it are to be sought," namely, together with those things situated within. //14//
On account of movement and the word [indicating it], for thus the mark is seen. (BS 1.3.15)
He states another reason for the small ether being Brahman: "Because of going" (gatīti).

Living beings—that is, individual souls—go day after day, every day, into this small [ether] which is the nature of Brahman residing in the heart during sleep; yet, although they remain in that very self, they do not know it because it is veiled by unreal ignorance, and therefore they rise up again. This is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Even if this small space (*dahara*) referred to by the word is accessible to the individual soul (*jīva*) during deep sleep, what follows regarding its being Brahman? Anticipating this doubt, he explains with the words "For it is seen thus" (*tathā hi*).
He states that it is also seen in common worldly experience with the words "In the world too.
Having explained the indicative mark of movement (*gati*), he explains the scriptural word (*śabda*) with the words "Thus" (*tathā*).
The sense is that the term "Brahmaloka" is not well-known as referring to either the individual soul (jīva) or the elemental ether (ākāśa).
He raises a doubt regarding its lack of established usage even for Brahman with the words "But surely... (nanu).
He provides the resolution by means of the *niṣādasthapati* maxim with the words "it should lead [to that]" (gamayet).
In the sixth [section], it was considered that the husband is a Niṣāda, because of the force of the word;
for after prescribing the Raudrī sacrifice, it is traditionally taught: "One should cause the Niṣādasthapati to sacrifice with this."
In this context, by the genitive compound "the lord (sthapati) of the Niṣādas," a member of the three higher castes (traivarṇika) is to be understood,

because of his capacity for [performing] the fire-rituals, the knowledge of the Vedas, and so forth; however, one should not understand a Niṣāda by the karmadhāraya compound "a Niṣāda who is also a lord."
When it is argued that [the Niṣāda] cannot [be the chief], the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:
the Niṣāda alone should be the chief (sthapati), because the word "Niṣāda" possesses the primary denotative power (śakti) with respect to the Niṣāda.

Since it is improper to assume that the heard genitive case-ending indicates a relationship with the meaning of the sixth [genitive] case— which is not actually heard— and since there is parsimony in assuming a connection with the preceding word for the heard accusative case-ending,
therefore, only the capacity of the Niṣāda to perform the sacrifice needs to be assumed.
This means that in the compound *brahmaloka*, it is a *karmadhāraya*.
He explains that "the gender also exists in a karmadhāraya" with the words "this very [point]. In the sūtra, the word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate the previously stated logical principles. //15//
And because its greatness, consisting of sustaining power, is perceived in this [body]. (BS 1.3.16)
He states that the small one (dahara) is the Supreme because it possesses the characteristic of supporting the entire world, using the word "dhṛteḥ" (from support).

Now, an objection is raised: "How so?"—for one might suspect that since the word "atha" (then/now) breaks the context of the small one, the "support" mentioned in the scripture cannot be a characteristic of the small one.

He replies with the words "The small one in this... and so forth, stating that because of the reference back to the subject already under discussion in the phrase "That Self," the word "atha" serves to introduce the injunction of the quality of support for the small one.
In the Śruti, the word *vidhṛti* ends in the suffix *ktic* because it denotes the agent;

however, in the Sūtra, the word *dhṛti*—due to its grammatical coordination with the word *mahiman*—ends in *ktin* and expresses "sustaining," since the suffix *ktin* is prescribed in the sense of an action according to the rule "striyāṃ ktin. This is the distinction.
He states that there is no tautology by saying "as in the case of water," [explaining] that the bridge is the cause of non-confusion, whereas the dam is the cause of stability;
he applies the Sūtra with the words "so here."

The meaning of the sūtra is that the "small" [ether] is the Supreme because the greatness of this support (*dhṛti*)—that is, the act of sustaining and governing—is found in this Supreme Self alone in another Vedic text.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase *dhṛteśca*, the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of being a governor, mentioned by the word "bridge" (*setu*), is to be understood.
Regarding that governance, he states the evidence from another Vedic text with the words "of this" (*etasya*).
Dhṛti said to him, "So be it. //16//
And because it is well-known. (BBs 1.3.17)

Because it shines and blazes on all sides, the word "space" (ākāśa) is well-known through its quality of pervasiveness in reference to Brahman, which is self-luminous; this is due to the frequency of its usage in that sense. //17//
If it be argued that "He" refers to the other [the individual soul] because of the reference to it, we say no, because of impossibility. (BS 1.3.18)

If it is argued that the "small" (dahara) space is the Supreme Self on the strength of the supplementary passage, "This Self is free from sin," etc., then one might suspect that the individual soul (jīva) could also be meant; therefore, [the author] refutes this with the words "the other" (itare).
He states the supplementary passage regarding the individual soul as well: "Now" (atha).
Immediately after the description of the small space, the pure Brahman, which is to be approached by the liberated, is described.

This serene being, the individual soul (jīva), having fully arisen from this aggregate of body and organs— that is, having distinguished itself from that [aggregate]— and having manifested and realized its own self in its true nature as Brahman, attains and reaches that very same inner, supreme light; thus it should be explained.

Just as the sentence "he sleeps with his mouth open" is explained as "having slept, he opens his mouth," so too [the text] refutes that light is not the Self by means of the word "this. Another scriptural passage states: "Having rejoiced and moved about in the state of perfect serenity..."
He states that "arising" (utthāna), like the states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], is also a mark of the individual soul (jīva), saying "likewise" (tathā).
He provides an illustration for the arising from that which is dependent on it, saying "just as" (yathā).

Anticipating the objection that the word "ether" (ākāśa) is never seen to refer to the individual soul anywhere, he says "and just as" (yathā ca) to show that it must be inferred by the force of the evidence of the aforementioned states and arising.

The objection being raised is: "In the absence of a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*), why should the individual soul (*jīva*) not be the small one? To this, the author states the restrictive factor with the words beginning "Not this" (*naitat*).
The meaning is that the individual soul cannot be the small one because the attributes heard in the scripture are impossible in the case of the small one.
If that is so, then there is a redundancy.
Regarding this, he says "atireka" (excess),
meaning that it is for the purpose of removing the suspicion of an additional [entity] based on the subsequent [passage].
What, then, is the interpretation of the reference to the individual soul (*jīva*)?
Regarding this, he says: "It will be stated"—that this reference is for the purpose of knowing Brahman, which is the soul's own place of deep sleep. //18//
If [the doubt] arises from what follows, [it is resolved thus]: "But [he whose] true nature has become manifest. (BS 1.3.19)

Anticipating the objection that the reason "because of impossibility" (*asaṃbhāvāt*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*), he refutes it with the words "If [it is argued] on account of what follows" (*uttarāccet*).
The doubt regarding the individual soul (*jīva*), which had been set aside by the Sūtra, is raised again on the strength of the passage concerning Prajāpati.

The meaning is that the impossibility [of the soul possessing such qualities] is not established, because the qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) are actually attributed to the soul itself in that context.
How is there a mention of the "living self" (jīva) there?
To this he says, beginning with "tatra" (therein):

although the word "jīva" does not appear at the outset, nevertheless, having introduced the Self characterized by qualities such as being free from sin (apahatapāpmatva), [the text speaks of] that very one.

The collective meaning is that because the three states beginning with waking are presented, the individual soul (jīva) is determined by the characteristic marks of those states; therefore, those qualities belong to him alone.
Prajāpati says to Indra: "This one who...

The mention of the eye is made because of its predominance; he says "the seer" to indicate that [the soul] exists in the waking state, which consists of perceiving objects through all the sense organs.

The grammatical connection is as follows: Prajāpati explains that it is the *jīva* alone who is being honored by objects consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanāmaya*)—this refers to the state of dreaming—and who is being worshipped—this refers to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
In that context, at that time, he has fallen asleep in such a way that this dreaming occurs.
He whose aggregate of instruments (*karaṇagrāma*) has been completely set at rest and cast away is *samasta*;
for this very reason, because his instruments have been withdrawn, he is free from the turbidity produced by them and is serene (*saṃprasanna*).

He dissolves the dream-like phenomenal world (*prapañca*) into mere ignorance; therefore, because of the presence of ignorance, this *prājña* is distinct from the liberated one. By means of his own consciousness, he is the witness of the causal body (*kāraṇaśarīra*), which is the object of that witnessing.

Having raised the doubt that, because of Brahmā’s statement in the fourth section, those qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) belong to that [Brahmā] itself, he declares that even in that section it is the individual soul (*jīva*), saying: "He said" (*nāha*).
The particle *aha* is used in the sense of distress;
for Indra spoke while feeling distressed.
Indeed, this man, while asleep in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), does not know himself as "I am Devadatta" and so forth;
nor indeed does he know these elements at all, but rather reaches utter dissolution.
Having perceived the defect [of this state], thinking, "I see nothing here to be enjoyed," he approached Prajāpati once again.
Having heard that defect, Prajāpati said, "This one" (*etam*).

The meaning is that, having begun with the statement, "I shall not explain anything other than this Self under discussion," he subsequently points out the individual soul (*jīva*) itself by means of a censure, beginning with, "O Maghavan, this body is indeed mortal.
Therefore, [the conclusion follows] from the words of Prajāpati.

Therefore, since its occurrence is not established, he states the final conclusion: "with regard to that" (*taṃ prati*). The meaning is that the object's state of being purified is its manifestation through the purification of the three states—that is, its becoming manifest through the mental modification (*vṛtti*) arising from the sentence.

If that is so, how can the term *jīva* (living being) be used in the masculine gender in the Sūtra, given that the state of being a *jīva* has ceased through knowledge? To this he says: "bhūtapūrva" (having been previously).

The meaning is that because the state of being a *jīva*—consisting in being reflected by ignorance and its effects—existed prior to knowledge, even after [the attainment of] knowledge, one who is of the nature of Brahman is still designated by the name *jīva*.
He states the purport of Prajāpati’s discourse—which consists of the four stages of Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turīya—with the words "This [is...
etc. Because it possesses birth and destruction, Prajāpati spoke to Indra and Virocana in order to make them understand that the body, which is like a reflection, is not the Self.

The Brāhmaṇa says, "Having looked at yourself in a bowl of water, tell me that form of yours which you do not recognize," and so forth; this is the meaning of the Śruti passage beginning with "in a bowl of water" (*udaśarāve*).
