Regarding efficient causes (*nimitta*) as well, there is no insistence on whether the effect residing in the material cause is itself ignorance, manifested through a specific configuration (*ghaṭanā*), or something else entirely.
He states the result of the establishment of the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) as the effect of grasping (*upādāna*) with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*).

Just as for one who has awakened from sleep, an eye of the same kind as the previous eye arises, and that [new eye] perceives only a form (*rūpa*) of the same kind as the previous form, and not taste (*rasa*) or other [objects], so too the worlds to be experienced, the groups of living beings which are the substrates of experience, and the karmas which are the causes of experience, by the power of the conditioned factors, are restricted to being exactly similar to the previous worlds and so forth; such is the meaning.
"Nikāyas" means collections.
Fearing that the example might be unestablished, he says "for not," meaning that just as there is no unique object for the sixth faculty, the mind.
The meaning is that because pleasure and so forth are cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*),
the contrary nature of their empirical usage is unreal; or alternatively,
it means that a sixth sense organ and its object do not exist.
He summarizes the meaning already stated with the words "Therefore, moreover" (ataśca).
The meaning is that, because of the similarity in conventional usage and because of their possibility, the individual entities being conventionally designated are indeed identical.
He applies this to the Sūtra with the words beginning "identical," etc.

The meaning is that the sacrificer, viewing himself through his future state and desiring, "May I become Agni, the eater of food," offered the oblation to be cooked on eight potsherds to Agni—the deity presiding over the *kṛttikā* constellation.
The plural number is used because of the multiplicity of individual constellations.
[Objection: But how can the sacrificer become the future Agni, having the same name and form as the Agni who is the intended object of the rite, in another *kalpa*?
In the same way, one should have stated it similarly for such passages as "Rudra indeed desired" or "Viṣṇu indeed desired";
however, that is incorrect, for Viṣṇu and Rudra do not possess the status of presiding persons (adhikāripuruṣa) in the same manner as Agni does.
Because it is heard in scripture that those two [Brahmā and Viṣṇu] are the causes of the world;

and because of the contradiction with such Śruti and Smṛti passages as "Rudra is indeed one" and "Viṣṇu is one," etc. In this Smṛti, the word "in the Vedas" (vedeṣu) is used in the locative case of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
At the end of the night and at the end of the dissolution;
the signs of the seasons, such as spring and the rest, are the new sprouts and so forth;
in their revolution, which occurs like the turning of a water-wheel.
The phrase "the entities (bhāvāḥ) are equal" refers to the categories (padārthāḥ); this is the ellipsis.

Therefore, even if one accepts that the gods possess physical bodies subject to birth and destruction, since there is no contradiction regarding their capacity for action or with respect to the Vedic word, it is established that the gods have the qualification for knowledge (vidyā). //30//
Jaimini [holds that] there is no entitlement [to the knowledge of Brahman] for those such as the Madhukas, because of the impossibility [of performing the required rituals]. (BS 1.3.31)
He objects: [the passage] "in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and so forth" means that the knowledge of Brahman does not qualify the gods and others for it,
because it is a form of knowledge.
The meaning is: "like the knowledge of the Madhu-vidyā and others."
He explains the illustration with the words beginning "How so? and so forth:

one should perform meditation by superimposing the name "honey" upon the sun—because it gladdens the gods, it is like honey—situated within the honeycomb that is the intermediate space, upon the bamboo staff known as the heavenly world (*dyuloka*).
In that regard, the sun's presiding over [the honey] is not logical.
He says, "Among the gods, etc.," because there is no distinction between the meditator and the object of meditation.

Anticipating the objection that the Vasus and others might have authority there, he says, "And again," because even they are objects of meditation and goals to be attained, and thus lack the status of being meditators.
The five flowers are the rituals prescribed in the four Vedas and the *praṇava*.
To them, the sacrificial substances such as Soma and clarified butter—known as the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), consisting of the red, white, black, dark-red, and secret [substances]—are offered.

These are brought from the solar orb by the solar-ray channels (*nāḍī*) situated in the five directions starting from the east and ending above; these channels have the form of apertures located within the honey and cake.
Having been transformed into the nature of fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food, they become the sustenance for the Vasus and other deities stationed in the five directions.
The meaning is that it has been stated that for one who meditates, there is the attainment of Vasu and the others.
He explains the meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*) found in the Sūtra with the words "likewise Agni" (*tathāgni*).
There are four feet (*pāda*) of the Brahman that is Space (*ākāśa*).
two ears,
two eyes, and two nostrils;

Regarding the statement "Speech is one," he says that one should perform meditation on the seven seers (*saptarṣi*) within the seven sense organs located at the head and the *camasa* vessels: "Likewise these two... Here, the right ear is Gautama, and the left is Bhāradvāja.
Thus, Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha are in the right eye and nostril; Jamadagni and Kaśyapa are in the left; and Atri is in the voice—this is the meaning.
In this case, because they are objects of meditation for the sages, the sages do not possess the qualification [for such meditation]. //31//
And because [the self] exists in light. (BBs 1.3.32)

Furthermore, he states that because they lack a physical body (*vigraha*), gods and others have no eligibility [for Vedic rites] anywhere, saying: "And because [the word] exists in reference to light" (*jyotiṣi bhāvāt*).

Since words such as "Āditya," "Sūrya," "Candra," "Śukra," and "Aṅgāraka" are found to be applied to spheres of light (*jyotiḥpiṇḍa*), the meaning is that there is no god whatsoever who possesses a physical body.
In the supplementary passage of the Madhu-vidyā, "The Āditya rises in the east and sets in the west," the word *āditya* is well-known to refer specifically to light.
"In that case, let the qualification belong to the masses of light alone";
to this he says, "And not...
Having raised the doubt regarding the qualification of fire and so forth, he says, "By this..."
The meaning is that words such as "fire," "wind," and "earth" denote insentient things.
The proponent of the established view (siddhāntin) raises an objection with the words "this might be so," and so forth;
[he refers to] mantras such as "the thunderbolt-handed Purandara."
Passages such as "He wept" are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*).
For it is said: "The gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant you desired enjoyments;
being satisfied, they satisfy him with auspicious fruits that fulfill all desires."
Such are the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

Even in the world, people depict Yama with a staff in his hand and Indra with a thunderbolt in his hand; thus, because the five factors such as physical form (vigraha) exist, there is no fault regarding lack of qualification [to perform rituals]. This is the meaning.
Embodiment, the enjoyment of oblations, sovereignty, graciousness,
and the bestowing of fruits— this pentad beginning with embodiment [constitutes the fivefold nature of the deity].
He refutes this by stating "not so," etc., on the grounds that there is a lack of evidence.
"And not here" means: not in the case of the analysis of the compound (vigraha), and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that either the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) or the mantras constitute the basis [for the existence of a deity], he says "the explanatory passages," and so forth.

The meaning is that the Mīmāṃsakas declare that mantras—being grasped by the injunctions of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) like rice and other materials—are intended for expressing what is connected to the performance, and are not directed toward unknown things such as the deity's physical form (*vigraha*). Therefore, the meaning is: "because of the absence of a physical form. //32//
But Bādarāyaṇa maintains that there is indeed [the presence of the organs] in the state of being, for it exists. (BS 1.3.33)
He refutes the prima facie position established by the two preceding sūtras with the words "But" (tu) and so forth:
"Brahma-vidyā does not qualify the gods and others,
because it is a form of knowledge (vidyā)."
He states that the reason given— “like the Madhu-vidyā and others”— is not decisive, saying “even though”:
[the Darśa and other rites] do not qualify a Brāhmaṇa.

He states the similarity of the fallacious appearance of the reason "because it is knowledge" by saying "nor is it," meaning that the principle— that whoever has the capacity for eligibility in a particular matter is the one entitled to it therein— is the same [in both cases], just as in the case of the Rājasūya sacrifice and others, because they are ritual actions (karma).
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that since it is not possible for everyone to have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for everything everywhere, therefore [the rule] is not set aside.
The meaning is: "That Brahman—whosoever among the gods and others realized it as their own inner self (*pratyak*), he became that Brahman.
Those gods then said to one another:

The meaning is that there is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) to this effect, namely that Indra and Virocana, the kings of the gods and the asuras respectively, went to Prajāpati, the bestower of the knowledge of Brahman.

Regarding the question asked by the Gandharva, "What here is the immortal Brahman?", Yājñavalkya replied, "Him" (*tam*); he states that this is an indicative mark of the eligibility of the gods and others for liberation, as it is heard in the *Mokṣadharmas*.

He says "Smārta" (based on Smṛti) because, just as although the word "eye" and so forth is applied to the physical globes in children, those learned in the scriptures accept sense organs distinct from the globes.
He says "jyotirādi" (beginning with light) to show that even when words such as "Sūrya" are applied to light and so forth, a deity possessing a body must be accepted;
the meaning is that this is because they are treated as sentient beings.
How can a single entity possess both an insentient and a sentient nature?
To this he replies: "Indeed, there is.

For thus the conventional usage of "deity" is heard in connection with having a physical form; for instance, there is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) related to the *subrahmaṇya*, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) belonging to the group of *udgātṛ* priests, which addresses Indra: "O Indra..."
"Come," and so forth;
therein, the address "O Medhātithi’s ram" is heard as a vocative for Indra.
He explains that [with the word] "meṣa": the meaning is that "meṣa" is an address to Indra, intended to make known that [Indra], having become a ram, carried off the sage.
As for the claim that the sun and other such entities are indeed insentient like clay and so forth,
that is not so;
for he says "clay," etc., because in every case there exists a dual aspect consisting of both the insentient and the sentient.
Regarding the question of what portion of the sun and so forth is insentient and what portion is sentient, he says: "But [in the case] of light and so on.
Mantras and the like are not authoritative with respect to their own literal meaning—such as a physical form appearing through the power of the words—[since that is not their intended referent].
He says "yadapi" (as for what was said) because [the passage] is intent on something else, like the sentence "Eat poison.
He says "atra brūmaḥ" (here we reply) to show that even from a sentence intent on something else, its own literal meaning is to be accepted provided there is no contradiction.
He illustrates the existence [of something] by mere cognition even when the object is devoid of intended meaning with the words "tathā hi" (for instance).
He raises an objection regarding the disparity—that there is cognition in the case of grass and so forth, but it does not exist in the case of a physical body—with the words "atrāha" (here he says).
"Vidhyuddeśa" refers to an injunctive statement.
On account of syntactic unity with that [injunction], the understanding in the *arthavādas* is precisely that "the injunction is praised.
A "narrative" (*vṛttānta*) is a matter of past fact;
the meaning is that there is no cognition whose object is such things as the [gods'] physical bodies (*vigraha*).
[Objection: "But surely, let there be a cognition of the analysis (*vigraha*) and so forth by means of a subordinate sentence (*avāntaravākya*. [Reply: To this he says, "Not so" (*na hi*).
The underlying intention is that there would also arise a cognition of drinking liquor (*surāpāna*).

He says, "To this it is replied," because such a view is incorrect due to the disparity between the syntactic unity of a word (*padaikavākyatva*) and the syntactic unity of a sentence (*vākyaikavākyatva*).

When the single negative particle (*nañ*) connects with the two words "one should drink liquor" (*surāṃ pibet*), then that single sentence consisting of those words produces a single experience of meaning; it does not, however, cause the two words to separately convey the drinking of liquor, because such [a meaning] cannot be logically established as a prohibition within a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), and thus it serves as no intermediary toward the experience of the sentence-meaning.

But an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), by conveying a connection between existing facts as a means for praise, enters into syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*) with the injunction; this is the sense in which there is an experience of the analytical breakdown (*vigraha*) and so forth.

[Objection: "But let there be a direct connection with the injunction itself, without the words situated in the *arthavāda* conveying an intermediate syntactic relation. To this he replies: "Just as... (*yathā hi*).
He demonstrates the impossibility of a direct connection by saying: "For not... (*na hi*).
Anticipating the objection that one might grasp the primary meaning of the *arthavāda* in all cases, he analyzes the *arthavādas* with the words: "In that case... (*tadyatra*).
The meaning is: among those *arthavādas*, in cases such as "Fire is the remedy for cold," and so forth;
since the non-difference [asserted in] "The sacrificial post is the sun" is sublated, it is a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*) based on qualities such as brilliance.

Where, however, as in "Vajrahasta Purandara," there is neither corroboration nor contradiction by other means of knowledge (*māna*), there it is a *bhūtārthavāda* (a statement of an existing fact). This is the meaning.
The phrase "having reflected thus" (*iti vimṛśya*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

He extends the following logical principle (*nyāya*) to the mantras: "The statement regarding the suffering of the body (*vigrahārtavāda*), even when taken in its literal sense, possesses a primary intentionality (*tātparya*); for, while being subordinate to another [meaning], it is a word whose meaning is unknown and uncontradicted, like the statements concerning the *prayāja* offerings. This he does by the words "by this" (*etena*).
The words [in the sūtra] serve as reasons for the refutation of those [interpretations] that merely restate the Vedānta or those that are mere figurative descriptions (guṇavāda).

Nor is there a split in the sentence (vākyabheda) even if it intends both meanings, because the intermediate meaning is contained within the meaning of the great sentence (mahāvākya); this is the intended sense.
He states "Moreover" (api ca) to show that the corporeal form of the deity must also be accepted on the grounds that the injunction would otherwise be untenable, just as in the case of heaven.

Now, one might object: since an injunction regarding action—which is by nature afflictive—is untenable without a fruit, let it be that heaven, established by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "that which is not mixed with suffering," is validated by the injunction.
But what is the untenability of the injunction without a corporeal form?
He says "no" to that; for since giving directed toward [an object] is untenable, one must accept its presence in the mind. Regarding this, he also cites scripture: "of whom...
Therefore, for the sake of its presence in the mind, a formal analysis (vigraha) must be accepted.

Furthermore, because it is recited in the section on ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*), the cognition of a physical form must be accepted as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the rite— just like the *prayāja* offerings— for without that,
the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of the rite cannot be established. Moreover,
he says "and not the word" (*na ca śabda...*) to show that it is improper to abandon the deity who possesses a clearly manifest form and instead hold that the deity is merely the word.
Nor should it be argued that "let the mere form (ākṛti) alone be the denotation of the word; what is the use of a physical body (vigraha)?
For there can be no connection between a form and an individual (vyakti) that is devoid of a body.
Therefore, since the word requires an object [to denote], one must accept a physical body as established by means of knowledge such as mantras; thus he says: "In that regard... (tatra).
Thus, he states "itihāsa" etc., to show that even historical accounts and the like, which are rooted in mantra and arthavāda, are authoritative regarding the embodied form (vigraha).
The meaning is that they exist as valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
He further states "pratyakṣa" etc., to show that the direct perception (pratyakṣa) of deities and so forth by yogins such as Vyāsa is also the source for historical accounts and the like.

He refutes the inference— "Vyāsa and others lacked direct perception of gods and such, because they were living beings, like us"— by means of an over-extension [of the argument], starting with the words "But he who... and so forth.
He might even say that there is no diversity in the world, [arguing]: "Everything is non-different from the jar, because it possesses the nature of a real entity (vastutva), like the jar."

Likewise, due to his unrestrained intellect, he would assert the non-existence of Kṣatriyas, the non-existence of the system of castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), and the lack of order regarding castes, stages of life, and so forth; and thus, the meaning is that there would be a sublation of the scriptural injunctions concerning the Rājasūya sacrifice and other rites, as well as the scriptural injunctions concerning the established order of duties for the Kṛta and other ages.
He states "moreover" (api ca) to show that the direct perception of gods and others is established even from the meaning of the *Yogasūtras*.
The meaning of the sūtra is that through the recitation of mantras, there is the presence of the deity and conversation with them.
He says "yoga" to show that because the greatness of yoga is established by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, yogis possess direct perception of gods and others.

The meaning is that for the yogi who has attained a body composed of light manifested through yoga— having conquered the qualities of yoga such as *aṇimā* and so forth by means of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon the five elements beginning with earth, starting from the soles of the feet up to the knees, from the knees up to the navel, from the navel up to the neck, from the neck up to the growth of the hair, and finally to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)— there is no touch of disease or other afflictions.
He states that "the consensus among painters and others" is also an authority regarding the analysis [of the compound], using the words "In the world," etc.
He concludes the section on the subject matter with "Therefore," etc.,
and states the fruit of this investigation with "The sequence," etc.

Only when there is eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) on the part of the gods and others do meditations that have the fruit of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) through the attainment of divinity become appropriate.
If the gods lacked eligibility, there would be no engagement in these meditations by those seeking gradual liberation due to the absence of [the capacity for] knowledge;
therefore, the point is that the establishment of engagement follows from the determination of eligibility. //33//
Because the hearing of disregard for that [body] and because of the rushing toward it by *śuc*, it is indeed indicated [that the body is the self]. (BBs 1.3.34)
This is indeed indicated by the word "śuka.
He states the connection of this [section] with the preceding one by means of the word "yathā" (just as).

In the previous [section], for the sake of establishing the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of gods and others, the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas with the existent reality (*bhūtārtha*), namely Brahman, was strengthened by stating the concordance of the mantras and other texts with the actual existence of the embodied forms (*vigraha*) and so forth.

In this regard, it should be understood that these two incidental sections (adhikaraṇas) are included within this chapter on "Harmonization" (samanvaya), because the application of the Vedic term *śūdra* to a Kṣatriya is stated here to further strengthen that [conclusion].
In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), even a Śūdra would proceed to listen to the Vedānta just like the twice-born.
In the established doctrine (siddhānta), the result is the absence of that [error].
In this context, the subject of inquiry is Vedānta;

regarding the doubt as to whether it qualifies a Śūdra or not—arising from the possibilities of its feasibility or infeasibility—the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is stated with the words "In that regard, even for a Śūdra," and so forth. Therefore, due to the absence of sacred fires and the lack of Vedic study, he is incapable.

He states that the Śūdra has the qualification [for knowledge] even on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the use of the word "Śūdra" for one seeking knowledge, saying: "And it occurs...
It is said that Jānaśruti, having offered six hundred cows and a chariot to his teacher Raikva, said, "Teach me.
Thereupon, Raikva, being destitute and desiring a bride, spoke as follows.
The particle *aha* expresses weariness.

A chariot that goes—meaning "one that travels"—yoked with a *hāra* (necklace) and a *niṣka* (gold ornament) is called a *hāretvā*. [The King says: "O Śūdra, let that [chariot] be yours along with the cows;
what is the use of this small amount [of wealth] which is of no benefit for my life as a householder? This is the intended meaning.

He states "therefore" (*tasmāt*) based on a logical mark (*liṅga*) supported by reasoning: that when there is the presence of desire for an object and so forth, engagement in the means to achieve the highest good (*śreyas*) is appropriate because it is natural.
He establishes his own conclusion (*siddhānta*) outside of the Sūtra itself with the words "there is no entitlement for a Śūdra," and so on.
The meaning is: "of one by whom the meaning of the Veda has been understood at first hearing."

The meaning is that the Śūdra lacks the qualification for the inquiry into Vedānta because he lacks the capacity for scriptural investigation of the Vedic meaning; this capacity consists of the Veda as refined by the rules of formal study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) and the superficial knowledge (*āpātajñāna*) arising therefrom. Since this [capacity] is absent, the logical grounds for the possibility of his possessing the desire [to know] and so forth are not established. Alternatively, the meaning is that only one by whom the Vedic meaning has been known and determined through the Veda refined by formal study possesses the qualification for the injunctions regarding the Vedic meanings, and no other.

For even one who has not studied the Veda would incur the contingency of being entitled to perform the rites according to the meaning of the Vedas, which would render the injunction to study (adhyayana-vidhi) purposeless.

Therefore, the meaning is that the Śūdra lacks entitlement to the injunctions for hearing [the scriptures] (śravaṇa) and so forth, which are the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman culminating in its fruit.

This is because the same logic applies: namely, the absence of the capacity obtained through the injunction to study, which consists in possessing knowledge of the meaning of the Veda already studied.
He states that the word "sacrifice" (yajña) is intended as an indicator for the meaning of the Veda, saying: "because the principle (nyāya) is common.
Therefore, the phrase "hence a Śūdra" means that the principle referred to by that pronoun is equal in both the knowledge of sacrifice and the knowledge of Brahman.
He refutes the previously mentioned indicative mark with the words: "as for what..."
The meaning is that the principle regarding the possibility of [the Śūdra] possessing the desire for knowledge and so forth has been refuted by the principle of incapacity.

Now, one might object: "In the case of the injunction 'one should cause the Niṣāda chief to sacrifice,' even though there is an absence of formal study, the Śūdra—by virtue of the word 'Śūdra'—should have the right to knowledge in this [Saṃvarga-vidyā], just as the Niṣāda has the right to the sacrifice.
Anticipating this doubt, he accepts the Śūdra's eligibility for the Saṃvarga-vidyā with the words "kāmam" (if you wish).
The meaning is: "because that is its object" and "because it is heard in that context.
In reality, however, because it occurs within an injunctive sentence, even the word *niṣāda* serves to designate the qualified person (*adhikārin*);
whereas the word *śūdra*, occurring in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) subordinate to the injunction for knowledge, does not indicate a qualified person.

Thinking that a word intended for another purpose cannot convey its own primary meaning due to the logical principle of incapacity (*asāmarthya*) and contradiction, he abandons his initial position and says "Arthavāda... [to introduce the refutation].
Then, raising the doubt as to what the meaning of the word "Śūdra" heard here might be, he states the meaning through the Sūtra with the words beginning "It is possible... and so forth.
A king named Jānaśruti was sleeping on the roof of his palace at night during the summer heat.
Then, the sages, gratified by his multitude of virtues such as the giving of food and other gifts, became swans and approached him in the form of a flight for his benefit;
among them, the last swan said to the lead swan:
"O Bhadrākṣa!"
"Do you not see the splendor of this Jānaśruti, which stands pervading the heavens?
It will consume you; do not go!
To him, the leader said:

"O, you speak these words to some wretched man who is devoid of knowledge, as if he were Raikva, who was accompanied by a *yugva*—a cart that moves along with it. For the splendor of Raikva, who is most devoted to Brahman (*brahmiṣṭha*), is insurmountable; such is not the case for one like you who does not know the Self. This is the meaning.
The intention of the swans was that the king, though distressed by our words, would come to know Raikva through his sign as a cart and thus become possessed of knowledge.
The word division is *kaṃ u are*;
the particle *u* has the sense of "also" (*api*).
The logical connection of the sūtra is as follows: upon hearing those words of disregard from the swans, grief arose in this king; that [grief] is indicated by Raikva through the word "śūdra.
The particle *hi* is intended to illuminate the maxim that when the literal and etymological meanings are obtainable, the unrelated conventional meaning must be abandoned.
Because of that *ādravaṇa*— that is,
because of the onset of that grief— he became a *śūdra*, having attained sorrow; or rather, by means of that grief as the agent, he was pursued and overtaken by the king.
The meaning is that he went to Raikva because of grief or by means of some instrument. //34//
And because of the attainment of the status of a Kṣatriya, and because of the indicative mark [found] later regarding Caitraratha. (BS 1.3.35)
He states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the etymological nature of the word *śūdra* in the passage beginning with "kṣatriyatva.
Following the injunction for the Saṃvarga-vidyā, an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) begins:

the meaning is that while King Abhipratārin—the son of Śunaka, of the Kapiga lineage, and a priest—and [King Kakṣasena], the son of Kakṣasena, were seated down to eat, being served by a cook, a young student (*baṭu*) begged from them.
Now, it might be objected that his status as a descendant of Citraratha (Caitrarathitva) is not heard [in this context]; therefore, he says: "And his being a descendant of Citraratha.
By the phrase "by means of this Dvirātra sacrifice," the connection of Citraratha with the Kāpeyas was already stated in the Chāndogya Śruti itself.
Furthermore, because Abhipratārin is also connected to them, his belonging to the lineage of Citraratha is established.
The meaning is that, as a general rule, those born of royal lineages have priests born of priestly lineages as their officiating priests (*yājaka*).
Now, let it be granted that Abhipratārin was a descendant of Citraratha;
however, how does that establish his status as a Kṣatriya?
Regarding this, he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
This means from Citraratha.

That the attendant (*kṣattṛ*) was a charioteer (*sūta*), his being sent out to search for Raikva, and Jānaśruti's giving of food, cows, and so forth, are indicative marks (*liṅga*) of Jānaśruti’s status as a Kṣatriya. //35//
Because of the reference to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and because of the statement regarding their absence. (BBs 1.3.36)
In this matter, it is established that the word *śūdra* is purely etymological (yaugika), and thus there is no entitlement for a *śūdra*.
Regarding this, he states another indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "sacramental rites" (*saṃskāra*).
It was previously stated that initiation (*upanayana*), which is a subsidiary element for the acquisition of the Veda, does not exist for a *śūdra*.

It is argued here that because the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*), which is an auxiliary to the acquisition of knowledge, is referred to in all [Vedic texts], and because the Śūdra lacks this, he has no entitlement to knowledge.
In the *Bhāṣya*, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes study, service to the teacher, and other such requirements.
The meaning is that the teacher initiated that disciple.

Nārada also, being a seeker of knowledge, approached Sanatkumāra while reciting a mantra; thus [the text] says "adhīhi" (teach), which means "instruct. Bharadvāja and the others, who were devoted to Brahman—meaning those who had mastered the Vedas and were established in the qualified Brahman—and who were searching for the supreme, attributeless Brahman, decided that this Pippalāda would explain everything they desired to know.
The meaning is that the six sages approached him.

Now, one might object: since the scripture states in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā that the king imparted the knowledge to the sages after having brought them near (*upanīya*), it follows that even one who has not undergone initiation (*anupanīta*) is eligible for knowledge; to this he replies with the words "to them" (*tān*).

In the preceding passage—"They, with fuel in their hands, returned in the forenoon"—it is shown that the Brāhmaṇas had come for the purpose of initiation (*upanayana*), and having thus indicated the attainment of initiation, it is [in effect] precluded [for others].

The meaning is that this is for the purpose of making known the traditional practice (ācāra) that those of superior caste must be instructed only after having been brought near by one of inferior caste.
"Of a single birth" means one who has not undergone initiation (anupanīta). "A sin" refers to that committed by eating what is unfit to be eaten (abhakṣyabhakṣaṇa). //36//
And because activity occurs when there is the ascertainment of the non-existence of that [object]. (BBs 1.3.37)
Satyakāma, whose father had died, asked his mother Jabālā, "To what lineage (*gotra*) do I belong?
His mother said to him, "Because I was occupied with serving my husband, I too do not know your father's lineage."
"But I am Jābāla by name, and you are Satyakāma by name; this much I know.
Then that Jābāla, having approached Gautama, was asked by him, "What is your lineage?
and he replied, "I do not know my lineage, nor does my mother know it; however, this much was told to me by my mother:"
Having approached the teacher for the purpose of initiation, [the boy] was told, "Say, 'I am Satyakāma Jābāla.
By this truthful statement, his lack of Śūdra status was determined.
This truth, though not belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, he spoke having discerned it clearly.
Having determined that "he does not deserve it," [the father said],
"O gentle one,
you have not departed from the truth; you have not abandoned the truth."
"Therefore, I shall initiate you;

fetch a fuel-stick for that purpose"—from this indicative mark (*liṅga*) of Gautama’s activity, he states that there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) for a Śūdra, saying: "In the absence of that... (Sūtra 37).
Because of the prohibition against hearing, studying, and understanding [the Veda], and because of the Smṛti. (BS 1.3.38)
He states that there is no entitlement [to Vedic study] because of the prohibition of hearing [the Veda] and so forth by means of mindfulness—this is expressed in the word "śravaṇa" (hearing).
The meaning is that for this Śūdra who hears the Veda being recited by the twice-born through negligence, the penance to be performed is the filling of both ears with molten lead and lac.
"Padyu" means possessed of feet; that is to say, having a mobile form.
And there is [the following]:
"memory" is the understood remainder;
"intellect" (mati) is the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas.
Giving is permanently prohibited for a Śūdra;
however, occasional giving (naimittika-dāna) certainly exists for him.
As for what was said regarding the observation of wisdom in Vidura and others—

Regarding this, he says "of those who... Although the attainment of the perfected ones (siddhas) is undeniable, he says "he should cause them to hear" in response to the question: how is knowledge to be obtained by practitioners (sādhakas) who are Śūdras? //38//
Because of trembling. (BsRp_1,3.10.39)
Regarding the word "kampanāt" (from trembling),
he states "avasitaḥ" (concluded) to address the concern that this [point] might also be merely incidental;
the meaning is "finished."
The *Kāṭhaka* recites:
"This which..."—the entire world has issued forth from, or been produced by, the vital breath (*prāṇa*); while that conscious self (*cidātman*), the impeller, exists, it moves and exerts itself.
And that cause called "vital breath" is the Great Brahman; it is "fear" because one fears from it.
Regarding that state of being a cause of fear, he provides an illustration: "like a thunderbolt.
The meaning is: "just as a raised thunderbolt causes fear, so it is.
He states, "those who [know]," referring to those who know this Brahman called *prāṇa* as being without distinction; they become liberated.
To the question, "How is this sentence cited in this Sūtra?", he says: "This [word].
The meaning is that because the sense of *ejati*—namely, trembling—is what is being defined in the Sūtra, a sentence containing the word *ejati* has been cited.

It is stated by the phrase "known from the word itself" (*śabdādeva pramitaḥ*) that no logical connection is required for this [cited sentence], as it is considered merely as a relevant incidental topic (*prāsaṅgika*).
In that regard, it was stated that in the passage concerning the thumb, the restatement of the individual soul (*jīva*) is for the purpose of knowing its identity with Brahman; however,
such is not possible here regarding the restatement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), because identity is impossible for the vital breath which is imagined as having a distinct nature of its own.

Therefore, by way of a counter-example, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this passage is devoted to the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*): "On account of its well-known [meaning], it refers to the fivefold function.

[Objection: But in passages such as "For this very reason, the vital breath," the scriptural mention of "breath" was interpreted as referring to Brahman on the basis of its indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Here too, the state of being the cause of all activity and fearlessness is a mark of Brahman; thus, since the matter has already been settled, there is no occasion for a prima facie view.
Therefore, he says: "And of air.
It is well known that having found its support—that is, having attained stability—in the vital air (prāṇa) as its cause, the world moves;
thus, the sense is that there is no clear mark of Brahman here.
And from the *vajra-liṅga* comes air; thus he says "air.
*Vyaṣṭi* means the particular, and *samaṣṭi* means the universal.
Immediately after [the prima facie view], he declares the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "Brahman alone.

He states—beginning with "In the preceding passage," etc.—that the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of being the substratum of all, which is supported by the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of the preceding and following sentences, sublates the scriptural mention of *prāṇa* that would otherwise cause a division of the sentence.
"Bright" (*śukram*) means self-luminous.
The meaning of the syllable "u" is that there is no world whatsoever that does not depend on Brahman and does not transcend it.
He explains the grammatical gender used in the Sūtra with the term "the state of being a mover":
the meaning is that Prāṇa must be the Supreme Self itself, because it is heard in scripture that everything, along with Vāyu, is subject to motion.

Anticipating the question of how the word "vajra" can apply to Brahman, he states that it is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*) by saying, "the word *vajra*. In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, in the passage "Vāyu alone is the individual manifestation," the term "immortality" (*amṛtatva*) refers to a relative immortality consisting in the conquest of premature death (*apamṛtyu*), not to absolute immortality; for after concluding the section on the meditation on Vāyu with those words, the text introduces the knowable Self with the words "Then Uṣasta questioned him," and subsequently describes the perishability of Vāyu and the other elements. This is what he means by the words beginning with "But as for [the statement] regarding Vāyu... and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that the Kāṭhaka passage is connected with that which is to be known. //39//
[The soul is] luminous because of the perception of light. (BBs 1.3.40)
Because of the mention of "light.
He cites the passage concerning Prajāpati’s knowledge from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, beginning with "This...
He states the doubt based on the two scriptural references to the "supreme light" with the word "therein..."

The meaning is that solar light destroys the darkness that obscures objects such as jars. In the preceding case, the scriptural mention of "Prāṇa" was interpreted as referring to Brahman because there was a supporting context for Brahman and because it was inappropriate to restrict the scope of the word "all. However, we do not see any such supporting context here for the passage beginning with "That Self which is free from evil," and thus he states the prima facie view by way of a counter-example, starting with the words "It is well known," etc. Under this prima facie view, the meditation would be on the Sun.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the fruit is liberation through the knowledge of Brahman.

Now, one might object: since it has already been stated in the *Jyotir-adhikaraṇa* that the word "light" (*jyotis*) refers to Brahman, how can there be a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? To this, he says: "Light.

In that context, regarding the passage on the *Gāyatrī*, the word "light" was made to abandon its own primary meaning because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the pronoun "which" (*yat*), which refers back to the Brahman under discussion.
The meaning is that this constitutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) because no reason is seen here for abandoning one's own [textual] purpose.

He states the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the state of being on the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*)—as a supporting factor for the scriptural mention of "light" (*jyotis*), saying: "And thus...
Having stated the mutual connection between the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) and the rays (*raśmayaḥ*) by means of the section beginning, "Now these channels of the heart... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.1).
Now, immediately after the cessation of perception, at the time when this death occurs,
he departs in such a manner that he goes upward by means of these rays connected to the channels;
having gone, it is said that he goes to the sun, which serves as the gateway to the world of Brahman.

In the same way, here too it must be stated that having risen from the body, having died, and having reached the supreme light called the Sun, one goes to the world of Brahman by means of that [light] and becomes manifest in one's own true nature; for the meaning is that the two gerund suffixes (*ktvā*) in "having risen" and "having reached" indicate that the light is situated on the path beginning with the rays of fire (*arcir-ādi-mārga*).

Thus, when it is argued that this passage concerns gradual liberation (*krama-mukti*) through the meditation on the Sun situated on the path, the author establishes the final conclusion with the word "evam" (thus).

The sense is this: since the Self alone, which was introduced as the subject to be explained, is the one to be explained here by the word "light," the scriptural mention of "light" (jyotiḥ-śruti)—which would cause a division of the sentence—is set aside by the scriptural mention of the "Supreme Person" (uttama-puruṣa-śruti), which is supported by the context (prakaraṇa) that ensures syntactical unity with the passage on light. Furthermore, he states "bodiless" (aśarīram) because, due to the indicative mark (liṅga) of the fruit consisting in bodilessness, the "light" is Brahman alone and not the sun.
Nor should it be argued that bodilessness (*aśarīratva*) would occur gradually through reaching the sun;
for, by the reference "that is the highest" (*sa uttamaḥ*), which qualifies the light as being supreme, there is a determination of bodilessness. Thus he says, "the highest.
He refutes the previously mentioned indicative mark (*liṅga*) with the words, "as for what [was said]..."

The intention is as follows: In the section on the channels (*nāḍīkhaṇḍa*), the attainment of the sun mentioned for the meditator on the "small space" (*dahara*) is not liberation; thus, the mention of the sun there is appropriate. However, in this Prajāpati discourse concerning knowledge devoid of attributes (*nirguṇavidyā*), the sun situated on the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) has no connection [to the goal] and would therefore be purposeless. Consequently, by rearranging the sequence of the scriptural text, it must be explained that one realizes one's own true nature and attains that very same Supreme Light (*paraṃ jyotiḥ*). //40//
Space is a distinct entity, because it is designated as being different from other things and so forth. (BS 1.3.41)
"Because of the designation [of 'space'].
He cites the *Chāndogya*: "Space.

Just as the hearing of the word "light" is set aside by the force of the opening statement, so too the words "Brahman" and so forth are set aside by the opening statement of "space"; thus he presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of this analogy: "the elemental [space]."
The fruit in both cases consists of the meditation on Ākāśa through its stated qualities and the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇa-brahma).

Anticipating the objection that this would result in redundancy with the sūtra "Ākāśas-talliṅgāt" (The [ether] is [Brahman], because of its characteristic marks), he refutes it by stating "and because of [the mention of] being the creator, etc.," noting that in the present context no such clear characteristic mark is heard.

It is logical that the well-known indicative mark "name" (*vai nāma*) and the scriptural mention of "ether" (*ākāśa-śruti*) should be set aside by the two mentions of "Brahman" and "Self" (*brahmātma-śruti*) found in the supplementary portion of the passage, as these latter are endowed with multiple indicative marks.

This is because it is determined that the purport of a sentence lies where there is a convergence of many means of knowledge; thus he establishes the final position with the words beginning "the Supreme alone," etc.
The meaning is that name and form—meaning word and object—are included within that [Brahman]; therefore, it is illogical for anything distinct from them to be their creator.

He raises the objection that "being the creator of names and so forth" is not a characteristic mark (liṅga) of Brahman, because it resides in the individual soul (jīva)— this is expressed by the word "nanu.

He refutes this with "bāḍham" (certainly), explaining that in the passage "by this living self," the agency of the soul is stated as being non-different from Brahman, since a direct [agency] is impossible.
Regarding what was said— that there is no clear indicative mark— he replies with the word "name" (nāma). In that case, however, there would be a redundancy.
Regarding this, he says: "Space" (*ākāśa*). This investigation is for the purpose of establishing that very point.

The sense is that there is no tautology, because it was stated there that the application of the word "space" to Brahman is taken as established, and that doubt and so forth arise with respect to it. //41//
On account of the difference [of the soul] in deep sleep and in departure. (BS 1.3.42)

By means of the distinction between deep sleep and departure [from the body], when Janaka asked "Which among those perceivable by the notion of 'I' is the Self?", Yājñavalkya replied: "This one who... [referring to the person within the heart].
"Consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) means composed of, or predominantly characterized by, the intellect (*buddhi*).
The seventh [case ending] has the sense of distinction (*vyatireka*);
the meaning is that he is distinct from both the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the intellect (*buddhi*).
He states his difference from mental activity (*vṛtti*) and from ignorance (*ajñāna*) by saying, "the inner light" (*antarjyotiḥ*).
The meaning is that "puruṣa" signifies the Full One (the Whole).
He expresses a doubt based on the observation of both genders [in the term]: "What then?
In the preceding section, it was stated that Ākāśa is Brahman because of the mention of its distinction from name and form.
That is incorrect;

for just as there is a statement of difference regarding the individual self (*jīvātman*) even though it is non-different [from Brahman] in the passage "embraced by the intelligent Self" (*prājñenātmanā saṃpariṣvaktaḥ*), so too a figurative statement of difference is possible—this is the connection with the objection.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is praise of the individual self as both the object and the agent of action.

In the established conclusion (siddhānta), the result is the realization of the identity of the essential nature of the Supreme Self (paramātman)—the conscious one (prājña) who is distinguished from the individual soul (jīva) only by a conceptual difference—by means of a restatement of that soul.
"Buddhānta" refers to the waking state.

Since the individual soul is mentioned at the beginning, middle, and end [of the passage], it follows that this sentence is intended as a praise of the soul; having reached this prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the author establishes the conclusion with the words beginning "parameśvara," etc.

If the sentence were merely intended as a praise of the individual soul (jīva), then the subsequent statement regarding the Supreme Knower (prājña)—who is distinct from the individual soul and previously unknown—would be irrelevant.

Therefore, when there is a conjunction of the known and the unknown, that which is unknown must be established by way of restating what is already known; this is the purport of the final conclusion (siddhānta), based on the maxim: "The purpose of a sentence lies in what is not already known" (apūrve vākyatātparyam).
He dispels the misconception that the "person" (puruṣa) is the body or the individual soul (jīva) by means of the passage beginning with "there, the person," and so forth.
Since the body cannot be denied because it is subject to sensation, the "person" must indeed be the individual soul;
however, the "wise one" (prājña), by conventional usage, is the Supreme Self alone—this is the meaning.
Mounted and presiding over it,
emitting and uttering terrible sounds,
when the intellect meditates, he meditates as it were; when it moves, he moves as it were.
He states "yataḥ" (since) to show that because it is said [in the scripture] to be "in reality devoid of all modification," the intent is not directed toward the transmigrating soul.
He states "tathā" (likewise) to show that unity is intended to be expressed in the concluding statement just as in the opening statement.
He explains [the meaning] with "yo 'yam" (this which...).

He states that the presentation of the various stages does not constitute a characteristic of the individual soul (*jīva*), because it aims at the oneness [of the Self] by means of purifying the referent of "thou" (*tvam*); thus he says, "Because [the Self] does not [awake] from the state of waking.
He states that non-transmigratoriness is understood through the question and answer; thus he says, "That which is beyond this," meaning immediately after the discrimination of desire and so forth.
"And it becomes" means: because he speaks thus, it is understood from that; such is the construction.
By that property of the state, he remains unaccompanied and untouched.
Because it is unattached, even in deep sleep the reality of the Self remains untouched by merit and demerit.
For since the Self in deep sleep transcends all sorrow, therefore "all sorrows are of the heart alone"—this is the meaning of the Śruti. //42//
[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after words such as *pati* and others. (Pāṇini 4.1.33)
He states another reason for the fact that the sentence has the identity of Brahman and the Self as its purport: "patyādi" (beginning with the Lord).
He explains the Sūtra: "itaśca" (for this reason also). "Vaśī" means independent.
"Not dependent" means [not subject to anything else].
"Īśāna" means possessing the power of control (*niyamana*).
The distinction is that sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) is the effect of that power.

Therefore, it is established that the thematic integration of the sixth chapter occurs when the meaning of "thou" (tvam) has been purified [of its limiting adjuncts] and unified [with the meaning of "that" (tat)]. //43//
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the venerable *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā*. //3//
Thus ends the third quarter (pāda) of the first chapter, titled "The Concordance of Indistinct Śruti Passages Establishing Brahman as the Object of Knowledge.
The Fourth Quarter of the First Chapter:
[The cause is] the Unmanifest, the Imperishable, the Unborn, and the support of the five classes of beings.
I salute Veditanyā, Priyā, Prakṛti, and the supreme Puruṣa. //1//

"Even for some, it is based on inference; if this is argued, we say no, because [the scripture] shows that the body is grasped as being presented through a metaphorical representation, and it demonstrates this.
In this pāda, in order to state the connection between the three topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) and the section concerning "Icchati" (I.1.5), he restates what has preceded: "Brahman," etc.
"By its being non-scriptural" means by the fact that the Pradhāna is devoid of Vedic words.
In the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, both the uniformity of interpretation (*gati-sāmānya*) and its non-scriptural nature (*aśabdatva*) were asserted.
In that [previous section], the uniformity of the Vedāntas' convergence upon Brahman was elaborated;

now, having raised the objection that the claim of the Pradhāna being "not based on scripture" (aśabda) is unestablished, that very point is being examined—this constitutes the connection by way of an objection (ākṣepasaṃgati).

Furthermore, since the concordance (samanvaya) of the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman is thereby strengthened by this examination of its lack of scriptural basis, the connection to the chapter (adhyāyasaṃgati) for these three sections should also be understood.

Here, the term "the unmanifest" (avyakta) is the subject of inquiry. Regarding the doubt—arising from both the Smṛti texts and the context of the passage—as to whether this refers to the Pradhāna or to the previously mentioned body, the opponent presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the term "the unmanifest" refers to the Pradhāna, which is not well-known [in the Vedas], just as it was shown in the sixth chapter that the [term] refers to the previously unknown Brahman. Thus he says: "The inferential [Pradhāna]."
By the word "api" (also/even), [the author] indicates that this objection regarding the lack of scriptural authority (*aśabdatva*) is raised while nevertheless accepting Brahman.

Thus, since Brahman and Pradhāna are alternative causes, the result is the failure of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that the Vedāntas are in harmony (*samanvaya*) with Brahman alone; whereas in the Siddhānta, that restrictive rule is established—this is the distinction.
The connection of this section (pāda) to the whole [chapter] should be understood as arising from the fact that the topics consist of an investigation of words (*padavicāra*).

He states "sound and so forth" (*śabdādi*) because the word *avyakta* refers to the Pradhāna due to its established usage in the Smṛtis and its etymological derivation (*yoga*), given that it is devoid of sound, touch, and other qualities.
To the question, "What harm is there if the Pradhāna is denotable by Vedic words? he replies, "That very same... (*tadeva*).
The scripture begins with "the one unborn" (ajāmekām) and so forth;
the traditional teaching (smṛti) begins with "nature (prakṛti) is said to be the cause" and so forth;
and the logical principle (nyāya) states that "whatever is limited is of an insentient nature."
The sense is that this would result in the refutation of the view that Brahman alone is the cause.
Stating the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the Sūtra, he establishes his own position with the words "Not this" (*naitat*).
He provides the reason for the absence of intent to deny the Vedic *pradhāna* with the words "For not... (*nahi*).

[Objection: But surely, because the Pradhāna is recognized here, it must be Vedic. To this he says: "For not here... [Objection: But when there is recognition of the word, the meaning is also recognized. Anticipating this, he says: "And that... [meaning], since the word is etymological (yaugika), in the absence of a restrictive factor, there can be no cognition of a specific meaning. Anticipating the objection that its cognition arises from conventional usage (rūḍhi), he asks: Is that convention worldly or based on Smṛti?
He says "not today" with the words "na ca";
he answers the second [objection] with "yā tu.
A human convention is not the cause for determining the meaning of the various eternal Vedas.
The meaning is that this is because the cognition of a person is diverse.
As for the claim that, due to the recognition of the sequence [of the Smṛti], the sequential object must be exclusively from the Smṛti, he says in response: "And not by sequence... etc.

The phrase "it being non-existent" (*asati*) is used with the negation (*nañ*) transposed from its original position; thus, it means "when there is recognition of that which is not of that form," i.e., of that which is contrary to that form.

He provides an example for the statement that "the cognition of that [object] does not exist when there is a cognition of an object contrary to it in place of the object whose form was previously known"—namely, "for indeed" (*na hi*).
Anticipating the objection that in the present case there is no contrary cognition, he states "by context" (*prakaraṇa*), meaning that by the force of the context, there is a cognition of the body.

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: "That which is arranged as a metaphorical representation of the body" (*śarīrarūpakavinyasta*) refers to the body itself being presented through the metaphor of its similarity to a chariot.

Since the term *avyakta* (the Unmanifest) here refers to that which was read in the middle position between the Self (*ātman*) and the intellect (*buddhi*) in the preceding passage, it does not denote the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) of the Sāṃkhya school; thus, the *pradhāna* is not Vedic. Anticipating the objection, "Why should the sequence found in the Smṛti (Sāṃkhya texts) be abandoned? he replies with the words beginning "For what reason? (*kutaḥ*), stating that the Vedic sequence is stronger because it is supported by the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other criteria.
He explains both of those with the words "for thus":
the fabrication of form (*rūpakakḷpti*) is the conceptualization of similarity;
the rein (*pragraha*) is the horse's bridle.

When the charioteer, which is the intellect (*buddhi*), is discerning (*vivekin*), it then draws back the horses of the senses from the path of treacherous objects by means of the mind. If, however, it is non-discerning, it then causes those [horses]—which are bound by the reins of the mind—to gallop forward. Thus, it is logical that the mind functions as the bridle for those horses.
Regarding those horses:
Regarding the paths as objects of experience:
one might ask, "Since enjoyment is possible for the conscious self (*cidātman*) by itself, what is the need for chariots and so forth? To this he says: "The self" (*ātma*).

Here "self" means the body; the sense is that the state of being an enjoyer arises through the false attribution (*saṅkalpanā*) of the body and other such things, and not inherently (*svataḥ*), because [the true self] is unattached (*asaṅga*).
Now, stating that one must proceed by means of chariots and so forth, he speaks the subsequent sentence preceded by a desire for clarification, beginning with "by those" (taiśca).
Although the body is the subject under discussion, he says "therein, whichever... (tatra ya eva) to ensure that the *pradhāna* is not taken as the referent of the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*).
Having thus cleared up the context, he establishes the body as the remainder through the passage beginning with "therein, the senses" (tatrendriya-).
Warding off the suspicion that the meaning has not been previously stated, he establishes its subsequent nature with the words "The objects":
the senses are called *grahas* because they seize and bind the human beast;
their status as *grahas* is dependent upon the objects.
Because they are ineffective when their objects are absent,
the objects (the *atigrahas*) are superior to the sense-organs (*grahas*), according to the hearing [of this] in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*.
The term "superiority" (*paratva*) refers to the intention of excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*).
The meaning is that [the distinction] is not made by way of internality.
Conceptual cognition is the mind (*manas*);
non-conceptual cognition is the intellect (*buddhi*) whose nature is ascertainment.
From the word "Self," it follows that He alone is beyond the intellect (*buddhi*); the ellipsis is that "He is recognized as such.

Alternatively, he says "or" to explain that the collective intellect (*samaṣṭibuddhi*), which is the object of terms such as "Brahmā" and so forth through its non-difference from Hiraṇyagarbha, is called "the Great One" (*mahat*).
The power of reflection,
the all-pervasive,
and the determination of existence.
Brahmā is the Self,
the substratum of the category of objects of enjoyment,
and the immediate determination.
The power of renown, the power of restraint,
and certainty regarding the three times.

The meaning is that the collective intellect (*samaṣṭibuddhi*) is the consciousness that manifests cognition and grasps all objects, including those that have passed away, which are superimposed [upon it].

Regarding the statement that this intellect belongs to Hiraṇyagarbha, he cites scripture with the words "He who... One might object: "But how can that [intellect] be mentioned when it is not the subject under discussion?"
And since it is asked what fault has been committed by the Pradhāna in that statement, he says: "And she...
The word *hiruk* means "separately.
The meaning is that while previously she was described as non-different from the individual intellect (*vyaṣṭibuddhi*), here her transcendence is stated through differentiation from it.
In that case, both the chariot and the charioteer would remain as the two remaining entities; to this he says "But in this [case]" (etasmiṃstu).
Therefore, he says "Thus, in this way" (tadevam), meaning that the chariot alone remains as the remainder.
The meaning is: "in those aforementioned six categories.
He states the result of the process of elimination (pariśeṣa) with the words "the others," the ellipsis being "whether it be the Veda or Yama."
The portion of the Sūtra beginning with "and shows" has been explained.

Furthermore, he states—beginning with the words "in the body"—that if the text is devoted to the oneness of Brahman and the Self, there is no room for the Pradhāna as asserted by the proponents of duality;
"experience" (bhoga) refers to sensation.

He states that there are indicative marks (*liṅga*) for the injunction of yoga— which serves as the cause for the knowledge of the hidden nature and the knowability of the *Kāṭhaka* text— intended toward its unity, beginning with the words "And thus this" (*tathā caiṣa*).
In the phrase "the foremost speech" (*vāg agryā*), the elision of the accusative case ending is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*), [as it arises from the maturation of meditative concentration].
And there is lengthening in the word *manasi*. //1//
But it is subtle, because of its suitability for that. (BBs 1.4.2)
He explains the Sūtra as a response to an objection, beginning with "This has been stated," and so forth.

The meaning is that because there is no difference between cause and effect, the term *avyakta* (the unmanifest), which denotes the primal material nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), indicates its transformation (*vikāra*). "With cows"—meaning with cow-products such as milk—mix the *matsara*, the Soma.
"Should make mixed" means that one should effect a blending. This is the second person plural form in the imperative (loṭ) of the root *śrī* (meaning "to cook").
He states the scriptural authority (*māna*) for the fact that the unmanifested cause is fit for the designation "unmanifested" by saying, "And scripture."
In that case, the meaning is: "Indeed, in its prior state, this world was unmanifest (avyākṛta).
It was in the state of potentiality (saṃskāra), which is power (śakti) in the form of a seed. //2//
Because it is dependent on that [the Supreme Lord], it is purposeful. (BS 1.4.3)
He explains the Sūtra as a response to the suspicion of a fallacy (*apasiddhānta*), beginning with "Here [the opponent] says," and so forth.
"Then" (*tarhi*) means at that time.
"This being the case" (*evaṃ sati*) means when the prior state designated as "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) is accepted.

He states with the words "To this it is replied," etc., that there is no deviation from established doctrine (apasiddhānta), because it is accepted that [the world] is imagined upon the Lord and is governed by Him.
It was previously stated that ignorance (avidyā) must be admitted for the sake of establishing the Lord as the creator of the immutable Brahman;
now he says that it must also be admitted for the sake of the distinction between bondage and liberation, using the words "Of the liberated ones," etc.

The meaning is that liberation must be accepted as resulting from the destruction of that [ignorance], for otherwise, even after creation, there would be the consequence of the liberated being bound again.
He states its distinction from the "real and independent Pradhāna" postulated by others with the words beginning with "avidyā."

"Māyāmayī" means comparable to well-known illusion; in common usage, it refers to that which is dependent on a magician, like an illusionist's trick. He states "mahāsuṣuptiḥ" (the great deep sleep) to indicate that she must also be accepted as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the differentiation of individual souls (*jīva*).
The plural expression "individual souls" (jīvas) is used because of the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (upādhis) such as the intellect (buddhi).
Regarding ignorance (avidyā), he cites scripture as well: "This very [is it]," etc.
It is called "space" (ākāśa) because it is the cause of space.
Because it lacks an end in the absence of knowledge, it is "imperishable" (akṣara);
because of its manifold activity, it is "māyā"—such is the distinction.

Now, he states that ignorance (avidyā) is fit to be designated by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta) because it is indefinable as being either identical to or different from Brahman: "the unmanifest," etc.

To the question, "How is that Great One (mahat) superior? he says: "That is called [the Great One]. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: when the intellect (*buddhi*) is the Great One, then its superiority is stated because it is the cause of that [ego].
Since a reflection is dependent upon its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), he states the superiority of the adjunct over the reflection: "But when... and so forth.
He clarifies the reason with the word "ignorance" (avidyā).
Even though the unmanifest (avyakta) is superior, what happens to the body?
To this he says: "And that" (tacceti).
[Objection: "But why is it not stated that the senses and so forth also possess the state of being unmanifest and the state of being higher, since they too are non-different from the Unmanifest?
To this, he says: "Even though...
He introduces the commentary by the author of the *Vṛtti* on the two sūtras with the words: "Others, however..."
The subtle parts of the five-fold elements (pañcīkṛtabhūta) are the initiators of the gross body.
It will be stated that for every individual soul, there exists a fixed subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) as the substratum of the subtle body-complex (liṅga).
The meaning is that upon attaining another body, one goes to the next world joined with that [subtle body].
Anticipating the objection as to how that [individual soul] can be superior to the Great [Self], he explains the second sūtra: "And because it is dependent on that" (tadadhīnatvāt ca).
Regarding the phrase "it has a purpose" (arthavat), he states the example found in the sūtra: "Just as... (yathā).
He refutes that explanation with the words "by them" (*taih*).
He raises an objection, fearing that even the primary subject—the gross [body]—might be abandoned due to the force of the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*), by saying "of what is recited" (*āmnātasya*).
Syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) consists in the fact that words conveying a single meaning ascend into a single cognition through mutual expectancy.
He provides the resolution: "No," [meaning] "In your view, since that [body] does not exist, how could there be comprehension of the object?
To the question, "Why should there not be cognition of the object even without it? he says: "For not... The meaning is this:

by the word "body" (śarīra), the gross body is intended through conventional usage; therefore, it would be improper to abandon that which is the subject under discussion and instead take the subtle elements—which are not the subject under discussion—by means of the term "unmanifest" (avyakta).
To the objection that there may be syntactic unity [between the two sentences], he says: "And not...
To the question, "What follows from that?", he says: "In that case...
When there is syntactic unity between sentences by virtue of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), the two bodies under discussion are to be understood by the term "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*).
The sense is that this is because the expectation [of the listener] is equal [to that of the speaker].
Purity is the certainty regarding the non-self;
for that purpose, only the subtle [meaning] which is expected should be grasped.

He raises an objection with the words "na ca" (but not so), on the grounds that because the subtle [body] is grasped as non-different from the self, it is difficult to purify; whereas for the gross [body], since the cognition of its being non-self and the resulting dispassion are easily attained through the perception of its foul odor and other such qualities—just like garlic—the [subtle body] is not comparable.
The meaning is: "by means of that state of being which consists in the presence of visible loathsomeness and disgust."
He refutes this with the words "since," [meaning]: here, impurity for the sake of dispassion is not intended,
because there is an absence of an injunction.

However, since the supreme state of Viṣṇu is intended to be expressed, the sense is that the aforementioned gross [nature] alone must be understood by the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) in order to demonstrate that [supreme state].

Furthermore, because the subtle [nature], which is included within the causal body (liṅga), is already grasped by the mention of the senses and so forth, it is not grasped separately by the two terms "unmanifest" and "body. Granting this for the sake of argument, he says: "in every way" (sarvathā).
The meaning is: "even when there is the apprehension of something gross or subtle.
"Let it be so named" means:
let the unmanifest (avyakta) be precisely that which is subtle. //3//
And because it is not stated that [the self] is an object of knowledge. (BBs 1,4.4)
Regarding the statement that "the unmanifest (avyakta) is not the Pradhāna," this Sūtra—"jñeyatva" (knowability)—is intended to provide another reason.
The meaning is that the distinction (antara), that is, the difference, of the Puruṣa from the Pradhāna—which consists of the qualities (guṇas) such as Sattva—is known through that [knowledge].
The connection is with the phrase "by those who say it is not possible," implying that the Pradhāna is remembered as being knowable.

He states "In some places" (*kvacicca*) to show that the Pradhāna is not only intended by them to be an object of knowledge as the counter-correlate of difference (*bhedapratiyogitva*), but also for the sake of attaining powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*) through its meditation.

He says "Nor is it untaught" (*na cānupadiṣṭam*) because, even in the absence of an injunction to know it, there is an implied knowability (*jñeyatva*) consisting in being accessible to the knowledge produced by the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*).

The meaning is this: knowledge that is taught can be understood as being fruitful, since teaching what is fruitless is impossible; and since no knowledge of the Unmanifest is taught, its accessibility through fruitful knowledge remains unestablished.
He states the conclusion: "Therefore," etc.
The meaning is: because it is not stated that [the self] is to be known through the fruitful knowledge desired by the Sāṃkhyas.
Now, one might object: since the body is also not mentioned as being an object of knowledge, how can it be included here?
Regarding this, he says: "But for us...

The meaning is that in our view, since the single entity called Viṣṇu alone is the object to be known, it is appropriate to introduce the body by means of the word "unmanifest" (avyakta) for the purpose of perceiving Him.
The intended sense is that the Pradhāna is not recognized merely from a common term, because there is no restrictive factor due to the non-mention of any characteristic mark found in the Smṛti. //4//
If it is argued that [the self] speaks, we say no; for the wise one is the subject, according to the context.
Anticipating the objection based on the indicative mark (liṅga), he refutes it with the words "If it is argued that [the text] says...
Here, the syntactical connection (anvaya) is: "For in this case, exactly such [a thing] is indicated.
The rest is clear. //5//
And thus, there is both the presentation and the question regarding these three alone. (BBs 1.4.6)
Furthermore, he states that the Pradhāna is not to be accepted here in the Kaṭhavallī because it is absent from both the questions and the answers: "Of the three.
When Mṛtyu said to Naciketas, "Choose three boons," Naciketas made his inquiry regarding those three alone, and Mṛtyu likewise provided the exposition concerning them alone.
The meaning is "not for anyone else.
He recites the three questions in sequence, beginning with "In that regard, first":
"O Death, do you remember the fire, the cause of heaven, which was granted as a boon to me by you?"
When a person has died, there exists a doubt as to whether or not there is something other than the body;
therefore, the meaning is that one should know this reality of the self without doubt.

He states the next three [verses] in sequence, beginning with "The reply also... The meaning is as follows: because the Virāj-self is to be meditated upon as the cause of the worlds, the fire-altar (agni) consisting of the worlds and so forth was taught by Death to Naciketas; he explained everything regarding those [bricks]—their essential nature, their number, and the manner in which the fire is built up.

The meaning is that, by the statement "Now, therefore, I shall declare Brahman," even though it is separated from the question regarding the individual soul (jīva), the passage beginning with "And as [the soul] having reached death... is the answer concerning the individual soul, because of its suitability.
As for the meaning of the sentence: "I shall declare how the self becomes after reaching death."
He states what was promised with the words "the womb" (*yonim*).
He explains the cause for obtaining the bodies of moving and non-moving beings with the words "as" (*yathā*);
"heard" (*śrutam*) refers to meditative worship (*upāsana*).
In the Sūtra, the first *ca* (and) has the sense of "because" (*yataḥ*).
Thus, since only three [entities] are introduced and questioned, the construction is: "Therefore, the Unmanifest is not the Pradhāna.
He introduces the Sūtra regarding the point already stated with the words: "Regarding this, he says."
He asks what follows from the two positions—that there is either one question or two questions—by saying, "And what [follows] from this" (*kiñcātaḥ*).
The suffix *-tasi* is used here in the sense of the locative case;
and in both these positions, the meaning is "what [is the consequence]? (*kimiti*).

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādin*) states, beginning with "That very [question]," that if the questions were identical, there would be a lack of consistency with the Sūtra; whereas if they were different, the status of *pradhāna* as being based on direct scriptural authority (*śrautatva*) would be established.

Taking the position that the questions are identical, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) says, "To this it is replied," with the understood sense being: "by which [explanation] the establishment of *pradhāna* might occur."
He explains—starting with the words "vara" and so on—that if one were to assume a fourth question, there would be a contradiction with the introduction concerning the three boons (*vara*).
That [speech] which has the granting of boons as its beginning is "that which begins with the granting of boons. "To the one sent" means to the one dispatched toward the world of Yama.
Furthermore, he first chose [this boon]: "May my father be well-disposed toward me when I have returned from here to the world of mortals.

Now, one might ask: why should there not be a distinction between the questions, such that the second boon is the science of the living self (*jīvavidyā*) and the third is the science of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)? To this, he says: "This which...

Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the statement that it is the third, beginning with the word "when deceased" (*prete*), the meaning is that the science of the individual self (*jīvātma-vidyā*) alone is the third boon.
Since the discourse has begun in this manner, it is not appropriate for there to be another question; thus he says, "In that regard" (*tatra*).

He raises an objection with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*), arguing that because the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—the two subjects to be questioned—are distinct, as evidenced by their respective characteristics of being subject to death and so forth versus being untouched by it, the distinction between the questions is established, and therefore the contradiction of the [single] statement is justified.
[The term] *gocaratvāt* means "because of being the object" or "because of being the locus."

It is not only because of the difference in the objects of inquiry that there is a difference in the questions, but also because of the lack of similarity between the two interrogative statements; thus he says, "by the shadow of the question.
He refutes the objection that the difference in the objects of inquiry is unestablished with the words beginning with "no" (na).

Furthermore, by denying birth and so forth in response to a question about Brahman, Yama indicates the identity of the two by describing the true nature of the individual soul (jīva); thus he says, "here and elsewhere."
In response to the objection that the statement of Śiva denying that [birth and so forth] is unestablished, he says: "It exists" (satī).
This means it is "possessed" (bhāgī), i.e., endowed with.
Therefore, by negating birth and other states attained by the individual soul (jīva) through ignorance, its true nature is declared; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, he states that the individual soul (jīva) is non-different from Brahman because it is the object of the knowledge that causes liberation, just like Brahman itself: "Likewise, in the dream... and so forth.
The internal state is that by which the cognizer perceives; the connection is that [he perceives] that as the Self.
