Therefore, it is established that the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa is consistent with the inner Brahman (pratyagbrahman). //22//
And [Brahman] is the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. (BS 1.4.23)
And [the word] "prakṛti" (primordial material cause).
In order to state the connection of this [term] with the defining aphorism (*lakṣaṇasūtra*), he recalls what has preceded: "yathā" (just as).
For in that [sūtra], the general causality of the world was stated as the definition of Brahman for the purpose of making it present to the intellect.

Having thus established the concordance of all the Vedāntas regarding Brahman as the object of cognition, [the author] now undertakes this [second chapter] because of a desire for specific knowledge— namely, whether that causality consists merely of agency, or whether it takes the dual form of both material causality (*prakṛtitva*) and agency. Thus, since general knowledge is the cause for inquiry into specific details, there is a logical connection (*saṅgati*) between the two.

Although it would have been more logical to place this immediately after that [section], nevertheless, since the refutation of the view that the Lord is merely the agent is easily accomplished by means of the Vedānta texts whose purport is certain, this has been written at the end of the section on *samanvaya*.
Because the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* is connected to the beginning of the chapter, this too is connected to the beginning of the chapter.
Furthermore, because the initial proposition regarding the knowledge of all things was primary in the preceding section, the view that the sentence refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) was refuted.
That is incorrect;
he objects that because of the distinction between the agent and the material cause, the proposition is figurative, using the words "In that regard, [the term] 'efficient cause'... and so forth.
The result of the preceding and subsequent positions is the establishment of duality and non-duality, as indicated by the phrase "preceded by deliberation."
Agency is established by the scriptural statement regarding "seeing";
and thus Brahman is not the material cause, because it possesses agency.
The meaning is: whoever is the maker of something is not of the same nature as that thing, just as the potter who makes a jar is not of the nature of the jar.
The world has a distinct agent and material cause.
He says "aneka... [in the verse], meaning: because it is an effect, like a jar.
Brahman is not the material cause, because it is the Lord (īśvara).
He says "like a king and so forth," [stating]: "Because of its lordship," etc.
The world does not have Brahman as its material cause, because it is of a different nature from that.
He says, "And it is an effect," meaning that whatever is thus [an effect] is such [dependent], like a jar which is distinct from its potter;
it is partless (niṣkala), without components (niravayava),
inactive (niṣkriya), and immovable (acala).
It is peaceful, immutable, faultless, and devoid of all defects;
the reason for this is that it is "untainted" (nirañjana).
The meaning is that it is empty like darkness or collyrium.

If one asks, "In that case, what is the similar material cause (*upādāna*) of the world? he replies: "By process of elimination" (*pāriśeṣyāt*). Thinking that when Brahman is negated, Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) remains as the alternative, he establishes his own position: "And [it is] Nature" (*prakṛtiśca*).
The word "ca" (and) indicates the apprehension of [the cause] as a *nimitta* (efficient cause).
Thus, he says "evam" (in this way), meaning that when causality consists of both forms, there is no contradiction between those two.
To the objection, "Why should it not be possible to know all effects simply from knowing the agent?", he replies: "But there is no non-distinction from the efficient cause."
Since clay and other materials serve as examples, it must be stated that Brahman, the subject of the illustration, is likewise the material cause; thus he says, "The example also...
The meaning is that since modification is merely a name beginning with speech and does not exist in reality, it is logical that knowledge of the modification follows from knowledge of the real cause.
For the sake of demonstrating the uniformity of the method of interpretation, he states both the proposition and the example in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* as well, saying, "So too elsewhere..."
The *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* also says: "In the same way, with respect to the Self.

Just as the pervasive manifestation in the thought "the jar manifests" is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and there are no modifications apart from that, so too this point is made clear by the following illustration:
a listener would not be able to perceive the specific sounds external to the general sound produced by a drum being beaten separately from the perception of that general sound.

By the apprehension of the universal (sāmānya), however, the specific sound produced by the striking of a drum is apprehended; or, by the apprehension of that [specific], its subordinate particular sounds are apprehended.

Therefore, the meaning is that particulars, which are to be grasped through the apprehension of the universal of sound, are superimposed upon the universal; likewise, jars and other objects, which are the manifested (bhāsya) by the self-luminous (bhāna) Self, are superimposed upon the Self.

Having stated that Brahman is the material cause (*prakṛti*) on the basis of the mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the non-contradiction of the proposition and the illustrative example, he states it by means of the ablative case-ending (*pañcamī*) as well, with the words "from which" (*yataḥ*). The syntactical connection is that in the scriptural text "from which indeed," the ablative case "from which" (*yataḥ*) is to be understood as denoting the material cause. The meaning of the grammatical rule (*sūtra*) is that the material cause of an agent of birth—that is, of an effect that is being born—is designated as the *apādāna* (ablative).
The result of this designation is that, by the rule "the ablative case is used for the source (*apādāna*"), the ablative case is obtained for the material cause (*prakṛti*).
Having thus established that Brahman is the material cause, he establishes its agency with the words "and the instrumental cause" (*nimittatvam*).
Brahman is to be presided over by an agent distinct from itself.
He states that the inference— "because it is a material cause, like clay and so forth"— is sublated by scripture with the words "prior to origination.
He also applies the Sūtra to the point that Brahman alone is the creator of the world, using the phrase "by another presiding agent" [Sūtra 2.1.23].
And because of the teaching regarding covetousness. (BBs 1.4.24)
He establishes, by means of four sūtras beginning with "kutaśca," that it is not contradictory for a single entity to possess a dual nature as a cause:
"abhidhyā" refers to the volition of creation. //24//
And because both [the individual soul and the Supreme Self] are explicitly mentioned. (BS 1.4.25)

The phrase "another cause for the increase" refers to the fact that the Sūtrakāra demonstrates—by means of the word "directly"—the non-apprehension of any other material cause, which is indicated by the restrictive particle "eva" in the expression "from space alone. This is the construction. //25//
Because of self-activity and because of transformation. (BS 1.4.26)
"Self-effort" (*ātmakṛti*) is effort belonging to the self.
The relationship of the self to the effort consists of being its object (*viṣayatva*) and its locus (*āśrayatva*).

One might object: "The locus of an action is established [prior to it], whereas the object is that which is to be accomplished; thus, for a single entity to possess both is contradictory. Anticipating this, he asks: "But how [is this]? (*kathaṃ punar iti*).
Just as clay is the object of an action because it is non-different from its intended transformation, so too is the self; thus he says, "because of transformation.
The words "the self" [are used], with the ellipsis "there is no contradiction."
He provides an example for the fact that even what is already established can be something to be accomplished, using the phrase "by way of modification" (*vikārātmanā*).

Now, one might object: since the word "Self" (*ātmānam*) is used in the accusative case in the scriptural statement regarding Brahman’s being "accomplished" as an effect, let it be that Brahman is the material cause, while the agent is someone else. To this he replies with the words "and by itself" (*svayam iti ca*).

Having explained the term "through transformation" (*pariṇāmāt*) in order to establish that Brahman is the object of the act of creation, he explains it in another way as well, stating that it is a separate Sūtra.

The meaning is that Brahman is the material cause (prakṛti), based on the scriptural statement regarding the grammatical coreferentiality of transformation— “Brahman is *sat* and *tyat*”— just as in the expression “an earthen pot” (*mṛd-ghaṭa*).
Here, *sat* refers to the three perceptible elements,
and *tyat* refers to the two imperceptible elements.
The meaning is that everything— from the definable, such as a jar,
to the indefinable, such as the form of a pigeon— became Brahman alone. In this Sūtra, the word "pariṇāma" (transformation) refers to the effect in general.

But it does not refer to a transformation consisting of a real effect, because the doctrine of illusory manifestation (vivarta-vāda) will be stated later in the passage beginning with "tadananyatvam" (its non-difference from that). //26//
For the womb is also sung [in the hymn]. BBs 1,4.27.
And because of the word *yoni*, it is said that [Brahman] is the material cause; thus he says, "and the *yoni*.
[It is] the agent (*kartāram*), possessing the power of action, and the Lord (*īśam*), the controller.
The inward-facing Puruṣa,
the full Brahman, and the womb, which is Prakṛti.
The meaning is that the wise perceive by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Now, one might object that the word "womb" (*yoni*) is seen to be used even for the female womb when there is no [actual] taking up [of elements]; therefore, he says: "of the female womb.
The meaning of the term "constituent part" (*avayava-śabda*) refers to blood.
The word *yoni* also has the meaning of "place," but that is not what is intended here by words such as *bhūtayoni*;
for that would contradict the remainder of the passage concerning the examples of the spider and so forth. Thus he says, "in some places.
O Indra, the *yoni* is for your *niṣada*, that is, for your sitting down.
The word "sthānam" means that [the place] was made by me; that is, it was created.

Having restated the inferences (anumāna) stated in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he states the sublation by scripture (āgamabādha) with the words beginning "yat punar... [i.e., "As for what..."]. Now, one might object: since inference is independent of scripture, there can be no sublation by it. To this he replies: "nahi... [i.e., "For not..."].
The subject (*pakṣa*)—the creator of the world—is established by scripture itself;
for an inference based on one possessing eternal agency is impossible due to its contradiction with the universal rule (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is an action is produced by a body.

Therefore, when the Lord as taught in scripture is taken as the subject to prove his non-being as a material cause (*anupādānatva*), there is indeed a sublation (*bādha*) by the scripture that teaches his nature as the material cause (*prakṛtitva*), which is the very basis upon which the inference depends. This is the meaning.
Regarding what was stated— that Brahman cannot be the material cause of the world because of its dissimilarity— the author replies with the words "Furthermore" (punar ca),
meaning starting from the sūtra "Not so, on account of dissimilarity" (na vilakṣaṇatvāt).
Therefore, it is established that the definition of Brahman consists of causality in both these forms. //27//
By this, all [cases] have been explained; they have been explained. 1.4.28.
By this, all [other views] are explained.
To state the purport of this section on extended application (*atideśādhikaraṇa*), he restates what has preceded with the words "because of seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*).
He states the reasons for the primary refutation of the doctrine of Pradhāna with the words "for that," and so forth.
If it is argued that the theories of atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth should be disregarded because they are weak, he says: "But even those...
Since one might ask how those [theories] can be counter-arguments if they are rootless, he says: "Of them..."
For instance, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, in order to make known that [Brahman] is the cause of the world, a father said to his son: "Break one of these banyan seeds.
The son replied, "It has been broken, O Venerable Sir."

Again, when the father asked, "What do you see here?", he replied, "Nothing, O Blessed One. Thereupon, the father said, "In that case, you do not see even the atom (aṇumātra). Thus, from the word "nothing" (na kiñcana), the doctrines of emptiness and intrinsic naturelessness are understood.
The doctrine of atoms (paramāṇuvāda) follows from the word "aṇu.
In this way, indicative marks such as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" and "Subtler than the subtle" are to be understood.

Here, when a doubt arises as to whether these doctrines of atoms and so forth are based on the Vedas (śrauta) or not, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they are Vedic because of the force of words like "non-existent" (asat), "atom" (aṇu), and so on; in response, the author extends [the previous reasoning] with the words "by this [same argument]."
Because this is an extended application (*atideśa*), there is no need for a separate introduction (*saṃgati*) and so forth.

Since the words "nothing" (*na kiṃcana*) and "non-existent" (*asat*) refer to an entity that is incapable of being perceived by the senses, and since the word "atom" (*aṇu*) intends something subtle, these doctrines lack scriptural authority; they are non-Vedic, just like the doctrine of the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*).
Furthermore, [the theory of Pradhāna] is sublated by the scriptural texts concerning Brahman as the cause;
therefore, it is established that Brahman alone is the supreme cause, and that the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all Vedānta texts refers to Him alone. //28//

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya) composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda. //4//
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter, titled "The Harmonization of Only Those Doubtful Words Beginning with the Unmanifest."
Thus ends the first chapter, named "Harmonization" (*Samanvaya*), in the venerable *Brahmasūtra-Śaṅkara-bhāṣya*.
